item.title: Ten Spiritualist Women Artists to Know - ARTnews.com
item.description:
When Spiritualism began as a movement in the mid-19th century, it attracted a host of believers—particularly women, because it granted them powers they couldn’t obtain elsewhere. “I time traveled to the worlds of remarkable women,” writes Jennifer Higgie in the prologue to her 2024 book about women artists of the past two centuries with a spiritualist bent, The Other Side: A Story of Women in Art and the Spirit World. “Women who found solace in the spiritual realm, because the physical one was too hostile to their seemingly limitless talents.”

Spiritualism with a capital S began as a movement in upstate New York in the 1840s, when sisters Kate and Margaret Fox claimed they could hear noises made by spirits. The pair soon became a traveling act, touring the United States as celebrity mediums and hosting public séances. The desire to commune with departed spirits soon spread across the Atlantic.

Artist mediums soon emerged as well, claiming to receive messages from spirits and translating them into bizarre and varied imagery. Some of the earliest nonrepresentational artworks—predating Wassily Kandinsky and other artists traditionally considered pioneers of abstraction—were by women trying to connect with nonphysical realms. “While the individual work of each artist is unique, the women involved in Spiritualism shared the same goal: to use art as a conduit to communicate with, and to learn from, other dimensions,” Higgie writes.

The development of abstract art was linked to spiritual ideas in Europe in the late-19th and early-20th centuries. This was explored in a landmark 1986 exhibition at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, “The Spiritual in Art: Abstract Painting 1890–1985.” It continues to be surveyed in shows such as the blockbuster 2018 Hilma af Klint exhibition at New York’s Guggenheim Museum, which positioned the Swedish artist as a trailblazer of abstraction; the current Minnie Evans retrospective at the Whitney Museum of American art, running through January 10, 2027; and the upcoming “Natural Magic: Women, Art, Sprit Worlds,” curated by Higgie, which will open at Turner Contemporary in February.

Here, we look at ten women of the 19th and 20th centuries who endeavored to commune with the otherworldly and recorded their experiences in their art. “The women surely understood something fundamental,” writes Higgie. “That the way we each make sense of our existence is never straightforward.”

item.title: The New Museum Spotlights New York City’s First Working-Class Entertainment Zone - ARTnews.com
item.description:
“A walk down 14th Street is more amazing than any work of art,” Allan Kaprow wrote in 1959, the same year he staged 18 Happenings in 6 Parts in a loft a block off the Bowery. What might he have said of that mile-long boulevard, “one of the great highways of humanity” per Theodor Roosevelt (the only New York police commissioner ever elected US president)?

The greatest architectural hodgepodge of its borough, the Bowery (from the Dutch bouwerie, meaning “homestead”) recapitulates the history of lower Manhattan. First a Lenape trail and then a sylvan lane, it was a briefly fashionable suburb before it morphed into New York City’s first working-class entertainment zone, a precursor to Times Square and Coney Island. In the late 19th century, the Devil’s Mile was an avatar of urban development—the site of an elevated train that cut a clamorous swath through the teeming neighborhoods of Lower Manhattan. By the early 20th century, the Bowery was the most famous skid row in America. A hundred years later it is the subject of a bold hybrid show at the New Museum.

“The Bowery: Devil’s Mile” opens with what might be a simulation of a show at the New York Historical Society—vintage maps and a 200-year-old marble milestone join 17th-century prints, among romantic views of no-longer-extant or never-existing Native villages. An imperious early 19th-century oil portrait of New Amsterdam’s irascible, much mythologized Director-General Peter Stuyvesant is upstaged by another, less decorous canvas from the same period by an unknown artist of the infamous Five Points slum, just a few blocks west of the Bowery. It’s a copy of George Catlin’s 1827 print, presenting a blurry Brueghelian tumult from a Caillebottesque perspective, that became something of an icon: Catlin’s image emblazoned the cover of Taylor Einbinder’s 2001 history Five Points and informed the design of Martin Scorsese’s 2002 passion project Gangs of New York.

Topical print images of newsworthy riots and fires give way to all manner of ephemera—tickets, handbills, souvenir postcards, stereo views, broadsides, and songbooks, not to mention advertisements for the dime museums and variety theaters that lined the Bowery from Chatham Square to Cooper Square throughout the 19th century. While much of the earlier material is culled from the New York Public Library, the most sensational paper artifacts mainly come from the collection of local archivist Adam Woodward, who has also provided the gallery’s centerpiece: a resplendent enameled 1836 pump wagon that once belonged to the volunteer firefighters known as the Lady Washington Engine Company No. 40.

The pump wagon’s relevance to Bowery culture will only be apparent in the exhibition’s final gallery, which is dominated by a comparable artifact, Brad Kalhammer’s installation Bowery Nation (1985–2012). A mélange the actual Devil’s Mile may be, but its representation is disinclined to break with historical chronology. This becomes clear when, moving on from ephemera, the exhibit turns cerebral. A ten-minute slideshow of the Danish journalist Jacob Riis’s photographs of hovel-housed immigrant families, accompanied by excerpts from his 1891 book How the Other Half Lives, is juxtaposed with Martha Rosler’s cool photo-installation, The Bowery in two inadequate descriptive systems, made some eight decades later. Whereas Riis uses documentation to expose, Rosler questions conventional representation. There are no people in her piece, simply 45 silver images of Bowery storefronts and gutters, typically littered with empty bottles. In lieu of captions, these are paired with placards giving slang terms for alcoholic intoxication. Nevertheless, Riis’s reportage washes over Rosler’s grid.

One feels the absence of Lionel Rogosin’s 1956 hybrid documentary On the Bowery. Instead, the show’s lone motion picture is a loop of the 1902 Edwin S. Porter comedy, How They Do Things on the Bowery, in which a visiting rube is lured into a Bowery saloon to be drugged and robbed. But the show more than makes do with the photography that comes to the fore in a long gallery featuring WPA work by Berenice Abbott and the photojournalist Weegee, as well as the younger street photographer Harvey Wang. There’s also a spooky Reginald Marsh canvas The Bowery Strokey’s Bar, painted in 1953 (the year before the artist died), in which a tabloid lies on the spectral pavement with the headline “Atom Bomb Burns Out Ghost Town.”

Taken by David Gadis, late 1970s photographs of the landmark punk venue CBGB (but not curiously an example of the club’s aggressive DIY handbills) segue into a small room devoted to Nan Goldin’s The Ballad of Sexual Dependency (1979-96), heralded as a barker might by its curated soundtrack. The outstanding artwork of the exhibition, Goldin’s slideshow, largely devoted to candid portraits of friends, many shot in her Bowery loft, remains stunningly raw. The emotion-charged images are simultaneously immediate and elegiac.

Exiting The Ballad, the viewer comes face to face with a white wall of 28 portraits in a variety of mediums by a fellow diarist and Bowery artist Billy Sullivan: The juxtaposition of these two vibrant portrait galleries is one of the show’s big ideas. The wall is flanked by works by Lynda Benglis, Eva Hesse and Tom Wesselmann, presumably produced in their Bowery lofts. (Context makes them newer iterations of the 1822 milestone.) The centerpiece is Kalhammer’s assemblage of 22 spidery birds and perhaps a hundred kachina dolls fashioned from found objects and refuse mounted on a sawhorse-supported twenty-five-foot-long wooden plank. Kalhammer’s Bowery Nation, which could have given its name to the exhibition, conveys the show’s intensely personal civic pride—its Campanilismo. Broadway is for tourists and celebrities, but every New Yorker has a Bowery connection. As for me, I can brag that, before World War I, my Polish-born grandmother was a 19-year-old barmaid at a dive near East 2nd Street, site of the Tin Palace jazz club, now an upscale pasta joint closed for renovation.

“Devil’s Mile” is a relatively compact exhibition but, in the tradition of the Bowery’s bare-knuckled boxing saloons, it punches above its weight. The show’s audacious yet unstated premise is that, as assertive a presence as anything else on the street, the physical New Museum is of a piece with the concert halls, curiosity cabinets, menageries, sideshows, beer gardens, Yiddish theaters, and Christian missions, not to mention nickelodeons, tattoo parlors, pawnshops, barber colleges, flop houses, wholesale lighting joints, and jazz clubs that have lined Roosevelt’s highway of humanity from Cooper Union to Chinatown. That it is, in other words, not only new, but a continuum.

item.title: Van Gogh Museum Reaches Agreement with Dutch Government on Contentious Renovation Budget - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Funding trouble has been brewing at the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam since at least 2023, when the museum began negotiating with the Dutch Ministry of Culture over the budget for a much-needed building renovation. In the summer of 2025, two years into the negotiations, museum director Emilie Gordenker told the New York Times that the current situation was “dangerous for the art and dangerous for our visitors.” The necessary repairs were so urgent that Gordenker worried the museum—one of the top tourist destinations in Amsterdam—might have to close.

On October 8 came news that the museum has reached an agreement with the Ministry of Education, Culture and Science following mediation talks that both parties entered into in order to avoid a public court case. The Van Gogh Museum will now be able to proceed with the planned three-year renovation, set to begin in the fall of 2028. During this time, the museum will remain partially open to the public, and the permanent collection—including iconic van Gogh paintings like Sunflowers, The Bedroom, and The Harvest—will be on view.

The museum’s statement does not specify the exact terms of the settlement, but in 2025 the Times noted that the renovation was expected to cost a total of $121 million, $88 million of which would go toward maintenance and structural modernization. The museum typically receives a $10 million annual subsidy from the government, and had asked for nearly $3 million more per year in order to finance the extensive upgrades, most of which have to do with climate control, accessibility, fire safety, security, and sustainability.

“We are relieved and grateful to be able to move forward with this important project,” Gordenker said about the settlement.

The background of the dispute is more complicated than a simple culture sector funding squabble. Van Gogh’s nephew, also named Vincent, inherited his uncle’s unsold artworks from his mother Jo (Theo van Gogh’s widow), and donated the entirety of the remaining estate (over 200 paintings, 500 drawings, and 800 letters, plus other art that the family had collected over the years) to the newly established Vincent van Gogh Foundation in 1960. In 1962, the Dutch state signed an agreement with the foundation, promising to build a museum dedicated to the artist and (crucially) taking responsibility for maintaining the museum-to-be. Therein lies the years-long dispute between the museum and the state regarding who is responsible for paying for the renovations.

Dutch architect Gerrit Rietveld was commissioned to design the Van Gogh Museum in 1963, and a decade later, it opened to the public on Amsterdam’s Museumplein. It has undergone several renovations over the past 50 years, and in 1999 a new wing designed by Kisho Kurokawa opened to house temporary exhibitions.

item.title: 15 Defining Photos From the Student Protests in France - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Students in France are approaching their third week of protests over a host of ills in the country's education system, spanning dilapidated infrastructure, teacher shortages, underfunding, and overburdened schedules. What began as a protest at one underdeveloped high school in Paris last month has surged into nationwide strikes including students, staff, parents, and activists, with more than 6,000 arrested, the overwhelming majority of whom are minors, according to France's interior ministry.

As the French government begins considering negotiations with students, police have brutalized and injured demonstrators at many protests. Saint-Denis Mayor Bally Bagayoko was tear-gassed while blockading students from riot police, a 15-year-old's hand was blown off by a police stun grenade (a weapon that has since been suspended by the interior ministry), and over 215 teenagers and 85 school staff have been injured since the protests began, according to French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu.

Activists hoisting painted cardboard signs alongside the French flag have become common sights across the nation, creating a visual lexicon of resistance. Much like water jugs became a symbol of student solidarity with Gaza in colleges across the United States, flaming trash cans have become strategic and emblematic blockades to school entrances across France, from the nation's smallest suburbs to the heart of Paris.

See some of the most striking photographs from the historic demonstrations, alongside protest art and placards calling for urgent education reform and an immediate end to police violence.

item.title: At the Fall’s First Major Auctions, Buyers Spent Carefully but Competed for the Right Works - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The first sales of the fall auction season offered some encouraging signs for an art market that has spent the last few years searching for them. Buyers were willing to spend, sometimes well beyond expectations. But they were picky on which works they spent their money.

Across recent sales at Christie’s, Phillips, and Sotheby’s in New York, bidders chased down established artists, recognizable bodies of work, and lots carrying estimates that left some room to run, with records and bidding wars along the way.

Sotheby’s achieved the highest-ever total for a Contemporary Curated sale on October 7, ringing up $38.6 million. The sale featured works picked by the Knicks center forward and six-time NBA All-Star Karl-Anthony Towns and Jordyn Woods, a model and socialite, along with the collection of architect Robert A.M. Stern, who died last year. The Stern selection totaled $8.7 million, surpassing its $5.5 million high estimate, and 90% of lots found buyers. The Stern group was led by Andy Warhol’s Flowers, selling for $6.3 million. Helen Frankenthaler’s 1974 canvas Return and Exit fetched $3 million, twice its low estimate. Other standout lots came from George Condo, Roy Lichtenstein, and Ad Reinhardt. Records were set for Annie Leibowitz at $140,800 and Fritz Scholder at $537,600.

It wasn’t all knockout results, however.A piece by Avery Singer, born in 1987 and represented by the international powerhouse Hauser & Wirth, reflected the much-commented-on downturn in the market for young artists. Her painting Kundry (2018) bore a low estimate of $600,000. It fetched $2.1 million at Sotheby’s New York in 2022, amid a frothier market; was withdrawn from a sale at the same house in 2025; and yesterday fell far short of its estimate, fetching just $243,200.

Meanwhile, Reflections on Pop, Sotheby’s sale of works from the collection of Lichtenstein and his wife Dorothy rang up at $8.5 million, just exceeding the presale high estimate, with 96% of works sold. The Pop master is the subject of a retrospective opening this week at New York’s Whitney Museum of American Art.

At Christie’s, a sale of postwar and contemporary art on October 1 brought in $28 million. The result was decent rather than spectacular, with the total reaching 86 percent of the sale’s aggregate low estimate.

Still, there was plenty of competition for the right material.

The sale was led by Wayne Thiebaud’s Coastal Farms (1997), which sold for $1.86 million, more than twice its $800,000 low estimate. A red Donald Judd sculpture from the collection of Barbara Jakobson followed at $1.3 million, while Sam Gilliam’s Region and Mind (1971) brought just over $1 million. A Josef Albers Homage to the Square painting sold for $960,000, more than doubling its $400,000 low estimate. (All prices reported include the buyer’s premium.)

In terms of the market, there’s little risk associated with those names. Thiebaud, Judd, Gilliam, and Albers all have established markets at this point, and their works are frequently represented in museum collections. But Christie’s also found room for price discovery farther down the scale. Judy Chicago’s Pasadena Lifesavers Blue Series #5 sold for $486,400, while Anni Albers’s Study for B brought $166,400 and Anicka Yi’s Counterfactual Imagination sold for $83,200. Christie’s said all three prices set auction records for the artists.

Phillips makes the selectivity argument even more clearly. Its modern and contemporary art sale on September 26 totaled $6.15 million, with 133 of 166 lots finding buyers, for an 80 percent sell-through rate.

Tom Wesselmann’s Drawing After Bedroom Painting #6 (1969) was the top lot at $348,300, landing comfortably within its $300,000 to $400,000 estimate. Yves Klein’s Monochrome bleu sans titre (IKB 321) and Rashid Johnson’s Untitled Anxious Red Drawing each brought $335,400. Works by Hans Hofmann and John Chamberlain followed at $258,000 apiece.


The more telling result may have come from Fairfield Porter. His 1969 painting Flowers on a Bank, estimated at just $50,000 to $70,000, sold for $148,350. Meanwhile, Cecily Brown’s Untitled (Paradise) and Oscar Murillo’s geographical avalanche also exceeded their high estimates, each selling for $141,900.

Taken together, the sales hardly amount to an all-clear for the art market.

But they do show buyers willing to compete again when the material and the price are right. And unlike a few years ago, when newly hot contemporary artists could seemingly leap from one auction record to another, much of the strongest bidding this time centered on artists whose markets have been built over decades. For an art market that has spent much of the downturn learning the difference between demand and hype, that may be the more useful sign.

item.title: EMΣT in Athens Wins European Art Museum Award for Social Impact - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The National Museum of Contemporary Art Athens (EMΣT) won this year's European Museum Academy Art Museum Award, edging out the Rijksmuseum and FENIX Museum of Migration in the Netherlands, Hastings Contemporary in the United Kingdom, Museum Gugging in Austria, and the National Gallery of Slovenia.

The academy conferred the award during a September 26 ceremony in Alicante, Spain, after the museum was shortlisted for the honor earlier in the month. Each year, a panel of judges visits award applicants across Europe, granting the distinction to the museum or gallery that best addresses its role as a social institution.

"Quality of production, originality of thought and a heartfelt belief in making a positive impact in everything the museum does in recent years helped EMΣT stand out in a highly competitive field of candidates," Samuel Gallacher, chair of the award jury, said in a statement.

EMΣT began operations in 2000 and moved between the Athens Concert Hall, Athens School of Fine Arts, Athens Conservatory, and various public spaces for the first 15 years of its history. In 2015, the museum moved into its permanent location in a former brewery. Its exhibitions have included solo exhibitions on Jannis Kounellis, Yang Fudong, Lawrence Abu Hamdan, Tala Madani, and Sammy Baloji, and an exhibition cycle asking What if Women Ruled the World? The museum also houses permanent collections that weave sociopolitical struggles in Greece with those in South Africa, the Middle East, and elsewhere.

item.title: A New AI Tool Wants to Fix the Gender Imbalance of Gallery Rosters - ARTnews.com
item.description:
A new AI tool is aimed at revealing the gender imbalance in gallery rosters. Hall W Rockefeller, who designed the program, is using it to advance the mission of her art organization, Less Than Half, which aims to raise the profile of women artists.

The AI tool analyzes a gallery’s artist roster to determine the percentage of male, female, and non-binary artists represented. Though the tool is not perfect, it purports to be capable of identifying artists who identify as non-binary, as well as decipher the gender breakdown of art collectives and duos. Any institution that appears to meet the diversity benchmark can display a “Less Than Half Approved” digital sticker on its website.

“I want people to notice the very apparent discrepancies and inequalities between men and women artists and the systematic ways in which women artists are kept from succeeding,” Rockefeller told Ocula. In addition to buying art made by women, “we want to support the people who are supporting women artists,” Rockefeller said. “That means supporting galleries who make a distinct point of representing women artists, supporting the development of their work, careers, and building legacies.”

Rockefeller has drawn on her family legacy, as well as her own art expertise as a writer and collector, to mobilize collectors, institutions, and the market using informed and more intentional purchasing power.

Art Basel and UBS’s 2025 Global Survey of Collecting found that high-net-worth women are more likely to collect women artists, with an average of nine percent more women artists in their collections. In 2024, they also spent 46 percent more than their male counterparts on art and antiques.

“This is a consumer that is more likely to buy, and more likely to take risks,” Rockefeller argued. “Especially for the middle market, the female collector is the figure that could really be the lifeline for a lot of these struggling mid-tier galleries we’re hearing so much about.”

Additionally, the UBS and Art Basel’s 2026 Art Market Report found that the gender gap widened at galleries with a turnover above $10 million, which is worth considering as trillions of dollars are expected to change hands in the coming decades.

“A lot of that wealth is going to women: to widows, to daughters,” Rockefeller added. “There’s a generation that is about to really come into their own, whether it’s inheriting money, or women are succeeding professionally as well, so I think there is a real opportunity for the big, blue-chip, international mega galleries to start courting that woman and taking her seriously.”

item.title: Cooper Union Strikes New Land-Lease Deal for New York’s Chrysler Building, With Plans to Restore Full-Tuition Scholarships - ARTnews.com
item.description:
New York’s iconic Chrysler Building, standing on land owned and leased by the Cooper Union for the Advancement of Science and Art, is transferring ownership to the commercial real-estate company Tishman Speyer and other investors, who are planning an extensive overhaul of the Art Deco landmark after years of neglect. The $235-million deal includes a 150-year ground lease with future rent to be paid to Cooper Union, which plans to use the funds to restore full-tuition scholarships to all undergraduates by 2028. (Students currently receive half-tuition scholarships valued at $22,275 per year, plus the prospect of extra aid based on needs and merits.)

Cooper Union, a private college founded by the industrialist Peter Cooper, has owned the land under the Chrysler Building since it was granted to the institution by Cooper’s children in 1902 as an ongoing source of financial support for the school. In a press release about the new deal, school president Steven W. McLaughlin said, “The significance of this agreement is ultimately about what it makes possible for generations of Cooper Union students. For more than a century, the Chrysler Building has helped sustain Peter Cooper’s vision of opening access to education by removing financial barriers. We have a responsibility to be caretakers of that promise, to build upon it, and to leave Cooper stronger for those who come after us. This agreement is part of an integrated financial plan that gives us the framework to confidently pursue that goal.”

The terms of the land lease were not disclosed, but Tishman Speyer chief executive Rob Speyer told the New York Times, “It’s a structure that’s going to be sustainable both for Cooper Union and for us.” (The Times also reported that in 2018, a year before the Chrysler Building’s last ownership change, “rent had skyrocketed from $7.75 million to $32.5 million”—though the Covid pandemic changed the building’s standing considerably after that.)

Of his company’s extensive makeover plans, which include upgrades to office spaces and common areas as well as a hospitality and wellness program, Speyer said, “We’re going to modernize the whole infrastructure of the building, whether it’s doing a total overhaul of the elevators, or the stainless steel at the crown of the building, polishing it so that it shines. Because this is a building that every New Yorker feels like they own. Because when you see it on the skyline, it’s your building.”

item.title: Woo Jin Joo Conjures Mythic Tales from Uncanny Sculptures of Fiber and Found Objects - Colossal
item.description:
Stumbling upon a battered end table or lost mitten is an opportunity for magic in Woo Jin Joo’s mind. The Seoul-born artist is known to gather furniture, garments, and other objects that have been left behind while walking near her home in London or commuting to her studio in Deptford. “I am not actively looking for anything in particular, but I discover them by happenstance, and they become meaningful; they provoke my imagination,” she says. “This is how I feel like we conjure meaning in our lives.”

Combined with clay and shiny, viscose thread, these found items transform into uncanny sculptures that often meld animal bodies with domestic fixtures. Human-sized figures cloaked in costumes of white and beige fringe slump on the floor or stand calmly against the wall, as if waiting to be spoken to. Other works similarly merge body parts with unusual shapes and forms, including the black boot-wearing ochre arch of “For Those Who Wade” or the totemic leg topped with a carved wooden table in “Murmur.”

Tapping into the strange and surreal is a way for Joo to transcend the limits of our perception and explore how mythology and folklore might provide different ways of gaining knowledge and wisdom. She believes that “even the most mundane interactions can harbour potential for meaning and transformation” and that her own experience living between cultures has allowed for a more fluid approach. “I’m Korean-Chinese, and I have been raised between the two countries. The culture and stories from these East Asian countries form my memory and psyche. But equally, the physicality of my living in London, and the physical encounter with certain objects is what brings out certain imagery or ideas,” she shares.

Like many artists who gravitate toward found objects, part of the appeal of a forgotten or discarded material, Joo explains, is the lives they’ve lived before coming into her possession, adding: “I am left to imagine, build, and find meaning in objects that has its own history. Naturally, it is not always that I discover an object that draws me, but I still have other creative ideas that exist within my imagination that I can turn to.”

Scale is also important for Joo, and several works stand as tall as the artist. Height and heft have a presence that a smaller piece hung on the wall can’t match, prompting viewers to move around the sculptures and consider the size of the works in comparison to their own bodies. “The larger sculptures feel extra enchanting to me too as the artist, from the process of ideation to production, of how what once lived in my mind comes to inhabit a corner of my studio space as a fully animated being,” she says.

If you’re in London, stop by Ruup & Form before November 13 to see Joo’s solo exhibition Bodily Inbetweenness. In early 2027, she’ll also have work on view at the Harley Foundation in Nottinghamshire. Until then, keep up with her practice on Instagram.

Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a Colossal Member today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article Woo Jin Joo Conjures Mythic Tales from Uncanny Sculptures of Fiber and Found Objects appeared first on Colossal.

item.title: Frank Gillette’s Anthropic Blues - Hyperallergic
item.description:
A hushed medley of ambient soundscapes greets the viewer as they enter Frank Gillette’s Spectra Obscura at Microscope Gallery. Field recordings capturing the woodlands and beaches of Eastern Long Island intertwine with percussive elements, melodic tones, and a selection of distorted electronics. Hailing from The Symbiotic Blues (2017–22), a trilogy of three-channel video works that run the length of the gallery’s east wall, this audio resonates subtly throughout the exhibition, creating an acoustic texture that matches the layered visual worlds on display. 

Since the 1960s, Gillette has been fashioning an ecology all his own — piercing video and media works full of strata, sharply tuned to the entanglements between nature, culture, and the devastation humans wreak upon the biosphere. Elegiac, urgent, and infinitesimal, the videos and Polaroids in Spectra Obscura express distinct sorts of disappearance, decay, and fleeting natural phenomena. The single-channel video “Symptomatic Syntax” (1981) features close-ups of slowly shifting aquatic milieu accompanied by sounds of running water and an intermittent voice-over delivering lines from J.M.E. Taggart’s 1908 book The Unreality of Time.

item.title: Medical Imaging and Art Meet in the Exhibition “Overexposed” - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The advent of cinema in the late 19th century allowed artists and scientists to record motion for the first time. Developed concurrently, X-ray technology extended vision beneath the skin, allowing people to view the body’s interior. Together, these tools produced spectacular new images that shaped modern conceptions of the body. 

Overexposed: Art, Technology, and the Body, a major exhibition on view at Museum of the Moving Image until January 2027, traces how innovations like cinema and X-ray imaging radically transformed the way we see — and understand — the human form. Bringing together decades of research films and contemporary works by 16 artists, the exhibition explores how looking beneath the skin has shaped ideas about science, power, care, and identity. 

"Through artworks and historical films, Overexposed reflects on the human desire to see inside the body, the technological means of doing so, along with possible social and political  consequences,” said Sonia Shechet Epstein, Curator of Science and Technology at Museum of the Moving Image, who organized the exhibition. 

Alongside the exhibition, the Museum is presenting a series of related events that have included a talk by Panteha Abareshi and screenings of Richard Fleischer’s Fantastic Voyage, David  Cronenberg’s Dead Ringers and The Brood, Claire Simon’s Our Body, and more. On November 5, in a program titled Visible Humans, ophthalmologist and photographer Benjamin Freeman and curator Elisabeth Sherman will discuss the Visible Human Project. 

The artists featured in Overexposed are Panteha Abareshi, Peggy Ahwesh, Zuza Banasińska, Lucien Castaing-Taylor and Véréna Paravel, Theo Jean and Ruth Cuthand, Barbara Hammer, Anna Kipervaser, Liz Magic Laser, Ana Mendieta, Agnes Questionmark, Donald Rodney, Courtney Stephens, Leslie Thornton, and Ron Vawter. 

An exhibition catalog, co-edited by Sonia Epstein and Elisabeth Sherman, is available in the MoMI Shop (onsite and online) and where books are sold. Lead support for Overexposed was provided by the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation and the Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts. Additional generous support was provided by Romy Cohen, The Gladys Krieble Delmas Foundation, Elaine Goldman, May & Samuel Rudin Family Foundation, and Doug Pugh. 

Overexposed: Art, Technology, and the Body is on view through January 3, 2027. 

Learn more at  movingimage.org.

item.title: I Wanted a Different Betty Parsons Exhibition - Hyperallergic
item.description:
ANNANDALE-ON-HUDSON, NY — It feels like a great deal of professional respect and admiration went into the making of Betty Parsons: An Expanded World at the Hessel Museum of Art. But there are also a couple glaring incongruities in the exhibition that make it feel off-kilter, and her work overall is fairly pedestrian. 

Still, admiration for Betty Parsons is well-deserved: She directed a gallery that thrust many luminaries of the late 20th century into the limelight. A very abbreviated list includes Agnes Martin, Barnett Newman, Barbara Chase-Riboud, Clyfford Still, Sonja Sekula, Mark Rothko, and Robert Rauschenberg. As the show’s verbiage puts it, her business was “ushering in the American avant-garde.” A multi-channel film by G. Anthony Svatek and Kaija Siirala playing in the galleries gives the viewer the nitty gritty of this labor: dealing with a brutally patriarchal art scene and working with limited budgets, all while being drawn to deeply feeling makers. In the film, Parsons says:

I was very critical of the male, because there were so many boring males around me ... athletic ... rich ... regressive, and ... insensitive, and I didn’t like any part of it. I thought they were all bloody horrors. So, when I did find someone who was sensitive and imaginative, well, it was just great. 

On the other hand, we also hear from Agnes Martin, who says: “I hate to tell the truth, but the truth is that she didn’t pay very well. So, I had to leave her in the end.” Parsons subsequently complains: “It’s tough going because you work very hard and all you get is a kick in the ass for it.” Most of her successful artists eventually left her for other galleries.

item.title: Psychedelic Paintings by Rafael Silveira Explore a World of ‘Visual Synonymies’ - Colossal
item.description:
Flowers for eyes, a horizon for a mouth… a popsicle for a holy relic? Rafael Silveira has long been interested in what he describes as “visual synonymies,” which he likens to “formal correspondences between seemingly unrelated things, moments in which one image unexpectedly recognizes itself in another.” The Brazilian artist’s surreal paintings replace facial features with landforms, flora, and fauna, sometimes hybridizing animals, figures, and other objects.

The works seen here were recently included in the artist’s solo exhibition Popsicledelic Trip at KP Projects Gallery in Los Angeles alongside a show by Silveira’s wife, the artist Flávia Itiberê. A series of vertical pieces with ornate, hand-carved wooden frames resemble the silhouette of popsicles, while figures hold giant versions of the frozen treats in a stylistic nod to religious art during the Renaissance.

The popsicle may seem like a quirky, even out-of-place reference within the context of these works, but for Silveira, the objects represent the broader idea that everything in the universe is connected. No matter how absurd it may seem at first glance—a man with a tree for a head or ice cream cones floating planet-like in a starry sky—the point is that they all really do exist simultaneously. Silveira juxtaposes objects and organisms in unlikely scenarios to challenge how we perceive the world around us and how even the same shape can have completely different associations.

One compositional form in particular, the tavola centinata, describes the shape of a canvas or relief with a squared base and rounded top. A feature commonly found in Gothic and early Renaissance paintings, it has the same silhouette as a classic popsicle. In a statement, Silveira says:

The connection is at once surprising and inevitable. One belongs to the sacred history of painting; the other to the realm of the ephemeral, the popular, the sweet, the melting. Bringing them together creates a bridge between devotional form and unstable matter, between permanence and disappearance, between the spiritual weight of the altarpiece and the fragile delight of something destined to dissolve.

See more of the artist’s work on Instagram.

Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a Colossal Member today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article Psychedelic Paintings by Rafael Silveira Explore a World of ‘Visual Synonymies’ appeared first on Colossal.

item.title: Sotheby’s To Offer $100 M. Collection of Ted and Ruth Baum, Led by $15 M. Paintings by Rothko and Ruscha - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Sotheby’s will offer the collection of cable television magnate Ted Baum and his wife, interior designer Ruth Baum, with the whole estimated to total in excess of $100 million. The collection includes works by leading American artists such as Roy Lichtenstein, Joan Mitchell, Ed Ruscha, Mark Rothko, and Tom Wesselmann, and major European figures including Alberto Burri, Lucio Fontana, Yves Klein, and Piero Manzoni. The group is led by a $10–15 million Rothko painting on paper and a Ruscha painting bearing the same estimate. Other top works are a Burri, a Fontana, and a Warhol, all tagged at $4–6 million. The remainder have not yet been assigned estimates.

Two dozen works will come to the block at a dedicated evening auction on November 16, with others following during a day sale on November 17 and yet more offered at various sales throughout next year; the collection consists of more than 130 works in total. Highlights will go on public display at Sotheby’s showrooms in London, Hong Kong, Paris, Los Angeles, and New York.

“From Joan Mitchell to David Hammons, the Baums knew what they liked, were insatiably curious, and kept pushing their eye,” said the couple’s advisor, New York’s Wendy Cromwell, in press materials. “The result of their shared passion is a collection that gallops through time, countries and genres. The Baums’ collection tells the story of what it means to collect contemporary art.”

The Baums had homes in New York; New Jersey; Southampton, New York; and Palm Beach, Florida, and were active in philanthropy in the areas where they lived. Ted Baum died in 2021; Ruth Baum followed this year. A gallery at the Norton Museum of Art, in West Palm Beach, is named for the collectors, who also funded the institution’s first contemporary art curator position; they also donated works by artists like Dale Chihuly and Leo Villareal, and Ruth was elected a life trustee in 2020. They served on boards and committees at New York’s Guggenheim Museum and Parrish Art Museum. Over the last two decades, Ruth supported organizations such as the Palm Beach Zoo and Conservation Society and the Armory Art Center in West Palm Beach; Palm Beach Dramaworks; and Planned Parenthood of Florida and New Jersey.

Their collecting began with a sketch by American artist John Sloan that Ruth bought at a charity auction in the 1970s, and they went on to snap up modern drawings and watercolors on paper by artists such as Fernand Léger and Pablo Picasso. They hoped that their collecting would peak with “one great painting,” and they felt they found it in 1983, when they bought Rothko’s untitled 1967 red-and-orange painting on paper, their first of many purchases of contemporary art.

“The Rothko hit us,” said Ruth, quoted in press materials. “That was it. We were children of the ’60s, and the art of that period spoke to us.”

In the 1990s, they went on to collect artists like Joan Mitchell along with Sam Francis, Hans Hofmann, Lichtenstein, and Wesselmann. In the 2000s they would add Ruscha’s Dimple (1964), in which a C-clamp seems to wrinkle the “e” at the end of the word, engaging Ted’s love of wordplay, and Warhol’s 1984 work The Scream (After Edvard Munch). They acquired the latter in 2006 at Sotheby’s London for £1.5 million ($2.7 million, or about $4.5 million adjusted for inflation).

“Ted and Ruth were among the most committed collectors of their generation,” said Oliver Barker, the house’s chairman for Europe, in press materials. “I was immediately struck by their inquisitiveness and the deep level of their research. No doubt they came to European abstraction via the touch points of post-war American abstraction. They instinctively understood that artists like Lucio Fontana and Yves Klein were vital to the history of 20th-century abstraction and could sit perfectly well situated in their beautiful interiors alongside Rothko, Mitchell and others.” The couple picked up their Fontana, Concetto Spaziale, Attese (1960), at Sotheby’s London in 2000 for just £333,500 ($485,232, or $934,155 adjusted for inflation).

The Baum collection announcement comes as the auction houses are working to ramp up excitement for their November art sales. On Monday, Sotheby’s main competitor, Christie’s, announced that a “distinguished collector” would offer $100 million in Old Masters and contemporary art, led by a Picasso estimated at $40 million; that collector is reportedly famed artist Jeff Koons. Days before, Sotheby’s revealed that it would offer 12 works from the holdings of Argentinian collecting couple Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier, expected to total a whopping $450 million and led by a $180 million Vincent van Gogh.

item.title: The Wealthiest Collectors Are Increasingly Relying on AI, Says Art Basel/UBS Report - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The fifth edition of the annual Art Basel & UBS Survey of Global Collecting, authored by arts economist Clare McAndrew and out today, delved into some new areas. For the first time this year, the author asked high-net-worth collectors how they got started on the road to collecting and how they think about granting access (whether physical or digital) to their holdings versus keeping them private. It also found that these well-to-do collectors are increasingly relying on artificial intelligence, considerably more than just last year.

To write the 235-page report, McAndrew surveyed 3,100 wealthy collectors over 10 key markets worldwide. While this is, on a global scale, a microscopic sample, it’s generally thought that the wealthiest collectors have outsize influence and can drive markets, so their attitudes are closely studied, not least of all by those who would like to sell to them.

As for what led new collectors into art buying, the influence of family was the most common entry point, says the report, which notes that was the route for 28 percent of respondents overall and for 40 percent of Gen Z respondents, whether through a family collection or a family member’s encouragement.

When it came to what they collected at first, painting was the most prevalent entry point for these collectors. Some 43 percet said a painting was among their first three purchases, tailed by sculpture at 25 percent, photography at 17 percent, or works on paper or digital art, both at 15 percent. Collecting segments like antiques, jewelry, and gems trailed behind, so the commonplace observation that buying other luxury collectibles might lead to art collecting did not seem to hold for this particular slice of the collectorate.

As for how well-heeled collectors are thinking about keeping their holdings private versus sharing them with the public, inconspicuous consumption appears to be the order of the day. Nearly two-thirds of the collectors surveyed preferred to keep their treasures mostly under wraps, sharing them only within family or a closed circle, while, at the other end of the scale, just 10 percent are seeking wide recognition. This plays out when they make loans to museums: 30 percent preferred to keep their loans private; 47 percent requested “discreet acknowledgement”; and only 17 percent required full public credit.

Perhaps surprisingly, the young Gen Z group were the most private when it came to sharing access to their collections. Some 39 percent restrict in-person access to close family, friends, and their household, nearly twice the share of any other generation. Even when sharing online, 36 percent of this generation restricts online access to their collections to private circles.

“Many purchases are driven less by the conspicuous consumption traditionally linked to the market than by a desire to build connections within close networks, where status comes less from price than from rarity, provenance, originality, and discovery,” said McAndrew in press materials. “Restricting access does not remove a collection’s signaling power; exclusivity can be part of the signal. Perhaps surprisingly, the youngest collectors were the most private, both in person and online. Gen Z collectors were the least likely to share details of their collections publicly online, preferring invitation-only spaces, with privacy central to their personal and cultural identity.”

Use of Artificial Intelligence On the Rise, Part of Increasing Tendency to Research

Use of artificial intelligence as a collecting resource has skyrocketed. In 2024, just 4 percent of collectors were using digital resources, such as apps or AI tools, for collecting advice and recommendations. This time around, some 22 percent are using apps or AI tools. And respondents are remarkably positive about AI, with two-thirds seeing the technology as improving artist and artwork discoverability and for personal advice and recommendations. Almost as many, meanwhile, found it good for provenance and authenticity verification and pricing and valuation analysis. And don’t rush to think that younger collectors are leaning more on AI tools: the differences between generations were minimal, with 23 percent of Gen Z using them compared to 21 percent of both Gen X and Boomers. And few are using them exclusively: only 12 percent used digital sources alone, with only 9 percent relying on a single source. Most commonly, that was the online press, followed by apps and AI tools.

More collectors this year are reporting that they’re undertaking moderate or significant research, be it market research or engaging with experts and other collectors, before buying—nearly three-quarters, up 10 percent from 2025. That number was a few points higher for Gen Z, at 80 percent.

Collectors are bullish on the art market overall: just over half expected growth over the remainder of 2026; about the same portion anticipate growth over the next 12 moths; and, taking a longer view, some 60 percent forecast growth over the coming decade.

Gen Z reported the highest average expenditure on fine art in 2025 and 2026, shelling out more than twice the amount of any older generation surveyed. Average spending across all age groups rose to $124,265 in 2025, a 13 percent increase from 2024. But Gen Z averaged $347,460, up some 19 percent. And that average continued to rise in the first half of 2026. And this age group were the highest spenders in almost every segment, spending more than twice as much as their peers not only on fine art but also on most collectibles.

A very small slice of even these wealthiest collectors were buying artworks priced above $1 million in 2025 and the first half of 2026—just 1 percent. (Even among these well-to-do buyers, about three-quarters spend under $50,000 in total on fine art.) But Gen Z was also most likely to spend at the highest levels; they accounted for some 13 percent of the collectors who did purchase $1 million artworks.

There has been a great deal of talk of the Great Wealth Transfer and its potential effect on the art market, including some very skeptical ones; McAndrew’s report says it’s happening.

“As a leading global wealth manager, UBS has been tracking the Great Wealth Transfer for several years, and the Art Basel and UBS Survey of Global Collecting 2026 confirms that it is well underway,” said Paul Donovan, chief economist at UBS Global Wealth Management, in press materials. “Gen Z reported the highest average spending, 40 percent entered collecting through family influence, and almost 90 percent retained inherited works. At the same time, younger collectors continue to favor traditional media such as painting and sculpture, suggesting that while collecting habits are evolving, aesthetic preferences remain more consistent across generations than is often assumed.”

item.title: Is the Tate’s ’90s Art and Fashion Show a Buzzing Delight or a Wardrobe Malfunction? Depends on Who You Ask - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Louis Vuitton had barely closed out Paris fashion week when the fashion world had one of the biggest nights of the year—in London. Donatella Versace, Givenchy’s Sarah Burton, Burberry’s Daniel Lee, and photographer Ellen von Unwerth were among the glittering crowd that turned out at Tate Britain for the opening of “The 90s: Art and Fashion,” on Tuesday night. This is perhaps not surprising, given that one of the curators is Edward Enninful, the former editor-in-chief of British Vogue, who brought back glamour to the Condé Nast title during his tenure from 2017 to 2024. (Enninful worked with Tate Britain curators Jessica Vaughan, Helen Little, Dominique Heyse-Moore, Alex Farquharson, and Celeste McEvoy on the show.)

Some among the British art press, however, were not impressed.

The Times of London’s chief art critic Waldemar Januszczak wrote that “I expected a celebration of the Nineties — instead it was a fashion disaster.” The Guardian’s Jonathan Jones agreed, writing “this isn’t an exhibition, it’s a magazine spread.” Giving the show one out of five stars, he wrote, “I hoped what I’d seen was a prologue to more art, bigger art, with enough space to appreciate it. But no. That’s it. You leave as dissatisfied as you might after flicking through a 30-year-old copy of The Face in a dentist’s waiting room.”

Not all the critics were as harsh—the Daily Telegraph’s chief art critic Alastair Sooke gave the show five stars and wrote that it left him “buzzing,” while The Independent’s Stephen Armstrong remarked that “the hope on the walls of this five-star exhibition is heartbreaking”—but it’s easy to understand why some are turning their noses up—the run-up to the opening has been more about the fashion than the art. Posters of Kate Moss photographed by Juergen Teller have been plastered over the city and praise for the exhibition has been handed largely to Enninful.

I spoke with one of the other curators, the Tate’s Jessica Vaughan, to find out a little more about the show, which opens to the public today. Speaking about the decade the show focuses on, she said, “there was this huge moment of growth and creativity, a time which really defined the parameters of what we now consider contemporary art. There was also this real boom in fashion and [the show] is about how they were feeding off one another and how the thematics were parallels in the things that these young creatives were interested in.”

The real goal of the exhibition, she said, is to spotlight Britain beyond the Young British Artists, or YBAs, who were predominantly white. “The story of the YBAs is really well-known and some of the criticism we’ve got so far is that we haven’t included those big names enough,” said Vaughn. “There are works by Tracey Emin and Damien Hirst there. We just wanted to spotlight other artists who we didn’t think got their dues and Edward always did that in fashion.” Those boldface names are paired with ones not typically associated with the YBAs, like Hamad Butt, Eileen Perrier, Yinka Shonibare, and Barbara Walker.

Important and poignant works in the exhibition often tackle queer themes, which largely were not historicized alongside the famous YBAs, whose art often privileged provocation. One of these is Familiars (1992), a three-part sculptural installation by Butt, a queer South Asian artist. The piece, which is in the Tate’s collection, includes vacuum-sealed glass bulbs containing toxic chemicals; viewers are invited to engage with sculpture—at the risk of cracking one of the bulbs and releasing toxic chemicals, a comment on homophobia and contagion during the AIDS crisis. When Familiars last showed at the Tate in the ’90s, one of the vials did crack, resulting in the whole gallery being evacuated. “It’s the idea that the thing that we’re most attracted to might be the thing that’s the most threatening to us and the work has a mythology around it,” Vaughn said of the work.

Another powerful work is Steve McQueen’s 1993 film Bear, depicting two Black men wrestling. They are simultaneously affectionate and combative, dripping with homoerotism. Vaughn argues that even though artists such as McQueen are equally as well-known as Hirst and Emin, they are rarely featured in the same context as the YBAs.

Another story being told in the exhibition is of female artists and the experience of inhabiting a female body. On display is Sam Taylor-Johnson’s Fuck, Suck, Spank, Wank (1993), a photograph of the artist wearing a T-shirt printed with those four words, her white denim jeans around her ankles. (The museum has recreated the t-shirt, and it’s for sale in the gift shop.) Not far away is Lucas’s now iconic photograph Chicken Knickers (1997), showing a raw whole chicken affixed to the front of a woman’s underwear. “We wanted to capture what it was to be a young woman at that time and to counter the images of Kate Moss by Corrine Day and others,” Vaughn said of the juxtaposition of these artworks with the Moss images that have dominated the show’s marketing campaign.

In other ways, the show is relevant to London today. Given that the UK is currently facing an upswing in right-wing politics—in September, British cryptocurrency billionaire Ben Delo donated £36 million to the far-right political party Reform UK, the biggest single donation a political party has received in the UK—the room that looks at life post–Margaret Thatcher feels prescient. It features disused urban spaces and the photography of Day and Juergen Teller. And given that more than a quarter of London’s late-night venues went dark between 2020 and 2025, there was a poignant nostalgia to the gallery dedicated to different types of nightlife in the UK in the ’90s, from queer parties to drum and bass to acid house. Perhaps those hard on the show didn’t catch how a reevaluation of the past might offer something for the present.

item.title: As Europe Enters Art Fair Season, London is Looking Fresh and Paris Continues to Shine - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Three years ago, dealer Thaddaeus Ropac started to question the health of the art market in London. The mixed auction results of 2022 and 2023 reflected what he saw as a stagnant period. And Paris, with the recent premiere of Art Basel, seemed to be emerging as the dominant location. “London lost part of the market because Paris became very attractive,” he told ARTnews in a recent interview. Still, Ropac is bullish on London: his gallery has just renewed its lease there for another 10 years. And he isn’t the only one. Global behemoth Hauser & Wirth, which has had a presence in the city since 2003, has planned a 15,000-square-foot gallery on Mayfair’s South Audley Street that is currently under construction.

In today’s uneven market, dealers and advisers are being especially picky about which fairs to attend. But as Europe braces for a double round of art fairs—Frieze in London from October 14–18, followed by Art Basel Paris from October 21–25—London is having something of a resurgence, even as Paris keeps its appeal. “Paris’s strength is its blockbuster museum exhibitions, which are attracting the Americans and international collectors,” said Ropac, whose gallery is doing both fairs. “Many of the American collectors now plan their trips so that they can combine London and Paris.”

“[Our] artists want to be in London,” said Zoe Sperling, a partner at Hauser & Wirth London, which is also doing both fairs. “We represent 15 artists and estates in the UK, the majority of whom call London home, but so many of our international artists want to exhibit here too. It’s evident that the city’s cultural pull remains very powerful.” To Ropac, London’s appeal is that it’s a city for working artists, and in that respect it has taken over from Berlin, which has “lost a bit of its attractiveness.” At Frieze, Ropac will show work by Denzil Forrester, Jordan Casteel, Oliver Beer, Mandy El-Sayegh, and Antony Gormley in its booth. “Frieze London reflects what’s going on in the studios and in the young scene,” he said. “We’re showing fresh contemporary works versus Paris, where we show important historical works,” including those by Marcel Duchamp, Lucio Fontana, Roy Lichtenstein, and Andy Warhol.

Looking across the pond, American gallerists are looking to strike a particular balance between the two fairs. Kenta Murakami, partner at New York’s Ortuzar gallery, said that while Paris may “seem to be the center at this point,” London continues to pull its weight. Ortuzar is participating in both Frieze and Art Basel Paris, showing historical work at Frieze’s sister fair, Frieze Masters, and showing primary market work at Art Basel Paris. “We think of the two fairs as one extended fair, split between two different cities in two very different contexts. They allow us to show the breadth of [our] program,” he said. “In a way, you can start a conversation in London that you might close in Paris,” he added. “From a sales numbers perspective, we look at [both fairs] holistically.”

At Frieze Masters, Ortuzar’s booth, with prices ranging from $50,000 to over $10 million, will span art from the 1940s to the ’90s by Josef Albers, Claire Falkenstein, Robert Ryman, Lynda Benglis, Joan Snyder, Suzanne Jackson, Jay DeFeo, and Agnes Martin. In Paris, the gallery will show works by living artists such as Takako Yamaguchi, Claudette Johnson, Suzanne Jackson, and Matt Connors, paired with historical works from the 1970s by Yoko Ono, Miyoko Ito, and André Cadere.

Some feel the comparison between London and Paris, ongoing since Art Basel launched in the City of Light, is unfair given that Art Basel’s Paris edition has begun to dominate all of the fairs, even its own flagship. “I think it would be really shortsighted to say that London wasn’t important,” said adviser Meredith Darrow. “[But] Paris has stolen the thunder of really every art fair, including Basel, Switzerland.” Bernard LaGrange, a senior adviser at Gagosian Art Advisory, agrees. “If you’re looking to sell an expensive work of art at a fair, you’re going to choose Art Basel Paris, maybe now above all others,” he told ARTnews. “Maybe Art Basel Switzerland, but it’s [one of] those two.”

Indeed, the highest prices at last year’s Art Basel Paris exceeded those at Frieze. In Paris, Hauser & Wirth sold a Gerhard Richter for $23 million, Pace sold an Amedeo Modigliani for just under $10 million, and David Zwirner sold a Ruth Asawa for $7.5 million. At Frieze, by contrast, the largest reported sales were in the low seven figures.

And yet, there could be a silver lining to the lower price tags in London. LaGrange thinks it could give Frieze an opportunity to rediscover its old identity. “Hopefully that allows Frieze to go back to being a place where you can discover what’s new and what’s exciting, which is what I think people loved going to Frieze to do before,” he said. “Then it just got a bit stale.”

Others see Art Basel Paris as the perfect place to experiment with cutting-edge, lower-price works. Participating for the first time, New York’s Mariposa is showing a large-scale installation of cut-out painted wooden figures by Drake Carr, priced between $10,000 and $15,000. “It’s a kind of daring presentation. What you pay for are the eyeballs on the work,” cofounder Alec Smyth said, noting that gallery views the fair as a marketing expenditure and the goal is to break even. “People from New York will fly to Paris to see Art Basel Paris, but they won’t necessarily go downtown to see your show. The reality is that art fairs still pull a really good crowd of collectors and just general art enthusiasts.”

London still has scale on its side. The city has a higher concentration of galleries than Paris, Frieze has more exhibitors than Art Basel, and the auction houses achieve higher totals. Last year, Frieze London and Frieze Masters together brought more than 280 galleries to Regent’s Park, compared with 203 exhibitors at Art Basel Paris. The difference was also apparent at Christie’s London, where the 20th- and 21st-century evening sale around Frieze totaled $142.9 million. The total for all four of the sales Christie’s held during Art Basel Paris came to only $107.4 million.

Paris, though, is gaining ground quickly. Last year, Christie’s total there was up 16 percent from the previous year, while Sotheby’s marquee modern and Surrealist sales totaled €89.7 million, more than 50 percent up from the previous year. Those sales included a €27 million Modigliani that became the most expensive work ever sold by Sotheby’s Paris.

The Cost of Doing Business

Whether a gallery chooses London or Paris—or both—ultimately comes down to the numbers. Ryan Stern, a director at the nomadic British gallery Sixty Six, said that taxes have become one of the biggest challenges to selling in London. The final invoice for a work staying in the UK includes a 20 percent VAT. “Sometimes that amount is enough to be an entire work in itself,” he told ARTnews. “That can deter someone from going through with it, and that’s a shame for younger collectors.”

London-based adviser Arianne Piper said Brexit’s end to temporary import fee exemptions and the added burden of customs red tape have undeniably forced Frieze London to pivot from a high-volume transactional hub to a more curated, talent-focused platform. “A decade on, top-tier international galleries that previously brought their highest-value primary and secondary inventory now split their offerings between London and Paris,” she said.

Taking up space at Frieze London is costly, and in an uncertain economy, even the big galleries are wary. At Regents Park, a small booth (between 30–50 square meters) costs of £597 per square meter; a medium one (50–70 square meters) is £618 per square meter; a large stand (70–90 square meters) is £640 per square meter; an XL booth (90–110 square meters) is £653 per square meter; and the biggest, an XXL, (110–130 square meters) is £671 per square meter. In total, the smallest fee a gallery can be charged just for the space without the additional furnishing and lighting, is £17,910 ($23,657), while an XXL gallery of 130 square meters costs £87,230 ($115,219).

Meanwhile, across the Channel, booths on the ground floor range from €880–€1,098.50 per square meter, while upstairs, prices range from €724.5–€849 per square meter. Art Basel Paris also offers a 25 percent discount for first-time exhibitors in the main Galleries section, and 15 percent off for a gallery’s sophomore outing there. The fair’s two smaller sectors, Emergence and Premise, are also 50 percent and 25 percent cheaper, respectively, than a Galleries booth. (At both fairs, the larger booths pay more per square meter as a way to help offset the cost of the smaller booths.)

In a sign of a collaborative trend among dealers and perhaps cost-cutting measures, this year’s Art Basel Paris will have a record 12 shared booths. Giving that a positive spin, Karim Crippa, the fair director, characterized it as “an edition of renewal and evolution, and we’re quite excited about that.”

By way of example, French dealer Edouard Montassut said his Paris booth cost about €35,000 with tax (about $39,200). That is just one reason he limits the number of fairs he does; the other is that too many of them demanded too much production from his artists, who work at a slower pace. “My artists don’t produce en masse, and that’s what I like. They’re not machines,” he said.

Zurich-based gallerist Eva Presenhuber estimated that the cost of participating in fairs has risen by about 50 percent, when factoring in all expenditures, over the last decade. She said this year the gallery will likely spend, all in, between $250,000 and $350,000 on its Art Basel Paris participation. “You have to sell at least $1 million just to cover that,” she said, which is “usually possible.” While that might seem high, she noted that fairs make up about 30 percent of their annual sales, though Art Basel in Switzerland remains its most important fair.

Presenhuber added that economic crises and global politics seem continue to dampen her clients’ moods overall—and their spending. “There’s a lot of panic in the world right now, which also reaches our clients, who are getting more and more quiet, and less excited,” she said. “There’s more hesitation, maybe due to overpriced works by younger artists over the last 10 years.”

But she insists that despite costs, fairs are essential for meeting new collectors. “More than ever, and if you’re not based in New York, then you need to do fairs—even if you’re in New York you need to do fairs,” she said.

One thing is for certain: collectors and art lovers will not be at a loss for delight at either London or Paris. Murakami, the Ortuzar partner, said the gallery was pulling out all the stops. “In this market, as soon as you have something that’s an A- or B+ work, it’s hard to place.”

item.title: European Parliament Installs Gilded Nude Statue Mocking Trump - Hyperallergic
item.description:
While President Donald Trump prioritizes adding his signature yellow-gold touch to historic fixtures within the Capitol, the European Parliament has satirized his self-monumentalizing proclivities by installing a gilded statue on its premises. The Strasbourg building is temporarily displaying Danish sculptor Jens Galschiøt's “The Orange Plague” (2025), which depicts a naked Trump sitting on the shoulders of a scrawny man straining under his weight.

Composed of copper and coated in 23-karat gold leaf, Trump's slumping figure presses his abdomen into the back of his carrier's head as he holds a small scale of justice in one hand and a scepteresque golf club with the other. The golf ball appears as a small globe, representing Trump's worldwide grip and his disregard for the planet's health.

In a project description, Galschiøt said that the sculpture references Hans Christian Andersen's The Emperor's New Clothes (1837), adding that Trump “believes the gold makes him great.”

“This sculpture has been made to address 'the elephant in the room' and start a necessary debate of how the United States is destroying the world's only chance to counter the climate catastrophe,” Galschiøt wrote.

He debuted the sculpture in Belém, Brazil, at the 30th United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP30) last November, and it has since traveled between Denmark and Germany.

“Nations as well as NGOs are afraid to openly raise the subject on how to deal with Trump and his policies, fearing tariffs, fund cuts, deportations, or the like,” Galschiøt explained in his statement, referencing what transpired during COP30 when various countries endorsed, and quickly reneged on, a pollution reduction agreement after the Trump administration threatened retribution.

This is not the first time the president has been stripped down to incite conversation. In 2024, an enormous, nude effigy of Trump was suspended on the outskirts of Las Vegas, and in 2016, several life-size sculptures of Trump were installed across the US, including in Union Square.

Galschiøt creates provocative sculptural and performance interventions addressing global issues of religious conflict, authoritarianism, racial intolerance, human rights violations, refugee crises, climate injustice, and world hunger. Among his best-known works is “Pillar of Shame” (1997), a sculpture commemorating those who were killed in the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre.

Danish politician and European Parliament member Per Clausen sponsored the temporary exhibition of “The Orange Plague,” which will only be in Strasbourg until Thursday, October 8, before it heads to Anatolia, Turkey, for COP31 next month.

item.title: Greek Prime Minister to “Ramp Up” Efforts Related to Parthenon Marbles Return - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis has continued to speak out regarding the Parthenon Marbles, vowing to “ramp up” his country’s efforts to retrieve the marble sculptures from the British Museum, The Guardian reported.

Mitsotakis has claimed that United Kingdom Prime Minister Andy Burnham was supportive of restitution efforts before assuming his current role, adding that he would raise the issue upon meeting Burnham.

“Unfortunately [talks] have not progressed,” Mitsotakis confirmed at a conference in Athens when asked about a “hybrid” deal with the museum to repatriate the fifth-century BCE marbles in exchange for other antiquities, namely, objects from the National Archaeological Museum in Athens, which is closed for renovations. “We will very clearly ramp up the intensity of our claims, not just with the British Museum, but also with the British government. I would also like to remind the audience that the new prime minister of the UK, unequivocally, was supportive of the return of the Parthenon sculptures before he became prime minister.” (Burham served as culture secretary under a previous administration.)

He additionally suggested a connection between the artworks’ return and Burnham’s reported comments about the UK strengthening its ties with the European Union. “For those of us who were saddened to see the United Kingdom leave the European family, we took great interest in the comments made by the UK PM,” said Mitsotakis, citing the possibility of “a stronger relationship between the UK and Europe.”

The Parthenon Marbles make up a monumental frieze sculpted to adorn the Parthenon in Greece. They were forcibly removed by British ambassador Lord Elgin more than 200 years ago and have yet to return to their homeland. Today, they remain in the British Museum’s collection. “The Parthenon sculptures will be part of this debate, this is not just an issue for Greece. It’s an issue for Europe,” Mitsotakis added.

Burnham, who has long supported the antiquities’ return to Athens over the last 25 years of his career, was considered by Greek officials to be the best hope of finally ending the feud. Mitsotakis’s right-wing administration has been pushing to reunify the masterpieces within view of the Acropolis.

“[The marbles] reunification in Athens would also set a precedent for a unique cultural partnership between Greece and the UK, and in particular between Greece and the British Museum,” he said. “I will certainly make the case very forcibly to the British PM when I meet him. I think the time has come. British public opinion supports reunification of the sculptures and I do believe that now is the time to push in this direction.”

These remarks are the latest in a string of increasingly aggressive statements calling for the marbles’ return. Late last month, Mitsotakis outwardly rejected the British Museum’s comparison between the British seizure of the Parthenon Marbles and the Bayeux Tapestry loan between England and France.

“There are striking similarities between the two pieces. Both were conceived as single works, intended to be seen and understood as a whole. In the case of the Parthenon sculptures, that relationship is also architectural: they were created as inseparable elements of the monument itself,” Mitsotakis previously penned in an op-ed. Yet, “nobody would seriously contemplate cutting what survives of the tapestry in two and displaying half in London and half in Bayeux, and claiming this was an adequate way to understand it. Yet that is exactly what happened to the Parthenon sculptures.”

item.title: Roy Lichtenstein Saw Our Pictures-Obsessed Moment Coming—and Deliberately Fed Into It - ARTnews.com
item.description:
If you, like me, cannot resist hate-reading a horribly misguided takedown of a great artist, check out the September 1963 issue of Artforum, which featured one of two screeds against Roy Lichtenstein by artist Erle Loran published that very month. (The other appeared in this magazine.) Loran was ticked off by Lichtenstein’s Portrait of Madame Cézanne (1963), a painting that borrowed Loran’s own diagram analyzing the Paul Cézanne work of the same name. As with the Loran diagram, Lichtenstein’s painting turns Madame Cézanne into a black outline, with letters and arrows diagramming her husband’s compositional choices.

In his Artforum article, sardonically titled “Cézanne and Lichtenstein: Problems of ‘Transformation,’” Loran stole back the Lichtenstein painting, setting an image of it alongside the original diagram, as if to convey the sense that the two are exactly the same. (In fact, they were not: Lichtenstein thinned out Loran’s outline and changed the shape of the arrows.) “A copy of anything, even when blown up to the monumental size of a billboard, is still a copy,” Loran complained. “Copies are not transformations.”

The irony of Loran’s essay is that he was right: Lichtenstein’s painting really was a copy, albeit not a perfect one. But what Loran did not understand was the intention behind Lichtenstein’s painting, whose purpose was not to transform Loran’s diagram but to translate it to a new venue and consider whether its meaning changed along the way. Brought from the page to the gallery wall, Loran’s diagram looks a bit like anti-art rather than reverent analysis of a masterpiece. Copies are not transformations, except when they are.

Lichtenstein would go on to copy a lot more imagery produced by others: famous paintings by Henri Matisse, comic books depicting emotionally tormented women, advertisements for appliances and medications. But what does it mean if Lichtenstein’s work has itself been copied endlessly, with his benday-like dots covering everything from cheap posters to throw pillows to haute couture?

A long-awaited Lichtenstein retrospective at the Whitney Museum in New York contends that his art’s ubiquity actually means it was a success. He saw our pictures-obsessed moment coming, the show implies, and even deliberately fed into it.

The Whitney show (through May 10) is titled “Like New,” which is something of a misnomer, given that it doesn’t radically upend one’s understanding of Lichtenstein. Doing so has simply become too difficult—this is the third Lichtenstein retrospective staged in the US in the past 35 years, after all. But the Whitney show does, at least, return some sangfroid to the Pop artist’s work. It suggests that, while he may have gleefully foraged from art history and painted with cheery reds and yellows, as past retrospectives proposed, he was really interested in mean-spirited aesthetic thievery more so than anything else.

This stylish show, organized by Whitney curator Meg Onli and artist Alex Da Corte, makes that much apparent with its opening. Walk the length of a gargantuan remake of a 1983 mural cannibalizing many of Lichtenstein’s signature motifs (brushstrokes, benday dots, and the like), and you end up at Image Duplicator (1963), a painting of two bulging eyes with raised brows. The image looks like it could be from the funny pages, and is fittingly given text in a comic font situated in a speech bubble: “What? Why did you ask that? What do you know about my image duplicator?” (Neither the picture nor the text, though respectively based on panels in X-Men and My Greatest Adventure, is faithfully appropriated, by the way.) Think of Lichtenstein as the curators’ own image duplicator, and recall that painting when you look at all the doubles and triples they’ve presented.

They offer, for example, Lichtenstein’s 1961 portraits of dealer Ivan Karp and artist Allan Kaprow. The two look virtually identical here, both donning white tuxedos and set against crimson backgrounds, even though they did not look alike in actuality. Later comes Modern Painting Triptych (1967), in which Lichtenstein offers three repeated views of an Art Deco ligature filled in with blue dots.

The duplication even goes meta at various points in the show. Alongside Lichtenstein’s originals, Da Corte and Onli feature appropriations of Lichtenstein in the form of paintings by Richard Pettibone and Sturtevant and a photograph by Louise Lawler, the last of whom is a leading figure of the appropriation-minded Pictures Generation of the 1980s. The curators have also organized an exhibition within an exhibition, producing a simulacrum of Lichtenstein’s 1962 Leo Castelli Gallery debut. Housed in a walk-in room situated within a larger exhibition hall, the Castelli copy is so faithful that even the gallery’s parquet floor has been reconstructed here.

Da Corte and Onli do not state that Lichtenstein was the only master appropriator of the Pop movement—no one can forget Andy Warhol’s contributions, which the Whitney memorably surveyed in 2018. Nor do they proclaim that Lichtenstein necessarily did anything entirely different from his peers. But they persuasively show that the iciness of Lichtenstein’s art—its “conceptual detachment,” per Onli’s catalog essay—inflects it with an unusual flavor that has often been forgotten as a result of its beautiful surfaces.

The curators smartly provide their image duplicator with an origin story. The show picks up in the 1940s, well before the onset of the Pop movement, with Lichtenstein’s time as a graduate student at Ohio State University. He spent time in Hoyt L. Sherman’s Visual Demonstration Center, where students learned in the dark as they were shown a succession of images meant to test how much they could perceive from the projections. The goal was to understand “perceptual unity,” as Sherman described it, and in a video Da Corte made for the exhibition, the co-curator imagines what it might have been like for Lichtenstein to see so many pictures nearly a century ago.

One might have expected Lichtenstein to opt for Op art as a result, but instead, he ultimately went Pop. Largely eliding Lichtenstein’s so-so abstractions of the 1950s, the show zooms forward to the ’60s, where one can see him directing mind-bending aesthetic strategies toward a visual language that recalls advertising. Here, one can find Golf Ball (1961), whose rounded surface is represented with rows of warping crescents. Through the ball’s circular shape and its lack of color, the painting knowingly winks at Piet Mondrian’s Composition 10 in Black and White (1915), then defiles the Dutch modernist’s aesthetic purity.

Such a gesture was something akin to a middle finger to abstraction at a time when most critics still prized it as the highest art form. (Lichtenstein would soon tackle Abstract Expressionism in much the same way, his brushstroke paintings of the mid-1960s being “a depiction of a grand gesture,” as he once put it.)
