But Lichtenstein also smartly directed his attention to artists that had themselves experimented with seriality, including Claude Monet, whose Rouen Cathedral paintings Lichtenstein remade with benday dots. One of Lichtenstein’s takes on Monet in this show features the cathedral buried beneath a matrix of black dots set atop a deep blue background, in what may count as an allusion to Ad Reinhardt’s blue-on-blue abstractions of the ’50s.

The Whitney reaches its apex somewhere around the Rouen Cathedral works and never quite again reaches the heights of that series. The show amasses an entire gallery of “Mirror” paintings from the ’70s, each depicting a circle of glass covered in dots, and a range of works produced between the ’70s and ’90s depicting artists’ studios in modes that variously recall Matisse and Picasso. There are also a few landscapes, including 1996’s Treetops Through the Fog, which takes its cues from both comics and the Chinese shanshui style of painting. But neither of these bodies of work thrill because they lack the barbs of Lichtenstein’s ’60s work, whose appropriations are more direct and therefore more striking.

My advice is to skim the last third of the show and head outdoors to see one of the show’s finest copies. On the Whitney’s facade, there’s a version of Lichtenstein’s mural for the 1963 New York World’s Fair Mural, a large version of the painting Girl in Window. (The source painting is one of many Lichtensteins held by the Whitney, which also owns the artist’s studio and now uses it as the home of its Independent Study Program.) Da Corte and his studio assistants personally painted this 32-foot-tall remake, which doubles as both a loving homage and a means of raising a great work to new heights. To quote Erle Loran once more, “A copy of anything, even when blown up to the monumental size of a billboard, is still a copy.” Fair enough, as this work demonstrates, but is that really such a bad thing?

item.title: Gertrude Abercrombie Painting, Bought for $30 at an Estate Sale, Sets $1.3 M. Auction Record - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Plucked from an estate sale in Kalamazoo, Michigan, for $30, Gertrude Abercombie’s Alderman Merriam’s Shells (1951) sold for $1.35 million at Freeman’s auction house on October 1.

The final bid far surpassed the lot’s $250,000 estimate, setting a new auction benchmark for the late Surrealist painter. For Freeman’s New York, success was almost guaranteed. Alderman Merriam’s Shells arrived on the block buoyed by its sensational rediscovery: the enigmatic still life of seashells scattered in darkness had vanished for decades, much to the dismay of Abercrombie’s ravenous market. In reality, it languished in Michigan until a sharp-eyed shopper rescued it from an estate sale.

“As happy as we are to have recaptured the record sale price for an artist we have long championed, we are even happier for our eagle-eyed consignor who saved this masterpiece,” Zack Wirsum, Freeman’s senior vice president, said in a statement.

Its eventual consignor, a collector of vinyl records and vintage furniture, arrived late to the sale, describing it as “picked over.” The painting was tucked away in a hallway at the rear of the building near the garage; further obscured in the lower-left corner of the canvas was the inscription “abercrombie ’51.”

“Uncertain but intrigued,” its finder brought the canvas to the Milwaukee Art Museum, which was then hosting an Abercrombie survey. As luck would have it, the exhibition catalog contained an archival photograph of the very painting, originally reproduced in a 1952 Chicago Review piece on Abercrombie’s exhibition at Newman Brown Gallery. The owner then contacted Susan Weininger, a prominent Abercrombie expert, who confirmed that the work was, in fact, Alderman Merriam’s Shells (1951).

According to Freeman’s, the shells belonged to Robert Merriam, who served as alderman of Chicago’s Hyde Park neighborhood, where Abercrombie lived and worked. Alderman Merriam’s Shells was exhibited in Chicago, New York, and Milwaukee in 1952 and 1953, but Abercrombie ultimately gifted the painting to John Reynolds, a doctor in Kalamazoo, as payment for an operation. The so-called “Queen of Chicago,” Abercrombie animated the city’s midcentury art scene, with artists and intellectuals gathering in her Hyde Park brownstone as if at a salon.

Her regional renown exploded onto the global art scene in 2018, when a Karma gallery show declared her a “critical, under-considered fixture of midcentury American Surrealism.” Since then, 80 of her paintings have fetched more than $100,000 at auction, with the majority exceeding their high estimates, according to the Artnet Price Database.

Alderman Merriam’s Shells depicted nine finely realized seashells, one suspended by a thread above a void. Sparse, aesthetic interiors were Abercrombie’s defining setting, while seashells became a recurring motif and “personal emblems,” according to Freeman’s. The house added that, “The shell is another kind of home, at once protective and confining, a contained space that may have also appealed to Abercrombie thematically.”

item.title: Rep. Jamie Raskin Wants the Smithsonian to Collect and Display Trump’s Propaganda, To Teach About Tyranny - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Democratic Maryland representative Jamie Raskin, a dogged antagonist to President Donald Trump who attempted to have him removed from office, has introduced legislation directing the Smithsonian Institution to preserve “artifacts reflecting the rise of government propaganda, corruption, and authoritarianism” during Trump’s two terms and place them in a permanent exhibition at the National Museum of American History (NMAH), a museum in the nation’s capital that is part of the Smithsonian Institution.

The Preserving and Remembering the History of Trump and other Tyrants Act comes partly in response to Trump’s order last month to have the Department of the Interior place signs outside NMAH, warning visitors that the curators express “personal, radical ideologies” in their galleries. The legislation also instructs officials from the National Park Service to remove any such signage installed without Congressional approval.

“Unlike President Trump’s project of censoring, whitewashing and fictionalizing American history, my legislation will forever preserve his manifestations of authoritarian narcissism and his propagandistic assault on American history and American democracy,” said Raskin in press materials. “To avoid repeating this descent into authoritarianism, we must study this corrupt President’s actions and allow the public to learn about the numerous tools he deployed while attempting to remake American history in his own image and according to his own autocratic and white nationalist beliefs.”

Trump has also hung massive banners bearing his scowling face on some federal buildings; Raskin’s bill directs Smithsonian staff to preserve them as well, along with media footage; the stories of Americans who “resisted and opposed the rise in authoritarianism in the United States”; and whatever else the Smithsonian’s secretary believes to be historically significant.

Neither the Smithsonian nor NMAH immediately responded to a request for comment.

Trump has long targeted the Smithsonian, a federal consortium of cultural and research institutions. It began, during his second term, with a March 2025 executive order targeting “divisive” and “anti-American” content in its exhibitions and calling for the restoration of “monuments, memorials, statues, [and] markers” that had been removed from public spaces since 2020. His persecution has continued up until now; last month, the administration accused the Smithsonian of discrimination and threatened to cut federal grants.

There is a pungent irony to Raskin’s legislation, as NMAH has been a particular focus for Trump, and its exhibitions have at least once softened their assessment of his presidency, reportedly under White House direction. In July 2025, the museum removed references to the two impeachments he suffered during his first term after a content review undertaken “following pressure from the White House to remove an art museum director,” as the Washington Post reported at the time. The museum soon restored the placard with fewer details. Raskin drafted articles of impeachment against Trump within hours of the January 6, 2021, attack on the US Capitol and served as the lead House impeachment manager during his second Senate trial, arguing that Trump incited a violent insurrection against the Constitution. The trial ended in a 57–43 vote to convict, falling short of the two-thirds threshold required.

Raskin’s bill comes amid strident debate over all three accusations leveled by Raskin, of “propaganda, corruption, and authoritarianism.” Regarding propaganda, there’s the debate over the White House illegally using $20 million in taxpayer funds to broadcast what are essentially campaign ads, during an election season, that boast of Trump’s accomplishments, to the tune of R&B singer Christian Berishaj (aka JMSN) singing his song “Love Me.” (The singer has issued a cease-and-desist letter.) Regarding corruption, the New York Times reported in July that in 2025, revenue from the president’s business holdings soared to $2.24 billion, expanding “primarily in areas in which he wields immense power and influence, like cryptocurrency.” And as regards authoritarianism, Trump recently was ordered by a judge to restore press access to reporters from Politico, CNN, and MS NOW after specifically banning them due to the content of their coverage, in violation of the First Amendment.

item.title: The Hellhounds of Genocide - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Editor’s Note: The following story contains mentions of sexual assault and harassment. To reach the National Sexual Assault Hotline, call 1-800-656-HOPE (4673) or visit online.rainn.org.

Ridikkuluz opens their solo show at Salma Sarriedine gallery with a painting of George W. Bush as a Sunday painter with a loafer stuffed in his mouth — an allusion to Iraqi journalist Muntadhar al-Zaidi hurling his shoes at the president during a 2008 press conference in Baghdad. In the work, “Ya Kalb (tribute to Al-Zaidi)” (2026), Bush paints a white poodle with glowing blue eyes. A demonic presence lurks in the dog, foreshadowing dangers to come. 

Ironically, that possessed poodle is the most docile dog in the entire show. Throughout, Ridikkuluz portrays Israeli soldiers as vicious dogs inflicting atrocities upon Palestinians and other Southwest Asian and North African (SWANA) individuals. Although the Israeli military’s weaponization of dogs has been ongoing for some time, the widely reported uptick in its use of dog attacks on Palestinians has drawn global condemnation. Meanwhile, in prisons, Israeli soldiers command dogs to sodomize, maul, and humiliate Palestinian men. In Ridikkuluz’s work, the irascible dog emerges as a symbol for the ongoing genocide and its unrestrained perpetrators. The show's title, Klab (كِلَاب), means "dogs" in Arabic, and is often used as an insult, taking on new meaning since the Israeli army’s latest offensive against Palestinians following October 7, 2023.

Later in the show, Ridikkuluz re-adapts Francisco de Goya's famous 1814 painting, “The 3rd of May 1808 in Madrid,” in which a Spanish man resists Napoleon's soldiers. “You’re Next - the Fifteenth of May” (2026) commemorates May 15, 1948 as the start of the Nakba (النَّكْبَة), or "catastrophe," in which an estimated 700,000 Palestinians were displaced, dispossessed, or killed during Israel’s formation between 1947 and 1949.

item.title: The Museum Director as Gardener - Hyperallergic
item.description:
When the Chazen Museum of Art at the University of Wisconsin–Madison (UW–Madison) reopens this November, visitors will see an innovative, object-centered approach to presenting the museum’s collection and experience the result of a new approach to museum leadership. Guiding the reinstallation of more than 25,000 works revealed that the skill and fortitude required for museum leadership has vastly changed.

In 2021, I published an op-ed in this publication arguing against the era of the director as a singular genius charting a course for everyone. I now understand what should replace it: leadership that pairs managerial acumen with creativity. I used to understand visionary and managerial leadership as opposites. I now believe that administration should be both managerial and creative, cultivating conditions for new possibilities. 

The collection reinstallation emerged through collaboration, experimentation, failure, trust-building and “sifting and winnowing,” a core value held by UW–Madison that comes from a 1894 statement by the board of regents: “Whatever may be the limitations which trammel inquiry elsewhere, we believe that the great state University of Wisconsin should ever encourage that continual and fearless sifting and winnowing by which alone the truth can be found.”

Sifting and winnowing is poetry grounded in something very real — the work needed to separate the grain from the chaff. Sifting is hard work, especially by hand. Winnowing, where you direct a current of air across the separated grains to lift and remove the chaff leaving only what is useful, is poetry embodied. But you can’t get to the poetry without first putting in the work.

item.title: More Than 18,000 Wildlife Species Populate Joel Sartore’s Ambitious ‘Photo Ark’ (So Far!) - Colossal
item.description:
Twenty years ago, National Geographic photographer Joel Sartore set out on a deceptively simple multi-year mission: to create a photo archive of biodiversity. Documenting around a thousand animals each year, his ultimate goal is a portrait catalogue showcasing more than 25,000 species. As of this writing, Sartore has documented 18,567 animals, including the new species of cat recently discovered in Bolivia. In zoos, aquariums, wildlife sanctuaries, and more, he collaborates with conservationists and researchers to document an awe-inspiring yet tiny fraction of life on our planet.

Sartore’s Photo Ark project illuminates animals against plain black or white backgrounds, highlighting their distinctive characteristics and expressions in an intimate and relatable format. “It’s the eye contact that moves people,” Sartore says. “It engages their feelings of compassion and a desire to help.”

Those feelings of care, ideally paired with the motivation to act, is what Photo Ark is all about. When Sartore began photographing animals in his hometown of Lincoln, Nebraska, in 2006, he recognized the power of bold, straightforward portraits to connect with viewers. The images not only introduce us to the incredible array of animals we coexist with, but spur efforts to protect them. Sartore says, “I want people to care, to fall in love, and to take action.”

In 2023, the Photo Ark Species Impact Initiative took things a step further by awarding conservationists grants to support their work. The project has also morphed into an all-ages educational initiative that National Geographic makes available in classrooms and through publications and broadcasts. “No matter its size, each animal is treated with the same amount of affection and respect,” National Geographic says. “The results are portraits that are not just stunningly beautiful, but also intimate and moving.”

Discover thousands of creatures on the Photo Ark site and learn how researchers are defending endangered and vulnerable species. You can also follow Sartore’s work on Instagram.

item.title: Dorothea Tanning Beyond Max Ernst’s Shadow - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Alyce Mahon’s new book Dorothea Tanning: A Surrealist World offers a panoramic, well-researched view of the artist’s life and work. Mahon grounds Tanning’s biography in womanhood — how Tanning faced immense pressure and beat odds, emerging as a standout artist on her own, despite often being attached to her husband, Max Ernst. Unfortunately, the work is overly ambitious and too academic, and fractures under this load. Although it offers moments of interesting, new insight, the book is bogged down by tedious cobbling together of others’ reviews of Tanning’s oeuvre, and a forced attempt to disentangle her from Ernst. The result is a book that is both lukewarm and overly defensive of its subject.

To be sure, A Surrealist World is an academic project written by a professor of art history. The book sounds intellectual, clearly targets other scholars, and offers a well-researched, comprehensive overview of Tanning’s life. Mahon begins with Tanning’s childhood as the daughter of Swedish immigrants in Galesburg, Illinois, a “small and sleepy town,” where “nothing happens but the wallpaper.” But Tanning had her eyes set on big things from the start, and soon made her way to Chicago, and eventually to New York in 1935. There, she took jobs as a commercial artist, creating advertisements for Macy’s and other corporate clients.

She quickly became enthralled with Surrealism after attending the Fantastic Art, Dada, Surrealism exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art in 1936. From there, her life followed its own surreal trajectory: in 1939, she visited Paris with a list in hand of artists she wanted to meet. Still an ingenue, she discovered Paris was an eerie ghost town, with war on the horizon. One of the artists she had hoped to meet in Paris was Ernst, whom she would later meet in New York in 1942 and marry in 1946.

item.title: Celebrating 60 Years of NYC's Millennium Film Workshop - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Millennium Film Workshop is a rare space in New York City that champions self-expression and experimentation in filmmaking. For over 60 years, Millennium has cultivated a thriving community of artists and creators, giving anyone interested in filmmaking access to resources such as camera equipment, workshop programs, a gallery, and the Millennium Film Journal. After all these years, the organization is far from aging. To celebrate the legacy of experimental filmmaking in New York City, the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) is hosting screenings in October, honoring Millennium Film Workshop and the Film-Makers’ Cooperative. 

In the 1960s, after the 35mm camera became popular, more people began using cameras to tell their stories. Experimental film first found its community during this period, as parameters expanded beyond the polished medium of high-budget films. Breaks in narrative and structure-based rules gave way to a more tactile viewing experience: sensorial through color, lighting, focus on the hyper-mundane, or surreal in nature. 

Filmmakers already working in this experimental format collectivized when, in 1961, Cinema 16, the only theater in NYC showing experimental film, rejected Stan Brakhage's Anticipation of the Night. In response, Jonas Mekas, Shirley Clarke, Ken and Flo Jacobs, and others formed the New American Cinema Group. That same year, the Film-Makers’ Cooperative was formed to distribute and archive this growing body of work.

item.title: Precarious Dwellings Perch Atop Rocks in Simon Laveuve’s 1/35-Scale Miniatures - Colossal
item.description:
When something’s stable, dependable, and strong, we might say it’s “like a rock.” Similarly, when things become difficult and challenges feel immovable, we might find ourselves “between a rock and a hard place.” These idioms suggest that perhaps especially when we face challenges, we find ways to beat the odds. And Simon Laveuve’s idiosyncratic, post-apocalyptic dwellings detail just that.

The artist’s 1/35-scale miniature domiciles perch atop stilts and boulders. Laveuve pairs tiny chairs, boxes of produce, fishing gear, and other daily essentials with objects that appear to have been scrounged from who-knows-where and repurposed into useful tools and furniture. While figures never occupy the scenes, evidence of their activities and lifestyle intimates their presence, as if the residents have simply slipped out to run a quick errand.

If you’re in Paris later this fall, see these works in person in the artist’s solo exhibition, Ancré dans la roche (Anchored in Rock). The title nods to Laveuve’s thematic throughline of dwellings in unexpected and often precarious places, where the anonymous builders make do with what’s available—a fitting metaphor for life amid contemporary political and economic turbulence. The work “speaks to this fundamental need: finding a place to hold on,” the artist tells Colossal. “And, from that point of anchorage, to live.”

Ancré dans la roche opens on November 12 and continues through December 22 at Loo & Lou Gallery, which will also present Laveuve’s work during Luxembourg Art Week from November 20 to 22. Check out the artist’s Instagram for updates.

item.title: How Printmaking Changed the Way Jean-Michel Basquiat Painted - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Jean-Michel Basquiat once offered a wonderfully concise explanation of his practice: “I collage my own hand.”

That line could serve as the motto for “Basquiat, the Blue Ribbon Paintings, and the Art of Reproduction,” a new exhibition at the Princeton University Art Museum centered on 11 paintings Basquiat made 1984, shown alongside other works by the artist.

The “Blue Ribbon” paintings, reunited here for the first time in more than three decades, are full of repeated images: anatomical drawings, logos, words, and the familiar Basquiat crowned figure. But they were never intended to be seen as straightforward copies of one another; the repetition is never exact. Basquiat shifts things around, paints over them, changes their colors and sometimes prints the same image twice, slightly out of register.

During a virtual walk-through of the exhibition, Alexandra Foradas, the museum’s curator of modern and contemporary art, provided a useful way of thinking about what Basquiat was doing. “He’s thinking like a printmaker, but he’s not making prints,” she said. “He’s incorporating reproductive technologies into all of his practice in various ways.

The exhibition goes back to Xerox works Basquiat made with Jennifer Stein in the late 1970s. The two used photographs, drawings, and scraps of paper to create sheets that they ran through a Xerox machine, then cut into postcards and sold outside museums in New York. They are modest things compared with the huge paintings that would follow, but the basic method is already there. Basquiat makes an image, reproduces it, cuts it up and gives it another life.

In Tuscany (1982), the process had become considerably more elaborate. Basquiat sent an assistant to a copy shop with his drawing of a headless Venus. The copies were cut up and pasted onto small stretched canvases, which were then nailed onto a larger wooden support. The exhibition is full of moments like this, where something familiar about Basquiat suddenly becomes much more literal.

Notary (1983) is an enormous collision of words, diagrams, figures, and references, including anatomical drawings derived from Leonardo da Vinci. Princeton has displayed some of the actual silkscreens used to make the painting nearby. Looking between them turns into a surprisingly entertaining game of “I Spy”: You spot an image on a screen and then find it buried in the painting. Another appears elsewhere, partly covered by whatever image Basquiat put down afterward. It makes the painting easier to understand without making it any less enigmatic.

Nearby, the exhibition traces some of the ideas behind this way of working by drawing connections to the work of Robert Rauschenberg and master printer Robert Blackburn, who worked with Rauschenberg. Basquiat, however, wasn’t simply imitating either artist.

Around the show’s midpoint, it shifts the context to several centuries in the past to Leonardo. On view are copies of a mass-market 1977 book featuring the Renaissance master’s anatomical drawings; Basquiat owned a copy, a fount of inspiration for him. Visitors can effectively view the book from Basquiat’s perspective, hopefully beginning to see how one inspired the other.

I told Foradas it reminded me of a copy of T.S. Eliot’s The Waste Land, featuring the poem being worked over in manuscript, complete with edits and annotations. There is something thrilling about seeing a famous work in progress, before it became entrenched in our collective memory: the crossed-out lines, the alternatives, the decisions. It is about as close as you can get to watching somebody think.

Foradas saw something similar in Basquiat. “You can see him thinking, annotating his own drawings,” she said. “He’s annotating his own practice as he moves through it.”

Foradas talked about how difficult that can be with artists who have become so famous that the legend begins to obscure the work that was done in the studio. Art doesn’t simply spring from an artist’s head “like Athena from Zeus’s skull,” she said. Each painting took time to develop: There was drawing and copying and moving things around. There were things that worked and things that needed another pass.

That is certainly the case with the “Blue Ribbon” paintings, which Basquiat worked on concurrently, laying all 11 canvases out on his studio floor and moving among them. He used the same screens repeatedly but changed their positions, added paint, and worked over the printed images by hand. One canvas begins with an area of thin black paint that Foradas compared to Helen Frankenthaler. Basquiat added gray, orange, red, and blue before finishing with silk-screened images. The surface feels built rather than simply painted.

“You get this sense of iteration and recomposition and editing over the course of the series,” Foradas said. Because Basquiat worked across the paintings at the same time, there isn’t really a first “Blue Ribbon” followed by ten attempts to improve it. They are variations being developed alongside one another. Each painting includes a version of a crowned silhouette. On one, Basquiat made the figure menacing, with glowing red eyes, while another iteration appears almost nervous.

Elsewhere, Basquiat printed the same screen twice, moving it only a few millimeters between impressions. The mistake-looking effect was almost certainly deliberate. By then, she said, Basquiat was too accomplished at silkscreening to accidentally move a screen so minutely.

A group of smaller works makes some of these experiments easier to see. One isolates the intestine image that appears in the “Blue Ribbon” paintings. Another is a loose watercolor that resembles a Color Field painting, rather than the technique typically associated with Basquiat. Foradas agreed with the comparison, noting that Color Field abstraction influences more of the “Blue Ribbon” paintings than one might expect. Once pointed it out, it’s hard to unsee.

All of this makes for a pretty convincing answer to one of the more persistent myths around Basquiat: the idea of the young, instinctive genius pouring images onto canvas almost faster than he could think. Foradas called the tendency to describe him as an “untrained genius” infantilizing. The word “primitive,” she added, still gets used about his work, despite being both “objectionable and incorrect.”

Princeton’s answer is mostly to show the receipts. There are the Xeroxes. There are the silkscreens. There are the books he studied and artists he learned from. There are images he drew, reproduced, rearranged, and returned to years later. There are collaborations with other artists, printers, and studio assistants.

There is, in other words, a lot of work. And hovering around this all is Warhol. “He is sort of the ghost in the corner of the exhibition,” Foradas said. Warhol is impossible to remove from the story of Basquiat and reproduction, but the exhibition resists making him the source of everything.

Rather, its final section looks at Basquiat’s relationship with printmaker and publisher Fred Hoffman through the lens of works like Tuxedo (1983). That work features small screens repeatedly reorganized across a much larger surface. (A version of Tuxedo, from an edition of 10, was on view in early 2024 at Gagosian’s LA outpost for “Made on Market Street,” a show dedicated to the work Basquiat made in Los Angeles in the early ’80s.)

While Warhol typically dominates in discussions of Basquiat’s connections to other artists, he just one of many—along Blackburn, Rauschenberg, Leonardo, and more. I went into the walk-through expecting a show about a group of Basquiat paintings I knew reasonably well. At first, “I collage my own hand” seems like a clever line, whipped up by a publicist. By the end of the show, it sounds more like a set of instructions.

item.title: Leon Black, You Can’t Hide - Hyperallergic
item.description:
If leaders of New York’s Museum of Modern Art thought that calls to remove board member Leon Black, an Epstein associate, would eventually die down, a group of two dozen protesters today proved them very much mistaken. Hear from an Epstein survivor, a feminist campaign group, and the organizer behind a roving Epstein files “bookmobile” — all of whom were outside MoMA today to remind the public of Black’s seedy ties to the sex offender. Staff Writer Anna Lee reports from the scene.

In more news today, the New Museum reveals the 36 artists and collectives in its upcoming triennial; and Independent Art Fair is acquired by Informa, a British conglomerate that owns several Miami art fairs and, of course, a yacht show in Monaco. I always thought “Independent” was an interesting name choice.

—Valentina Di Liscia, senior editor

MoMA Helping “Sanitize” Leon Black’s Reputation, Protesters Say

Over two dozen people assembled down the street from the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) today, October 6, calling for the removal of disgraced billionaire Leon Black from the museum board over his ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Black has also faced multiple rape allegations, which he denies, none of which have resulted in a conviction.

Among those in attendance were members of the feminist campaign We Are UltraViolet and its Epstein Accountability Project, the research initiative Time & Memory Project, and the mobile Epstein-Trump Reading Room, created by the Institute for Primary Facts.

item.title: Ten Out of Ten: Top 200 Collector Joop van Caldenborgh Reflects on His Museum Voorlinden’s First Decade - ARTnews.com
item.description:
A decade ago, Dutch industrialist Joop van Caldenborgh opened the Museum Voorlinden in Wassenaar, Netherlands. To mark the institution’s anniversary, he spoke to ARTnews about his journey as a collector, the museum’s history and anniversary plans, and his latest acquisitions.

ARTnews: How did you start collecting?

Joop van Caldenborgh: When I was a young boy, I collected stamps, sugar packs, cigar tins—all kinds of little things that could be collected. When it became art, it was the same kind of habit. I bought my first piece of art when I was 16, using my newspaper delivery money, but that is not “collecting.” It takes time before you really are a “collector.”

When did you realize you had risen to that status?

I was certainly much older, maybe in my early 40s, when my wife said to me, “Why do you still buy art that you cannot hang anymore?” I realized I had this disease of being a collector: somebody who buys although they have nowhere left to hang the art. That is the whole idea of collecting. Only after a certain time do you realize you have to do something with it.

Is that what led you to create the Museum Voorlinden?

It was never my intention to start a museum. That came late in life and was unexpected. The idea started in 2010 when my son, who now runs the family company, Caldic, said to me, “Why don’t you make an exhibition at the Kunsthal Rotterdam?” With Suzanne Swarts, who is the now director of the Museum Voorlinden, we organized an exhibition, “I promise to love you: Caldic Collection,” named after a Tracey Emin work we own. I remember well how much fun it was to do that and afterward said, “We need our own exhibition space.” We didn’t dare to call it a museum; it was an exhibition space. In 2011, we bought the Voorlinden Estate, which is about 100 acres with an old mansion on the property. It also happens to be very close to where I live. It took five years to open because we had to get governmental permission to build the museum as it’s in nature and very close to the sea.

What are some cornerstones of the collection?

That’s difficult to answer. I have six children; if you ask which one is my favorite, you’re in trouble. It’s the same with the art. All the art is collected with a certain devotion and emotion. All of the works are loved. What I can tell you is that when I started, I collected the more abstract works of the Zero [movement], from the late ’50s and early ’60s. I have a bit of a mathematical mind, so I liked that kind of art—and nobody understood it. Everybody said I was crazy. At the museum, some of the cornerstones, which are permanent, are a James Turrell skyspace, Ron Mueck’s Couple under an Umbrella (2013), a large Richard Serra that he made for us, and a swimming pool by Leandro Erlich, which is maybe the most Instagrammable part of the museum.

What makes an artwork a trophy?

For me, a trophy is not defined by the price of an artwork, but by the strength of my connection to it. I like artworks that move me emotionally. They don’t have to be beautiful or made by a famous artist. The real question is simple: do I like it? I fell in love with a monumental outdoor sculpture by Tracey Emin and acquired it for our sculpture garden last year. But equally rewarding are works by artists who are still being discovered, who haven’t already secured their place in art history. That is one of the great pleasures of collecting contemporary art: encountering extraordinary minds and talking to artists about their work, life, and philosophy. It helped me see things differently and discover that there are a multitude of ways you can look at the world, far beyond the notion of trophies.

How would you characterize the past decade of the museum being open to the public?

It’s very strange if you never thought of building a museum. I was always in a business-to-business [industry], not business-to-consumers, and museums are consumer-facing. How you approach the public is different. I’m lucky we have a director who understands that very well. It’s not my forte. But what I am most proud of is if I look out of window from the mansion and see the entrance of the museum at 11 o’clock in the morning, I see a line waiting to go inside. When I go into the museum, I see people enjoying themselves. That they visited makes me happy.

What differentiates the Museum Voorlinden from other collector museums around the world?

There are many very good collector museums in the world, and I am rather modest. But I think we combine art, architecture, and nature together very well. It’s beautiful nature around here; the architecture is very fine. In the museum, we have hardly any objects that disturb you from looking at art. We have a kind of a dialogue between the museum’s park and what’s inside.

What are some of your recent acquisitions, and what drew you to them?

It’s often like love at first sight. A work simply stops you in your tracks and just feels right. Sometimes I can immediately imagine it at Voorlinden. That was the case with Kader Attia’s Resonance (2025), an installation of suspended birdcages fitted with bells. It is visually striking, but it also captures a paradox of contemporary life. We are constantly connected, yet often isolated, each with our own voice while genuine dialogue can be hard to achieve.

Another is an extraordinary eight-meter-long painting, Oceanic Underwater (2025), by Howardena Pindell. It is made up of thousands of tiny sprayed dots, but when viewed from a distance, it’s like looking at an ocean. It is immersive and almost meditative. The closer you look, the more you appreciate the labor and precision that went into its making.

To celebrate the museum’s 10-year anniversary, you are opening “Celebrating the Icons of Art” in September. How did that come about?

It was Suzanne’s idea to make this “Icons” exhibition and have it use the whole museum. Alongside works from our collection, we will have loans from museums around the world—we will get their icons. We will have pieces by Claude Monet, Joan Miró, Francis Bacon, Louise Bourgeois, David Hockney, Ron Mueck, Daniel Buren, and Damien Hirst. It will be the most experimental and biggest exhibition we have made in the past 10 years.

What else is coming up for the Museum Voorlinden?

Early next year we will have an Olafur Eliasson show at the museum, followed by a Nicolas Party exhibition. Eliasson will also use the whole museum. We have a number of works by Eliasson, and he is also making special works for the exhibition. We only own one work by Party, but maybe there’s an opportunity to get more. I don’t know.

What are you looking forward to for the next decade?

I hope I will be here for the next 10 years. We still have a lot of exhibitions that we would like to make.

item.title: Hannah Lim Draws on Her British-Singaporean Heritage in Sculptural Snuff Bottles - Colossal
item.description:
In playful, anthropomorphized sculptures, Hannah Lim takes inspiration from historical ceramics, classical Chinese literature, and her British-Singaporean heritage. For several years, the London-based artist has been interested in the 17th- and 18th-century design phenomenon known as Chinoiserie, in which European producers mimicked Chinese and other Asian motifs, appropriating a variety of regional aesthetics that catered to a Western market. “In my own work, I attempt to reclaim and re-imagine this practice in a more conscientious way,” Lim says in a statement. “My sculptures often draw inspiration from specific cultural styles or processes.”

Snuff bottles represent a consumer trend that emerged in China in the 17th century. Its namesake substance, which originated in the Americas, is a kind of powdered, scented tobacco that’s scooped with a tiny spoon and inhaled directly into the nose. As in Europe, its popularity spread especially among the affluent. When Lim observed several examples in museum collections around the U.K., she was fascinated by their ornate designs and variation and began experimenting with sculpting similar motifs. Then, she began to scale up.

A typical snuff bottle is diminutive and jewel-like, typically just a couple of inches in diameter so that it could be both portable and easily tucked away. Lim’s are several inches tall and usually need to be held with both hands. “Initially, my own snuff bottle works were designed in a way to highlight certain personal aspects of my heritage. Over time, they’ve come to reflect different points in my research,” Lim tells Colossal. “Each of my own snuff bottles also has a hanging charm hidden within its lid. The hanging charm references the tiny spoon attached to the lid of traditional snuff bottles.”

For the structure, Lim uses a combination of polymer clay and Jesmonite, a casting material made by blending a mineral powder with liquid acrylic polymer. She also applies chalk, acrylic paint, and a layer of gloss to give each piece its finishing touches, including small painted or relief portraits of animals and imaginary creatures.

Inspiration comes from a wide range of mythological writings, particularly an ancient Chinese tome called The Classic of Mountains and Seas, which is a mostly fantastical account of more than 550 mountains and 300 waterways. “I’ve been attempting to interpret the text through my work, using the enchanting alchemic descriptions of these creatures as inspiration for my most recent series of sculptures and paintings,” the artist says.

Lim is continuing to experiment with scale and materials, especially through the use of metal, and recent sculptures like “Orchid Table” incorporate laser-cut elements. She’s also frequently making bespoke frames that serve as extensions of her paintings, and she plans to incorporate motifs onto the frames themselves.

If you’re in the U.K., see Lim’s solo exhibition Reimaginings through November 14 at the Museum of East Asian Art in Bath. She’ll also have some works on view later this month with Cynthia Corbett Gallery in Paris, and later this year, she’ll unveil a new public artwork in Paddington, London. See more and follow updates on the artist’s Instagram.

Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a Colossal Member today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article Hannah Lim Draws on Her British-Singaporean Heritage in Sculptural Snuff Bottles appeared first on Colossal.

item.title: The Zaha Hadid Foundation Is Reopening the Late Architect’s Former HQ as a Public Arts Space - ARTnews.com
item.description:
To mark the 10-year anniversary of Zaha Hadid’s death, the Zaha Hadid Foundation is reopening the architect’s former headquarters on October 29. The former Victorian schoolhouse, located at 10 Bowling Green Lane in Clerkenwell, will be repurposed as a public cultural space for architecture, design and the related arts.

The newly-refurbished space will include galleries, a learning space, lecture hall and collection display. The spaces will be used to host exhibitions, talks, workshops and creative residencies.

“It was Zaha’s wish for the foundation to preserve her legacy while carrying her ideas forward: advancing education, supporting future generations and contributing to the wider field of architecture,” said Rana Hadid, chair of the trustees of the Zaha Hadid Foundation, in a statement.

She added, “At the heart of that mission is her extraordinary archive, a profound record of her work, imagination and intellectual life. This next step will allow us to safeguard that archive, open it to wider audiences, and create new opportunities for learning, scholarship and creative discovery, ensuring that Zaha’s ideas continue to inspire generations to come.”

Katherine Nolan and Alex Butterworth, from the London-based Studio KA, spearheaded the renovation of the Grade II-listed schoolhouse built in the early 1870s. The pair have restored some of the building’s original features, while adding new flooring and taking hints from Hadid’s paintings for the finishing touches. Nolan and Butterworth have kept the memory of Hadid alive in the nuanced details such as the Z-shaped door pulls and shard-like flooring insets that the Iraqi-British architect incorporated herself.

Aric Chen, director of the Zaha Hadid Foundation, said in a statement that the organization is “thrilled” to see this “next evolution” of the site. “It will be where Zaha’s legacy will live on both through our programs and exhibitions drawn from her archive, and through her forward-looking ethos as we actively engage with architectural culture today,” he said.

The space will open to the press and private viewings on October 29, followed by the public opening on November 3. A new exhibition, titled “Zaha Hadid: Architecture of Performance”, will inaugurate the location. Curated by Catherine Howe and Libby Sellers, the show celebrates the stage and set designs Hadid imagined for contemporary dance, classical opera and pop music.

item.title: Zurich-Based Dealer Eva Presenhuber to Close ‘Sentimental’ Vienna Gallery Space - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Dealer Eva Presenhuber told ARTnews she is closing her space in Vienna in early December, in a decision that the influential gallerist said had more to do with local conditions in Vienna, where several galleries have recently announced they are shuttering, than the overall financial stability of her Zurich-based business. The gallery in Austria is currently showing an exhibition of works by Angela Bulloch until October 23, which will be followed by a final exhibition of works by Austrian designer Nina Hollein, from November 11 to December 4. Shortly afterward, the gallery will close.

Presenhuber, who has been in the business for over 35 years and is one of Europe’s most respected dealers, said she opened her Vienna space in April 2022 on a “sentimental” whim, mostly out of affection for her native Austria. When an ideal location became available, she said she jumped at the opportunity. And while Vienna was no financial boon, it was a different kind of success story, she explained, by contributing to the celebration of artists from her program with no less than 18 solo and 17 group institutional exhibitions in the region, in just five years.

Nevertheless, when the lease for the Vienna space was due to end this year, and despite her Zurich galleries “doing fine,” Presenhuber reasoned it was time to close, given the added expense it had come to represent. Indeed, a slower art market has indirectly weighed on her decision to close, as the gallery’s overall sales have dropped by about 40 percent over the last three years.

Presenhuber explained the art market is still in a period of adjustment for many galleries who, like hers, are seeing “more hesitation” from collectors. “There’s a lot of panic in the world right now, which also reaches our clients, who are getting more and more quiet, and less excited,” Presenhuber said.

As competition rises from other galleries as well as auction houses, Presenhuber said a generation of her once-dedicated collectors are getting older and not only acquiring less, but wondering what to do with their thousands of artworks. It’s unclear, she said, who, if anyone, will replace them.

Presenhuber is one of several Vienna galleries planning to close or reduce their footprint. Dealer Emanuel Layre is scaling back his gallery after 15 years in the Austrian capital, as ARTnews reported earlier, and according to Die Presse, Zeller van Almsick gallery will also close after nine years. They are joined by gallery Exile, founded in 2008 by Christian Siekmeier, which announced it is closing on October 18.

item.title: ‘Jodi,’ Sotheby’s Newly-Minted Nanotyrannus, Hits the Auction Block With $9 M. Estimate - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Sotheby’s may have been hoping that the dinosaur skeleton known as “Jodi” was, in fact, a youthful T. rex, given the name recognition and resulting price tags that have accompanied this species of sought-after dinosaur.

Instead, the auction house’s latest high-profile specimen is a Nanotyrannus, a mid-size tyrannosaurid genus that, according to Artnet, had previously been for sale for $20 million at Frieze Masters in 2023. At the time, the skeleton was called “Chomper” and was being sold by the London gallery David Aaron. According to a statement from Sotheby’s, “Jodi” is one of only three known Nanotyrannus specimens.

Named for Jodi Pierson, the rancher who discovered the fossil on her land in Montana in 2019, “Jodi” is the first Nanotyrannus to be put up for sale at auction since the new genus was confirmed in a study published in Nature magazine last fall. The Nature article, which refers to “Jodi” as NCSM 40000, further identifies two subspecies of Nanotyrannus: N. lancensis and Nanotyrannus lethaeus, and spells out many morphological differences, for example, Nanotyrannus’s longer limbs, bigger claws, additional teeth, and smaller overall body compared to the T. rex.

“Jodi’s” $8 million-$9 million estimate quite a bit less than the record-breaking hammer price of “Gus,” a 67-million-year-old Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton that sold at Sotheby’s three months ago. The 20-foot-long skeleton will be on view for two weeks at Sotheby’s galleries in the Breuer Building starting on October 13 until the live sale on October 27.

item.title: “Thinking From Black” Is a Glossary of Possibility - Hyperallergic
item.description:
In 1979, Barbadian poet and scholar Kamau Brathwaite declared, “The hurricane does not roar in pentameter.” In the speech at Harvard University, he discussed the diasporic linguistics that proliferate throughout the Caribbean, and the failure of colonial English-language strictures to encapsulate the archipelago’s perspective. His oration was later published as History of the Voice: The Development of Nation Language in Anglophone Caribbean Poetry (1984). He identifies these communications as “nation language” — an amalgamation of sonic and verbal nuances that synthesizes African influences into a creolized Caribbean tongue. Nation language, Brathwaite explains, is “an English which is like a howl, or a shout or a machine-gun or the wind or a wave. It is also like the blues.” 

I thought of Brathwaite’s epic speech-essay often while reading the newly released Thinking From Black: A Lexicon (2026), edited by Tina Campt, Kaiama L. Glover, Canisia Lubrin, Tavia Nyong’o, Christina Sharpe, and Alexander Ghedi Weheliye. These scholars are members of the Practicing Refusal Collective, a cohort of Black feminist academics convening since 2015. Thinking From Black was born out of the coalition’s goal of expanding the critical conversation around Black life across disciplines. The collective’s members, including artists, poets, and historians, mull over words of their choosing in this book and offer definitions of phrases from which Blackness proliferates — “traditional or speculative,” written or not. The entries in Thinking From Black offer no easy explanations or definitions of any given idea. Instead, by calling itself a “diasporic glossary,” the book becomes a launching pad from which readers can ruminate on the calamity, the pleasures, the ceremony, and the emergency plaguing Black life internationally.

item.title: Ayé A. Aton Returns to His Earthly Roots - Hyperallergic
item.description:
In the 1960s, Robert Underwood left his small Kentucky town as a teenager and became Sun Ra’s protégé. He became the percussionist for Ra’s Arkestra and returned home in 2016 as Ayé A. Aton. Over seven decades on the road, Aton explored vast distances of space and time, studying the mysteries of outer space and Ancient Egypt under Ra’s mentorship, then turning to art in a self-directed inquiry into the visual culture of West and Central Africa. In later years, Aton’s research into his African ancestry deepened, and his work turned away from Ra’s Afrofuturism toward a more historically grounded approach.

Ayé A. Aton: Image from the Past celebrates this later period in the artist’s life with a small but luminous exhibition of 16 paintings created between 2004 and 2012. In a representative grouping of six works on paper, each piece recalls a Central or West African mask, rendered in Aton’s own freeform style. Faces appear fragmented, with curving, amorphous shapes against a swirling background of marbleized acrylic. Other elements surround the masks, such as patterned shields in “Ngbaka People of the Congo” (2012), but more often, Aton adds geometric forms suggestive of the cosmos or figurative shapes that resemble winged animals or spirits.

item.title: These Are the Artists in the 2027 New Museum Triennial - Hyperallergic
item.description:
After a five-year pause, the New Museum in Manhattan will open its sixth triennial for emerging artists in its newly expanded building on February 4, 2027. Titled The Outside Expands, the triennial will feature 36 artists and collectives representing 34 nations, making it the most internationally focused edition to date. A complete list of participants is included at the end of this article.

New Museum Curator Vivian Crockett co-organized The Outside Expands with Isabella Rjeille, a curator at Museu de Arte de São Paulo Assis Chateaubriand (MASP) in Brazil. The pair was inspired by “X Galeria (X Gallery)” (1979), an urban intervention staged by the Brazilian collective 3NÓS3 during the United States-backed civil-military dictatorship that gripped the nation for over 20 years.

Members of the collective duct-taped large X's on the entrances of various galleries in São Paulo, and accompanied them with the following message: “O que está dentro fica, o que está fora se expande” (“What is inside remains, what is outside expands”). During the period of profound repression and human rights violations, 3NÓS3 called on Brazil's artists and scholars to practice beyond institutional frameworks — a demand that's becoming increasingly relevant today.

item.title: The State Russian Museum Has Restored Ivan Aivazovsky Seascape Painting Ahead of Major Retrospective - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The State Russian Museum in Saint Petersburg has restored Ivan Aivazovsky’s The Ninth Wave (1850) ahead of a retrospective on the Russian artist opening on October 16, according to Russian state media LenTV24.

The restoration of the painting started in June and will be exhibited in the Benois Wing of the museum. In the 120 years that the State Russian Museum has owned the painting, only minor conservation has been carried out.

“The Russian Museum has no canvases in unsatisfactory condition, but we understand that one day this painting, which is over a century and a half old … will require comprehensive scientific restoration. Especially given the high standards of conservation maintained at the Russian Museum,” said Alla Manilova, general director of the Russian Museum in a statement in June. “The Ninth Wave is the most beloved painting among our visitors, according to our attendants. We are fully aware of the immense responsibility – the public is eagerly awaiting the results.”

The Ninth Wave depicts the sea after a night storm with the sun shining through. The painting borrows its name from the old maritime belief that the ninth wave is the largest and most powerful wave in a sequence of ocean waves.

The State Russian Museum revealed that the museum’s specialists repaired areas of peeling, applying primer and paint across the entire surface of the canvas and completed the restoration with a varnish coating. The specialists also restored the painting’s linden wood frame by cutting out over 100 missing fragments from it and covering it with gold leaf. The Ninth Wave will be presented alongside over 200 works by Aivazovsky including The Creation of the World (1841) and The Flood (1864).

item.title: A Triumphant Tribute to Latine Visual Culture - Hyperallergic
item.description:
La Feria, the single-day media and print fair run by The Latinx Project at New York University (NYU), returned for its third edition on Saturday, October 3, just as the northeastern coast’s humidity retreated. Forty-six entities gathered to celebrate contemporary media and assert Latinx/e art’s place in the art historical canon, displaying zines, academic books, textiles, and prints of many sizes that embody a plethora of printmaking techniques — some even made in real time. 

While artists are required to submit an application to table, there is no fee, unlike at other art and media fairs. La Feria also connects publishers and organizations with other artists, true to the ethos of access and experimentation that is at the heart of printmaking. Essye Klempner, director of Programming and Partnerships at the Elizabeth Foundation for the Arts’ Robert Blackburn Printmaking Workshop (RBPW), presented works produced by both staff and workshop members, among them Shellyne Rodriguez, Belinda Lee Medina, and Moses Ros.

“What you see here is a collection of work by artists that use the workshop. This includes the work of interns, to show the true ecosystem of printing workshop communities,” Klempner told Hyperallergic.

item.title: Photographer Elizaveta Porodina Turns Her Luminous Lens to Insects - Colossal
item.description:
Perhaps best known for her luminous portraits in collaboration with legacy magazines and fashion houses, photographer Elizaveta Porodina has also captured the smaller, yet no less striking, creatures walking this planet. Commissioned for the climate-focused publication Atmos, a radiant series of images highlights beetles, butterflies, and mantises in her signature ethereal style and saturated color. The body of work focuses on the concept of biomimicry and accompanies a feature on Janine Benyus, who coined the term.

The portraits shown here are also included in Porodina’s new monograph Found Dreams, edited by Nadine Barth and released by Prestel, alongside her more cinematic, fashion-focused imagery. Pick up your copy from Bookshop, and dive into an archive of her work on Instagram.

item.title: Independent Art Fair Purchased by British Conglomerate - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Shortly after closing the books on its dedicated 20th-century edition late last month, Independent Art Fair revealed that it was acquired by Informa, a London publishing, research, business intelligence, and exhibitions conglomerate.

Independent's cofounder and creative director Elizabeth Dee confirmed the partnership to Artnews, noting that Informa acquired the New York City-based fair in 2025 and was behind both the May and September iterations this year. Dee has not responded to Hyperallergic's request for comment.

While not overtly disclosed, Informa's hand now becomes evident through the original Independent Art Fair's shift to Pier 36 this May, which nearly doubled the participant lineup compared to its previous launchpad at Spring Studios, and in Independent 20th Century's controversial debut at the Sotheby's Breuer building last month after four years at the Battery Maritime building.

Dee also told the publication that she was staying on board to oversee the now twice-annual event, which she launched in 2010 alongside curator Darren Flook, and was adamant that Informa was “committed to Independent's creative and curatorial autonomy.” The fair's scrappy beginnings at the Dia Center for Art's old headquarters were later refined into spatially attuned curations of 20th- and 21st-century art.

item.title: Amok Island’s Geometric Murals Teem with Vibrant Local Flora and Fauna - Colossal
item.description:
This year, an international team of scientists announced the discovery of a new species of wild cat in Bolivia, and research initiatives like Ocean Census continue to document hundreds of new marine species annually. Yet species are probably disappearing faster than we can find them. It’s difficult to gauge what goes extinct every year when we’re still so far from comprehending just how many different types of organisms there are in the first place. Possibly thousands of species disappear every year, however, and at a rate accelerated by human-caused habitat loss, pollution, and climate change.

For Amok Island, who was born in Amsterdam and is currently based in Fremantle, Western Australia, the fragility of the earth’s biodiversity plays a central role in vibrant, large-scale murals.

Across his home state and other parts of the world, Amok Island portrays mammals, crustaceans, flowers, and more that reflect creatures and specimens found in those regions. Flocks of migrating birds swoop across industrial infrastructure, flowers bloom on community buildings, and roosters, butterflies, and cats adorn walls in urban spaces. Showcasing the beauty of living things that locals can learn about and enjoy nearby, Amok Island shines a light on the continued importance of conservation.

See more on the artist’s Instagram.

item.title: The Year of the Trophy: An Introduction to the 2026 Edition of the ARTnews Top 200 Collectors List - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The past two auction seasons in New York have seemed to buoy hope in an art market that has been variably described as shaky or going through a correction. At the top end of the market is the competition for “trophy works,” pieces by canonical, blue-chip names that typically have sterling provenance—and that count, if nothing else, as smart investments. Look no further than Constantin Brâncuși’s Danaïde (ca. 1913) and Jackson Pollock’s Number 7A, 1948, both of which sold for over $100 million this past May; Mark Rothko’s Brown and Blacks in Reds (1957), for $85.8 million, also in May; or Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914–16), which brought in $236.4 million last November. The Brâncuși and the Pollock came from S.I. Newhouse’s collection; the Rothko from Agnes Gund’s holdings; and the Klimt from Leonard A. Lauder. All three of those collectors were fixtures on the Top 200 list from the early 1990s until their recent deaths.

If these sales give any sense of where the market stands today, it would certainly be “The Year of the Trophy.” But is that the full story? “The market for Brâncuși’s Danaïde or Klimt’s portraits represents a tiny, highly visible peak of an iceberg,” said São Paulo–based Pedro Barbosa, whose collection focuses on Conceptual art and archival materials. “It is an asset class operating largely on extreme rarity, consensus history, and wealth preservation. It reflects the financial markets far more than it reflects the living ecosystem of art.”

[Explore the 2026 edition of the ARTnews Top 200 Collectors list.]

In this year’s annual survey, we posed several questions to our Top 200 Collectors, chief among them: What makes an artwork a trophy? “A trophy is a work the art world has finished arguing about,” Jennifer and Alec Litowitz told ARTnews. Jenny Yeh, on the other hand, pointed out that “the definition of a trophy is [not] fixed. Every generation reshapes the art historical canon, and what is considered a trophy today may not be the same decades from now.” (Centuries ago, the ultimate trophy was a sprawling history painting; tastes change.)

Several collectors said a trophy work can never tell the full story of an oeuvre, a movement, or an era. “A great artwork can inspire generations. A great archive can allow generations to rewrite history,” said Ariel Marcelo Aisiks, who collects artworks as well as artists’ archives. “Markets are very good at measuring price,” said Anita Blanchard and Martin Nesbitt. “They are less reliable at measuring cultural significance, intellectual importance, or the ability of an artwork to change how we understand ourselves and the world around us.”

Often, it’s nuances like this that are left out of the trophy headlines. As Suzanne Deal Booth put it, if you only pay attention to those eight- and nine-figure prices or record-smashing successes, you’re missing out on “all of the small moments of trial and triumph that led the artist’s work to be regarded as a trophy in the first place.” When it comes to being a collector, Darlene Pérez said, the headlines don’t cover “the relationships—the years [spent] getting to know artists, galleries, and curators before acquiring a work. Those conversations, studio visits, and friendships are what make collecting meaningful.”

“The goal should not be to collect a trophy by breaking auction records,” said Ryan Zurrer. “The mark of a truly great eye for collecting is seeing the future first and being the first to recognize that a work will become iconic and meaningful as a trophy artwork over time. Then the real challenge is combining that recognition with the conviction to take action and acquire an iconic work before it breaks records in secondary sales.” Grażyna Kulczyk struck a similar sentiment: “Art history has its own rhythm, and in my view, it does not move at the pace of the art market.”

item.title: The Met’s Krasner and Pollock Show Is a Breathtaking Upending - Hyperallergic
item.description:
I was married to an artist once. It was not a good experience, although calling it “an experience” makes it sound like a unified, parsable thing, and it wasn’t that, either. We’re all adults here, is what I’m getting at — so no one should imagine that anyone has bulletproof insight into anyone else’s romantic relationship, much less their own. Certainly, once a relationship is over, it becomes a moving target in permanence: the good, the bad, and the ugly all trading places, each a microcosm in which various genres of chaos and ecstasy hold sway. And whatever we may think of other people’s marriages, we must take care. What we believe we know is almost always something we meant to say about ourselves. The phone call is coming from inside the building. If you see something, well, see something.

The Met’s new show, Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous, is by any reckoning one of the most gorgeously designed and ingeniously installed exhibitions in the museum’s history. Yet its strength is in its unfussiness, because there’s no mystery about the subtext here. Although the title hints at deeper questions about the restorative power of memory, we all know why we’ve come to these mostly windowless galleries tucked into a somewhat hard-to-access section of the museum’s second floor. We want to stare at somebody else’s marriage. Even more than this, we want to know how she did it. How did Lee Krasner make these intricate and small and big and brash paintings? How did she survive being married to a man who was briefly the most famous artist in America, and who died while driving under the influence? How did she — unlike Edith Metzger, a passenger in the car Pollock crashed on the night of August 11, 1956 — make it out alive, and, moreover, what did it mean for her art?

I arrived at the entry to Past Continuous having fought my way through the Saturday afternoon crowds that can make a visit to The Met these days feel more like a punishment than a brush with transcendence. A narrow hallway illuminated by a silent video of collaged film and photographic images of Krasner and Pollock’s Long Island cottage leads to rooms containing artworks. I lingered here, starting to feel dreamy, until another visitor, apparently also studying the pictures of Krasner and Pollock posed together, exclaimed sharply to her companion, “The lady was a homely lady, not pretty!” She then added, as if to either soften or authenticate the blow, “I knew her!” Gosh, I thought to myself, misogyny is alive and well, especially at soon-to-be-blockbuster retrospectives. Startled out of my communion with grainy images of painters' supplies and verdant marshland, I moved on.

item.title: The British Museum Will Extend Its Hours Amid ‘Extraordinary’ Demand for Bayeux Tapestry - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Crowds of visitors have swarmed the British Museum since the Bayeux Tapestry arrived in London from its home in Normandy, France, earlier this fall. Along with unprecedented attendance figures and fervent international interest in the 230-foot-long textile have come some visitor experience snafus, including closing early due to an unrelated gala dinner and being sued by a blind man for not providing audio tours.

In response to some of these issues, which have resulted in visitors not being able to fully experience the 11th-century tapestry—or, in some cases, being turned away, despite having secured tickets to the sold-out exhibition—the British Museum has announced various changes to the overall visitor experience.

“You don’t want anyone that comes to see [the Bayeux Tapestry] to have a bad experience, so our focus is very much on getting it right and learning lessons,” Nicholas Cullinan, director of the British Museum, told the BBC. Cullinan noted that the museum has already welcomed nearly 1000,000 visitors in the three weeks since the exhibition opened.

These include extending the museum’s hours of operations, though the museum has not specified how much earlier or later than normal it might remain open for tapestry enthusiasts. (As of now, the museum is open from 10am to 6pm Sunday through Wednesday, and until 9pm Thursday through Saturday.) According to the New York Times, the British Museum “has a careful plan for light hour allocations” in order to comply with the French government’s strict guidelines.

The museum also plans to provide an audio guide as part of the exhibition’s app, something it had initially avoided in favor of self-guided tours. Now, however, audio guides will both make the exhibition accessible for blind and low-vision visitors as well as, perhaps, help all visitors move through the space more efficiently. For those waiting in long lines—some as long as two hours—additional seating and clearer signage will added.

The British Museum is rolling out these tweak just in time for the next member ticket booking window to open on October 6. Starting then, tickets will be available for the three-month block of January 1 through March 31, 2027.

item.title: In Vatican Address, Pope Leo Denounces AI-Generated Art: ‘The Church Needs Artists’ - ARTnews.com
item.description:
In a Friday address at the Vatican, Pope Leo told artists and curators that the Church needs them, especially in the age of AI. The pontiff weighed in at the very moment when some experts are predicting that artificial intelligence could wipe out humankind within a decade, and just three days after US president Donald Trump rallied some of the world’s top architects of frontier AI models at the White House to sign an agreement to regulate themselves.

The pope spoke to the artists and curators at the Vatican’s Apostolic Palace, telling them that the Church needs them and adding, “This is especially true in this age of artificial intelligence, in which we urgently need to distinguish human art from what is produced by machines.” The address came on the occasion of an exhibition, “The Art of Possibility: Weaving Together,” organized by the Vatican’s Dicastery for Culture and Education.

“There is an ontological difference—even before an aesthetic one—between art and what a machine can generate through statistical calculation based on millions of images created by others. Algorithms lack the spark of the human, whereas ‘authentic culture and art preserve this spark,’” the pontiff said, quoting his own May encyclical letter, “Magnifica Humanitas… On Safeguarding the Human Person in the Time of Artificial Intelligence.”

The Pope cited a predecessor, Paul VI, saying to artists in 1964, “We need you.” Leo reiterated that and went on to say that the church’s ministry was “to make the world of the spirit… inspiring. And in this task, which translates the invisible world into accessible, intelligible forms, you are masters.”

The pontiff accompanied the address with a post to the same effect on X, the social media platform owned by Elon Musk, whose own efforts in the field earned him a spot at the president’s September 29 meeting:

“We live in the age of search engines that offer us thousands of instantaneous answers,” Leo told the artists and curators on Friday. “Yet, no matter how powerful they may be, they merely return what already exists and tend to give us what we already want.”

Art, he added, “is a different kind of ‘search engine,’” adding, “It does not proceed by indexing but by inquiry. Indeed, its inquiry is a focused attention that is not satisfied with the mere sum of facts, for it never ceases to dig deeper, seeking the thread that unites them. Your art, when it resists homogenization, when it draws our gaze, when it compels us to pause before that which cannot be consumed, is a form of cultural and spiritual regeneration.”

Concluded the Pope, “Dear artists, dear curators, know that the Church looks upon you with esteem, gratitude and hope; that she needs you, and that she wishes to walk alongside you, so that together we may safeguard the grandeur of humanity entrusted to us. May God bless all of you and your work!”

item.title: Pre-Columbian Archaeology Meets Science Fiction in Max Lehman’s Quirky Sculptures - Colossal
item.description:
In archaeology, discoveries typically prompt more questions than answers. For Max Lehman, who studies Pre-Columbian art history, what we don’t know—and may never—about ancient peoples and civilizations is what makes the discipline so compelling. The ancient Mayans, for example, bedecked their elaborate temples with images on carved rock slabs, and the Aztec sun stone, or calendar stone, is a remarkable example of Mexica sculpture.

Lehman’s work has one foot in the advanced civilizations of the past and another in the distant future, a time long after today’s developments around robotic and machine learning technologies. His current show Ancestral Androids at Hecho a Mano delves into a kind of future past inspired by science fiction, where modern tech and prehistoric visual culture merge in unexpected and idiosyncratic ways.

The New Mexico-based artist imagines his pieces being excavated by archaeologists many years down the line, when their exact origin and function have been lost to time. “I resist providing complete explanations because archaeology rarely offers certainty,” Lehman says in a statement. “We reconstruct civilizations from fragments, projecting ourselves into the spaces left empty by time.”

Lehman’s work also nudges the nature of information itself, as we find ourselves in an era of data and archives (digital and otherwise) at a scale unprecedented in human history. It begs the question: in the next thousand years or more, what information will remain? And how will AI influence which stories are told and what is considered fact or myth? These technologies are already reshaping our minds.

“Artists understandably worry about AI appropriating their ideas,” Lehman says. “My own work, however, remains deeply rooted in the physical act of making—there is still no machine that can throw a ceramic vessel with the intuition, hesitation, and accumulated experience of human hands. Clay continues to preserve evidence of the maker in ways that cannot be simulated.”

Vividly colorful characters with titles like “The Mother of Machines” and “Sapphire Sage” nod to sacred figures with enigmatic associations. They’re cartoonish, and occasionally clownish, with expressions that read as slightly unsettling. It’s almost as if the characters are devoid of any real feeling, like both a robot or a carved stone. Additional faces often appear on bellies or foreheads, suggesting collectivity and shared consciousness. “The sculptures ask us to consider what happens when artificial beings become old enough to have ancestors, old enough to leave ruins, and old enough for their own history to become myth,” the artist says.

Ancestral Androids continues through November 1 in Santa Fe. See more on Lehman’s Instagram.
