item.title: Elaina Richardson Looks Back at 26 Years as President of Yaddo - Hyperallergic
item.description:
After 26 years at the helm of Yaddo, the storied artist retreat currently celebrating its 100th anniversary, Elaina Richardson is moving on. She will be succeeded by Cyra Levenson, deputy director of Learning and Engagement at the Guggenheim Museum, as announced last week.

James Baldwin, Truman Capote, Sylvia Plath, Leonard Bernstein, Jacob Lawrence, and Philip Guston are just a few of the alumni of the prestigious art residency in Saratoga Springs, New York. Sprawling over the 400-acre estate purchased in 1881 by financier Spencer Trask and writer Katrina Trask, the coveted residency's artists, writers, and composers boast 90 Pulitzer Prizes, 36 MacArthur Fellowships, 73 National Book Awards, and a Nobel Prize in Literature, among other accolades.

A journalist by trade, Richardson came to Yaddo after seven years at the fashion magazine Elle, culminating in the role of editor-in-chief. During her tenure, she navigated the residency out of a financial crisis, increasing its endowment from $8 million to about $40 million. She has also diversified the pool of residents, opened the organization to the world, upgraded its facilities, and steered it out of the troubled waters of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Born to a working-class family in Glasgow, Scotland, Richardson is a bit of an outlier in the professional worlds she’s inhabited over the past quarter century. Despite presiding over one of the most esteemed art institutions in the United States, she keeps humble, straightforward, and BS-free. You won’t hear a word of artspeak from Richardson. No condescension, no fake flattery, and no beating around the bush. On top of that, she’s got a good sense of humor.

I met Richardson at her Manhattan apartment for a conversation about her time at Yaddo, the changing nature of art residencies, and what it takes to support artists today. The interview has been edited and condensed for clarity. 

Hyperallergic: Let’s start at the end. Why are you leaving?  

Elaina Richardson: Mainly because it feels healthy to do it. And it feels safe to do it, or at least felt so when I announced the decision. "Safe" meaning for Yaddo as a place. There have been times before when I thought this would be the natural moment to leave. For example, when my daughter was going to college, I thought this would be a good moment to sort of think about, you know, what else is out there. But then the stock market crashed, and everything kind of fell.

item.title: Rana Begum Sees What You Don’t - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The London-based artist Rana Begum’s show at Lehmann Maupin — her first solo show in New York — is a perceptual mindfuck, in the best possible way. Across 18 works drawn from different series that thread through the artist’s career, we see her using simple, industrial materials — glass, automotive parts, chain link, metal — to create complex, phenomenological, and even paradoxical experiences of color and light. 

“There are three core elements in my work: light, form, and color,” Begum told me during a walk-through of her show a few days before it opened. “Those three things coexist in each work. There’s a different kind of balance for each series. One will be more about light and the next will be more about form, and so on. But either way, the three coexist in the work, and you can’t take any one away.”

One of the first works in the show, “No. 1628” (2026), is composed of a series of powder-coated aluminum bars mounted to the wall; the sides of each bar are painted a vivid, almost neon, yellow and pink, respectively. But the precise distance of the bars from one another creates strange optical effects as you walk around the piece, so that other phantom hues and even geometric patterns emerge — it’s like a lenticular photograph, but one that depends only on color and light, not imagery. 

“I think all my work has a sense of time as well,” Begum added. “You have to observe, see how the work shifts and changes through the day.” This quality was perceptible even over the course of my hour-long visit to the gallery — the piece, installed near a window, seemed preternaturally responsive to small changes in the position of the sun.

“This series, which I started around 2007, is an anchor for me,” she added. “Just mentally, it’s crazy that this is happening in your eye and brain, right?”

item.title: Through Fictional Self-Portraits, Tang Shuo Visualizes an Ancestral Archive - Colossal
item.description:
As a child in Dashishan Village in southern China, Tang Shuo was afraid of snakes. He and several generations of the Tang family lived together in a small community and farmed the land, tending to crops and sheep and encountering the occasional reptile. In a vivid new painting on linen, the artist confronts this adolescent fear as he envisions himself grasping a sleek, black serpent, its recently shed skin lying beneath them.

Long interested in his ancestry and familial connection to the land, Tang once again journeys to his home territory for Borrowed History, his first solo exhibition in New York. This body of work extends the artist’s approach to questioning how our heritage informs our understanding of who we are and how we got here. Working from photographs of himself, Tang renders his likeness in a variety of positions he envisions his kin having occupied. There’s “The Migrant” carrying a small sack slung over his back, for example, and “The Settler” hoisting a tree trunk with tools and bones scattered in the background.

Tinged with magical realism—Tang cites Gabriel García Márquez’s One Hundred Years of Solitude as an influence—the paintings reach backward to imagine the lives of the artist’s ancestors. Lush forests and candy-colored clouds envelop the scenes as a way to connect eras and generations. Nature and the terrain occupied, the artist suggests, is the throughline that tethers him to those who came before.

Although the specific scenes are fictional, Tang also considers his practice to be one of archiving “a world that is disappearing,” a statement says. “When he was a child, more than two hundred people lived in Dashishan; today, only a dozen or so remain. He continues to document the inhabitants and stories of the village and will eventually publish a book recording its history, which he describes as his ‘own bible.'”

Borrowed History is on view from October 8 to November 7 at Plato Gallery. Explore more of Tang’s works on Instagram.

item.title: Monumental Sculptures by Sharif Bey Meditate on Identity and Objecthood in ‘Homecoming’ - Colossal
item.description:
From nail-cloaked ceramic vessels to larger-than-life busts influenced by African and Oceanic visual culture, Sharif Bey’s bold works summon the complexities of heritage, identity, and society. In his ceramic and mixed-media Guardian Series and Crown Series, calm yet imposing figures evoke the Benin Bronzes, ceremonial masking traditions, the giant Moai stone heads of Easter Island, and more.

Bey has long been interested in the commanding nature of objects, especially the ways in which colonialist forces have mined cultural heritage. The Benin Bronzes, which artisans created during the 14th century in what is now Nigeria, are a prime example: British troops looted thousands of plaques in 1897, and The British Museum, The Met, the Smithsonian, Chicago’s Field Museum, and more keep them in their collections. Some have been repatriated, but most remain in Western institutional collections.

In Sharif Bey: Homecoming at The Andy Warhol Museum, the title of which nods to the artist’s background growing up in Pittsburgh, works like “Crown Series: Iris” and “Guardian Series: Blink” possess a deified air. Ceramic beads complement rusty nails, spikes, and chains that mimic hair and garments and also nod to a past filled with brutality and violence, especially—but not limited to—the transatlantic slave trade.

With their eyes closed, Bey’s figures exude a serene power and dignity in the face of historical injustices, which are woven into the fabric of our present. The show pairs the artist’s work with pieces by Andy Warhol and Jean-Michel Basquiat from the institution’s permanent collection, delving into the way all three explore themes of identity and society.

If you’re in Pittsburgh, you can see Homecoming through October 12. Discover more on Bey’s Instagram.

item.title: Tom of Finland Foundation Turmoil - Hyperallergic
item.description:
It’s a lovely day for upholding labor rights. As Whitney Museum of American Art workers celebrate a new contract, Staff Writer Rhea Nayyar brings us a hopeful update from unions at three other institutions: the American Folk Art Museum, Brooklyn Museum, and the Guggenheim.

What better reminder of why we fight for culture than a show of beautiful new paintings? Hyperallergic Editor-at-Large Hrag Vartanian writes movingly about Mala Iqbal's vignettes of the metropolis and its familiar strangers, on view at JJ Murphy in Manhattan.

It’s also Banned Books Week, when we defend freedom of expression even more vociferously than usual. If you’re in NYC, head to the Brooklyn Public Library for a timely talk with artist and author Christopher Myers, film producer Karin Chien, and publisher Namrata Tripathi, moderated by Vartanian.

—Valentina Di Liscia, senior editor

Mala Iqbal Paints the Space We Share With Strangers

Figures jostle the surface of every Mala Iqbal canvas with the energy of a great metropolis. Many are bathed in an orange and yellow glow, a tinge of artifice for people who live under electric light, places where even the sun isn’t enough. Some of the paintings forgo that effect, like “Through the Curtains” (2026). Left to right, we see a scene of collapse, which is obscured by a tulle curtain rendering like a faded negative; a figure reacts, almost numbly; and ultimately another curtain finishes the scene with a pictograph-like pattern — life, transformed by a screen, experienced by someone, and turned into an indecipherable language. I view it as a metaphor for how our screens deliver collapse and violence with every scroll, faster than we can process it. | Hrag Vartanian

item.title: An Exhibition Devoted to Lee Krasner and Jackson Pollock Argues for Krasner’s Equal Significance - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Lee Krasner’s art has always been tough to is tough to define, because she was constantly changing and reinventing her work. Unlike her fellow Abstract Expressionists, whose paintings could be easily recognized by certain characteristics, Krasner worked in cycles.

“Krasner refused to become a serial painter with a repeated trademark format,” wrote art historian Barbara Rose in the catalog for Krasner’s 1983 traveling retrospective, which opened at the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston. “A painting by Krasner is recognized by its style, its rhythm, its mastery of color and nuance, its fine detail, and its floral, naturalistic, or organic imagery.”

Krasner was also hard for art historians to assess because she was self-effacing and bad about documenting her work (which she sometimes destroyed). And she reputedly had a prickly personality, alienating major critics. Add all this to the fact that for many years she was known mainly as the wife and then the widow of Jackson Pollock, and it’s no wonder that Krasner’s recognition came late in the game.

Toward the end of her life, and in the decades since, Krasner has been celebrated for her organic, calligraphic forms, strong colors, and rhythmic lines. Now, an exhibition at the Metropolitan Museum of Art titled “Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous” will showcase her paintings alongside works by Pollock, celebrating them as “artistic peers and life partners.” The Met was the site of Krasner’s memorial service in 1984; now, more than 40 years later, it is fitting that it’s the venue for this major two-artist show.

item.title: What Changing Views of the Young British Artists Say About the Art World Today - ARTnews.com
item.description:
In his latest bestseller, London Falling, Patrick Radden Keefe refers to art in his prologue to illustrate the way the city of London changed near the end of the 20th century: In 1988, a group of young artists used a derelict warehouse in the docklands of southeast London as the venue for their first group exhibition, “Freeze.” He doesn’t say anything else, assuming the reader will know who those artists became: the Young British Artists, or YBAs.

Arguably Britain’s most famous artistic group ever, the YBAs were a symptom of their moment. They rocketed to fame in the early ’90s, as London was undergoing a profound renaissance—or rupture, depending on how you look back on it now. Their legacy has ebbed and flowed in parallel with Britain’s national image, peaking in the heady atmosphere of the end of the millennium and gaining nuance as it has fallen ever since. And that legacy has continued to be reexamined in notable exhibitions, among them shows for Tracey Emin at Tate Modern earlier this year, Jenny Saville at London’s National Portrait Gallery in 2025, and Sarah Lucas at Tate Britain in 2023—as well as “The 90s: Art and Fashion,” an exhibition devoted to the art and pop culture of the YBA decade opening at Tate Britain in October.

Making a definite list of who is an “official” YBA is difficult. The designation is sometimes reserved for the artists included in the original “Freeze” exhibition, while other times it applies to those in collector Charles Saatchi’s “Young British Artists” exhibitions from 1992 to 1995, and still other times to the artist list for the Royal Academy’s 1997 “Sensation” show. Many, but not all, of the members in the orbit of Damien Hirst graduated from Goldsmiths in the late 1980s and early ’90s, and there are dozens of other exhibitions that pulled together different arrangements of artists. Then there are the questions of who was friends with who or might be dating, and of course what the media made of it all at the time. With that said, the key YBAs are definitely Hirst, Emin, Lucas, Saville, Marc Quinn, the Chapman Brothers, Gary Hume, Michael Landy, Gillian Wearing, Chris Ofili, Angus Fairhurst, Rachel Whiteread, and Anya Gallaccio.

When “Freeze” opened in its East End warehouse in 1988, it was a scene. In his memoir about being a YBA groupie, Lucky Kunst, critic and curator Gregor Muir described the way the exhibition marked the start of a new culture of packed openings and the feeling of a real community of artists and art people who went to all of them, drank and drugged excessively, and knew each other well. Genuine friendship between the artists was the glue that held the group together, more than any guiding aesthetic qualities or artistic questions in search of answers. If pressed, one could say that YBA artists shared a desire to shock. But whether through revulsion, violence, sex, or strange new ways of using space or materials, the artists in the YBA set sought reactions from viewers—with good or bad mattering less than the intensity of the reaction itself.

IN 1992, THE BRITISH-IRAQI ad man andcollector Charles Saatchi hosted the first “Young British Artists” exhibition at his gallery near Sloane Square in West London, the first time the moniker was officially enlisted. The exhibition debuted Hirst’s infamous shark in a formaldehyde tank, with the title The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living (1991). Around the same time, three more defining YBA works were exhibited elsewhere in London: Marc Quinn’s Self (1991), a sculpture of his own head made with eight pints of his own frozen blood; Sarah Lucas’s Two Fried Eggs and a Kebab (1992), a table on which the foods in the title were arranged to suggest a set of breasts and a vagina; and Rachel Whiteread’s Ghost (1990), a plaster cast of an entire room of an abandoned Victorian house. These four works, along with Tracey Emin’s My Bed (1998), stunned the international art world and have defined the YBA image and legacy ever since. I would wager that many readers can picture some or all of them right now—they have become genuinely iconic.

The YBAs were the beneficiaries—or maybe victims—of superb branding. Saatchi, whose advertising firm Saatchi & Saatchi was most famous for masterminding the brand strategy of Margaret Thatcher’s final two election campaigns, purchased a huge volume of work directly from the artists who would become known as the YBAs, including the works mentioned above. While the amounts he paid were not negligible by the metrics of the time (he bought Quinn’s Self for £13,000 in 1991 and Emin’s My Bed for £150,000 in 2000, for example), he resold the works with a mark-up of over 1,000 percent (he sold Self in 2005 for approximately £1.5 million and My Bed in 2014 for about £2.5 million).

In 1997, the Royal Academy hosted a blockbuster exhibition of works in Saatchi’s collection, titled “Sensation,” that broke visitor records and also garnered significant criticism for basically being a preliminary saleroom for one man’s collection. Saatchi was unprecedented in London—no collectors of his wealth and strategic mindset were buying in the city at the time. He had more or less free rein to buy anything he wanted, and to manufacture a frenzy around the artists he collected to make his investments so lucrative. After all, he was an ad man.

By 1998, the year after “Sensation,” the Observer writer Andrew Anthony wrote in an article titled “Why Be a YBA?” that “increasingly, the artists and the surrounding world of dealers, gallerists, hangers-on, [and] parties have become more ‘interesting’ than their art.” The line between them, he noted, “had already been blurred,” but by the turn of the millennium it had fully been erased. Throughout the decade from “Freeze” in 1988 to this moment of flux in 1998, the YBAs’ relationship to the “establishment” had been paradoxical. They promoted themselves as disrupters who had come from outside the art world to shake things up. But they were graduates of prestigious art schools who were in with major dealers and collectors within a few years of graduation: chiefly Saatchi and Jay Jopling, the Old Etonian son of a member of Thatcher’s cabinet who founded the gallery White Cube. They exhibited in major museum exhibitions around Europe and North America, and while those shows did garner some controversy (the Clintons and Rudy Giuliani agreed that the Brooklyn Museum’s iteration of “Sensation” was deeply offensive), they were also huge platforms that conferred institutional legitimacy.

The media personas of some of the YBAs, most famously Emin, pulled in the other direction. Emin was famous for appearing drunk on television, throwing drug-fueled multi-day benders, and being brazenly promiscuous, working class, and generally unfazed by anyone’s expectation that she be anything but herself. Her behavior epitomized the fuck-it attitude of her YBA peers. But she, too, became the establishment: first by being a punk celebrity, which made her a household name, and eventually by sticking around long enough and commanding high enough prices at auction to win mainstream acceptance culminating in her blockbuster Tate Modern show this year.

IT’S NO ACCIDENT that the YBAs gettingthe most attention now, both in museums and on the art market, are women. Saville’s 1992 painting Propped sold for over £9 million in 2018, breaking records for the most expensive work ever sold by a female living artist at the time. Emin’s commercially minded paintings and neon works do what they’re meant to: Several of her post-cancer canvases have sold for seven figures, although none has beaten the £2.5 million record set by My Bed in 2014. Some of the YBAs never made eminently sellable paintings but have still grown into respected art world fixtures as they continue making installations or transient work. Rachel Whiteread’s sculptural practice has always had a quiet, stable monumentality, and it continues to stand the test of time. Anya Gallaccio’s interest in decay and mortality pivoted nicely into a tactful, timely engagement with eco-consciousness and connection to place.

Many of the male YBAs have evolved rather less, and their desire to offend in order to provoke no longer holds the inciting power it once did. For example, Tom Whyman pointed out when writing about an online furor over the Chapman Brothers for ArtReview in 2023 that they are too big to cancel, because for their collectors “any such ‘cancellation’ would negatively impact their investment.” Hirst’s work now rivals that of Jeff Koons in seeming specifically conceived for asset-class collectors. His truly heinous series of sculptures “Treasures from the Wreck of the Unbelievable” premiered in 2017 at the Pinault Collection’s Palazzo Grassi and Punta della Dogana in Venice before being allocated to other collectors in editions of multiples of various works, which he said earned him a final total of $330 million. I saw some of them installed at Rome’s Galleria Borghese in 2021 and found them utterly foul—and comically empty when seen alongside the complexity of Bernini’s work. When the image of the artist transcends his art, it might result in good sales, but it doesn’t make the art meaningful.

“I GOT LUCKY AT WHITE CUBE,” reads a T-shirt currently for sale from Plaster, a London-based art brand run by Milo Astaire and Finn Constantine (once just a magazine, now a physical shop, event space, and creator of content). The shirt could have just as easily been sold in 1995, when Jay Jopling was hawking Hirsts from his first gallery location in St. James, with openings that overflowed into the street and what one imagines was a fine white dusting of cocaine covering the loos. It mimics the shirts that Sarah Lucas and Tracey Emin sold out of The Shop, the space they opened in the East End in 1993, with slogans like “Have you wanked over me yet” and “I’m so fucky” drawn in black marker. Though it was only open for six months, The Shop epitomized the genuine energy of the YBAs when they were just starting out: goofy, for sale, and always keen to hang out. “Lots of people now say they went to The Shop when they didn’t, but we know exactly who did because we were there every day,” Emin said years later.

After the peak of fame and power with the Royal Academy exhibition in 1997, which toured to the Hamburger Bahnhof in Berlin and the Brooklyn Museum of Art, there was a dearth of interest in the YBAs for a decade or so. But when the Olympics came to London in 2012, bringing with them a very un-British wave of nostalgia and civic pride, interest revived and exhibitions were staged around the city to celebrate the legacy of the early days of the group. Since then, big-name YBAs have mostly found platforms in solo retrospectives and other shows, like Tate Britain’s forthcoming “The 90s: Art and Fashion,” that offer new looks back to the YBA decade.

While British art has always suffered from an air of provinciality, the YBAs seemed poised to change that when they put Britain on the proverbial map of contemporary art in a way it had never been before. But British art, like Britain itself, continues to suffer something of an identity complex. The YBA legacy has traced the rise and fall of perceptions of Britain itself, both at home and abroad. Stepping into the spotlight alongside Tony Blair’s New Labour, Kate Moss, Vivienne Westwood, and the Beckhams, the energy around YBAs in the ’90s epitomized Cool Britannia. But the fashionable-at-the-time nakedness of the YBAs’ desire for money, most completely embodied by Hirst, quickly became crass.

Though the conventional story told about the YBAs is one of friendship and community, what stands out now is their allegiance to neoliberal individualism. The flashy, shocking work that made the group seem invincible ended up making it banal, appearing now to be little more than branding. And Britain itself, after the financial and cultural boom of the ’90s, has in the post-recession era settled into its new role as butler to the world, to borrow a phrase from writer and money-laundering muckraker Oliver Bullough.

The stiff-upper-lip self-deprecation that now leads your average Londoner to say that Britain is shit embodies a malaise that makes the optimism of Cool Britannia feel very far away indeed. With hindsight, it’s obvious that the YBA moment was defined by a Faustian sale of the self to the highest bidder that encapsulates the intensifying symbiosis of the market and art itself. It is a soulless ethos for artmaking, but one that continues to echo through the global art ecosystem.

item.title: Maia Ruth Lee Invites Us to Embody the Interval - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Translation never arrives in Maia Ruth Lee’s solo exhibition at Tina Kim Gallery, Double Vision. Instead, it is a condition to be embodied and probed. Much like her parents — Bible translators who moved to Nepal and developed a written alphabet for the oral Sherpa language — Lee unfolds the act of translation in her new show.

Grid-like patterning inspired by the luggage at Kathmandu airport, illegible glyphs, and images from the family archive act as a recurring visual language across canvas, latex, and steel. The works draw on motifs of migration, but the motifs themselves migrate across the gallery, mutating as they take on new forms. Stacking, for instance, evokes playfulness in the modular canvases of the B.B. Tetris series (all 2026) and heaviness in “Expandable Luggage” (2026), where the growing height perhaps suggests a belabored migration. Here, translation acts as a migration of a kind: some things carry across while others are left behind.

item.title: Swiss Government to Fund Research into Holdings of Cultural Artifacts - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The Swiss government will provide $2.4 million in funding for research into the provenance of objects in its museums and collections, the Swiss Federal Office of Culture announced earlier this week. Funding for 26 projects from 2027–2028 was awarded following a public call for proposals.

A core focus will be on items acquired by Swiss institutions in colonial, archaeological, and Nazi-era contexts. The winning projects range from initiatives involving several museums to collaborations with communities of origin to the individual cataloging of archives and databases.

Participants include major museums as well as collections with limited experience in provenance research. The aim is to help a variety of institutions gain insights into the origins of their collections, providing a basis for further actions.

For example, $120,000 will fund a collaboration between the Natural History Museum in Basel and the Gadjah Mada University in Indonesia. The project will trace the provenance of 189 Indonesian human remains in the Natural History Museum’s collection, the circumstances of their acquisition, and their potential descendent communities, with the aim of establishing a basis for restitution dialogues.

A further $120,000 will go to a joint project involving nine Swiss museums, including the Museum of Cultures Basel and the Bern Historical Museum. Together, the institutions will research over 6,300 artifacts from Cameroon held in their collections. The focus, according to their proposal, will be on contexts of appropriation, chains of ownership, and the significance of the artifacts to contemporary Cameroon.

Funding will also go into research into Nazi-looted art, with several art museums investigating works from the Nazi era with unclear provenance. The Kunstmuseum Basel will receive $120,000 to examine 336 drawings in its collection with provenances previously flagged as problematic, as well as the fates of the drawings’ sellers and the museum’s collection strategies between 1933 and 1945.

item.title: Queer Artists Say Tom of Finland Foundation Has Lost Its Way - Hyperallergic
item.description:
LOS ANGELES — For over four decades, the Tom of Finland Foundation has been a vital hub for queer artists. Now, an acrimonious rift between the foundation’s board and its co-founder leaves its future uncertain.

The nonprofit foundation was established in 1984 to preserve the art and legacy of Tom of Finland (born Touko Laaksonen, 1920–1991), whose erotic depictions of hypermasculine men — sailors, lumberjacks, and leather-clad bikers — have become iconic images of queer culture. Over the years, its scope grew beyond Tom’s work. The foundation began supporting contemporary artists through exhibitions and acquisitions, and in 2011, it started an artist residency program based out of its headquarters, an Echo Park craftsman home known affectionately as “TOM House.” 

On Monday, September 28, a group of 41 former artist residents released an open letter to the foundation’s board in which they expressed concern over “the lack of transparency and abrupt interruption of several programs by the current administration,” specifically the Artist-in-Residence (AIR) program, which they say was “discontinued without prior communication or warning.” They also claim that “nearly the entire staff” of the House was laid off this past June. 

The letter asks the board to “guarantee the continuation of the Foundation’s mission, not only by preserving the legacy of Tom of Finland and his work, but also by maintaining an active commitment to new generations of queer and erotic artists through a residency program, mentorship, support, exhibitions, research, and access to the Foundation’s unique archive.”

Carta Monir, a 2022 AIR and coordinator of the open letter, told Hyperallergic that the board was “refusing to answer any questions.” 

“It felt vital to write the letter,” Monir said. “It’s clear that, unless there’s public scrutiny, they won’t be transparent.”

item.title: Gaia Alari’s Lilting Animations are Drawn Frame by Frame - Colossal
item.description:
Gaia Alari’s works are defined by a distinct, effervescent visual language. Made from thousands of handmade drawings on paper, the artist’s elaborate animations put on strikingly tactile performances as fleeting marks of oil pastel and charcoal dance across the screen.

Meandering botanical forms, gestural bodies, and sweeping birds converge into fluid loops that create a rhythm reminiscent of a stream of consciousness. Whether Alari is collaborating with a brand, exploring personal interests, or creating static illustrations, it’s clear that each piece tells a distinct story. Watch more from the artist on Vimeo and keep up with her explorations on Instagram.

item.title: Tomás Saraceno Returns to the Past to Envision a More Just Future - Colossal
item.description:
How might we visualize the inextricable web of space, time, and matter, enormous concepts that are so systemic they can almost become abstract? Rendering these connections in a tangible, accessible, and even participatory manner continues to ground Tomás Saraceno’s multidisciplinary practice. Born in Argentina and based in Berlin, the artist plays with scale and spectacle to draw our attention to the life-giving ecosystems in which we’re all bound, merging art, architecture, and science into alluring works.

At Haus der Kunst, Saraceno’s ecological and collaborative projects take center stage for a sweeping presentation titled Ancestral Futures. Spanning more than two decades, the solo exhibition emerges from the central premise that the knowledge we’ve gained in the past is critical to understanding and creating our shared tomorrow.

Called “the art world’s favorite arachnophile,” Saraceno frequently returns to the spider and its web as a metaphor for and example of the networks that undergird life. Interactive installations invite visitors to crawl through sprawling structures, while the decade-long Webs of At-tent(s)ion series welcomes several species of spiders into the museum to spin their sticky structures inside boxes. Continually returning to the web is a clear reminder that we’re all connected to one another and that nature’s processes are cyclical.

Saraceno also adapts his interest in solar-powered air balloons for the museum. An immersive cavern made of crowd-sourced plastic bags inflates with the help of willing visitors who ride stationary bicycles to power the project. Others can wander inside, where they become enveloped by a colorful patchwork of brands and remnants of humanity’s culture of disposability and consumerism.

Perhaps the most impressive works in the exhibition are those created as part of Saraceno’s ongoing collaboration with Indigenous communities of Red Atacama, in the basin of Salinas Grandes in northwestern Argentina. Eleven weavers loaned their handmade blankets, which are presented together as a vibrant, soft space for lounging at the show’s opening. Immersion into the landscape of Salinas Grandes follows with galleries filled with sand, water, salt, and more.

Several works reference The Sanctuary of Water, the multi-pronged project Saraceno and the people of Salinas Grandes are undertaking together. The collaboration, the museum says, “emerges in solidarity with the communities’
resistance to lithium mining in one of the world’s largest lithium-rich regions. Their struggle highlights the continuing legacy of colonial exploitation: While international corporations profit from resources such as lithium—essential for technologies including electric cars—the environmental and social costs are borne by local communities.”

As a permanent land work, “The Sanctuary of Water” is organized around a large reflective pond that captures the sky above, skewing boundaries between land and air. “In our worldview,” says the collaborative project’s website, “Pacha names the inseparable weave of space, time, and matter. It is one living body, sustained by the water that flows through them all.”

If you’re in Munich, you can see Ancestral Futures through February 7. Otherwise, explore more of the artist’s collaboration with the communities of Salinas Grandes on the project’s website.

item.title: After 30 Years, Fondation Beyeler Enters Its Next Chapter With a $144.9 M. Peter Zumthor–Designed Expansion - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The Fondation Beyeler in Switzerland is marking its transition from youth to adulthood after nearly three decades—or in astrological speak, it’s in Saturn return—with a $144.9 million expansion and a cosmologically minded exhibition to inaugurate the space.

To mark the occasion, the museum tapped Basel-born architect Peter Zumthor, who recently completed a new building for the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, to design three new structures: a 16,000-square-foot gallery building named after Swiss entrepreneur and billionaire Hansjörg Wyss; the Ammann Pavilion, a performance venue nodding to Swiss art dealers Thomas and Doris Ammann; and Erlen Torhaus, an office space that borrows its name from the Lange Erlen in Riehen, a park that stretches from Basel to Riehen, where Zumthor was given permission to build on.

But the decision to expand the Beyeler’s Renzo Piano–designed gallery and attach a critically acclaimed starchitect like Zumthor was not a business decision, Beyeler director Sam Keller told ARTnews over cigarettes under clear blue skies last week. Instead, he said, “it was an artistic and cultural decision. First of all, it’s not the goal of the expansion to have more visitors. We love visitors and we’re happy if they’re coming, but we are already the most visited art museum in the country,” he said, noting that it welcomes 500,000 visitors annually. “The point was to have both a spatial and conceptual expansion.”

In choosing an architect, Keller and his jury made a long list of 100 architects from all over the world that have past experience of building spaces that balance the display of art with the surrounding natural environment. For the Fondation Beyeler, the surrounding nature preserve and park, the Naturschutzgebiet Eisweiher, is an integral part of its campus. The 11-firm shortlist included Made In Architects, SANAA, and Tod Williams Billie Tsien Architects, with Zumthor’s design winning out in 2016. In the decade it took to complete, as the architectural plans were refined, the Beyeler hosted workshops with artists to get their input as to what kind of gallery spaces would best benefit the museum and ultimately the art on view.

Keller praised Zumthor for the architect’s understanding of light, saying, “He elevates and enhances the environment in which he works in. [Some] architects that come from the south think they have to block the light, but in the north you have to invite it in.”

Beyond his sensitivity to light, Zumthor has also delicately handled how the new Beyeler buildings coexist with their environs. The Wyss gallery, for example, has been constructed in a Y-shape to conserve the park’s old trees. The architect worked to create the crushed exterior of the museum using rammed concrete with crushed limestone from a quarry in Laufen, about 12 miles from the museum. Each block of concrete-limestone mixture was hand-rammed by 11 workers to create a distinctive block. “I like art museums that really only serve art,” Zumthor said. “The museum itself was meant to be just for the art.”

Serving the Art on View

The inaugural exhibition for the expanded Beyeler, titled “Constellations,” actually starts in the existing, somewhat grey Piano building, where the light comes in from the top. Here, visitors make their way through an exhibition featuring waif Alberto Giacometti sculptures, a room full of Picassos, Fischli/Weiss’s comical sculpture Animal (1986), and more. When compared to the Zumthor expansion, the Piano building feels stagnant, though its most charming attraction is still the glass-walled gallery that looks onto a water lily pond.

Even though the new Wyss Gallery is only a few minutes’ walk away from the Piano building, Zumthor’s creation holds its own: It has one foot in the park and the other on a grey-paved museum plaza. Yet, there’s a sense that it has been there forever, somehow hiding among the trees and residential houses next to the museum.

But what disconnects Piano- and Zumthor-designed galleries in architecture connects them in curation. “Constellations” continues in the Wyss gallery, where the light comes in through the side, illuminating a suite of scattered Roni Horn glass-and-water sculptures that change hues as the light shifts throughout the day. The vast space’s high ceilings also give artworks on display breathing room. Constantin Brâncuși’s marble-and-limestone sculpture L’oiseau (1923/1947), for example, commands the space, while Wolfgang Tillmans’s 2022 photograph tree filling window imitates an open window in a closed space.

Outside the Museum

With its expansion now complete, the Beyeler will next turn its attention to how to better integrate the Naturschutzgebiet Eisweiher into its overall programming. As part of Zumthor’s overall plan for the campus and in collaboration with landscape architecture firm Vogt Landschaftsarchitekten, the museum has doubled the surrounding park to just under five acres, dotting it with sculptures by Rachel Whiteread, Louise Bourgeois, and Fischli/Weiss. They will soon activate a new greenhouse with educational programming led by the Beyeler’s inaugural botanical curator Rahel Kesselring.

“We realized that we have very high-quality architecture, art, curators, and conservators, but we actually know very little about our natural environment and we look at our museum as a garden, we’re planting things that will bear fruit in future generations,” Keller said.

Keller’s mission with the expansion of Fondation Beyeler was to treat visitors—all half a million of them annually—as humans rather than as ticket holders. The museum now has up to six entrances and exits that visitors can come in and out of to curate their own journey. “People like the freedom and it means we also trust them and we’re giving them some responsibilities,” said Keller.

item.title: Fall of Freedom Returns With Hundreds of Anti-Authoritarian Art Actions - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The art and activism initiative Fall of Freedom is anchoring its second year with hundreds of events across the United States this weekend, October 2 through October 4. Public artworks, concerts, and exhibitions are among this year’s line-up, uniting artists and cultural organizations in the fight against an increasingly authoritarian Trump administration.

Organized by a group of cultural workers including artists Dread Scott and Jenny Polak, playwright Lynn Nottage, and writer and curator Laura Raicovich, Fall of Freedom saw a successful inaugural run last November. Since then, Trump's attacks on the arts and freedom of speech have escalated, as evidenced by his ongoing efforts to stamp his name on the Kennedy Center, repeated threats to strip federal funding from and influence programming at the Smithsonian Institution, and targeting of public artworks like Joel Shapiro’s “Blue” (2019) and José de Rivera’s “Infinity” (1967).

“Fascism in the United States is advancing and metastasizing," Scott told Hyperallergic over email. "Migrants are being deported in record numbers. The rule of law is in tatters. And the arts are assaulted. They want to silence us. But artists and musicians are unruly and we refuse to be quiet."

Along with fellow playwright and MacArthur “Genius” Fellowship grant recipient Dominique Morisseau, Nottage conceived Undersiege, a production with monologues from over 40 Black women and femmes, as an anchor event for Fall of Freedom. The National Black Theatre and the Studio Museum in Harlem will present the performance at the uptown museum on Friday, October 2.

"Artists are collectively using this moment to say our voices won't and can't be silenced," Nottage told Hyperallergic over email.

"It is beautiful to witness how many people across the country have responded to this call to action by organizing concerts, readings, workshops, exhibits and salons centering art as a form of resistance, celebration and liberation," Nottage added.

Fall of Freedom organizers scaled up the movement earlier this year, hosting a round of art and activism events nationwide around May Day.

This fall’s program includes a Roger Guenver Smith one-man show honoring painter Jean-Michel Basquiat at the New York Theatre Workshop; a workshop in Little Rock, Arkansas focused on zine-making — a practice under scrutiny by the Trump administration; and a convening at the Kennedy Center in DC where participants are encouraged to bring and share their favorite stories about the institution. During Fall of Freedom last year, organizers carried out a dance protest at the Kennedy Center in response to Trump's authoritarian policies.

The name “Fall of Freedom” is a play on words, meant to signify both the hope and uncertainty of the current political climate. Kris Grey, a transgender and nonbinary artist who participated in Fall of Freedom's first edition, wrote an essay for Hyperallergic last year explaining that they were motivated by both impulses.

"A core ethos of the project is the belief that creativity, in and of itself, is a practice of resistance," Grey wrote. "Art is not a luxury in moments like this; it is a survival strategy."

item.title: The Overlooked Black Architect Who Shaped a Landmark Smithsonian Museum - Hyperallergic
item.description:
On the concourse level of the Smithsonian Institution’s National Museum of African American History and Culture is a small exhibition, easily missed if you are focused on the elevator that takes you down to begin this site’s profound historical journey. Titled A Century in the Making, the display details the long development of a building that at last made a permanent home for Black history on the National Mall in Washington, DC. One panel, headlined “An Architectural Marvel,” describes the competition that culminated in this bronze-colored icon. A photograph shows the winning team: architects Philip Freelon, J. Max Bond Jr., and David Adjaye. 

As Freelon Adjaye Bond/SmithGroup, they shaped this building together. Yet in the decade since the museum opened in September 2016, the spotlight has shone most brightly on the Ghanaian-British Adjaye. With a growing reputation as a globetrotting starchitect, his fame quickly eclipsed that of his teammates. The museum was “Adjaye’s stunning building,” a Guardian review explained; “Adjaye’s radically inventive design” (Vogue); and “Adjaye’s structure” (the New Yorker). When the full team name was invoked, it was often only in passing. 

Architecture has long been told as a story of heroic individuals acting alone. For those seeking an auteur to celebrate, Adjaye’s talent and growing fame fit the bill, but much has changed over the last few years. In July of 2023, the Financial Times reported the stories of three female former employees who accused Adjaye of serious sexual misconduct. As he withdrew from the limelight in the aftermath, he revealed in stark relief the danger of upholding the trope of the long genius. 

In September, the National Museum of African American History and Culture celebrated its 10th anniversary. Coming at a moment of jubilation but also existential threat — as the Trump administration seeks to narrow, if not erase, the history told in Smithsonian landmarks like this one — the birthday offers an occasion to consider the team that designed this building and, in particular, the unsung member who first pushed for it: J. Max Bond Jr. To understand the importance of the so-called “Blacksonian,” we must look beyond its filigreed façade to the tale of collective struggle and resistance chronicled within its galleries. Likewise, to understand the long-germinating ideas that made this museum a profound interruption of the monumental status quo, we must look to Bond, the subject of a biography I have just published, Max Bond: The Life and Work of the People’s Architect.

Bond, who died of cancer in 2009, just before his teammates won the museum’s design competition, was exceptionally successful as a Black American architect in an often hostile field, but never a “star.” In fact, he was deeply skeptical of his profession’s obsession with stardom. “We as architects should question whether or not the ‘Star System’ serves our interests as a group,” he wrote in an unpublished 1993 essay. For him, architecture was a process of slow collaboration and incubation, not a flash-of-brilliance napkin sketch; and the architect, by extension, was only one of myriad participants in the decades-long shaping of a building. In Bond’s view, architecture required not simply virtuosic form but virtuosic function, especially for the benefit of its inhabitants. Like the social movements for racial equality that spanned his decades-long career, buildings and city plans succeeded when they were democratic, shaped collectively, and celebratory of people — especially Black people — who had been disenfranchised.

item.title: Rebecca Ness Stakes Her Claim to Art History - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Inheritance makes me think of money. Handing down heirlooms after a loved one passes, or being next in line for the deed to the family house. A one-way street, an open-and-shut door. But to Rebecca Ness, inheritance is akin to transformation: taking something old and making it new. Her latest show explores this by revisiting and updating historical paintings in contemporary contexts. Here she proclaims that all of art history belongs as much to her as to anyone else.

In Inheritance, Manet’s “A Bar at the Folies Bergère” (1882) becomes a crowded and sweaty scene at the West Village lesbian institution Cubbyhole. The 19th-century trompe l’oeil board paintings by William Harnett and John F. Peto are updated on a corkboard with cut-out and crumpled pages from art history textbooks and photos of the artist, a Pinterest board brought to life.

item.title: Rare Cache of Ancient Roman Sculptures Discovered at Chartres - ARTnews.com
item.description:
A new archeological excavation at the Saint-Martin-au Val sanctuary in Chartres, France, has unearthed a collection of fragments of Roman stone statues and sculpted reliefs, reports Heritage Daily. Archaeologists also found evidence of a water system that may have played a role in ancient rituals.

A monumental Gallo-Roman religious complex, the walled sanctuary occupied over 25 acres and enclosed a massive temple with walkways, a portico, and several other structures. Begun around 70–80 CE, it seems to have been abandoned by 130 CE—perhaps without ever having been completed. It is considered one of the most important Roman religious structures still surviving in France and is notable for its preserved wooden ceiling.

The discoveries were made during the 2026 excavation campaign, which resumed this year after a four-year break. Among the most significant were the fragments of statuary, which were found in and around a large basin. Researchers believe some depict mythological scenes and may once have decorated the part of the sanctuary’s façade overlooking the basin. The quantity of fragments is especially noteworthy because surviving Roman sculptures are rarely found in Chartres.

The basin itself, more than six feet deep and lined with white marble, was discovered, along with two additional basins, in 2022. This year, archaeologists uncovered a platform on its eastern side that was reached by steps and separated from the water by a balustrade. They also found a drain connected to the platform by a pipe, suggesting a system for controlling water.

An opening in the basin’s western side appears to have provided access to the water, perhaps so visitors could perform a ritual cleansing before proceeding further into the sanctuary. Further research will be needed to determine the relationship between basin, platform, and surrounding architecture.

The city of Chartres and C’Chartres Archéologie offered rare public access to the excavations this past September during the 2026 European Heritage Days.

item.title: In Chicago, teamLab Expands Our Perceptions Through Boundary-Breaking Installations - Colossal
item.description:
Against a patchwork wall of hammered copper, a black veil appears to billow in mesmerizing motion. The fabric-like layer writhes and twists against the glimmering backdrop, revealing its diaphanous texture as it unfolds to translucence. Like a curtain flapping in an open window, the digital projection floats across the metallic surface of one of teamLab’s latest works.

Part of teamLab: Everything Exists in Infinite Continuity at the Smart Museum of Art, “Sea of Darkness, Memory Shining from the Depths” is one of several new commissions from the international art collective. Founded by Toshiyuki Inoko in 2001, teamLab consists of hundreds of artists, animators, musicians, mathematicians, developers, engineers, and more who tap into the provocative intersection of art, science, and technology.

The collective has long been interested in the limits of human perception and imagination. Through interactive and immersive installations, they invite viewers into a world where boundaries are suspended and continuity in space and time are key. teamLab was one of the earliest adopters of incorporating digital technologies into experiential works, and they continue to use basic software and programs most people have access to.

Today, encountering such elegant, yet technologically simple digital works is rare as we witness the exponential rise of AI and a collective outsourcing of much of our lives. In contrast to the tech evangelists and the luddites, teamLab’s approach is decidedly human without eschewing the digital. Works like “Order in Chaos” respond to physical touch, shooting a cacophony of vibrant lines across the floor, walls, and a grid of screens in the gallery. Riotous in energy, the piece “is an attempt to expand painting from a completed image, or a perspective illusion of space, into a spatiotemporal pictorial space that is continuous with the real space,” the collective says.

Bridging divides between time and location also emerges in “Continuous Life and Death at the Now of Eternity II,” which corresponds to its current exhibition’s environment. While on view in Chicago, for example, the floral piece brightens as the sun rises and darkens when it sets. As fall turns to winter, so will the ecosystem on the screen.

Closing the exhibition is one of teamLab’s most ingenious pieces, “The World of Irreversible Change.” Depicting a serene animated community as it goes about its day, the paneled digital work is programmed to respond to human touch by triggering a year-long, irreversible state of war and bloodshed between the inhabitants if the piece is tapped too many times. Several editions of “The World of Irreversible Change” were created, although the iteration on view at the Smart Museum is the only to exist in its original, pristine condition (it’s understandably cordoned off for preservation).

As Inoko tells us during a walkthrough of the exhibition, when the battle breaks out, the community can never return to its quieter days of peace. Eventually, all the people die, and the once thriving metropolis turns desolate. After a few years, shrubs begin to pop up and later still, bird song rings through the skies. But humanity never returns, a poetic if not cautionary tale for our era.

teamLab: Everything Exists in Infinite Continuity is on view through February 21 at the Smart Museum of Art. Explore more of teamLab’s works on its website and YouTube.
