item.title: Strong Hong Kong Evening Sales, Totaling a Combined $184.6 M., Mask Key Hurdles in Asia’s Art Market - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Editor’s Note: This story originally appeared in On Balance, the ARTnews newsletter about the art market and beyond. Sign up here to receive it every Wednesday.

The Hong Kong art market’s recovery remains uneven, with a mixed macroeconomic backdrop in Asia weighing on collector budgets, as evidenced by this week’s round of auctions in the special administrative region.

Mainland Chinese equities dropped to a 13-month low this month, while the Japanese yen dipped to a multi-decade low in June. In contrast, South Korea’s economy gained traction on the back of strong semiconductor exports, while capital from the Middle East has continued to flow into financial centers like Hong Kong and Singapore amid prolonged geopolitical friction.

With China’s domestic market continuing to face headwinds, commercial galleries are already bearing the brunt. The abrupt closure earlier this month of Tang Contemporary’s Wong Chuk Hang space in Hong Kong after months of accumulated rent arrears, which the gallery attributed to a sharp contraction in sales, sent shock waves across the market.

The top international auction houses have reflected the market’s cautious tone, too. Staged between September 28–30, the modern and contemporary art evening sales at Christie’s, Sotheby’s, and Phillips in Hong Kong generated a combined $184.6 million, a steady increase from the $164.9 million achieved during this past spring season. (All figures are reported in USD and inclusive of buyer’s premium, unless otherwise noted.)

However, unlike those March auctions, which delivered two white-glove auctions, the autumn season yielded just one, at Christie’s. Notably, Christie’s achieved its perfect sell-through rate only after withdrawing two major lots prior to the sale: Jonas Wood’s Wood Grain Pot 4 (2016) and Cheong Soo Pieng’s 1926 Paysage (Landscape).

Firing the first shot of the auction season was Sotheby’s on Monday. The evening opened with a single-owner collection sale of billionaire Joe Lewis’s holdings of paintings and works on paper by Léonard Tsuguharu Foujita. Continuing the momentum of a Sotheby’s London sale from Lewis’s collection earlier this year, the Hong Kong auction realized $8.7 million. Of the 15 works offered, 80 percent sold above their high estimates. The top lot for this portion of the evening was Foujita’s 1949 oil-and-ink painting Le rêve (Hommage à La Fontaine), which sold for $3.38 million against an estimate of $510,000–$765,000.

Yet as the evening progressed to the main marquee sale, buyer caution and risk aversion became clear. While the opening lot—Wood – Rift I by Chinese artist Hu Xiaoyuan—surpassed its high estimate by over 160 percent to fetch $212,080 and establish a new auction record for the artist, momentum quickly faltered as the second and third lots both failed to sell. The biggest surprise came when the season’s top lot—Mark Rothko’s 1965 Chapel-series masterpiece Untitled (Plum and Dark Brown)—was withdrawn prior to bidding. It had been estimated to sell for between $9.94 million and $16.3 million.

Without the Lewis portion, the Sotheby’s evening sale concluded with a total of $87.3 million and an 88.5 percent sell-through rate. Inclusive of the Lewis sale, the house reported a 91 percent sell-through rate and $124.3 million haul, its highest total since fall 2023. The main auction’s top lot ended up being Yoshitomo Nara’s 1994 painting Present for $9.13 million; the work made its return to the market after last appearing at auction at Sotheby’s New York in 2004.

At Christie’s on Tuesday night, the underbidding activity was buoyant for many European Old Masters and established contemporary Asian artists, from Peter Paul Rubens to Liu Ye, now in his 60s.

In one standout moment during the Old Master offerings, intense bidding escalated for Rubens’s Landscape with Willows (1577-1640) between two phone buyers until Rebecca Yang, Christie’s China chairman, brought down the hammer at $1.5 million, or 150 percent above its low estimate, drawing a sharp burst of excitement and applause from the salesroom floor.

Ada Tsui, vice president for Christie’s Asia Pacific, said she was particularly impressed by the bidding on Liu’s work, noting that the lot sparked a head-to-head battle between a Hong Kong–based collector and a Western buyer. “The underbidding activity was remarkably strong, and the Western collector went all out to fight for that piece.”

However, performance across other marquee lots was mixed. Yayoi Kusama’s 2011 A-Pumpkin (YHP) hammered at $5.99 million—2.08 percent below its low estimate—realizing roughly $300,000 less than a comparable painting of the exact same dimensions sold at Sotheby’s the previous evening. Meanwhile, Gerhard Richter’s Abstraktes Bild (1991) hammered at $3.568 million, falling 26 percent short of its low estimate; with premium, it sold for $4.47 million.

“We took a bit of a risk by bringing this particular Richter work to the evening sale,” Cristian Albu, head of auction and private sales for Christie’s Asia Pacific, told ARTnews, noting that while Richter created prolifically across diverse media, this marked the first time Christie’s presented a painting executed in oil on wood in Asia.

While the auction house was pleased with the result—given that the consignor had acquired the piece in 2006 at Christie’s London for a fraction of its current value—Albu reflected that a dedicated exhibition in Asia showing the full breadth of the artist’s material possibilities might have helped collectors better contextualize the work for collectors in the region.

Regarding Kusama’s performance, both Tsui and Albu deemed the final result solid despite the below-estimate hammer. “The artist’s passing was priced in a long time ago because of her age, and we think this is a very respectable price with the buyer’s premium—over $7 million,” Tsui said. “With sales of very comparable works scheduled back-to-back with our competitor, having multiple clients bidding at that level is encouraging.”

Ultimately, Tsui observed, performance often comes down to the specific work, its medium, and individual collector taste. She noted that Asian collectors are deeply familiar with Richter’s oeuvre, pointing to the sale of the Marian Goodman collection in New York in April, where buyers from Asia acquired or underbid on more than half of the seven abstract paintings on offer.

At the end of the night, Christie’s marquee 20th- and 21st-century evening sale generated $92.6 million, a 28 percent increase year-on-year, though the latest result was supported by 14 additional lots compared to last year’s offerings.

Synthesizing the broader season, auction house veteran Yuki Terase, cofounder of advisory firm Art Intelligence Global, highlighted the structural challenges currently facing top-tier secondary market offerings. With a global art calendar packed tightly with international fairs, major gallery shows, and private secondary market inventory, buyers returning from the summer break were met with a sudden influx of choices.

“We have a vast pool of collectors who can comfortably and intuitively spend up to a few million dollars, but once you cross into eight figures and above, the buyer pool shrinks dramatically,” Terase told ARTnews.

She pointed out that top-tier market trophies in Asia this season—such as Jean-Michel Basquiat’s Ancient Scientist (1984), which sold at Christie’s for $9.81 million to become the most expensive work sold at auction in Asia this season—exemplify this dynamic. Though leading the regional market, the hammer price of $7.97 million landed just 11.61 percent above its low estimate. Having previously changed hands in Hong Kong at a joint Phillips and Poly Auction sale in December 2020, the work demonstrates how premier eight-figure lots increasingly rely on unlocking fresh capital and attracting new high-net-worth buyers to the market, rather than simply depending on existing participants to re-engage.

At Phillips on Wednesday night, the autumn sale marked the house’s first Hong Kong evening auction since the departure of Asia chairman Jonathan Crockett earlier this month and an overall staff exodus from the house globally. Acting as interim lead, Dina Zhang, head of modern and contemporary art for China, actively dispelled market rumors that Phillips might scale back its regional presence. Instead, Zhang emphasized that the firm is focusing on client retention and acquisition through tailored service and a more flexible consignment strategy, incorporating experimental and edgy works and expanding into category niches that larger competitors may overlook.

“I think we remain very competitive in certain categories and within specific price ranges,” Zhang told ARTnews. “Whenever we are competing for a major consignment against other houses, I always ask clients to give us a fair shot. Even if we lose the bid, I ask them for transparent feedback so we know the real reason.”

Across a lean catalog of 16 lots, Phillips’ Modern & Contemporary Art Evening Sale generated over $6.4 million, concluding with a sell-through rate of 87.5 precent. The sale’s top lot was another Richter, 1983’s Abstraktes Bild (522-1), which sold for $2.93 million, or about $1.54 million less than the Sotheby’s Richter, painted eight years later.

item.title: Brazil’s Inhotim Marks 20 Years and Looks to a Future Beyond Its Founder - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Twenty years after it opened to the public, Inhotim is going through one of the most decisive transitions in its history. The contemporary art museum and botanical garden, which collector Bernardo Paz imagined on an unprecedented scale in the Brazilian mining town of Brumadinho, with individual pavilions for specific artists, monumental works, and paths stretching across 346 acres, recorded its highest annual attendance in 2025, welcoming 365,000 visitors. But Paz, who donated the land, galleries, and 326 works to Inhotim in 2022, is no longer involved in its operations. (He announced earlier this year that he is building another museum right next door, on land that Inhotim had planned to expand.)

Adviser Allan Schwartzman, a cofounder of Inhotim and now chief curatorial adviser to the forthcoming Museu Bernardo Paz, described the two projects as “two halves of a body.” They share a founder, a border, and a similar ambition: to create experiences around artworks that could not be presented in the same way inside a conventional museum. As Inhotim took shape before its public opening in 2006, even its founders did not know whether people would travel roughly 37 miles southeast from Belo Horizonte to visit. “We thought maybe if a couple hundred people came a week, we would be successful,” Schwartzman told ARTnews in a Zoom interview. “Well, now you get up to 10,000 people on a nice weekend day.”

For more than a decade, Paz, a former mining magnate, provided the funds to acquire artworks, commission large-scale projects, and build pavilions for individual artists. But over time, the challenge of sustaining the institution made it necessary to create a board, which was established in 2012 to handle the decision-making, donating, and fundraising, according to Schwartzman. The separation did not happen all at once, and it was not free of controversy. Paz stepped down as chair of Inhotim’s board in 2017, the same year a lower court convicted him of money laundering. (An appeals court acquitted him in 2020.) Five years later, he donated Inhotim to Inhotim, including all the art and its lush 140-hectare botanical garden.

As Paz starts building again, Inhotim is currently marking its 20th anniversary from a position of strength. The museum now has 19 galleries that display more than 900 works; 12 spaces are permanently dedicated to the work of individual artists, while seven are used for temporary exhibitions. Alongside the mining companies, Inhotim is one of the area’s main employers, with nearly 70 percent of staff living in Brumadinho. Since its opening, Inhotim has welcomed nearly 5 million visitors from around the world.

Among Inhotim’s best-known attractions are the pavilions dedicated to Yayoi Kusama, Adriana Varejão, Hélio Oiticica, Doug Aitken, and Tunga. They include immersive installations, monumental works, and site-specific projects made possible by the museum’s scale, many of which could not be presented in the same way in a conventional museum setting. Together, they reflect Inhotim’s defining idea: artworks conceived in close relationship with architecture and the surrounding landscape.

Speaking about the institution’s future, Inhotim curator Deri Andrade told ARTnews, “Brazilian artists will always be part of our curatorial program, but we are also turning our attention to Latin America. I would say we are looking at the world as a whole, with a very diverse program.”

The 20th anniversary program shows how this vision is already taking shape. Three exhibitions that opened in April focus on Brazilian artists and the museum’s history. The most high-profile is a major survey of Dalton Paula. Curated by Beatriz Lemos, “Dupla Cura” includes works from 1999 to the present, across painting, installation, photography, and video, exploring Black memory, Afro-Brazilian spirituality, childhood, and healing.

Outdoors, Laís Myrrha’s Contraplano takes the form of a concrete structure inspired by an Oscar Niemeyer building in Belo Horizonte. Set in an area shaped by mining, the work brings elements of Brazilian modernism and structures of power into dialogue with Minas Gerais’s landscape.

For his exhibition, titled “Tororoma,” a Tupí term evoking a river in full flow, davi de jesus do nascimento transforms a gallery renovated for the project into an experience inspired by the São Francisco River, to the north of Inhotim. The installation combines paintings, video, carved riverboat figureheads called carrancas, and a sprawling network of roots cast from molds taken from trees in his hometown of Pirapora, in northern Minas Gerais.

The anniversary program will continue on November 14 with “À Céu Aberto,” an exhibition based on archival research and works from Inhotim’s collection, and the reopening of Janet Cardiff’s The Murder of Crows.

For Andrade, Inhotim’s future will be shaped by both new commissions and a renewed focus on what the museum already owns. “The next step will be to revisit our own collection,” he said. “If you compare Inhotim with other museums, you will find that our collection is small. We have fewer than 1,000 works.”

According to Andrade, this renewed emphasis on commissions returns to one of Inhotim’s founding ideas: inviting artists to develop works specifically for the site. Future programs will combine new projects with a reassessment of the collection and the permanent galleries, both structurally and curatorially.

Asked whether Paz’s departure had caused the museum to lose sponsors, Andrade replied: “On the contrary, with his departure, we began to raise money through cultural incentive laws to maintain the museum, at the municipal, state, and federal levels,” he told ARTnews. (Inhotim is now a private nonprofit that benefits from Brazil’s federal Rouanet Law and Minas Gerais’s state cultural incentive law, as well as donations from private individuals and foundations.)

Still, what is being built at Inhotim’s edge cannot be separated from the established institution’s future. According to Schwartzman, Paz was already thinking about what would come next after completing the donation. “And once he did that, Bernardo said, ‘I’m ready for another project,’” the adviser recalled.

As one of the area’s largest landowners, Paz turned to another part of his portfolio, which happened to be directly beside Inhotim. Two of the projects planned for the Museu Bernardo Paz, opening next September, were initially intended for Inhotim: a Michael Heizer commission and a home for a major work by Anish Kapoor.

“I think it becomes a kind of part two in [his] thinking,” Schwartzman said. “Institutionally, how these two entities end up functioning, of course, needs to necessarily remain different.”

Schwartzman said there had not yet been formal conversations between Paz and Inhotim’s administration, but he could imagine the two museums coming together one day. (Inhotim declined to comment on a possible future collaboration with Museu Bernardo Paz.)

“The challenge from 2026 onward,” Júlia Rebouças, Inhotim’s artistic director, wrote in an email to ARTnews, “is to build a lasting Inhotim that continues to be innovative and relevant.”

item.title: Milwaukee Art Museum Returns Two Jars to David Drake’s Descendants - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The Milwaukee Art Museum has returned two 19th-century stoneware vessels by Dave (David) Drake to the descendants of the African-American ceramicist under an ownership transfer agreement that allows the objects to be displayed long-term. While the hefty jars serve as examples of ceramic mastery, Drake had also inscribed them with his name and brief poems during a time when Black literacy was criminalized in the antebellum South.

“For our family, this agreement is about more than the ownership of these two vessels,” said Yaba Baker, Drake's fourth great-grandson, in a press statement on the return. “It is about recognizing David Drake as our ancestor whose voice, expertise, and creativity have endured for over 175 years.”

Colloquially known as Dave the Potter, Drake was born into slavery around 1801 on a plantation in the Carolinas. Little is known about Drake's early life, but a handful of records show that as a late teen, Harvey Drake and Abner Landrum brought him to work in their pottery business in Edgefield, South Carolina — the epicenter of ceramic production in the American South during the 19th century.

Drake became a master potter known for throwing particularly large works, and surreptitiously learned to read and write at great risk, as South Carolina had instituted anti-literacy laws for enslaved and free African Americans through the Negro Act of 1740. The act also forbade African Americans from earning their own money or moving abroad, implementing harsh corporal or even deadly penalties. Regardless, Drake exercised his agency by incising his name into his pottery and displayed his expertise by authoring original rhyming couplets.

item.title: UK’s Ashmolean Museum Joins Forces with Samdani Art Foundation to Build Bangladeshi Art Collection - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The Ashmolean Museum at the University of Oxford in the UK and the Samdani Art Foundation (SAF) based in Dhaka have joined forces on a new program focused on contemporary art from Bangladesh. The partnership will bring a Bangladeshi artist to Oxford each year and will also see the museum build a dedicated collection of contemporary Bangladeshi art.

The first artist selected for the Ashmolean Samdani Visiting Artist program is Munem Wasif, a Dhaka-based artist and curator. Wasif is spending two weeks at the museum, where he’s working with its collections and archives. His practice brings together photography, moving image, archival materials, and found objects, often exploring ideas around impermanence, insecurity, and memory. During his time at the Ashmolean, Wasif will be looking at the colonial history of Bengal and considering how the museum’s collections might connect with his existing work.

“For years, my practice has returned to the colonial history of Bengal, often through the fragments that remain,” Wasif said in a statement. “I’m interested in encountering objects and artworks firsthand, and seeing how they might connect with questions I have been exploring through photography, prints, and textiles.”

The partnership also gives the Ashmolean a new way to expand its holdings of contemporary art from Bangladesh. In collaboration with SAF, the museum will acquire works by Bangladeshi artists each year. It has already bought works by Ashfika Rahman with support from the foundation. The new acquisitions will add to the Ashmolean’s existing collection of South Asian art, which it says is among the most extensive in the UK outside London. The museum will also work with SAF on research into Bangladesh’s contemporary art scene.

Mallica Kumbera Landrus, curator of Indian, Himalayan, and Southeast Asian art at the Ashmolean, said the SAF partnership would strengthen the museum’s connections with artists from Bangladesh. “The museum has remarkable collections from across South Asia, and this partnership gives us an exciting opportunity to develop that story through contemporary Bangladeshi art and artists,” she said. The program builds on SAF’s 15 years of work supporting artists and cultural initiatives in Bangladesh and creating opportunities for artists to work internationally. The foundation, established by Nadia and Rajeeb Samdani, has supported projects including the Dhaka Art Summit and the Samdani Art Award.

Nadia Samdani, SAF’s president, said the partnership would extend that work into a new institutional setting. “We are proud to see this vision take shape at a world-leading institution,” she said.
The foundation has recently supported the first UK solo museum exhibition by a Bangladesh-based artist, with Soma Surovi Jannat presenting her work at the Ashmolean in March 2026. Jannat was the winner of the 2020 Samdani Art Award.

SAF has also announced a partnership with the Kunsthalle Basel for the Samdani Art Award in November 2026, when eight finalists will take part in Regionale 27 alongside artists from the Basel region. In Bangladesh, the foundation runs Srihatta—the Samdani Art Centre and Sculpture Park in Sylhet. The center hosts artist residencies and community projects and is one of the founding organizations of Photosynthesis, an international residency network supported by the Getty Foundation. Its first Photosynthesis residency at Srihatta is due to begin in December 2026, with Indian interdisciplinary artist Himali Singh Soin.

item.title: Paint Isn’t Just Paint at the New York Studio School - Hyperallergic
item.description:
I went to This Heat at the New York Studio School, curated by Jacob Brooks and spread across two galleries now twice the size after recent renovations, to see the works of Brenda Goodman and Steve DiBenedetto, and learn about those of Bendix Harms. I have followed and written about the first two for many years; I knew nothing about the last. 

I was intrigued by the exhibition announcement because it paired two longtime veterans of the New York art world with someone unknown to me. Was there a formal connection between these artists, and what was it? I have long felt there was a complex and nuanced dialogue within contemporary art about the relationship between abstraction and figuration, opacity and transparency, as seen in Goodman and DiBenedetto's work. I also believe that neither has settled into a signature style nor succumbed to the pressures to be simultaneously socially relevant and self-serving, our current Scylla and Charybdis that few contemporary artists have successfully navigated. They have not turned their back on the world; they have addressed it in unexpected and disarming ways, with humor and imagination. How would Harms’s work add to this dialogue, and did it have to? There was something off-kilter and unscholarly about this grouping, which we need more of in curating. 

There are 17 works in the exhibition. Three are by Harms, with the remaining 14 evenly divided between Goodman and DiBenedetto. This imbalance required this viewer, at least, to keep changing my focus to see what was strong about each artist individually, to consider the ways they were and were not in conversation with each other, and to try and downplay this consideration to see the works for themselves. This presented an unexpected but not unwelcome challenge, pushing me out of my comfort zone.

I decided that comparing the work of these artists was a dead end. Together, Harms’s work consisted of less than one-third of the exhibition, though having a non-New York artist was a great intervention because the New York Studio School has often struck me as an insular atmosphere whose pedagogy was based on a narrow idea about art. After leaving the show, I sat in the school’s reception area and read the brochure Brooks wrote, learning that Harms is inspired by his immediate circumstances and paints directly on canvas using a palette knife. I decided to dig deeper and learned that he is a 59-year-old German artist living on a remote farm in northern Denmark. 

In “Tears of No Return” (2020), we see a flattened, layered space occupied by two large birds (one green and the other blue) with puffed-up chests, a black cat with yellow pupils and lines of blood dripping from its mouth, and a large turquoise green face with one eye visible, crying. A turquoise arm and hand hover protectively above the green bird, which has four red claw marks embedded in its chest. The comically grotesque view conveys the violence of a world occupied by predatory cats and defenseless birds. The man’s tears emphasize his inability to ensure that harmony prevails. What’s he supposed to do? Punish the cat and deny its natural instincts?

Harms’s humor inflects the work of Goodman and DiBenedetto in unexpected ways. Goodman has stated that her work is about “pain and sadness.” Done between 2020 and 2026, the six paintings of varying sizes and one intimately scaled work on paper include titles such as “Covid 3” (2021), “Covid 5” (2021), and “Not That Again” (2024). Moving between abstraction and figuration, and across different mediums, Goodman roots her paintings in personal experience but never quite becomes narrative. In “Mounting Thoughts” (2024), a painting I kept returning to, I could not tell exactly what I was looking at. Three conical shapes lie in a pile on a table, which tilts up toward the picture plane. 

The brown shape on the left and behind the pile could be the tops of one-piece chair backs. We seem to be viewing a gloomy room. Does the pile of grayish-white cones refer to the mounting thoughts alluded to in the title? What is the black oozing out of the spaces between the forms, and where do they come from? Throughout her seven-decade career, Goodman has moved back and forth between the explicit and enigmatic without losing any power. “Mounting Thoughts” falls on the side of the opaque. I did not expect the oddball absurdity of the painting, which became more apparent because of the proximity of Harms’s weirdly cheerful, brightly colored paintings.

Many of DiBenedetto’s paintings strike as a weird combination of the grotesque and comic, like an armless creature trying to apply lipstick with its nose. That humor, which I see as arising out of anger, despair, and tenderness, marked by a commitment to exploring altered states, infuses these process-driven paintings with figural presences that seem both primordial and post-apocalyptic. Like Goodman, I always feel like I am looking at something that exists — a lifeform — but cannot name. In “Isotope Plus" (2026), the largest painting of the seven DiBenedetto works in the exhibition, a flattened, multi-limbed form takes up much of the luminous blue ground. The latest incarnation of the artist’s long preoccupation with octopi, this form seems like a body turned inside out; there are vacuoles of color (or are they eyes?) dispersed across the orange and brown surface. 

While I have been looking and writing about DiBenedetto’s paintings for a long time, it never occurred to me before that the paint could be seen as an ectoplasm, a spiritual substance or energy excreted by a body in a trance state. Psychical researcher Gustav Geley’s description of the material as "very variable in appearance, being sometimes vaporous, sometimes a plastic paste, sometimes a bundle of fine threads, or a membrane with swellings or fringes, or a fine fabric-like tissue" echoes DiBenedetto’s paint surfaces. Paint is not just paint. 

The feeling that paint is more than just a physical medium comes through clearly in the work, connecting him with artists as diverse as Alfred Jensen and Antonin Artaud, who believed art could open the viewer’s consciousness to a higher order. At the same time, with titles such as “Lettuce Leaf Control Panel” (2026) and “Your Problem is Obvious” (2026), DiBenedetto associates the artist with the shaman trickster. That tension between serious and self-mocking, cosmic and comic, is a much-needed breath of fresh air in this narcissistic world.

This Heat: Brenda Goodman, Steve DiBenedetto, and Bendix Harms continues at New York Studio School (8 West 8th Street, Greenwich Village, Manhattan) through October 18. The exhibition was curated by Jacob Brooks.

item.title: A New Exhibition Explores Edmonia Lewis’s Montana Connection - Hyperallergic
item.description:
“I think as historians, we spend so much time asking ourselves how someone as prominent as Edmonia Lewis could be overlooked, but there are generations of artists who have been looking closely at her since the 1860s,” Melissa Ragain, the curator of a new exhibition at Montana’s Tinworks Art on the late Black and Indigenous artist’s legacy, tells Hyperallergic.

On view at the Bozeman nonprofit art space through April 2027, Chisel & Razor: The Artistic Legacies of Edmonia and Samuel Lewis bridges the lives, work, and influence of the expatriate sculptor and her benefactor brother, a Bozeman businessman and performer. While the first installment centered on Samuel, the exhibition’s second act, opening October 11, looks to Edmonia.

Organized in conjunction with a separate presentation of Edmonia's original works at Bozeman’s Museum of the Rockies, the Tinworks Art exhibition deliberately does not include her artworks, and instead brings together the work of contemporary artists to make sense of her life and legacy. Building upon the works of Edgar Arcenaux, Terry Adkins, Sonya Clark, Maud Sulter, Gisela Torres, and Nate Young included in Act I, the second installment will include Sanford Biggers, Andrea Carlson, Kelly Church, Athena LaTocha, and a new commission by Auriea Harvey.

In "Edmonia Triumphalis" (2026), Harvey, who, like Lewis, is a Black Catholic expat artist working in Rome, imagines a speculative tale in which Edmonia travels to Bozeman to visit Samuel. She synthesizes sculptural and research-based processes into an arch formed from local earth and a fountain inspired by the same classical flourishes that influenced Lewis, linking the disparate contexts of Rome and Montana while conveying the ever-contemporary nature of Edmonia’s work.

item.title: Art Collector Ken Griffin Gives $3 B., the Largest Donation in the History of Higher Education, to Carnegie Mellon For a Miami Campus - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Billionaire hedge funder and ARTnews Top 200 collector Kenneth C. Griffin has made the largest-ever donation in the history of higher education, giving $3 billion to Carnegie Mellon University (CMU) in Pittsburgh. The school will launch a purpose-built Miami outpost with $2 billion of the gift, which also supports the main campus to the tune of $1 billion. It’s additionally the largest gift Griffin has ever given.

The Miami campus, located in the city’s Wynwood district, will support more than 3,500 students, from college to PhD levels, with nearly 300 faculty and over 600 staff. Construction is slated to get underway in 2027, with the first students enrolling in 2028. The Pittsburgh gift will be divided between “flexible support for the school’s highest priorities” and an investment in its school of computer science, which will be renamed for Griffin, who will join the school’s board of trustees, according to press materials.

The founding CEO of Citadel, a hedge fund and financial services company, gave the gift via Griffin Catalyst, his philanthropic organization, which had previously doled out some $2 billion in education, science and medicine, civic engagement, and upward mobility.

“The opportunity to bring Carnegie Mellon to Miami places our city at the heart of humanistic and scientific advancement and amplifies the University’s international reach and impact,” said Griffin. “It is a tremendous privilege to be part of this historic moment. CMU Miami represents a generational opportunity to build a new center of research and intellectual life—one that will attract exceptional students, scholars, and researchers from across the globe and rank among the world’s most important academic institutions.”

The Miami school promises to “invert the traditional higher education model” by organizing itself around “societal challenges rather than academic majors,” according to the announcement. It will focus on areas including human health and biological discovery; national security and strategic capabilities; energy and climate resilience; and advanced manufacturing and industrial transformation. The school’s interdisciplinary approach will see humanities, arts, and design playing “an essential role in bringing creativity, context and a deep understanding of the human experience.”

CMU has strengths in computing, robotics, and machine learning, per press materials, which note that the school was first to create a drama program, a robotics institute, a human-computer interaction institute, a department of engineering and public policy, and a computer science college.

Founded in 1900 by industrialist Andrew Carnegie, CMU ranks third nationally in graduate earnings by academic major in the 2027 U.S. News & World Report rankings of best colleges, which also puts it first in undergraduate computer science and among the top five in some 17 undergraduate specialty categories.

“Throughout our history, CMU has anticipated moments of profound technological change and responded with new ways of thinking and solving problems,” said CMU president Farnam Jahanian. “Artificial intelligence represents one of the defining intellectual developments of our time, and it demands that we rethink how we educate students, conduct research and partner with others.”

Griffin collects artworks by a range of historical and contemporary artists, including Jean-Michel Basquiat, Paul Cézanne, Njideka Akunyili Crosby, Jasper Johns, Willem de Kooning, and Jackson Pollock. His buying also extends to rare historical documents including the U.S. Constitution and Apex, a record-setting Stegosaurus. He recently lent a painting by Leonardo da Vinci and his studio to New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art, which hung it without so much as a press release.

Griffin announced in 2022 that in addition to moving his family to the Sunshine State, he would move his then-$51 billion hedge fund’s headquarters from Chicago to Miami, citing the state’s business-friendly policies; Florida does not collect state income tax. Griffin was the subject of some unwanted attention in April for a $238 million New York City penthouse amid Democratic Socialist mayor Zohran Mamdani’s quest to tax luxury properties whose owners do not live full-time in the city.

Griffin’s commitment to Miami also includes a superyacht marina complex, a loan of paintings by Basquiat to the Pérez Art Museum, and a loan transfer of blue-chip works to the Norton Museum of Art in West Palm Beach from the Art Institute of Chicago.

item.title: Manuel Álvarez Bravo's Solitary Gaze - Hyperallergic
item.description:
A small room sprouts off the side of Yancey Richardson’s sunlit Chelsea gallery, and though it’s about the size of a parking space, it often contains the best stuff. Right now, it holds a suite of nine photographs by the Mexican photographer and modernist titan Manuel Álvarez Bravo.

If you’re unfamiliar with Álvarez Bravo’s work, it’s worth a visit. The show features some of his most famous images, printed during his lifetime, that together echo an erotic, dreamy vision of solitude; all but one depict lone figures. In my favorite, “Los perros durmiendo ladran o Los sueños han de creers (Sleeping Dogs Bark or Dreams are for Believing)” (1966), a little dog naps by himself in the sun, his reclining paws mirroring the diagonal posts of a propped-up fence. Human dreamers likewise abound, sleeping outside, as do beautiful young women who look away from the camera.

item.title: Artists Rights Society Launches Partnership with Samsung to License Artworks on Digital Displays - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The New York–based Artists Rights Society (ARS), which represents more than 120,000 artists for licensing images of their works in the United States, has announced a partnership with Samsung Art Store to display the work of ARS-represented artists on Samsung TVs.

The collaboration launches with the work of LeRoy Neiman, who is known for his expressionist depictions of sports, leisure, and other facets of Americana. A collection of 33 of Neiman’s work is now available to license via the Samsung Art Store, with more artists on deck to join his work in the coming months.

“LeRoy Neiman’s work has always had a remarkable ability to connect with audiences through its energy, color, and celebration of life,” Neiman Foundation executive director Tara Zabor told ARTnews in an email. “We’re thrilled to partner with Samsung and ARS to bring his art into homes around the world, introducing new audiences to his distinctive artistic vision while extending the reach of his enduring legacy.”

In a statement, Samsung director of business development Kyle Menges said, “We’re honored to partner with ARS to celebrate the legacy of artists like LeRoy Neiman, while ensuring that the estates entrusted with their legacies are fairly recognized and compensated.”

In the art world, ARS handles the licensing for any publication of their artists’ in any form, ranging from both editorial and commercial uses. On the editorial side, this includes the licenses for reproductions in books like exhibition catalogs, scholarly tomes, and even the covers of novels, as well as publications, for news coverage and criticism for exhibitions as well as general use. ARS rates can vary based on the type of use and the distribution for a specific project but can be around $130 for web use or around $250 for print reproductions in the interiors, with covers costing more.

The Samsung partnership then represents a new revenue stream for ARS artists, particularly at a time when art publications have reduced their print schedules or folded completely. A paid subscription for the Samsung Art Store currently costs $4.99 per month (plus taxes and fees). “For nearly 40 years, our job at ARS has been to help artists encounter new audiences through licensing agreements that reflect the times and respect their practices,” Katarina Feder, ARS’s vice president and director of business development, said in a statement.

The Neiman works, along with digital reproductions of ARS-represented artists for the future, join some 5,000 artworks by 800 that Samsung Art Store subscribers already have access too, many of which of are done via partnerships with institutions like the Musée d’Orsay in Paris, the Museum of Modern Art, and the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. The majority of these works have now entered the public domain and primarily date to before the 20th century, though some have been licensed via ARS through special agreements.

“Samsung Art Store’s paid subscribers are able to enjoy artwork from ARS, museums and artists from around the world on Samsung’s Art TVs,” Andrea Fisher-Scherer, ARS’s managing director for merchandise licensing, told ARTnews by email. “In all cases, rightsholders are compensated for the use of their intellectual property on the Art Store.”

item.title: Arthur Jafa’s Vital New Museum Survey Is a Horror Show for the Ages - ARTnews.com
item.description:
In a self-portrait from 1988, Arthur Jafa holds his camera to a mirror and stares upward, meeting both his own reflected face and the gaze of his viewer simultaneously. When it was first published in Artforum, the photograph was called Self-Portrait. But at some point, Jafa changed it to Monster, the title it holds today.

The renaming of Monster is, I think, a telling gesture, especially because Jafa’s films and videos are filled with terrifying creatures. Some are human, some are not, and most end up getting ignored, for whatever reason, by the critics and curators who write about Jafa’s oeuvre, which may just count as the most influential body of work produced by any living artist active today.

Think, for example, of Love Is the Message, The Message Is Death (2016), the video that is justly regarded as Jafa’s magnum opus. Across seven minutes, Jafa montages an astonishing array of visual material related to Black life in the US, from the police killing of Walter Scott to grainy footage of the Notorious B.I.G. rapping. Set to Kanye West’s “Ultralight Beam,” the piece is typically regarded as a salute to the survival of Black Americans in spite of so much death and disaster. But Jafa also includes two appropriated movie clips that seem at odds with that notion: one showing the monster from Cloverfield, laying waste to New York City; the other showing the Xenomorph from Alien salivating before chowing down on its prey.

More monsters show up in APEX (2013), which features 841 images played in quick succession across eight and a half minutes. In between pictures of partially mutilated heads, faraway planets, and African masks, there is a picture of the poster for Jaws and a still from a “Lord of the Rings” movie showing Gollum, whose madness turned him into a scaly-skinned, sharp-toothed cave dweller. And even more monsters can be found in sculptural works such as LeRage (2017), which shows a grayscale version of the Incredible Hulk smashing his fist into the ground and sending debris flying.

Given this horde of creatures, it’s possible to call Jafa’s art a horror show. Certainly, his recently opened New Museum survey, the exquisite “I Am Tony” (on view through January 3), makes the case that this is a fair description.

Curators Massimiliano Gioni and Gary Carrion-Murayari have parceled nearly four decades’ worth of art across two floors of the New York museum, casting much of the exhibition in inky darkness. Stare deep enough into the show’s abyss, and you will find a mix of terror and transcendence that is appropriate to Jafa’s oeuvre. I was only somewhat surprised to encounter the Xenomorph once more, this time in The Last Wave (2020), a wall-filling mural in which the alien is set alongside images of a solar eclipse, a New Order album cover, Michael Jackson performing, Billie Holliday in her coffin, and countless other visions.

Billed as his largest show to date, the exhibition is a vital one for Jafa, whose route to the center of the art world was unconventional. Having been obsessed with movies since childhood, Jafa went on to make a significant contribution to film history during the 1990s, lensing features directed by Spike Lee, Julie Dash (to whom he was once married), and John Akomfrah. He also worked as a second-unit cinematographer on Stanley Kubrick’s Eyes Wide Shut. But Jafa’s New Museum exhibition, which is less a typical survey than an immersive project in its own right, shows that he was making art simultaneously, even when most mainstream galleries weren’t showing it.

The show largely elides the cinematic part of his career and focuses instead on his visual art, which it presents in a nonlinear manner. Visitors can, of course, find well-known works by Jafa, including The White Album (2019), the video essay about whiteness that won him the Golden Lion at the 2019 Venice Biennale. But these pieces do not form the show’s core. Love Is the Message, his most acclaimed work, is so deemphasized that it is relegated to a small side gallery, where its triumphant song can barely be heard amid his other videos’ screams and rumbles.

The great revelation of the exhibition is Jafa’s early work, which begins the impulse toward horror seen throughout his more recent work. Notebooks (1988–2007), a series of binders featuring images appropriated from books, magazines, and other print sources, is given a hallway of its own. One of the binders combines an advertisement for an MF DOOM album and a photograph by Cindy Sherman that shows the artist maniacally smiling while wearing a silvery mask. The collage enacts an uneasy racial dynamic: MF DOOM was a Black rapper known for cloaking his face in metal, while Sherman is a white artist whose disguises have included blackface.

The sense of menace was continued more obliquely in 2002 with My Black Death, for which Jafa exhibited his own Pontiac Trans Am, part of which he crushed and left alongside the vehicle’s front half. Rarely exhibited and here remade with another Trans Am as MBD_Trans Am (2026), the piece is paired with an ominous booming sound that is both alluring and repellent.

This collision of horror and beauty is key to Jafa’s work, which proposes terror as a basic condition of life. “For me personally, I think Black being is intrinsically bound up with horror,” Jafa once told the curator Helen Molesworth. “I don’t think you can get around it. It can’t be reconciled, or theorized away. One has to accept it, to live with it.” Or, as Simone White puts in the catalog for the Jafa show, the work evinces the line of thinking that “blackness cannot exist without terror. Including intrablack terror.” (She also notes that this conception of Blackness is “not a settled thing” among many thinkers, and goes on to praise Jafa for “the whiff of shit he stirs up in powerful circles of black criticism.”)

Jafa’s remarks to Molesworth may help explain his cryptic 2021 video AGHDRA, in which a computer-generated ocean churns on for well over an hour, its waters filled with broken rocks. Set beneath a gorgeous sun at what may either be dawn or dusk, this sea occasionally stutters and reverses before continuing to roll all over again. Like MBD_Trans Am, the video has a foreboding din for its score, except that in this case the horror is even more explicit. For what it’s worth, back in 2021, Jafa told me that the piece has its roots in a Godzilla movie he saw in Tokyo with his son and a friend.

AGHDRA is presented in a large, dim gallery at the end of the New Museum show alongside a “Picture Unit,” a walk-in structure resembling a maze whose walls are lined with more scary imagery, including a vision of white eyes peeking out from a void. Neither AGHDRA nor the “Picture Unit” contain any of the monsters seen elsewhere in the exhibition, but they do not need to, either, to make their point. They are about the sense that danger lurks everywhere.

It’s a sentiment Jafa makes explicit with a metal plaque appended to a wall near the exhibition’s end. When I went to the show, I just about missed this work because of the lack of light, but once I saw the sculpture, I couldn’t unsee the words that it bears: “AMERICA IS A SATANIC CULT.” The true monsters are all around us. There is no escape.

item.title: Blind Man Sues the British Museum Over Lack of Bayeux Tapestry Audio Tours - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The Bayeux Tapestry at the British Museum is nothing short of controversy. In its latest, the museum is being sued by a blind man over a lack of audio guides at the exhibition, according to The Telegraph.

The lawsuit was filed by Yusuf Ali Osman, a registered blind man who has no sight in both eyes, with the law firm Leigh Day. A letter was sent to the museum by the law firm outlining that the British Museum failed to comply with the Equality Act.

“The Museum is committed to making the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition as accessible as possible and has worked with specialist access consultants to inform the exhibition experience,” said a spokesperson for the museum in a statement. “Provisions include a sensory map to help visitors prepare for their visit, as well as dedicated tours during the exhibition run, which will include an in-person audio-described tour. We are also exploring including a separate audio-described tour as part of the exhibition’s app-based audio guide.”

Prior to Osman’s visit, he had called the British Museum to ask if audio guides would be available and he was told they would not be. According to Leigh Day, the museum said it would be restricting the number of visitors who can enter the gallery and that self-guided visits would be prioritized over programmed tours and events as a result of the exhibition’s popularity. The museum has been giving visitors 40-minute viewing slots and has also banned photography in hopes of moving queues.

Osman is seeking damages from the British Museum and is also asking for the museum to change its policies and provide disability awareness training. “I want to be able to visit the Bayeux Tapestry and experience it for myself. I understand that there are important restrictions around how the tapestry is displayed, but it is disappointing to find that blind visitors are not being offered an audio-described way of experiencing it,” he said. “I hope that this legal action will help make sure that blind and partially sighted people are properly considered when major exhibitions are planned, so that we can enjoy and engage with our national cultural institutions on a more equal footing.”

item.title: Eddy Firmin Interrogates History and Colonizing Forces in Provocative Sculptures - Colossal
item.description:
Hailing from the French West Indies in the Caribbean—specifically the island of Guadeloupe—and currently based in Montréal, multi-disciplinary artist Eddy Firmin is deeply interested in the history and politics of colonization and identity. His home region’s inextricable ties to the dark legacy of slavery informs a practice that interrogates how knowledge is shared and passed down through generations.

Throughout more than three centuries, upwards of 20 million or more people were transported to the Western Hemisphere to be sold as slaves in what is now viewed as one of the most atrocious crimes against humanity ever perpetrated. Millions died due to exhaustion, disease, and brutal transport and living conditions.

Chattel slavery was particularly extreme in the Caribbean, where roughly 40 percent of those taken from Africa were put to work on sugar cane plantations owned by European capitalists. Myriad African traditions crossed the Atlantic with members of their displaced communities, taking on new forms and evolving into tools for resistance.

One of these traditions is known as Gwoka, an Afro-Caribbean custom that involves music, dance, and storytelling. It continues today in contemporary form, taking place during festivals and other events, furthering a legacy of resilience that enslaved people drew on for mutual support and perseverance.

In Gwoka and similar artistic endeavors, technical ability and aesthetics “aim to seduce and mesmerize, while the hidden message fosters resistance to dominant discourse in the arts as in the social space,” Firmin says in a statement. Music and the way it’s broadcasted continues thematically in a large-scale collaborative work made with Afro-Caribbean and Franco-Canadian artist Géraldine Entiope titled “Pa ka tann ?!” A vibrant, elaborately patterned DJ booth with monumental speakers is set on top of a small car, from which Caribbean music can be played and celebrated.

The artist often works with ceramics, recontextualizing symbolic motifs and patterns and testing our associations with materials and their applications. Punching bags and tools are made of porcelain, while sculptures drawing on the African masking traditions are paired with glossy corporate branding.

Busts of Black men, often depicting Firmin himself, mirror the types of marble and alabaster sculptures that historically honored affluent or influential European figures. In the artist’s reimagining, we are confronted by uneasy, contemporary relationships. The self-portrait titled “Sans Signe” (“Without Sign”), for instance, portrays a man with a metal collar around his neck and the seemingly incongruent monogram pattern of Louis Vuitton emblazoned across his face. Eyes closed, he may even be blinded.

The public occasionally scrutinizes fashion brands’ ethics, such as the enormous backlash Nike faced in the 1990s due to its reliance on overseas sweatshops. But most people never see or even think about how the products they purchase are made. Just because it’s not immediately apparent doesn’t mean that the corporate messaging and reliance on material possessions isn’t altering the very fabric of global society. Firmin prompts us to consider how much agency anyone has in a capitalist system where enormous wealth increasingly concentrates for a slim few while most people struggle to get by.

The artist also interprets consumerism as yet another colonizing force: when corporate interests and the demand for manufactured goods increasingly influence daily life, what happens to local and Indigenous customs, value systems, creativity, and autonomy? Here, shackles serve as a stark reminder of both a grim past and a present peril.

If you’re in Toronto, a few of Firmin’s works will go on view starting October 9 in the exhibition After the Island: Caribbean Canadian Ceramics at the Gardiner Museum. See more and follow updates on the artist’s Instagram.

item.title: The Agony and Ecstasy of Johanna Hedva - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Korean-American artist, writer, and composer Johanna Hedva’s exhibition Gravity, My / Favorite Enemy, at the Center for Art, Research and Alliances (CARA), is created with its own demise in mind. 

The show’s first work, “The Clock Is Always Wrong (Other Mouth)” (2023–ongoing) consists of a glass vial suspended from the ceiling by hooks and chains with a viscous, ink-black liquid slowly dripping from its spout and seeping into the carpeted gallery floor. This sculpture is said to contain enough of this liquid to last until December — its emptiness will signal the show’s closure. 

This sense of finality is ever-present in Hedva’s practice across mediums: In addition to their visual art, they are an accomplished writer whose prose, poems, and essays such as “Sick Woman Theory” (2016) view the encroaching doom of illness and death as sites of exploration rather than hopelessness. Gravity, My / Favorite Enemy showcases a selection of six works that certainly grapple with these larger ideas of surrendering oneself to the cosmos, but aren’t quite convincing enough for one to follow Hedva into the void. 

On the main second-floor gallery, “I’m Not Punished by What You Like to Be Punished by” (2026) consists of a light-tan jersey fabric stretched out over a panel of charred wood and puddled onto the floor. The edge of the fabric is adorned with Indian temple hair — hair shorn during Hindu rituals and often sold to Western consumers in tracks to fund temple upkeep. This hair also appears in the sculpture “I’ll Take More” (2026), where a mane is draped over the piece’s wood frame, and a preserved luna moth is suspended by a piano string jutting out from the panel.

item.title: How to Write About an Indian Artist for Western Readers - Hyperallergic
Artists Deserve to Afford Pets - Hyperallergic
item.description:
From David Hockney’s beloved dachshunds to Frida Kahlo’s menagerie of parrots, the history of art is a history of animals. Through the ages, artists have formed deep bonds with their pets, who offer emotional support, portrait inspiration, and the purest of all loves. But today, many artists who are pet parents say they can barely afford healthcare for their sick, injured, aging, or even perfectly healthy friends. In a moving and necessary piece, Staff Writer Rhea Nayyar speaks to artists and cultural workers about the increasingly prohibitive costs of caring for those who care for us.

Today's issue is all about art beyond traditional spaces. Izzy DeSantis spotlights four artists exploring biodegradable, climate-friendly art materials, and in Rome, Anthony Majanlahti visits an astonishing mosaic under the Baths of Trajan. Plus, Staff Writer Anna Lee reports on “Tidal Crossing,” Jean Shin’s expansive new installation at the Brooklyn Army Terminal.  

Hyperallergic members in NYC, you still have time to RSVP for tonight’s event at the International Studio & Curatorial Program. Not a member yet? Join here. I’ll see you there!

— Valentina Di Liscia, senior editor

How Are Artists Affording Pet Care?

Imagine this — you make a significant sale that covers your apartment and studio rent for the month and a chunk of some credit card debt, and before you know it, your beloved dachshund stops eating and suddenly needs a couple of teeth extracted. In the blink of an eye, you’re another $1,400 (at best) in the hole you’ve been persistently digging yourself out of. Even worse, the problem spreads, and the dog needs more teeth removed within months.

Animal companions may be some of the most meaningful bonds of a lifetime, but it’s no walk in the park to account for exorbitant veterinary care while running on the check-to-check treadmill. So how are animal-loving artists and cultural workers managing with soaring prices as private equity gobbles up the veterinary sphere, and how are they budgeting for financing medical care to do right by their pets? | Rhea Nayyar

item.title: A Workforce of Creatures Chugs Along in Kate Renshaw-Lewis’ Hand-Drawn Film ‘Busy Bodies’ - Colossal
item.description:
Reuben “Rube” Goldberg (1883-1970) was known for his comic strips, political cartoons, and unique inventions. His most enduring legacy, however, is arguably the Rube Goldberg machine. Still bearing his name, these contraptions are often comical or playful due to their “overengineered” nature, using complex sequences of simple chain reactions like rolling ramps, weight and pulley systems, domino chains, and pendulum swings.

“Busy Bodies,” created by animator Kate Renshaw-Lewis, is a short film inspired by these straightforward yet intricate mechanisms. The animation presents an imaginative process for what seems to be the creation of red rubber gloves and the packaging of vague fish products. As tiny hat-wearing creatures—reminiscent of factory workers—complete their assigned tasks like clockwork, Renshaw-Lewis emphasizes “the mystery and absurdity behind how we get items that are so readily available to us,” she says.

The moving image is entirely hand-drawn, combining inkjet and screen printing techniques. Throughout the film a satisfying flow of tasks ensues, leading up to a climax that abstracts the visuals into shifting colors and outlines. This “under the hood” perspective provides viewers with a larger understanding of the painstakingly manual process behind the work.

Renshaw-Lewis’ film won the Grand Jury Prize for best animated short at Slamdance Film Festival, and it was nominated for Best Film at Sundance Film Festival. Watch more from the artist on Vimeo, and find some behind-the-scenes tidbits on Instagram.

item.title: The Counterpublic Triennial Pollinates a Budding St. Louis - Hyperallergic
item.description:
ST. LOUIS — Suspended mid-leap with nothing below, the future lies outside of the frame. What’s certain is the split-second decision: to soar forward or look back over one’s shoulder; to plunge into the unknown or pause — perhaps, to plummet.

Inspired by the moment in a video game when a character jumps off a cliff and is suspended midair — taken from artist Alice Bucknell’s commissioned work of the same name — Coyote Time marks the third edition of the Counterpublic Triennial, a sweeping exhibition of public art well suited for a city that can feel both frozen in time and ripe for a wildly revitalized future.

Counterpublic’s roots go back to 2015, when original co-founders James McAnally and Brea Youngblood sought to integrate the project of their gallery, The Luminary, into the urban fabric of the surrounding neighborhood. Incorporated in 2021 as its own non-profit organization, the three-month exhibition has since exploded in both renown and ambition — nearly doubling the number of artists from 2023 to cascade across St. Louis City and into the Metro East region beyond the Mississippi River.

Creatively pollinating parks, community gardens, vacant lots, and even an abandoned vending machine factory, this year’s Counterpublic is organized into five major hubs and boasts an international guest curatorial team, including Stefanie Hessler, Raphael Fonseca, and Wanda Nanibush. The exhibition features major artists like Glenn Ligon, Rirkrit Tiravanija, and Nick Cave, alongside regionally notable artists such as Rachel Youn, Anika Todd, and Jamie Lee Harris. On its opening weekend, visitors flocked from near and far despite the stifling heat, a current running through the city rivaling that of its mighty river.

At its best, Counterpublic artworks invigorate, channeling the energy of St. Louis’s established arts districts to empty, under-utilized, or under-recognized urban spaces — capillaries warming appendages gone numb from decades of neglect. Hipsters rub shoulders with retirees; elites share tables with the hoi polloi; outsiders are forced to reassess, if not jettison, the harmful preconceptions wrought by a “flyover” mindset toward the region.

item.title: Nuanced Portraits of India’s Female Bodybuilders - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
Keerthana Kunnath’s Not What You Saw began organically, after the photographer met a handful of female bodybuilders from the Kerala region of South India. The group later grew to more than a dozen, and Kunnath began to embed herself within the community. She came to understand the full weight of their commitment: the physical demands of the sport, the emotional strain, and the financial pressures of choosing this career. Determined to build visibility and respect for these women, she got to know their friends and families, spent time with them in their homes outside the shoots, and followed them to competitions. The project is both documentation and provocation: a tribute to trailblazing women and a call to rethink cultural constructs of gender and beauty. The artist’s visual language is striking and graceful, characterised by a rich colour palette. Foam, Amsterdam’s display of her works opens up vital conversations about gender, sexuality and mental health, topics that are rarely discussed in her homeland of India. Aesthetica spoke to the artist about how important visibility is for the women in her images. 

A: Not What You Saw began when you met a handful of female bodybuilders from the Kerala region of South India. What was it about the women that you initially wanted to document? 

KK: I was immediately drawn to their muscular bodies, but also to the grace and softness that existed alongside that strength. There was something about seeing these very powerful women in the context of Kerala that felt unfamiliar to me. I wanted to photograph them as Malayali women who are also bodybuilders. Two things that, to me, felt almost strange to see in the same sentence. 

A: Can you tell us a bit about the bodybuilding community in Kerala? 

KK: It’s a very small and relatively new group, especially when it comes to women. Men’s bodybuilding has been much more established and visible in Kerala, whereas there are still only a handful of women competing. Because of that, the community is quite close knit. The women are supportive of each other, and they encourage one another to keep going in a space that can feel very male-dominated. 

A: You spend a lot of time with the women, as well as their friends and family, in their quiet, domestic moments as well as during training. Why was it important to capture these spaces alongside the gym? 

KK: I wanted to get to know them beyond bodybuilding. I was interested in the contrast between the physicality we usually associate with strength training and the quieter, more ordinary parts of their lives as daughters, mothers, friends, partners, and people with their own ambitions and responsibilities. Through our conversations, I realised how much they were navigating alongside the sport. It was important for me to hold space for all of those different parts of who they are, rather than reducing them to their bodies. Spending time with them at home, with their families and in their everyday environments allowed me to see those quieter layers, which became an important part of how I understood and photographed them. 

A: How did spending time with these figures shape how you viewed strength? 

KK: I had initially been drawn to their physicality; the muscle, the discipline, the physical transformation. But the more I got to know them, the more I realised that wasn’t the strength that stayed with me. There is a much quieter resilience in choosing a path that isn’t expected of you, especially as a woman, and continuing to do it despite the ideas and expectations around womanhood. For me, that became one of the most powerful parts of the work: realising that strength can be as much about conviction and self-belief as it is about the body. Spending time with them made me rethink what I was initially looking at. Bodybuilding isn’t a very mainstream path for women in Kerala, and they are constantly having to negotiate that with their families, their communities and sometimes with their own ideas of what a woman is supposed to be. They make space for this part of themselves, and continue despite all adversity, which helped me realise that the physical strength was only the most visible part of it.

A: Were there any particular stories or experiences that have particularly stayed with you? 

KK: One moment that has stayed with me was seeing Kavitha’s mother come to support her at a competition. Kavitha is 40, and her mother didn’t really know much about bodybuilding or what was happening around her, but she was completely there for her daughter. When Kavitha won the trophy, her mother had this huge smile that I found really moving. She may never have imagined this for herself or for Kavitha, but seeing her daughter on that stage, doing something so unexpected, was special. 

A: Your images have a softness, despite the physical power of the bodies. How did you balance this? 

KK: I think that softness came quite naturally from the connection I built with the women. The more time I spent with them, the less I saw them simply as strong bodies and the more I saw them as whole people. We’re all much more complicated than what is visible on the outside, and I think that comes through. 

A: How does your work challenge what wider society sees as acceptable for women’s bodies? 

KK: I didn’t set out to challenge an idea of how a woman’s body should look. Through the process of making the work, I realised how much we attach meaning to a woman’s body and how quickly we decide whether it looks feminine, attractive, strong or acceptable. For me, the series is about sitting with that discomfort a little longer. A muscular female body can exist without needing to be explained or softened, and femininity doesn’t have to disappear when the body becomes stronger. I think the photographs are an attempt to make space for that without telling the viewer what they should think. 

A: What do you hope your subjects see when they look at these photographs of themselves? 

KK: I hope they see a side of themselves that they don’t always get to see. I’ve photographed them in so many different situations. Training, competing, at home, with their families and I hope the images hold all of those versions of them. I also hope they feel proud when they look at them. Many of them have had to make their own way in a sport that is still unfamiliar for women in Kerala. I’d like the photographs to remind them of how far they’ve come, and maybe, on a difficult day, give them a reason to keep going. 

Keerthana Kunnath: Not What You Saw is at Foam, Amsterdam from 18 September – 27 November: foam.org

Words: Emma Jacob & Keerthana Kunnath

item.title: The Art of Eli Schläppi: Abstraction and Lived Experience - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
“I paint myself because I am the subject I know best.” These are the now infamous words of renowned artist Frida Kahlo. It’s a sentiment echoed across disciplines and eras, such as Jackson Pollock’s declaration that: “Every good painter paints what he is.” Or, in writing, the age-old adage that you must “write what you know.” They all boil down to the same philosophy: the work we create is fundamentally tied up with our own personal experiences. Our creative output is often shaped by our nationality, upbringing, family, friends and education. Nowhere is this truer than in the work of Eli Schläppi, an artist whose work unfolds at the intersection of painting, philosophy and lived experience. 

Her paintings are rooted in her Swiss heritage and informed by her background as a Cantonally Licensed Naturopathic Doctor. They’re also enriched by years of engagement with Chinese medicine, Daoist thought and East Asian calligraphic tradition. There’s no doubt, Schläppi is an artist whose life is writ large in her practice. Her paintings emerge from an attentive observation of natural phenomena and a profound awareness of movement and perception. Rivers, volcanic landscapes, northern skies, light and ecological systems all become materials for a painterly language that acts as a record of Schläppi’s interactions with the world. Her abstract pieces are bold and confident, offering the decisive strokes of a practitioner who approaches art as a means of understanding life as something in constant motion. 

The artist has a clear message in her work: humanity is not separate from the natural world, we are an integral part of it. Her celebrated Not green but blue river series, inspired by the glacial waters of Switzerland’s Aare River, “rejects traditional landscape representation in favour of embodied gesture.” Sweeping blue lines traverse the canvas, echoing the ferocity of a flowing river and suggesting it as a life force itself, rather than an inanimate part of the landscape. Meanwhile, Sky-Elbe-Beach is also inspired by a river, the Elbe in Hamburg. Here, layers of blue dissolve distinction between sky and water, generating a sense of place that transcends the geographical and becomes something more universal. 

In other works, Schläppi explores a more geological side of the landscape. Lanzarote is inspired by the volcanic parts of the Canary Islands, and the paintings take on more vivid yellow and orange hues. Angular shapes move like tectonic shifts and currents of molten rock, whilst more intricate networks – a change from the artist’s usual style – represent erosion, sedimentation and renewal. Here, the works capture the perpetual activity of the world. It’s an intelligent and nuanced perspective, acknowledging and accepting that we exist in a state of constant destruction and formation, where stability and change coexist. 

What sets Schläppi apart is her commitment to the authenticity of gesture and material. She prioritises direct bodily engagement over our era of digital production and technological mediation. Here, her involvement with Chinese philosophy comes to the fore, with Daoist concepts of flow, balance and transformation resonating throughout her paintings. Elsewhere, the influence of calligraphy informs her understanding of gesture as an extension of our innermost selves. Ultimately, her work is a fascinating representation of her experiences. There’s a synthesis of Western abstraction and Eastern philosophical thought, resulting in work that transcends cultural boundaries whilst remaining deeply personal. 

Words: Emma Jacob

Image Credits:

All images courtesy Eli Schläppi.

item.title: Please No Photos! A Short Film Focuses on Tourists’ Obsession with Capturing the Moment - Colossal
item.description:
If you find yourself feeling impatient at the slow, meditative opening scenes of “The Spectacle,” just wait. The short documentary from The New Yorker visits a slew of stunning vistas primarily across Norway, showcasing star-dappled night skies and awe-inspiring mountaintop views. We’re witness to landscapes that appear untouched by humanity, until director Yasmin van Dorp plops us down amidst hordes of tourists.

What was a serene environment is suddenly a chaotic display of phones and cameras. A parent attempts to coax their child out atop the famous Norwegian boulder Kjeragbolten for a photo, assistants fluff formal gowns so their wearer appears windswept, and selfie sticks and drone controls abound. Van Dorp puts the contemporary tourism industry in full focus, confronting viewers with our inability to be present and the strange desire to see some of the world’s most spectacular sights filtered through a tiny screen.

item.title: Staff at Three Major Museums Vote to Strike - Hyperallergic
item.description:
I was heading down to Sunset Park on Sunday afternoon to visit a close friend when, as an absentminded creature of routine, I accidentally embarked on my usual journey to Atlantic Terminal. I’ve made this ultimately harmless mistake multiple times now, but I still get frustrated with myself for arriving somewhere later than I intended because of something so easily preventable. 

In this instance, however, I was in the wrong place at the right time for once. Because if I hadn’t accidentally sent myself uptown, I wouldn’t have gotten to see this:

As one can imagine, my whole day was made because of this serendipitous little treasure named Benji. I’d hazard a guess that many others felt similarly when encountering the gilded cavatappi inflatable on the High Line. Staff writer Anna Lee reported that the shimmering serpentine installation was backed by the luxury jewelry company Bulgari for New York Fashion Week. Evidently, my little friend Benji got the memo about Fashion Week before any of us did. 

I’ve been making a lot of collages to ease myself back into art-making without an agenda after sheepishly neglecting my studio for a summer spent outdoors. I was delighted to see that the Brooklyn Public Library began offering a craft supply lending program last week!

Between the Library’s rentable woodworking kits and Cricut machine and the recent inauguration of Brooklyn Creative Reuse’s brick-and-mortar shop in Industry City, it’s heartening to see these community-driven efforts to mitigate the costly barriers to entry for craft and artmaking. Resources like these are a salve for the sore soul amid the embattled landscape of higher arts education — the School of Visual Arts is shutting down its graduate photography and video practice program because of the school’s financial struggles and the general decline in enrollment.

It’s been a big day for museums today. Senior Editor Valentina Di Liscia brings us to The Met’s groundbreaking ceremony for the construction of its forthcoming Tang Wing for Contemporary Art, while unionized staff at the Whitney Museum, the Brooklyn Museum, and the American Folk Art Museum hit the ground running with a vote to authorize strike action if fair contracts aren’t reached.  

Don’t miss Hyperallergic Editor-in-Chief Hakim Bishara’s interview with Alfredo Jaar on the occasion of the Chilean artist’s solo exhibition at Galerie Lelong, contributing critic Channelle Chevelle Russell’s experience at the Drawing Center’s show for the late artist Pope.L, and reflections by artists and art workers on the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attack and its reverberating cultural impact around the globe.

Alfredo Jaar Is Still Trying to Change the World

In April of 1987, when Reaganism was running amok and Henry Kissinger was fiddling with world affairs like a puppet master from hell, a relatively unknown 31-year-old Chilean artist named Alfredo Jaar staged his billboard installation A Logo for America smack dab in the heart of Times Square. It instantly became one of the most discussed works of political art in the contemporary canon.

Appearing between ads for tomato sauce and a Mexican restaurant, the 42-second LED animation bewildered New Yorkers with the message “This Is Not America” superimposed on a map of the United States, followed by an image of the US flag with the text, “This Is Not America’s Flag.” Next, the “R” in America shifted into a dancing map of South, Central, and North America. | Hakim Bishara
