item.title: Met Museum Breaks Ground on New Modern and Contemporary Wing - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The Metropolitan Museum of Art officially broke ground today, September 15, on its forthcoming Tang Wing for modern and contemporary art, designed by Frida Escobedo. The Mexican architect joined Met Director Max Hollein and elected officials in a morning ceremony at the museum's European Sculpture Court.

Escobedo, the first woman to design a wing at The Met, also clinched another “first” earlier this year, when she participated in the museum's inaugural public event held entirely in Spanish. At today's ceremony, she began her remarks with a nod to a Spanish expression for groundbreaking — la primera piedra, or “the first stone” — a phrase that made her think of the four piles of uncarved stone blocks atop the columns on The Met's Fifth Avenue facade. The curious pyramidal slabs are a vestige of architect Richard Morris Hunt's 1894 expansion plan, which called for sculpted statues that never materialized.

“It suggested the idea of becoming — that architecture, and perhaps institutions too, are never entirely finished,” Escobedo said in her address. “They continue changing, accumulating, and adding meaning.”

Replacing the Lila Acheson Wallace Wing at the southwest corner of The Met's building complex, the 126,000-square-foot Tang Wing will expand the museum's 20th- and 21st-century art galleries by nearly 50%, adding 69,500 square feet of exhibition space while improving accessibility and reducing energy consumption. The new wing is slated to open in 2030.

item.title: Staff at Whitney Museum, Brooklyn Museum, and American Folk Art Museum Authorize Strike - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Unionized workers at the Whitney Museum of American Art, the Brooklyn Museum, and the American Folk Art Museum (AFAM) have voted to authorize a strike action if they don't receive fair offers for union contracts with their respective institutions.

“Staff should be able to afford to live in the city they work in,” said AFAM's Director of Information Technology, Richard Ho, who has worked at the museum for 25 years. “AFAM staff voted unanimously to unionize to address pressing concerns about workplace rights and wages that lag below inflation.”

Strike dates have not been set, but the three union groups organized with United Auto Workers (UAW) Local 2110 also voted to set a strike deadline if necessary, making note that each museum has a major exhibition opening in early October. The strike vote follows that of the Guggenheim Museum union, which voted to authorize strike action this June after six months of stalled contract negotiations.

Ratified in 2023, inaugural three-year union contracts at the Whitney and the Brooklyn Museum expired this summer. The Brooklyn Museum contract was ratified the day before its union planned to strike, averting the action entirely after stalled negotiations since 2021. The AFAM union, which officially banded in 2024, has been in negotiation with the museum for an inaugural contract for the last two years.

item.title: Mildred Howard Enters History Through the Everyday - Hyperallergic
item.description:
OAKLAND, Calif. — Mildred Howard works in a magical time signature. Poetics of Memory, the legendary Bay Area artist’s first museum survey, open through October 18 at the Oakland Museum of California, traces a path through more than 50 years of her career, from early copy-machine collages to multimedia assemblages and large-scale gallery installations. Howard has long punctuated the Bay Area landscape through public art commissions, including a giant golden frame installed in San Francisco’s shipyard and blue glass etched with poetry on the city’s Fillmore Street Bridge. Her work plays out in the major key of American history, while sounding the blue notes of everyday experience that make up a human life, creating space to engage the dissonance and harmonies between past and present.

Entering the exhibition, visitors are greeted by large-scale bronze keys and a padlock, commemorating the Longshoremen's union leader Harry Bridges, who Howard has said opened doors to workers’ rights previously closed. A version of the sculpture was publicly installed in San Francisco in 2001. The understated piece sets the stage for the rest of the show, exemplifying Howard’s engagement with history through everyday objects, shifting scale, and lyrical interpretation.

Howard achieves a dreamy quality in her work, creating a niche outside of time where viewers can look at the world from outside its usual cacophony, a gap in the noise, an eye in the storm. “Magnolia Blossoms for John” (1979), one of the earliest works in the show, is a photocopy collage that combines flowers and hands, reminiscent of a still from Maya Deren’s dreamy 1943 short film “Meshes of the Afternoon.” In another, an untitled Xerox collage from 1979, a person’s face is shrouded by lace in surreal fashion, again prefiguring one of Howard’s career-long interests. Often, shrouds and veils appear in her work to communicate the layering of historical narratives by creating multiple temporal surfaces that coexist within a single frame.

The latest work in the show, “Moving Stills” (2026), is a large-scale installation featuring a triptych of film stills projected for 31 minutes, shot by Howard at 14, documenting her first trip to the South to meet her extended family. The film, recently rediscovered in one of her late mother’s handbags, is projected through layers of lace fabric, diffusing the already grainy and fragmented images into a dreamlike softness that evokes the feeling of a distant memory. The piece acts as a throughline in Howard's practice, linking an early film experiment to her recent exploration of personal narrative.

item.title: Painter William T. Williams Has Stayed Curious on the Canvas for Six Decades - ARTnews.com
item.description:
“There’s something to learn every time I go in the studio,” William T. Williams told me this past spring. “Anything that I did yesterday I have to forget, and I have to enter the studio and enter the paintings as if it’s the first time that I’ve had engagement.” He likes to keep the process “as open as possible,” but still, he is always “thinking about two or three steps ahead.” He keeps at it until he has followed “where the paintings are taking me, [then I] just go with that until I’ve exhausted it.”

We were standing in his sun-drenched studio behind his home in Connecticut, where sets of windows on three walls illuminate the interior for several hours each day. Williams and his wife, Pat, have split their time between here and New York for the past 15 years, and it’s a sharp contrast to the New York studio he’s had since 1968, which he intentionally kept free of natural light. “I boarded the windows up in the back, because I wanted to have a certain set light,” he said. “When we came up here, it was just the opposite. We decided to open the studio up, and that has influenced the paintings because of the angle of light and the geometry that the light brings in the afternoon.” The paintings, he said, have become more vertical. He might turn a canvas around and place it against a window to see the light pass through it. “That begins to inform me,” he said.

Works in progress stood on two walls, and one lay on the floor: bands and rectangles of cracked paint butting against each other in a sense of organized chaos. A decade and a half’s worth of paint drips cover the floor. An equally paint-stained table holds the various mixtures of Golden paint that he’s currently using. In one corner are shelves holding smaller variations of his abstractions, which he described as “the key to everything.” Some might be the details of a section he’s trying to work out; others are miniatures of a larger canvas. Depending on where he is in the process, in-progress canvases will likely feature sections covered in blue painter’s tape, or cut-up Post-its in different shades, which he uses “to indicate where something’s going to be, but not necessarily the color,” he said. His latest abstract paintings feature two-inch vertical bands made up of different rectangles of color, roughly the size of the Post-its he uses to mark them out.

After laying down a clear layer for the underpainting, Williams begins to build up thin layers on different sections of the canvas, adjusting the thickness for the application as he goes. “Each new layer brings another element that I have to orchestrate,” he said. He leaves gaps between layers to create their signature cracked appearance, which is his way of exposing “the building up of the layers.” Most of these paintings take at least six months, though some he’s worked on for years, making subtle adjustments, for example, to one color, “changing the blue ever so slightly, tonally, and coming back into it.”

Each layer of paint is slightly different, depending on which solution of paint he’s using. Some are thinned with different amounts of alcohol, which speeds up the drying; others are thinned with water, which reduces the sheen of the surface. Getting the consistency just how he wanted it took years of experimentation. “The drying time is important,” he noted. Instead of using a palette, Williams works from plastic cups that contain each of these mixtures, allowing him to easily go back and make touch-ups if need be, or to re-up a solution when he runs out.

At the core of the work is a dedication to formalism—and to breaking down its conventions. “I want art that doesn’t just sit on the wall,” he said. “I want it to be as irritable as possible. It’s finding a hidden way or system that does that.” He is interested in what abstraction can channel. “There’s a twist that happens in terms of: If I’m not going to paint protest paintings, if I’m not going to paint a narrative painting where there’s a story, how do I talk about those kinds of feelings that led me to want to do dissonance, or something that’s off-kilter?”

Color, he says, is “the most difficult element in painting. If you’re doing something representational, the color will do what you want it to do because you’re simulating something. If you’re in abstraction, it’s the most difficult element to control. To get it outside of a prescribed thing, to get there to be some poetry or some magic in it, requires something else. There has to be something that’s offbeat, something that’s off-key in it to make it work.”

With his recent canvases, he wanted to play with the idea of figure versus ground. Jonquil (2021) features a cracked yellow background with a single band of yellow going down it; a third of the way down the band is a single red square, which whether it was “sitting in front of the plane, or sliding in back of that plane, or being a hole in that plane, that’s what began to interest me,” Williams explained. Though these newer works might look drastically different from his “Diamond in a Box” series from the late 1960s, in which planes of various colors and geometric forms collide and overlap in a harmonious dissonance, Williams sees them as being in dialogue with each other, though the earlier pieces don’t have nearly as many layers of paint. As he began to multiply these squares in later canvases, he started to see a relationship with his paintings from years ago. “That’s very much part of the paintings from the late ’60s: things passing in back and in front. That was just isolating one of those gestures.”

“There is a constant sense where you see him asking and answering questions in the space of the work, and he has done that for decades,” Thelma Golden, the director and chief curator of the Studio Museum in Harlem, told me. “What we then have is the legacy of not only this incredible practice but also the legacy of this incredible person who has been so committed to creating art, creating space, creating meaning.”

WILLIAMS WAS BORN in Cross Creek, North Carolina, in 1942. The family moved to New York when he was 4 years old, settling in Queens. Until he was about 14, his parents would send him back to North Carolina every summer, almost as soon as school let out. Williams had a penchant for drawing as a kid, and early on, two people nurtured his interest in the arts. Tommy Hemans, who ran a community center in the housing project where Williams lived, gave him materials, and Mrs. Ross, who taught his junior high school art class, suggested to his parents that he would benefit from attending the School of Industrial Art (now the High School of Art and Design). There, he found himself surrounded by artists, both as professors and classmates, for the first time. “It was an immersion in the idea of what art is and what it can be—the power of what it can be. That early training was helpful,” he said. He first went to New York Community College, studying advertising production for two years. He got a job at Billboard Music Week, but estimates he lasted from May to July, when he saw an ad seeking applications to the Pratt Institute.

When Williams enrolled in Pratt in 1962, he started out in the graphic design department, but switched to painting in his sophomore year. His initial assignments, from academically trained painters who had students make figurative paintings, weren’t especially inspiring. His grades, he said, “were dismal, and I was really unhappy.” What marked a turning point was taking a class with painter Richard Bové. Without him, Williams said, “I would not be painting.” Bové told Williams to go see an exhibition of Hans Hofmann at the Kootz Gallery. “What struck me was the exuberance of paint and the physicality of paint, and just the sheer amount that Hofmann was using,” Williams said. “That sense that it’s a material that has a life of its own. For me, painting became about material.”

In 1965, during his junior year at Pratt, the faculty selected Williams to spend the summer studying at the Skowhegan School of Painting & Sculpture in Maine, where, as he recalls it, he was the only student working in abstraction. “I arrived there struggling with trying to get away from the Abstract Expressionists,” he said. In Alfred Leslie, a second-generation Ab-Exer who had recently started making realistic figurative paintings, however, he found an instructor with whom he could have freewheeling conversations about scale and technique.

At Skowhegan, Williams won the Leonard Bocour Award, whose namesake had founded Bocour Artist Colors, the legendary paint manufacturer. Upon his return to New York, he met Bocour and visited the factory on West 52nd Street; for the next 15 years or so, Bocour would be one of Williams’s main patrons. “He was the person who invested in me, in terms of believing in me as an artist.” Bocour, who himself was an artist, shared painterly knowledge, too. If Williams was struggling to get the paint to lay how he wanted it to, Bocour would visit Williams’s studio, or Williams would head to the factory to meet up with a technician. “I’d show him the problem, and he’d show me how to fix it,” he said. Though, in one instance, the advice from a fellow artist using a home remedy, adding Ivory Soap to the paint, allowed the paint “to sink into the canvas miraculously.”

His time at Pratt, Williams said, “gave me confidence that this thing called ‘art’ was important, and that it was something that I could do the rest of my life.” Coming from a blue-collar background, “there was a disconnect,” he said, between “the idea of art and making a living.” Bové and the other faculty, like Philip Pearlstein and Alex Katz, encouraged him to go to grad school at Yale, where, he recalled, painter Al Held “greeted me with his way of saying, ‘I like your work, and I like you, but you’re going to have to work.’”

After graduate school, Williams began his “Diamond in a Box” series, drawing on a shape he had known in childhood from the quilts of his grandmother and aunts and the design on the front of his mother’s phonograph. “It worked for me because it forces the eye to go to the top, then the two sides, then the bottom,” he said. “Any geometry had to play in relationship to that diamond.” Then he embarked on his “Shimmer Series,” inspired by how the light would flicker over the lake at Skowhegan, and how it would shimmer over Jamaica Bay during his early morning subway rides from Far Rockaway to Manhattan during high school. These canvases use just one color, Dioxazine Purple, which gives the impression of small waves rippling. By the late ’70s, he’d moved on to his “Roller” series (1978–82), using paint rollers and a wet-on-wet technique to apply some 15 layers of paint to the canvas. It was the most anti-art gesture he could think of; during the five or so years he worked in that way, he said, “the surfaces were getting more texture. I was getting marks out of them that I couldn’t make,” he said. By the early ’80s, he’d developed a palette that was “much richer and much wider,” which led to “overloading paintings with color. It’s just a lot of devilish things that interest me in terms of making a work of art. Painting is play to me—it’s work, but it’s play.”

That sense of play has made Williams something of an iconoclast. “He has existed outside of any one movement,” said Eric Booker, a curator who has worked with him, “and he hasn’t really been swayed by that. He’s stayed a very steady course that is true to him and what inspires him.” While his work is most certainly in dialogue with the history of 20th-century abstraction, Booker said, “there is always something in Bill’s paintings that remains entirely his own.”

FOR ALMOST AS LONG as he has been making art, Williams has been teaching it. Through an introduction from art historian Dore Ashton, he got a job at the School of Visual Arts in 1970, and was soon teaching at both SVA and Pratt; the following year, he moved to join the faculty of Brooklyn College via an invitation from Pearlstein, who was one of several Pratt professors now teaching at the public university. He shared an office with Pearlstein, Harry Holtzman, Allan D’Arcangelo, and Jimmy Ernst, all of whom he described as helping him navigate teaching by being able to talk with artists who “had lived a generation of art prior to me, as opposed to reading about it.” Williams stayed for nearly 40 years, retiring in 2008.

Among the artists he influenced at Brooklyn College was Nari Ward, who took Williams’s undergrad course New Materials, where students made a work from a New York telephone directory. “He was the right person at the right time,” Ward said, noting that when he began to move away from 2D art into sculpture, Williams suggested artists to look at—like David Hammons and Martin Puryear—then told him to “think about how they’re working, and how different is your engagement with this material.” Ward also took instruction from Williams’s own practice and his handling of paint. “I saw him negotiating both this sense of control over [the medium] and at the same time allowing a way to let go of that control to make the material teach him what needs to happen.”

Teaching wasn’t the only way in which Williams changed artists’ fates. In 1968, as he was finishing up his MFA at Yale, he wrote a proposal for an artist residency program. “It was the idea of, how do you go from being a student into making art your life’s work?” he explained. “One of the things that I saw missing was an infrastructure that was supportive of specifically minority artists. So many of them I met were self-taught. Others I met who had formal education always talked about what happens after school.” His proposal included a multipronged approach that would provide artists with a place to make their work (the residency component); supporters to buy their work (patrons) and to write about it (scholars and critics); and the venue to tie it all together (the museum). “Those are the components that come together in terms of an artist,” he said.

He shared the proposal with Ashton, who connected him with someone on the Junior Council (now the Contemporary Arts Council) of the Museum of Modern Art, who told him about a new institution Uptown that was being founded to support Black artists. Serendipitously, it was to be called the Studio Museum in Harlem, with the idea of it having a studio already baked in. He met with the founding trustees, who included Eleanor Holmes Norton and Betty Blayton-Taylor, and supporter Charles Cowles, and they were enthusiastic. Formally implemented in 1969 with Valerie Maynard as the first resident, the program still exists to this day; alumni include some of the most prominent artists in the world, like Kerry James Marshall, David Hammons, Simone Leigh, Lauren Halsey, Kehinde Wiley, Julie Mehretu, and Titus Kaphar, some of whom have gone on to establish similar programs elsewhere. “It lives at the center of the life of this institution,” said Studio Museum director Thelma Golden. Williams “connected the possibility of what it meant to create opportunity for artists, to mentor artists, to create a space for artists to fully engage with their creativity.”

Williams was also working outside the museum. Alongside artists Melvin Edwards, Guy Ciarcia, and Billy Rose, he started the Smokehouse Associates, which produced nine murals around Harlem between 1968 and 1970. (A fragment of only one of them still exists, though Williams’s archives contain photo documentation of the others.) The artists engaged community members—a block association, a church, elders—to help them figure out what was needed for the space and even to help paint. Eric Booker, who curated an exhibition on Smokehouse at the Studio Museum in 2017, said he sees the project as “decentralizing the arts, which lives at the heart of [Williams’s] ethos as an artist and as an educator.” Mona Hadler, an art historian who conducted an oral history with Williams, believes that the works proved “abstraction can uplift” and that an artwork “need not be figurative to have a message.”

A given mural’s design and coloration were responsive to the site and the surrounding environs of that particular section of Harlem. “The community’s reaction is evident in the documentation,” Booker said. “You see children and elderly people inhabiting and participating in these spaces. There’s always this sense of a joyful possibility in the way that they’re interacting with these spaces. That means of social empowerment was important to the collective’s mission. It was less about the works themselves and more about the process of making the works, and what that did for the surrounding community.”

Williams compared the relationship between a mural and its site to the very nature of painting, especially his most recent work with multiple layers of paint. “By its nature, you’re layering material. You can go at it in terms of layering the material so that it’s seamless, or you can layer the material where there’s a dialogue between what’s underneath and what’s on top.”

WILLIAMS WORKED IN AN UNOFFICIAL CAPACITY for the Studio Museum for about a year. During that time, he organized one exhibition, 1969’s “X to the Fourth Power,” a four-person group show featuring only abstract art—a challenge, as he saw it, to the institution and its audience. Williams showed a “Diamond in the Box” painting, alongside a 100-foot chain sculpture by Melvin Edwards, whom he had met through Al Held; a large-scale beveled painting by Sam Gilliam, whom he had cold-called; and an 8-by-16-foot painting by Steven Kelsey, a white artist who had been his classmate at Yale. The reaction to it, Williams told me, was “bewilderment.” As art historian Kellie Jones explained in a 2019 essay, abstract art “did not match up with what some thought of as representative of Harlem, particularly in the heady days of the Black Arts Movement.”

That wasn’t the only response, however. Williams recalled one line from the show’s review in The New York Times: “To a large extent, the exhibition succeeds in making its point that art is art whether the artist is black or white, whether the work is exhibited in Harlem or in a posh downtown establishment.” “It was just blatant racism in terms of the first premise being that [Black artists are] not capable of doing [abstraction], and I think that was implicit in a lot of things,” he said. “I think that exhibition ended that discussion.”

Pushing that discussion further in a 1971 essay in ARTnews called “It’s Not Enough to Say ‘Black Is Beautiful,’” the artist Frank Bowling wrote, “Much of the discussion surrounding painting and sculpture by blacks seems completely concerned with notions about Black Art, not with the works themselves or their delivery.” According to Williams, he and his friends Edwards, Gilliam, and Jack Whitten spent a lot of time discussing “what art could be instead of what it had been” and debating “the idea of what is an aesthetic,” a formal approach to abstraction that was unique to each artist. Because of the era’s “blatant racism,” particularly within art criticism, it wasn’t a conversation that much of the art world was ready to have.

In terms of his own paintings, Williams told me, “the early writing about the work made an assumption that the dissonance that was in the work was by default rather than by decision. The spatial cancellation in the paintings was by decision, not by default.” He deliberately gave his paintings titles that had “absolutely nothing” to do with their content, in order to “force the viewer to just look at the paintings and have a relationship with what they were looking at, rather than me giving them a prompt or a narrative.” Sister of Neckbone (1970), for instance, is an abstract painting with planes of color at oblique angles stacked on each other, broken up by lines and arcs. Valerie Cassel Oliver, curator of modern and contemporary art at the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts, included Sister of Neckbone in her 2021 exhibition “The Dirty South: Contemporary Art, Material Culture, and the Sonic Impulse,” in a section that was “a meditation on the Black body itself.” The work’s title, she said, refers to “how people within the Black community give honorifics to each other,” some of which might be based on their bodies. The titular “Sister of Neckbone” acknowledges this woman and her role in that specific community, or as Cassel Oliver put it, it “is another way of honoring Black bodies, which is a very Southern thing to do.”

“The titles are events that a group of people have experienced,” Williams explained. Rather than provide a narrative, his naming mechanism comes from “wanting someone who has had that experience to walk in, see that painting, and laugh, because that experience is so important…. They and the painting are having an experience. There’s no looking. It’s of the present. Looking is, ‘That thing is there, and I’m here, and I’m looking at it.’ Experiencing it is, ‘It and I are one in the same.’ … Looking excludes people; experiencing doesn’t exclude anyone.” In the New York art world of the late 1960s, he recalled, people would often say, “That’s a good reading of that painting,” which he felt implied that there is “a prescribed literature or a prerequisite to experiencing the painting. What I’m suggesting is there are no prescribed things for my paintings. All you have to do is stand in front of it and experience it. You don’t need a narrative. You don’t need a PhD. You don’t need previous art experiences. It’s just you and that object. That’s it.”

AHEAD OF THE “X TO THE FOURTH POWER” show, Williams and Edwards spent a day clearing out the space and getting it ready for the exhibition. “The human energy that was put into that show bonded Mel, Sam, and me together for 50 years,” Williams recalled. “What came through that is a bond in terms of this idea of making art and what it was about. Meeting two other artists who were as demanding and as committed as I was—it was divine.” Their friendship lasted until both his friends’ deaths, Gilliam in 2022 and Edwards this past March.

It’s difficult to overstate just how important these friendships were to Williams. “Every time I come into the studio and work, they’re present—they’re there saying, ‘You keep going,’” Williams said. “It’s knowing that there were two other human beings with the same kind of absolute commitment to what they were doing. The dialogue continues even after they’ve passed away.” He recalled visiting Edwards’s studio in New Jersey and Gilliam’s studio in Washington, D.C., over the years, and being amazed “at just the sheer body of ideas and sheer body of engagement,” he said. “There’s a whole history back there that people are not aware of [in terms of] the amount of interaction, the amount of discussion, and the amount of thinking.”

Toward the end of my visit, I noticed what at first seemed to me to be a sculpture. Behind one wooden column were dozens upon dozens of dried-out paintbrushes dipped in various colors. I asked Williams about it. He paused and took a deep breath. “It’s a memorial,” he told me. Each time a friend he’s known for a long time—artists, musicians, poets, and more—dies, he will take the “brush that I’m working [with] that day, stop, leave the paint on it, let it dry, and put it on the memorial.” Brushes for Gilliam and Whitten are among them, as well as one for Edwards, which joined the ranks in March. “It has gotten very full,” Williams added, “but it didn’t start out that way. [They’re] always there.”

item.title: Brooklyn Museum, American Folk Art Museum, and Whitney Museum Unions Vote in Favor of Strikes - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Unionized staff at three New York City cultural institutions—the Brooklyn Museum, the American Folk Art Museum, and the Whitney Museum of American Art—voted in favor of strike action if they do not receive satisfactory offers on their contracts, Local 2110 UAW announced today.

Local 2110 UAW, which represents workers at a broad network of museums and cultural institutions across the country, said its members voted overwhelmingly to authorize the union’s elected bargaining committee to call a strike. No strike deadline has been set, as contract negotiations remain ongoing.

“It’s not that we want to strike,” Derrick Charles, a membership associate at the Whitney and union chairperson, said in a statement. “We’d rather be working and doing our jobs but our wages are untenable for making ends meet in New York City.”

One of the museum’s most front-facing employees, Charles works in the lobby selling admission and answering visitors’ questions. He has held the position since 2018 and earns $24 an hour. The 2026 NYC True Cost of Living Measure Annual Report (TCOL) from the New York City government estimates that a single New Yorker without children must earn $34 an hour to meet the city’s current cost of living.

In a statement on behalf of the unionized staff, Local 2110 UAW said all three museums must raise their minimum pay rates, noting that average wages for their staff fall below the $71,000 annual salary that the TCOL report identifies as the minimum required for a single adult to afford to live in New York City.

Staff at the American Folk Art Museum (Afam) voted unanimously to unionize with UAW Local 2110 in June 2024. The union represents employees across various departments, including education, curatorial, visitor services, and IT. The museum has two locations: its galleries on the Upper West Side of Manhattan and a center in Queens.

A spokesperson for the Afam told ARTnews that its leadership is “committed to continuing to bargain in good faith toward a fair and mutually beneficial contract.”

Roughly 200 Whitney employees unionized in 2021, following two rounds of layoffs that reduced the workforce by 20 percent. They ratified their first collective bargaining agreement after 16 months of negotiations, securing layoff protections, minimum pay increases, and an average 15 percent retroactive wage increase, among other provisions. Negotiations for their second contract were marked by a union rally outside the museum’s annual gala on May 19, with members carrying signs that read, among other slogans, “We love fair contracts.”

In response to the strike vote, a spokesperson for the Whitney Museum told ARTnews that it “continues bargaining in good faith and remains committed to arriving at a fair, reasonable contract that respects the needs of all parties.”

Meanwhile, the months leading up to today’s announcement have been fraught for the Brooklyn Museum unions. Last year, museum leadership reversed plans to lay off more than a dozen workers following a $2.5 million grant from the New York City Council. Citing a widening deficit, the Brooklyn Museum had announced plans to cut more than 10 percent of its staff in February 2025, prompting backlash from the two unions representing museum workers, DC 37 Local 1502 and UAW Local 2110. The unions said the cuts had been announced without attempts to negotiate with their bargaining units.

Brooklyn union members rallied outside the museum for weeks, eventually prompting action from city leaders, including a special oversight hearing on February 28. There, Committee on Civil Service and Labor Chair Carmen De La Rosa said layoffs “should be the absolute last resort.”

Elizabeth St. George, an assistant curator at the Brooklyn Museum, said in a statement that she was concerned about health care and job security. “I’ve never expected to get rich as a curator, but I want to be able to rely on having a job with affordable health care and a reasonable salary so I can concentrate on doing the work I love.”

The Brooklyn Museum did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication.

item.title: Three Works of Sacred Art Stolen From Spanish Churches as Authorities Warn of Rise in Art Theft - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Three works of religious art were stolen from two churches in the Spanish city of Valladolid, the latest in a string of thefts from museums and churches across Spain and Europe.

Two works disappeared from the Church of San Pablo: a small Station of the Cross depicting Jesus falling for the second time, decorated with a silver relief, and a 17th-century copy of an Ecce Homo by Spanish Renaissance painter Luis de Morales. A nearby church, Vera Cruz, meanwhile lost a roughly two-foot-tall polychrome wooden carving of an angel carrying a torch, according to El País.

The thefts occurred only days apart, and authorities are investigating whether the same person was responsible. The prior of San Pablo suspects its two works were taken during an evening Mass on September 10, while parishioners were facing the altar. A sacristan told the local newspaper El Diario de Valladolid that several people saw a man leaving the church carrying a large plastic bag. Church officials initially discovered that the Ecce Homo was gone and reported the theft, only to realize later that the Station of the Cross had disappeared as well.

The Archbishopric of Valladolid has since asked churches throughout the archdiocese to exercise “extreme precautions and surveillance” and urged them to keep updated inventories, preferably with photographs, of their holdings. It has also encouraged churches and religious orders to report suspected thefts as quickly as possible.

The Valladolid thefts come amid a notable run of robberies targeting art and antiquities. This summer, 220 19th-century gold coins were stolen from the Provincial Museum of Albacete, while 149 coins belonging to the so-called Villanueva Treasure were taken from the Provincial Archaeological Museum of Badajoz in April. More recently, pieces from the Bronze Age Treasure of Villena were stolen from a museum in Alicante.

Then there are the ancient Celtic gold coins that were stolen from a museum in Germany, the $4.5 million jewelry heist from a French museum devoted to the Decorative arts, and, most famously, the Louvre heist, a smash and grab job worth more than $100 million in royal jewels.

Europol, unsurprisingly, has noticed the trend. Jean-Yves Goriou, head of the European Union’s organized crime unit, told El País that the agency had observed “a clear and pronounced increase in the number of museum robberies” reported by national authorities, with gold objects particularly attractive to thieves because of the metal’s high market price.

Churches are a particularly easy target. They can sit nearly empty for hours at a time, and during services, the people who are there tend, quite reasonably, to be looking at the altar rather than keeping watch over the art. In Valladolid, that may have been all the opening the thief needed.

item.title: The Legacy of Colonialism Haunts Hew Locke’s Era-Defying Flotilla - Colossal
item.description:
Although Hew Locke’s practice revolves around geographically bound objects—superimposed drawings of Guyanese homes and his suspended flotilla among them—the artist traces the reaches of empire that extend far beyond any singular era or point on a map. How people, capital, cargo, and ideas traverse the globe has long been central to Locke’s work, an investigation he continues in The Wanderers on view at P·P·O·W.

Returning to the artist’s Odyssey series, the solo presentation hangs a fleet of miniature ships from the gallery ceiling. The flotilla features a wide array of boats, from tankers and fishing vessels to the towering galleons of the 16th century, which Locke embellishes with tiny pennants strung between the masts, foliage springing from the sides, and coats of colorful paint that appear as vibrantly aged patina. Referencing the global history of trade and exploitation, the ships all journey together toward un undetermined future, the legacy of their pasts in tow.

Conquest and the desire for control and wealth also appear in Locke’s lavish busts, which adorn Parian ware (a porcelain that emerged in the mid-19th century as an economical dupe for marble) with a trove of glittering baubles. Titled as Souvenirs, these mixed-media sculptures depict figures like Queen Victoria and George Washington and revel in artifice and ostentatious displays of power that soar high in the air.

Several skeletons are embedded within the costuming, gesturing toward memento mori and implicating these powerhouses in the afterlives of their colonial projects. The figures appear haunted by death and, as Locke says, are “weighed down by the literal burden of history.”

The Wanderers is on view through October 24 in New York. Find more from Locke on Instagram.

item.title: “Excavation Record I – Sayonara” by Artist Kosuke Ajiro - BOOOOOOOM! – CREATE * INSPIRE * COMMUNITY * ART * DESIGN * MUSIC * FILM * PHOTO * PROJECTS
item.description:
Kosuke Ajiro

GR gallery is pleased to present Excavation Record I – Sayonara, the first solo exhibition in the United States by Japanese artist Kosuke Ajiro. The exhibition introduces Ajiro’s distinctive practice through the figure of the archeologist, who ventures into a whimsical and enigmatic imagined realm known as the “Kingdom of Sally.” Across the exhibition, each work reveals a fragment of this mysterious world, uncovering earthbound creatures and curious details before opening onto a vast, fantastical expanse. Moving between the familiar and the otherworldly, Ajiro’s works invite the viewer on a journey of mystery, magic, transformation, and discovery. As the story gradually reveals itself, viewers are invited to witness the rise and fall of the ‘Kingdom of Sally’ and participate in piecing together the discovered fragments that will one day rest in a temple dedicated to the art of storytelling. In Excavation Record I – Sayonara, Ajiro presents a body of mythology originating from the kingdom known as the “Sally Mythology.” The seventh chapter of this mythos, Sayonara, is believed to recount the end of the world, depicting a cataclysmic event comparable to Ragnarök in Norse mythology. Adopting the persona of an excavator, Ajiro positions himself not as the creator of these artworks, but as an archeologist and historian uncovering, reconditioning and presenting traces of a lost civilization. The exhibition unveils thirty artifacts as revealed historical fragments of an ancient mural excavated near Tokyo Skytree, depicting the events of Sayonara which Ajiro then restored onto canvas. By placing himself within the mythology and inviting viewers to assume the role of fellow discoverers, Ajiro creates an immersive narrative where the pieces act as records of the kingdom, tracing it from ancient times to its demise during the medieval period.

on display until October 24.
