item.title: Joan Mitchell Foundation Publishes Extensive Report on Artist Legacy Stewardship - ARTnews.com
item.description:
What does it take to preserve an artist’s legacy? “You can only learn how to do this by doing it,” Solana Chehtman, director of artist programs at the Joan Mitchell Foundation, offered in response to a question that animates an ambitious new report titled Creating Future Memory: Building the Field of Artist Legacy Stewardship, published by the Mitchell Foundation. “There are so many ways in which people can have a hand in this work, and we want to a raise awareness and give visibility to efforts happening around the country.”

Related Articles

The ARTnews Accord: Solana Chehtman and Chris Sharp on Why Artists Should Take Estate Planning Seriously

Joan Mitchell Foundation Announces 2024 Fellowship Recipients

The 80-page report, now available for free download at the foundation’s website, is an extension of the enterprise’s long-running Creating a Living Legacy (CALL) initiative and a 2025 convening that brought together 145 figures working on matters related to preservation and longevity for artists and their work. Among the attendees at the gathering in New York were archivists, conservators, grantmakers, estate executors, leaders of artist-endowed foundations, and, of course, artists themselves.

“What we heard from participants at the convening was both inspiring and sobering: across the country, individuals, collectives, and organizations are doing extraordinary work to preserve artistic legacies—yet these efforts remain largely disconnected from one another and chronically under-resourced,” Chehtman said in a press release announcing the report. In an interview at the foundation’s office in Chelsea last week, she added, “At the convening you could see people identifying each other and learning that they were not alone in doing this work.”

The Creating Future Memory report focuses on three main subject areas—“Access to Knowledge,” “Funding and Resources,” and “Coordination and Collaboration”—and offers directives gleaned from the CALL initiative, which began in 2007 as a way to serve Mitchell’s stated desire for the foundation to “aid and assist” artists upon her death in 1992.

“What’s our obligation to keep an artist’s work out of the dumpster?” asked Christa Blatchford, the foundation’s executive director. “We realized, as an entity that stewards a legacy, we have a unique vantage and opportunity to talk about that.”

One passage in the Creating Future Memory report cites Mikiko Ino, who has worked to preserve her late husband Kikuo Saito’s legacy, recalling, “Kikuo always said there are two deaths: the first is physical, and the second is when nobody talks about you.” After his passing, she said, “I decided to never give him the second death.”

A resounding pull-quote from Amalia Mesa-Bains, an artist and curator who attended the convening, reads: “They’re running with a big eraser right behind us. Remembering is a defiant act.”

About the pressing needs and disquieting realities of legacy cultivation for artists, the report claims, “Too often, these efforts are approached as a series of isolated tasks, rather than as part of a coordinated, sustained process. In reality, legacy stewardship operates as a complex web of mostly invisible and often under-resourced tasks, in which each actor—artists, estate leaders, archivists, conservators, lawyers, and other supporters and arts workers—contributes complementary labor and knowledge.”

In the foundation’s office, Chehtman said, “Our mission is to aid and support artists, but it cannot be just on the shoulders of artists, because legacy is by nature communal.” She also stressed a sense of urgency undergirding work of the kind: “Given everything that is happening in the country and in the world, there are lot of communities and a lot of artists who are at risk.”

Alongside the Creating Future Memory report, the Joan Mitchell Foundation has launched a new “Legacy Field Map” to help build a crowd-sourced network of organizations working toward similar ends. The foundation is soliciting submissions and will vet candidates to be added to a resource that will expand over time. “Many of these people don’t know each other,” Chehtman said of workers in the field, “and they don’t know of each other either.”

At the core of the report and the map is an integral question, according to Chehtman: “How can we see this field not only as artists and their family members and foundation leaders but also everyone in the art field who can have an impact?”

item.title: Federal Judge Again Rules Trump Cannot Add Name to Kennedy Center - ARTnews.com
item.description:
A federal judge on Tuesday ruled that the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts could not inscribe “renovated and restored by President Donald J. Trump” on the venue’s facade, dealing another setback to the Trump-appointed Kennedy Center’s months-long campaign to memorialize the president somewhere on the institution’s premises.

US District Judge Christopher R. Cooper, who has presided over several legal challenges brought by Trump over the issue, wrote that any such change to the Kennedy Center would violate his earlier ruling, which held that his name was illegally inscribed on the building last December.

“Simply put, defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress’s blessing,” Cooper wrote in his recent decision. “The board resolution bucks a federal court order and a statute Congress enacted.”

The Kennedy Center board voted in August to change the venue’s name to “The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump,” in recognition of what the board characterized as the president’s philanthropic contributions. The board has also proposed naming the center’s plaza after Trump and, if the newly established Trump Kennedy Center Fund reaches $100 million, adding a separate inscription that would read, “Endowed by the Trump Kennedy Center Fund.”

Hours before Judge Cooper released his ruling, Trump turned to social media to describe the Kennedy Center as in a “virtual state of collapse,” denounce the judge as “very hostile and conflicted,” and predict that the venue was “destined to doom” unless it was allowed to close for renovations, as the board had previously sought to do.

Cooper has rebuffed successive attempts by the Trump administration to intervene at the center. In May 2026, he ruled that only Congress had the authority to rename the center, dedicated as a living memorial to President John F. Kennedy, or close it for two years of renovations, as the board sought to do that February.

In his Tuesday ruling, Cooper called the board’s August decision “linguistic gymnastics” and declined to rule on whether the proposed “Endowed by The Trump Kennedy Center Fund” inscription was legal, since the board said it depended on reaching a fundraising goal. But he suggested he would likely reject the addition if the goal were reached, saying it would violate his prior order “just as plainly” as the initial name change.

The Justice Department has argued that the president’s name should be added to the building to honor his “ongoing” contributions to its upkeep, including $258 million in congressional funding for capital restoration in 2025. Trump’s lawyers said his “efforts and prestige” offer the “sole hope for the Center’s financial survival and structural renewal,” arguing that without his involvement, the Kennedy Center will “continue to be in a financial and structural death spiral.”

The president’s opponents in the Capitol disagree. “The law is extremely clear: The John F. Kennedy Center is named for President Kennedy — and no one else,” lawyers for U.S. Rep. Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat and ex officio member of the Kennedy Center board, said in a statement to press Tuesday. “But President Trump is holding the Kennedy Center hostage unless he can put his name on this sacred memorial. The Court just rejected this proposal for the second time. This unlawfulness is as breathtaking as it is wrong, and it needs to stop.”

item.title: How Monumental Environmental Works by Meg Webster Cultivate Reconnection - Colossal
item.description:
In Derrick Jensen’s 1995 book Listening to the Land, Chickasaw poet and environmentalist Linda Hogan said, “There is a way that nature speaks, that land speaks. Most of the time we are simply not patient enough, quiet enough, to pay attention to the story.” Decades on, we continue to grapple with an increasing detachment from nature as unfettered urban development continues, the current administration rolls back environmental protections for emissions and public lands, and escalating reliance on A.I. in work and daily life has led to a massive surge in data center construction.

Our collective clamoring for so-called progress and our obsession with creature comforts and endless technological advancements mean we’re removing ourselves both physically and psychologically from a world humans were once much more in tune with. For artist Meg Webster, this fraying relationship to our environment has long informed an interdisciplinary practice that advocates for nature.

Through immersive environmental installations and large-scale sculptures made from organic materials, Webster interrogates the delicate yet resilient balancing act sustained by the earth’s ecosystems, which are being continually degraded. In direct opposition to the extractive processes society relies on for fossil fuels and other natural resources, the artist invites us to commune with them instead: elements such as soil, salt, sand, and more can be experienced by walking around and into unexpectedly precise geometric forms.

For Sculpture Milwaukee, an aluminum and glass spiral fitted with an irrigation system nourishes an intimate garden. At Paula Cooper Gallery earlier this year, a monumental installation made from plant cuttings loosely unfurled in a coiled, almost fox-like form. And a long-term installation at Dia Beacon filled the organization’s post-industrial space with monumental sculptures made of salt, earth, beeswax, and dried brush.

The works most recently at Dia, which included installations like “Cono di Sale (Salt Cone)” (1988) and “Wall of Wax “(1990), draw on the post-minimalist tradition of using easily accessible materials, but unlike the movement’s predecessor, not obscuring the way it was constructed. Webster’s pieces are simultaneously meticulous and organic; she creates precise domes, cones, and concave slabs that are fragile, even precarious, yet they also possess an inherent strength.

Webster’s works incorporate ancient shapes, such as spirals, which manifest often in her installations. Ubiquitous and universal, these forms were carved into stone thousands of years ago at places like the Newgrange passage tomb in Ireland and on carefully selected slabs of sandstone in the American Southwest, where Ancestral Puebloans observed the solstices. Webster’s “Soft Broch,” which she first created in 1984, is a tribute to the unique drystone towers found in Scotland, which may have been fortified, high-status homes and the nucleus of local Iron Age communities.

Works like “Glen” (1967) and “Concave Room for Bees” (2016), the latter of which was installed at Socrates Sculpture Park along the East River in Queens, are rooted in the Land Art movement of the mid-20th century. Both installations evoke ancient Roman amphitheaters, except in Webster’s imagining, these open-air spaces are attended by pollinators, and flowers are the entertainment. It’s not just a visually striking garden; we’re also reminded how essential insects are to plants’ survival and vice versa, and how both continue to dramatically decline due to habitat loss, pesticides, and other human-triggered factors.

Webster’s oeuvre is also characterized by a beautiful sense of openness, both literally and conceptually. The work is never didactic; it is meant to be experienced and interpreted uniquely by the viewer. One can walk inside of many of her works, and in the case of “Glass Spiral” in Milwaukee, peer out from wherever you are to see different vantage points of the piece. In “Thicket,” visitors enter what feels like the beginning of a maze. And “Soft Broch” envelops you within its textural, organic walls.

In “outdoor installations designed to enhance the community’s appreciation for and understanding of the earth’s ecosystem,” Paula Cooper Gallery says, Webster venerates the natural world, giving us the opportunity to immersively do the same and, hopefully, to continue to do so outside of the gallery walls.

Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a Colossal Member today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article How Monumental Environmental Works by Meg Webster Cultivate Reconnection appeared first on Colossal.

item.title: The Many Islands of “America” - Hyperallergic
item.description:
WATERVILLE, Maine — At the entrance of the conceptually ambitious exhibition Imagining an Archipelago: Art from Cuba, Guam, the Philippines, Puerto Rico, and Their Diasporas at the Colby College Museum of Art are four works that embody many of its themes. A painting by Cuban-born Zilia Sánchez is composed of white marks that hover between fully abstract, figurative, and cosmological, traced on a gray-black ground, as if we are looking down at a body or up from a boat to the sky — either way, trying to find our bearings. Félix González-Torres’s “Untitled (USA Today)” (1990) lays out candies in wrappers of red, white, and blue for viewers to consume over time, incorporating the colors of the American flag (along with the patriotism it implies) into our very bodies. The letters of a 2023 concrete poem by the CHamoru scholar and poet Craig Santos Perez spell out “Archipelagoes resemble constellations,” spaced out like an archipelago or constellation — or both — on the wall. A series of photographs by Juana Valdés, “On the Malecón” (2000), documents a performance in Havana, done in the wake of a mass migration of Cubans to the United States to escape economic privation, in which she set afloat paper boats fashioned from the torn-out pages of a 19th-century novel exploring the country’s racial and social hierarchies. 

The sea, the stars, “America” as a thing to be consumed, the archipelago, waves of colonization, enslavement, migration, and diaspora that complicate any sense of identity: All of these ideas run through artworks by more than 40 contemporary artists and collectives. Though geographically disconnected, their islands of origin share a common history, playing key, if hardly willing, roles in the US’s transformation into a colonial power: All were brought under US control at the end of the War of 1898 (also known as the Spanish-American War), handed over by Spain as part of the Treaty of Paris. 

Despite the historical conceit at the heart of the show, its curator, Jessamine Batario, takes pains to ensure that these places, and the art that emerges from them, are not reduced to an unnuanced sameness. The exhibition, on the contrary, is an attempt at archipelagic thinking. Introduced by Édouard Glissant and expanded upon by many others since, archipelagic thinking asks us to consider the specific forms of relation and solidarity made possible by seeing the world from the perspective of archipelagoes, islands that retain their distinctiveness even while existing as a collective. 

The exhibition is divided into two floors, one organized by region, the other by theme. Among the artists in the section on the Philippines, migrant labor plays a major role — not surprising, as wealth sent back to the country by Overseas Filipino Workers (an official designation) accounts for nearly 9% of the country’s GDP. In “Export Quality (Value Studies: Uniforms)” (2023), Thea Canlas fashions work uniforms for a factory laborer and a maid out of delicate piña cloth, a material usually reserved for finery worn on special occasions. Jerome Reyes’s newly commissioned projection of text fragments — “Those who care for everyone/ The Anointed salvaged/ That save all except themselves/ Who tends to you” — coalesces into a poem that speaks to the role Filipino health care workers played, and the price they paid, during the COVID-19 crisis. “Where My Uncles Went,” a 1996 sculpture by Carlos Villa, draws upon the history of an earlier wave of migrant workers to the US in the 1920s and 30s. These so-called manongs (uncles) are represented here by a floating fedora mounted onto a wooden shadow box frame, surrounded by a spare geometric arrangement of lines suggesting a revolving door. This uncle is the Invisible Man, a subtle indictment of how those who benefit from labor fail to perceive it.

Two works that are themselves archipelagos — Teresita Fernández’s “Archipelago (Garland)” (2020), fashioned out of fragments of charcoal, and Sara Jimenez’s “the seas breathing us in and out” (2026), a ceramic and textile installation newly commissioned for the show — imagine the ocean as a means of connection. Fernández’s is an alternative geography, a “map” composed from the fused coastal contours of the islands of the Caribbean, while Jimenez’s, in its configuration of fragmented body parts, faces, flora, and fauna, alludes to the maritime route that connected the Philippines and Mexico. 

A video work by Beatriz Santiago Muñoz (“Ojos para mis enemigos,” 2014) follows a man who walks through a decommissioned, crumbling US Navy base in Puerto Rico; two panels of found photographs by Sherwin Rivera Tibayan offer a view into the world of Filipinos serving in the US Navy (“Untitled Collage Frame #1 and #2,” 2025); and a photo of a doctored Cracker Jack box by Miguel Luciano (“Cracker Juan,” 1998) turns an acerbic eye on the way the US military exploits Puerto Ricans: “Highest Combat Fatalities in US!” “Citizenship Prize Inside.” Together, these and other works offer up a complicated view of these islands and their people’s relation to US militarism. 

In a section on food, Maia Cruz Palileo’s gorgeous little paintings of domestic scenes (“Still Life with Banana Catsup” and “The Old Table,” both 2014) hang alongside Edra Soto’s deadpan video “Happy Hour, La Hora Feliz” (2020), a close-up view of the artist preparing party snacks from an array of American processed food — food that came to replace Puerto Rico’s island-grown crops, as the soundtrack explains. Elsewhere, Daniel Lind-Ramos’s “Vencedor: 1797” (2018–19), an assemblage of found objects that commemorates the Black Puerto Ricans who sided with Spain to fend off a British invasion, and Reynier Leyva Novo’s exacting resin casts of the guns, machetes, and a bullet used by the leaders of Cuba’s 19th-century wars of independence (“The Desire to Die for Others,” 2012), speak to fraught notions of sovereignty. 

Batario, during a walkthrough, said that she had intended for the show to be fully thematic, but a number of the artists demurred, pointing out that viewers probably couldn’t identify the places in question on a map, let alone have an idea of their cultures and histories. The comment has stuck with me, not least because I had to consult an atlas to confirm where every place stood in relation to the others, but also because it underlines just how necessary this show is now, as we contend with a new phase of American expansionist ambitions.

Imagining an Archipelago: Art from Cuba, Guam, the Philippines, Puerto Rico, and Their Diasporas continues at the Colby College Museum of Art (5600 Mayflower Hill Drive, Waterville) through June 6, 2027. The exhibition was curated by Jessamine Batario.

item.title: The Black Schoolhouse in New Orleans Looks to Offer a New Model of Arts Education and Community Building - ARTnews.com
item.description:
In New Orleans’s historic Seventh Ward, a series of repurposed shipping containers will soon host what its founders hope will be a new model of arts education and community building.

Artists Joseph Cuillier and Shani Peters founded the Black School a decade ago, slowly setting up the groundwork for a physical space. Now, after more than five years of fundraising and community outreach, they will open the Black Schoolhouse next month as the physical manifestation of the Black School.

Located at 1660 N. Roman Street, the Black Schoolhouse has been built from the ground up in refurbished, copper-painted shipping containers. It will host exhibitions and afterschool programs for art making, as well as provide the community with a garden, kitchen, library, and space for art making. In 2022, they received a two-year grant of $1.95 million from the Mellon Foundation.

“I see it as a bridging of worlds,” Cuillier told ARTnews in a recent video interview. “I see us as a place to share serious contemporary art, a place to educate the next generation of artists, and a place to teach cultural practices.”

“We have a need for these third spaces that bring community together that allow us to talk [instead of] being isolated on the internet,” Peters added. “Life is just getting more and more split apart. We see the rupture in society as a whole, so we that we need these spaces. We know we need art and creativity. We’re trying to put it together in one, and hopefully influence and inspire many more people to do the same.”

Origins

The Black School initially came together as an art project in 2016, “a moment in time where I think a lot of Black folks and folks who are conscious about the world were trying to figure out what their role was—I’m speaking specifically about the Black Lives Matter movement,” Cuillier said. “There was a lot of political upheaval, and I think a lot of people were committing to racial justice as an organizing focus.”

The duo had met two years earlier, in 2014, through mutual friend groups of artists and creatives in New York, where they had both moved for graduate school. “As we got to know each other, we realized we both had very similar ideas of wanting to create a formal art education program rooted in Black history,” Peters said.

Both Cuillier and Peters, who are also life partners, come from families of educators, and both chose to be artists. “It was a matter of looking back at those histories and those family legacies and fusing it with our pursuit as artists that the Black School emerged,” Cuillier said. Peters added, “We both see ourselves as continuing these family legacies, not having to start over every generation of Black movement work.”

The venture centered, according to Cuillier, around the question of “how can we pair this new commitment to racial justice with the kind of social practice art making that we were interested in practicing?”

Initially, the Black School hosted artmaking workshops, like screen printing or collage, in high schools and middle schools in New York that was “rooted in the young folks’ social reality,” Cuillier said. “We would ask them what they love about their community, and what they want to change about their community. That would be the basis of the content of the work.”

They soon expanded Black School’s reach to host one-off workshops in Newark, Houston, New Orleans, and Michigan, where Peters grew up. As the program developed, they added additional components like Black Love Fest, an annual art festival, and the Design Studio, a graphic design firm with an apprenticeship program.

Setting Up in New Orleans

When the pandemic hit, they had to pause their programming. “It also was an opportunity for us to launch a project that we had been working on quietly,” Cuillier said. Around this time, they started thinking about the long-term plans for the Black School and soon set up a crowdfunding campaign, which raised $300,000 in six months.

They settled on New Orleans, where Cuillier is originally from, because they knew that New York would likely be too expensive and prohibit them from realizing the Black Schoolhouse and raising their growing family. “We started one lifetime project. Why not make it two?” Peters joked. They relocated to the Crescent City in 2021.

Prior to the pandemic, the couple had also deepened their connection with the city’s art scene in 2019 by collaborating with the art department at Xavier University. That year, Peters participated in the Joan Mitchell Foundation’s residency program in New Orleans.

After moving there full-time, they began looking for land in the Seventh Ward, where members of Cuillier’s family have lived for over a century. He characterized the neighborhood as a site of “contemporary and historical place for Black self-determination.” They decided to buy a plot of land, instead of an existing structure, because “we knew we wanted to build something,” he said, with the selected plot being large enough to accommodate a garden.

Just before closing, Hurricane Ida hit. The couple immediately got to work, organizing a trash pickup for the neighborhood when city services had been suspended for weeks. The following month, the sale closed and they hosted an intention-setting event that included a storytelling circle and a cookout.

“That’s where we kicked off sharing the idea for a building, researching how exactly to do it, and making sure that we were factoring in the input of our neighbors,” Peters said, noting that they had decided not to create any renderings without that initial feedback. They spent the next year going door to door to meet the neighbors and present them with the idea.

They next hosted two community workshops with paper models of the shipping-container designs, one at the New Orleans African American Museum in the nearby Tremé neighborhood and the other outside the Dollar General three blocks from their plot of land. “We wanted to make sure we were getting everybody’s input: those that care to go to an art museum, and those that might say, ‘What the hell is the art museum or art center?’ We wanted to be engaged with the entire community,” Peters said.

Once they met with their architectural teams, they went back to their door-to-door approach over the next six months and hosted the first Black Love Fest in New Orleans to get further community input on the initial drawings. “For the most part, people almost unanimously embraced it,” Cuillier recalled. “The main response was ‘Yes, do it. How soon can you do it?’”

That focus on being completely invested in community buy-in came from their approach as artists. Often, Peters said, social practice art is defined as “an outsider dropping in” and “fixing things for people.” Peters said her project would do this, but she also noted that she was “already connected with these people. That gives a different type of sense and understanding.”

The Black Schoolhouse founders also see their project as a counter to the Seventh Ward’s ongoing gentrification, whose pace only got faster after Hurricane Katrina in 2005. “That’s why the land was even accessible and affordable to us. It’s a neighborhood that’s definitely still feeling the loss and the tragedy of Hurricane Katrina,” Peters said.

A Schoolhouse in a Shipping Container

The design of the Black Schoolhouse is also a singular addition to this part of New Orleans.

“We knew we wanted to explore new architecture technology, especially something that’s climate resilient, being in New Orleans,” Cuillier said of the decision to use shipping containers.

To realize the Black Schoolhouse, they worked with New Orleans–based Whawn Allen as the project’s architect of record and Lo-Tek as the shipping-container design specialists, and brought on the apprentices in the Design Studio to assist. An architectural tour with Malik Bartholomew, a seventh-generation New Orleanian and local historian who founded Know NOLA Tours, helped round out the design process.

In addition to being low-cost, shipping containers are extremely durable and won’t absorb water in the way that wood does; the strength of the material also allowed them to design a cantilever roof. There are also countless containers that have been decommissioned and take up space in landfills, presenting “an opportunity for upcycling,” said Cuillier, who noted that they have a “similar geometry” to shotgun houses, which are ubiquitous in this part of the city. Solar panels, donated by local nonprofit Footprint Projects, and a system to capture rainwater also round out the Black Schoolhouse’s commitment to sustainability in design.

The gesture is about “taking inspiration from the traditional architecture of New Orleans but also presenting something that was very Afrofuturist and forward-facing in nature,” Cuillier said. “I see us as practical Afrofuturists.”

They were also influenced by the Rosenwald School project, a partnership between Sears Roebuck president Julius Rosenwald and Booker T. Washington, the founding president of the Tuskegee Institute. Together, they built nearly 5,000 schools, primarily for the education of African American children in the South between 1913 and 1932. Built to a uniform design, the realization of each school also required buy-in from the community, which was required to raise half the funds for their construction, with the other half coming from the Rosenwald Fund.

“That’s how we educated ourselves in these simple structures that we built for ourselves, by ourselves,” Peters said. “We got the motivation to do it [because] if they could do nearly 5,000, we can do one.”

“I left my visit to The Black Schoolhouse both impressed and inspired by what is being built right here in the Seventh Ward,” Louisiana State Senator Royce Duplessis told ARTnews in a statement. “At a moment when there is a national effort to retreat from diversity and equity—and from institutions that proudly embrace Black history and identity—The Black School is leaning in. They are creating a space rooted in Black history, creativity, education, and community that honors the past while investing boldly in the next generation. I am proud that this extraordinary project will call our community home.”

Cuillier and Peters thought of painting the exterior different colors, as an homage to Caribbean architecture, but the gesture felt forced. Black would also have been ideal, they said, but that, too, was a nonstarter, given how hot New Orleans can get. They settled on copper, finding resonance in its ability to recall certain skin tones. The paint has a ceramic additive that also blocks heat.

Among the community requests that are reflected in the final design are a combination of indoor and outdoor spaces, with the deck being able to double the interior gallery’s square footage; balconies that will give different views of the city; and a community kitchen and garden that will include fruit trees as well as jasmine, a traditional scent common in New Orleans.

“New Orleans is a singular culture across the board, from language and food to dance and music,” Peters said. “People have unique memories of food that they’ve eaten that is being lost with gentrification. The garden helps us to bring back some of that ancestral memory.”

The Opening and Beyond

When the Black Schoolhouse opens on October 10, it will serve as an open-door community center, where people can drop by during the week and enjoy the facilities, including a gallery, a library, a computer lab, a meditation space, and a garden.

“The Black Schoolhouse holds tremendous potential to provide intergenerational art training and resources to the historic Seventh Ward and the City of New Orleans,” New Orleans city council member Eugene J. Green, whose district includes much of the Seventh Ward, told ARTnews in a statement. “As a member of the City Council, I am often called on to connect residents with local programs and resources that expand their horizons and create new opportunities. The Black Schoolhouse will be a valuable addition to our community, strengthening both the people it serves and the institutions that support them.”

Its inaugural exhibition will take the title “The Making of The Black School” and trace the first decade of its history. Curated by Ryan N. Dennis, co-director and chief curator of the Contemporary Arts Museum Houston, the show will bring together various archival materials to help narrate “the organization’s process of imagining, building, and sustaining a Black-centered educational ecosystem,” according to an exhibition description. The show will also include archival materials on the Rosenwald Schools, the Freedom Schools, and the Black Panther Liberation Schools, placing it “within a broader continuum of Black educational innovation.”

The core programming will begin in the afternoon as an after-school program for local children. On the weekends, the programming will focus on serving all ages, with the annual Black Love Fest becoming weekly Black Love Saturdays. Periodically, the weekend programming will also feature workshops on the People’s Movement Assembly, “a tried-and-true movement practice for community co-governance,” Peters said. “We’re marrying these worlds of art and politics through that system. Now that we have the building to gather people in, we’ll use that system to formally gather folks around community power building, but always with culture and art as part of the process.”

“The art is the tool by which we plan on building these alternative systems of governance,” Cuillier added. “I think artists have always created new models, and we’re curious about how those models could live just in a poor, working-class Black community in New Orleans—outside of the art world. How can we use our creative problem solving to address some of the major issues that are facing our community?”

Other long-term goals include adding an after-school program that will serve as a pipeline for its design apprenticeship, now in its eighth cohort, as well as a residency program for artists to come spend time in New Orleans without the expectation of having to make an exhibition. They also want to develop a model curriculum for their after-school programming that can be shared with other communities.

In thinking of the future of the Black Schoolhouse, Cuillier pointed to the example of Jerome “Big Duck” Smith, who founded the nonprofit Tamborine & Fan in 1968 to serve the Sixth and Seventh Wards of New Orleans. “What he did was pass on the cultural and creative traditions of the community, but also pair that with activism,” Cuillier said. “We see the Black School as a continuation of that—a passing of the baton, using art and culture.”

He continued, “I see us as like a leadership engine, creating pathways for creatives to step into more community leadership roles in New Orleans. … We know Black art and culture has affected the whole world many times over, so we’re looking at how we can harness that to create the changes we hope to see in the community. We’re hoping the legacy of the Black School will be as a change-maker—for the better.”

item.title: Stolen 16th-century Flemish Panel Given to Spain’s Fine Arts Museum of La Coruña, Brazilian Artist Marlies Ritter Has Died, and More: Morning Links for September 15, 2026 - ARTnews.com
item.description:
To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter.

Good Morning!

  • Spain’s Fine Arts Museum of La Coruña has received a recovered, stolen 16th-century Flemish panel painting of a biblical scene from the government.
  • Brazilian artist Marlies Ritter has died at 84.
  • Ching-Ling Wang will become the first Nancy Chang Lee Curator of Chinese Art at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Asian Art.

The Headlines

RETURN TO SENDER. Spain’s Fine Arts Museum of La Coruña has received a recovered, stolen 16th-century Flemish panel painting of a biblical scene from the government, according to Finistre sull’Arte. The painting by an anonymous “master,” likely from Antwerp, featuring Mary and a baby Jesus, greeted by Saint Anne and Saint Joseph, seen tipping his hat, was found over the course of an international sting operation that involved Spain’s Guardia Civil, the Ministry of Culture, and Italy’s Carabinieri. Along with the panel, investigators seized 60 other smuggled cultural objects considered Spanish national heritage and property, including works by Amedeo Modigliani and Pieter Brueghel. The objects had been illegally exported to Italy from a villa in Marbella, Spain, and sold to galleries and private collections across Italy and elsewhere. The other recovered artworks are being distributed to several national Spanish museums.

IN MEMORIAM. Brazilian artist Marlies Ritter has died, reports ArtReview. Born Maria Luise Ritter, she was 84 years old when she passed away on September 11, according to a statement on Instagram by the Fundação Vera Chaves Barcellos in Brazil (FVCB). Ritter was known for her ceramics, use of repetition, and doll heads attached to unlikely bodies, creating an unsettling effect. As demonstrated by her 2025 retrospective at FVCB, “Thinking with Your Hands,” she also wrote and worked with fabric, woodcuts, paper, and photography. “A reference in ceramics and an artist of multiple languages, Marlies produced countless works in which affection, daily life, and memory are immortalized in every detail, in gesture, in repetition, and in moments of dilated time,” FVCB added. “Her poetics represents a true communion between her being and her work, enabling different reflections and new perspectives.”

The Digest

Ching-Ling Wang will become the first Nancy Chang Lee Curator of Chinese Art at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Asian Art (NMAA) and will leave his current post as curator at the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam. [ArtAsiaPacific]

New York’s School of Visual Arts (SVA) is ending its photography, video, and related media MFA program by the end of 2027–28 academic year. [Artforum]

A British family had no idea their garden ornament in the home for decades was in fact a valuable marble sculpture by Harriet Goodhue Hosmer, the 19th-century American feminist, considered the country’s first female professional sculptor. [BBC]

The Pope has inaugurated a new artwork by JR on the Vatican façade, ahead of the September 25 opening of the exhibition AQVUA, about water as a source of both life and destruction. [Le Figaro]

The Louvre is looking to Asia for sponsors of its over €1 billion ($1.2 billion) architectural renovation project, which is still €360 million ($415 million) short of its targeted budget. [South China Morning Post]

Pro-Palestinian activists protested at the British Museum’s Bayeux Tapestry exhibition opening weekend. [ARTnews]

The Kicker

GIFT THAT KEEPS GIVING. There’s nothing like a “pleasant surprise” gift, as Switzerland’s Musée des beaux-arts de La Chaux-de-Fonds recently described it. The institution would know. When they began going through the inventory for a donation from Swiss collector Philippe Bodenmann, they expected to find 150 artworks. Instead, they found 218, reports The Art Newspaper. The entire collection, including several works by Joseph Kosuth, Lawrence Weiner, Royden Rabinowitch, Olivier Mosset, Marcia Hafif, and Günther Förg, among others, is now on view in the museum until January 3, 2027. “When we first announced the donation project … not all of the portfolios had yet been opened, and the inventory was not fully completed,” explained David Lemaire, the museum’s director. He said two donated works fill key gaps in the institution’s collection: Kosuth’s “pivotal” Intentio (project), 1985, and Andreas Christen’s “particularly spectacular” untitled monochrome relief from 1998.

item.title: British Museum U-turns on Photography of Bayeux Tapestry, While Conservators Discover Two New Small Breaks After Arrival in UK - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The Bayeux Tapestry has taken the British Museum and London by storm with tickets selling out, merchandise being flaunted all over social media, and bookshops placing volumes on the history of the Bayeux Tapestry at every till. But it seems visitors are already disappointed by their experience at the museum as the British Museum has made a U-turn on allowing photography, according to the Substack Maxwell Museum.

It’s unclear as to why the British Museum has banned photography without a reason. “Signs at the entrance say its [sic] prohibited, despite your e-ticket saying it’s allowed. The exhibition’s webpage says photos are banned too, but it was saying the opposite just yesterday on the opening day (I’ve checked on the Wayback Machine archive),” writes Maxwell Blowfield, author of the Substack. “I’ve asked the British Museum why there’s been the sudden change, but have not heard back at time of writing.”

The British Museum did not answer a request for further comment about the use of photography in the exhibition from ARTnews.

Upon its arrival in Britain, the Bayeux Tapestry has been scrutinized to minute detail. Thalia Bajon-Bouzid, one of the tapestry’s conservators, recently told the New York Times that her team had discovered two new small breaks “among its millions of threads while checking its condition after it arrived in England.” She added that the thread breaks were both “a few millimeters long.”

A spokesperson for the British Museum said that the “British Museum received the draft of condition report B last week. This report compares the Tapestry’s condition upon its arrival in London in July 2026 with photographs taken in September 2025, before it was taken off display in Bayeux.” That July condition check was the last full one conducted on the tapestry, with the one previous to that being in 2020. (The tapestry coming off display planned as part of the Bayeux Tapestry Museum’s ongoing renovations.)

The British Museum spokesperson added that the report has not been finalized yet and it’s still to be agreed on by both French and British Museum conservation teams, who carried out the condition checks together. “We can confirm though that from initial reading of the report it strongly suggests the Tapestry’s condition is virtually unchanged,” said the spokesperson.

item.title: Fotografiska Tallinn Celebrates Vivian Maier’s Rediscovered Archive - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
Vivian Maier’s (1926-2009) story is one of the most remarkable in the history of photography. During nearly 40 years working as a nanny, she walked the streets of New York and Chicago with a camera around her neck, often accompanied by the children in her care. At the height of the American Drean, Maier belonged to an invisible working-class and remained a quiet witness to the world around her. Where others saw ordinary daily life, she saw an endless source of images, at t times through a child’s eyes: colourful characters, fleeting encounters, strange coincidences and the tragicomic moments of everyday life. The artist documented post-war America from the 1950s to the late 1980s with an extraordinary instinct, creating a unique visual portrait of the era, with life itself in the leading role. Yet, the French-American photographer remained unknown during her lifetime, before the chance discover of her archive brought her extraordinary talent to the world and posthumously established her among the great names of 20th century photography. Now, Fotografiska Tallin opens Vivian Maier: Unseen Work. 

The exhibition follows on from two hugely successful shows at Fotografiska New York and Shanghai, demonstrating the truly international appeal of Maier’s work. Maarja Loorents, Head of Exhibitions and Co-Founder of Fotografiska Tallinn explained: “Vivian Maier’s story is extraordinary, but what matters even more is how powerfully her photographs speak even without knowing that story. The exhibition offers an excellent overview of the work of one of the most gifted street photographers of the last century, from her iconic images of the streets of Chicago and New York to her more abstract work and colour photography.” Vivian Maier: Unseen Work features 230 monochrome and colour prints as well as exclusive access to audio recordings and super 8 films, which are a fascinating insight into her worldview.

Maier’s work is distinct in its ability to balance the urban fabric and architectural details of the city and the margins of everyday life. She frequently focused the camera on people who had stepped out of the constant flow of the streets and remained at its edges, waiting, watching or simply dozing. Her visual language brings together humanist American street photography traditions, intersperse with striking self-portraits in which Maier herself occasionally enters the frame. Colour and film became part of her later work, as she experimented with movement and kinetic sequences, bringing elements of cinematic language into her practice. Her vast archive, only discovered in 2007, comprises more than 120,000 negatives as well as her own documentary films and audio recordings. Its chance discovery placed her within the ranks of the 20th century’s influential figures, including Henri Cartier-Bresson, Diane Arbus and Robert Frank. 

This exhibition is testament to an almost unparalleled career. The fact that Maier captured these photographs for the simple reason that she wanted to document her surroundings gives them an authenticity that’s often difficult to find. Her work maintains a distinct voice, a unique perspective and a clear vision – unaffected by external influence. Vivian Maier: Unseen Works is a testament to why her photographs are so enduring, revealing a perfect time capsule of 20th century urban life. 

Vivian Maier: Unseen Works is at Fotografiska, Tallinn from 19 September: tallinn.fotografiska.com

Words: Emma Jacob

Image Credits:

2. Vivian Maier. New York, NY, July 27, 1954 © Estate of Vivian Maier, Courtesy of Maloof Collection and Howard Greenberg Gallery, NY.
3. Vivian Maier. Self-Portrait, New York, NY, 1953 © Estate of Vivian Maier, Courtesy of Maloof Collection and Howard Greenberg Gallery, NY.

item.title: Alfredo Jaar’s America - Hyperallergic
item.description:
In April 1987, a message flashed across the screens of Times Square: “This Is Not America.” Chilean artist Alfredo Jaar’s A Logo for America has one very clear message at its center: “America” consists of many countries, not just the United States. Almost 40 years later, on the occasion of the work’s return to New York, Editor-in-Chief Hakim Bishara sits down with the artist to talk about “America” and a US that is radically transformed and yet, Jaar says, essentially the same. He’s a pessimist of the intellect — hard not to be, right? — but certainly a warrior at heart. 

To Jaar’s point, it’s not 1987 anymore, but we’ve got yet another strongman leader waging yet another culture war here in the US. Trump’s latest target: abstract sculpture? He wants to erect a 30-foot-tall statue of George Washington in place of José de Rivera’s rotating stainless steel Möbius strip outside the National Museum of American History in Washington, which, in his words, “tells visitors nothing about America, inspires no one, and honors none of our Great American Heroes.” Tell me you don’t understand art without telling me you don’t understand art, Mr. President.

Much more in today’s issue, including James McNeill Whistler’s mellifluous paintings at Tate Britain, a Keith Haring mural that might make Philadelphia’s Register of Historic Places, and protests over a sponsor of the Bayeux Tapestry’s financing of a community center in an illegal Israeli settlement in the Occupied West Bank. 

— Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor

Alfredo Jaar Is Still Trying to Change the World

In April of 1987, when Reaganism was running amok and Henry Kissinger was fiddling with world affairs like a puppet master from hell, a relatively unknown 31-year-old Chilean artist named Alfredo Jaar staged his billboard installation A Logo for America smack dab in the heart of Times Square. It instantly became one of the most discussed works of political art in the contemporary canon. 

Appearing between ads for tomato sauce and a Mexican restaurant, the 42-second LED animation bewildered New Yorkers with the message “This Is Not America” superimposed on a map of the United States, followed by an image of the US flag with the text, “This Is Not America’s Flag.” Next, the “R” in America shifted into a dancing map of South, Central, and North America. The message to US citizens and their leaders was simple but provocative: Stop hijacking the name “America” while you’re just one of many countries in it.

Almost 40 years later, the basic fact that America is a continent, not a country, still has to be explained to US citizens who see themselves as the only Americans out there. | Hakim Bishara

item.title: Light & Magic: The Birth of Art Photography - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
Photography’s emergence as an art form was also a battle over who controlled the image. Pictorialism placed authorship, materiality and artistic intention at the heart of photographic culture from the late 19th century onwards. Light & Magic: The Birth of Art Photography, opening at Tate Modern this autumn, brings together more than 200 rare vintage prints by over 80 artists across Europe, North and South America, Asia and Australia. Rather than presenting Pictorialism as a transitional episode between Victorian photography and Modernism, the exhibition reveals a movement with its own ambitions, networks and visual languages, asking us to look beyond the established centres of the medium.

Pictorialism began at a moment when photography was caught between mechanical reproduction and artistic expression. Photographers manipulated negatives, papers, chemicals and printing processes to resist the assumption that a photograph was merely a transparent record of the world. Soft focus, atmospheric effects, tonal variation and elaborate composition became strategies for asserting individual vision, while painting, Symbolism and other contemporary art forms provided important points of dialogue. However, this history has often been flattened into a European and North American narrative, with Pictorialism positioned as a conservative precursor to the sharper visual language of Modernism. Curated by Charmaine Toh, Acting Head of Curatorial at Tate Modern, and Genevieve Barton, Assistant Curator, International Art, Light & Magic instead extends the movement across cultures and decades.

Every photographic canon is also a story about exclusion. What survives, what enters collections and what is repeatedly exhibited can determine which practices come to stand for an entire medium. By placing celebrated figures alongside photographers whose work has received considerably less attention, Tate’s exhibition complicates the familiar hierarchy between centre and periphery. Adolph de Meyer and Clarence H. White appear alongside Long Chin-san, Luo Bonian and Shapoor N. Bhedwar, producing a field in which different photographic traditions can be read in relation rather than isolation. Long Chin-san’s Pavilion Fairyland, with its evocation of traditional Chinese ink painting, is particularly revealing, demonstrating that photographic modernity did not require a rejection of inherited visual languages.

Softness becomes a form of authorship in Emma Barton’s The Awakening (1903). Rather than presenting the portrait as an unmediated record, Barton builds an image through delicacy, atmosphere and controlled tonal effects. The result sits at an interesting distance from photography’s supposed obligation to document, suggesting that the camera can be as imaginative as it is evidential. That tension feels particularly relevant now. As photographic manipulation and AI-generated imagery continue to complicate ideas of truth, Barton’s insistence on intervention looks like an early claim for the artist’s agency.

A photograph, in Pictorialism, was never simply what happened inside the camera. Paper, chemistry, surface and tone all became part of the image’s identity, turning the print into something closer to a crafted object than a neutral document. Peter Henry Emerson’s A Norfolk Boat-Yard (1886) sits within this exploration of process, while pairs of prints reveal just how radically different techniques could alter the same image. A functioning darkroom extends the point into the gallery itself, making visible the labour that is usually hidden behind the finished photograph. At a time when so much image-making happens without a physical trace, that emphasis on touch and process feels particularly resonant.

Performance enters the picture through the rise of studio photography, where constructed environments, costumes and theatrical poses allowed photographers to move beyond the conventions of straightforward portraiture. Bertram Park, Yvonne Gregory and Cavendish Morton developed images in which identity could be staged, stylised and transformed, while Yevonde’s Goddesses series pushes this impulse into colour through experimental Vivex prints. Such work makes photography appear less like a passive witness than a form of production, anticipating contemporary concerns with self-fashioning, celebrity and mediated identity. Portraiture here becomes a space in which the subject is not simply recorded but actively invented. What appears at first to be an historical curiosity consequently opens onto a larger cultural question about the extent to which images construct the identities they claim merely to depict.

Photographic societies, salons and camera clubs were equally important to Pictorialism’s development. These networks created an international infrastructure through which images, techniques and arguments could circulate, offering photographers an alternative geography to the conventional museum-centred history of modern art. London’s Royal Photographic Society forms one important node, but Light & Magic also draws attention to organisations including Guangshe in Shanghai, The New Line Group in South Korea and the Photographic Society of Singapore. Their journals, books and exhibition cultures reveal a sophisticated print ecology in which photography was debated and disseminated long before the arrival of today’s globalised art market. Publications such as Camera Work, Shashinkai: The Monthly Photographic Journal and USSR in Construction demonstrate how magazines could operate not merely as records, but as active spaces for constructing artistic communities and circulating new visual ideas.

The networked history of Pictorialism also challenges the seductive myth of the isolated photographic genius. Artistic movements rarely develop through individual innovation alone; they depend upon infrastructures of publication, criticism, collecting and exhibition that determine whose experiments become visible. Pictorialism’s camera clubs and salons functioned as laboratories for this process, connecting practitioners across national boundaries while also establishing standards of taste and legitimacy. Tate’s curatorial strategy is strongest when it allows these systems to become part of the story rather than treating them as background information. The exhibition participates in a wider art-historical shift towards understanding modernism as plural, interconnected and institutionally produced.

The boundary between Pictorialism and Modernism proves far less stable than photographic history has often suggested. Lionel Wendt’s solarised portraits from the 1930s and Shigeru Onishi’s experimental compositions of the 1950s demonstrate that pictorial strategies did not simply disappear when Modernist photography gained critical authority. Instead, abstraction, solarisation, distortion and formal experimentation could develop alongside – and sometimes through – an older investment in photographic manipulation. Edward Steichen, Paul Strand and Edward Weston further complicate any clean division between movements, their careers crossing from Pictorialist practices into forms of modernism that would later become canonical. Steichen’s Primo Carnera and Strand’s Miss Thomson, New Mexico, both from around 1922, consequently operate as evidence of a medium negotiating competing ideas of progress.

Modernism’s mythology depends, in part, on the language of rupture – the old image giving way to the new. Yet the works gathered here suggest something more interesting: photographic modernity was built through inheritance as much as rejection. Light & Magic proposes that photography’s identity was formed through contradiction, borrowing and persistent reinvention. Pictorialism could be decorative and experimental, conservative and radical, deeply invested in tradition while simultaneously testing the possibilities of a new medium. Those tensions make the movement particularly relevant now, as distinctions between photographic, digital and computational image-making become increasingly unstable.

Few moments make London’s position within the international art world more visible than Frieze Week. Galleries, collectors, museums, curators and artists converge on the capital, turning the city into a particularly dense site of exchange between the commercial and institutional spheres. Tate Modern’s decision to open Light & Magic during this period gives the exhibition an added resonance, placing a reassessment of photographic history within one of the busiest moments of the global art calendar. The timing also offers a reminder of the UK’s continuing cultural reach, while the exhibition itself resists any straightforward idea of London as the centre. Its story moves outward – towards Shanghai, Singapore, Seoul, Sri Lanka and beyond – making the capital a meeting point rather than the endpoint.

What materialises is a history of photography defined by possibility. Pictorialism gave photographers permission to manipulate, stage, soften, colour and reimagine the world in front of the lens, while the societies, journals and salons surrounding the movement created an international culture in which those ideas could travel. Tate’s exhibition restores that sense of experimentation, placing familiar names alongside artists and networks that have received far less attention. Photography did not have to become less photographic in order to become art; its artistic potential was found precisely in what could be done with the medium. More than a history of an early movement, Light & Magic is a reminder that the photograph has always been an inventive form – one whose boundaries remain open to being remade.

Light & Magic: The Birth of Art Photography is at Tate Modern, London from 14 October – 21 February: tate.org.uk

Words: Anna Müller
