item.title: Another Abstract Public Artwork Faces Trump’s Senseless Ire - Hyperallergic
item.description:
In a Truth Social post criticizing the Smithsonian Institution's “ideological activism” on Friday, September 11, President Donald Trump called on the National Museum of American History (NMAH) to erect a 30-foot-tall statue of George Washington and develop a five-year exhibition on “America’s Greatest Hero.”

In Trump's eyes, the colossal statue would ideally replace José de Rivera's kinetic sculpture “Infinity” (1967), the United States government's first abstract art commission, which has stood outside the NMAH entrance facing the National Mall for almost 60 years.

Deriding the late American abstractionist's stainless steel Möbius strip, which rotates on its axis every eight minutes, Trump called it a “strange modernist sculpture” that “tells visitors nothing about America, inspires no one, and honors none of our Great American Heroes.”

The president led with a call for the Smithsonian to display an existing 11-foot-tall statue of Washington outside the NMAH's Flag Hall for a dedicated Constitution Day celebration this Thursday, September 17. The gesture of replacing the work with an enormous statue, he said, would be underpinned by an urgently produced exhibition about Washington's life and work in anticipation of his 300th birthday, which is coming up ... in 2032.

Trump claimed that the NMAH had “failed to give George Washington and our other Founding Fathers the celebration they deserve” in its America 250 programming under the Smithsonian's “recently ended” leadership, referencing Secretary Lonnie Bunch III's retirement announcement. He also needled NMAH's now-defunct Center for Restorative History and its Decolonization Working Group for “focus[ing] attention overwhelmingly on those who have been oppressed.”

item.title: 300-Pound Faun Sculpture Stolen from French Zoo in the ’90s Heads Home - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Three decades after it was stolen from a zoo under the cover of night, a 19th-century bronze sculpture was recovered from the United States and returned to its rightful home in the north of France, where it is now on display at the Musée de Picardie in Amiens.

According to a press release issued by the London-based Art Loss Register (ALR), Alfred Lepère’s Faune Chasseur was identified as part of due diligence preceding a proposed sale by one of ALR’s auction-house clients. The sculpture was commissioned by the French State in 1863 and is owned by the state and listed in its national collection managed by Centre National des Arts Plastiques. It was showcased at the Amiens Zoo before it was stolen in 1993.

“The recovery of this remarkable sculpture demonstrates why thorough due diligence is so important within the art market, where a stolen work can disappear for decades into private hands,” said Charlotte Chambers-Farah, ALR’s business development and client manager. “Despite the considerable weight and size of this monumental sculpture, its whereabouts were unknown for more than 30 years before it appeared in a US auction catalogue more than 4,000 miles from where it was stolen. There were no obvious indications to the auction house that it had a problematic provenance, but by checking the work against our global database, its hidden past was established before it could be sold.”

Acknowledging the recent rash of art crimes that have roiled art institutions around the world, most prominently the Louvre, Chamber-Farah added, “At a time when thefts in public institutions are once again targeting items for their material value, this recovery offers grounds for hope that their disappearance over a prolonged period does not necessarily mean that they have been melted down for scrap.”

item.title: Prized Gertrude Abercrombie Painting, Priced at $30 at an Estate Sale, Heads to Auction for $250,000 - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Missing for decades, a Gertrude Abercrombie painting will find itself some collector’s prize this October at Freeman’s.

Of the lots scheduled for Freeman’s postwar and contemporary art auction, Alderman Merriam’s Shells (1951), by the celebrated Chicagoan artist, surely has the best story. According to the house, the enigmatic still life of seashells scattered in a deep void was spotted this summer at a “picked-over” estate sale in Michigan. Hung in a corner of a dark hallway, it carried a $30 price tag and a nearly overlooked signature in the corner reading “Abercrombie.”

“Uncertain but intrigued,” its finder brought the canvas to the Milwaukee Art Museum, which was then hosting an Abercrombie survey. In a serendipitous stroke, the exhibition catalog included an archival photograph of the very painting, which had originally been illustrated in a 1952 Chicago Review piece on Abercrombie’s exhibition at Newman Brown Gallery.

Authenticated by leading Abercrombie scholar Susan Weininger, then handed to Freeman’s (a sponsor of the Milwaukee show), Alderman Merriam’s Shells’s $30 price tag was replaced with a $150,000–$250,000 estimate. Bids will start at $75,000.

Haunting but visually restrained, the painting depicts nine delicately rendered seashells, one suspended by a thread against a black background. The shells belonged to Robert Merriam, an alderman in Chicago’s Hyde Park neighborhood, where the artist lived and worked, the auction house said.

In a statement, Zachary Wirsum, senior vice president and head of Freeman’s postwar and contemporary art department, marveled at the fact he’d only recently told visitors to the Milwaukee show that Abercrombie’s paintings still occasionally appear at estate sales. “Little did I know that one of those ‘once in a while’s would occur less than a month later,” he said.

item.title: Using AI, Scientists Recreate the Sights and Sounds of 2,500-Year-Old Tombs - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The Etruscan painted tombs of Tarquinia, Italy, dating from around the 7th to the 1st century BCE, have long been celebrated for their vivid iconography and remarkable state of preservation. Now, archaeologists have used AI to examine how sight and sound may have affected Etruscan mourners of the time.

Focusing on two 5th-century BCE painted tombs at Tarquinia, the Tomba del Gallo and the Tomba dei Demoni Azzurri (“Tomb of the Blue Demon”) as case studies, researchers used acoustic science and AI modeling to recreate each tomb’s distinct experiential strategy. Their findings suggest that these tombs were intended not simply to memorialize the dead but to create an ambient experience for the living.

“Etruscan tomb architecture was structurally designed in a manner that produce[d] somatic and affective responses,” say archaeologists Maurizio Forte of Duke University and Jacqueline Ortoleva of the University of Oxford, who coauthored a study recently published in August in the Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory.

To prove their point, Forte and Otoleva attempted to reproduce the aural and visual conditions of the tombs when they were built. Their acoustic survey involved playing recorded handclaps at different locations and measuring how those reverberated through each tomb. To mimic the visual experience of a 5th-century audience, Forte and Otoleva used AI to map movement routes through the tombs while imagining how those tombs may have looked in candlelight.

“The dromos (entrance passage), with its narrowing walls and descending axis, created a liminal transition that physically oriented the body before it entered the chamber,” the authors write, “We suggest that [the tombs’] images were not purely commemorative but instead had the potential to activate the sensorium of those present.”

“For example,” they continue, “Torch light flickering across painted dancers created movement; incense and the smell of libations layered the olfactory register onto the visual. Sound—lamentation, music, the movement of offerings—completed what we might now call an immersive environment.”

According to Forte and Otoliva, while the two tombs were built in the same general period, they may have induced different responses in their visitors. While the Tomba del Gallo seems to have prioritized a calm experience, the Tomb of the Blue Demon likely precipitated feelings of disembodiment and disorientation. They note that it’s unclear whether the tomb builders intentionally designed these effects or whether they emerged from the space and materials at hand.

What remains, however, is the builders’ deliberation in constructing emotive and sensory experience. “The implications of the present study extend well beyond Tarquinia,” Forte and Otoliva conclude. “If Etruscan funerary architects were deliberately engineering spatial geometry, pictorial content, and acoustic experiences inside the tomb space, then we must fundamentally reconsider the category of ‘funerary architecture’ across the ancient Mediterranean and beyond.”

item.title: James McNeill Whistler’s Music for the Eyes - Hyperallergic
item.description:
LONDON — James McNeill Whistler is at once ubiquitous and obscure. Born in 1834 in Massachusetts, he spent some of his childhood in St. Petersburg, Russia before moving to Paris and then London to study art. While he recalls the motifs and methods of European heavyweights such as Courbet, Renoir, Singer-Sargent, and Constable, Whistler’s work diverges in its technical progression. Whistler prioritized aesthetic effect over iconographic content, confining each piece to a limited chromatic palette in search of the sublime and forgoing faithful representational accuracy. Like music composed primarily for aural pleasure, his work avoids sharp or jarring notes in color, tone, or composition for aesthetic pleasure. In fact, Whistler often used musical titles like harmonies, symphonies, or arrangements to emphasize this; his most famous work, the 1871 portrait of his mother, is called “Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1."

James McNeill Whistler at the Tate Britain is the first major solo exhibition of his work in the last 30 years, and this exhibition has been five years in the making. Part of Whistler’s relative obscurity in the United Kingdom stems from stipulations in major bequests that prevent loaning his work, most significantly from the collections at the Smithsonian Institution and the Hunterian at the University of Glasgow. Many may be familiar with Whistler’s work through reproductions, but this exhibition matters precisely because the ‘harmonious’ limited palette and subtle paint application are lost in photographic reproduction.  

A fantastically singular technique distinguishes Whistler from contemporaries and other stylistic schools. Curators Carol Jacobi, Isobel Muir, and James Finch emphasize Whistler’s individuality through a laser-focused visual analysis of his paintstrokes, and by opening the show with a pseudo-reproduction of his studio, complete with theater windows. The curators take it a step further by presenting his brushes and palette to describe the physical process of making the strokes. A caption, for example, explains how in a nearby portrait of Effie Deans (or “Arrangement in Yellow and Gray,” 1876–68) he “created the folds of her skirt with a stiff, flat-ended brush … [pressing] harder against the canvas to deepen the shadow at the hem.” There is plenty more of this glorious catnip for anyone remotely interested in painterly technique. Interestingly, a technique peculiar to Whistler is using a loaded brush with excess paint spilling at its edges to create a thicker framing ridge on either side of the stroke. It is an ingeniously economical application simultaneously of both outline and fill, and once you spot it, it’s everywhere.

There is a sense of immense discipline in Whistler’s arc from traditional models to aesthetic tonality, such that he himself eventually disappears. A strict economy characterizes his efforts, from an early watercolor of “The Thames at Battersea” (c.1876–68) delineated fantastically by only about five light blobs, through to a distinct precision and restriction in what he actually applies and even takes away. Comparing this to the show-boating of Singer-Sargent’s loose, cutting-corners virtuosic brushwork, or the trowel-applied thickness of Manet hacking away in his painterly constructions, not a single brushstroke is in excess, with Whistler even wiping away to leave a mere trace of pigment. A quote pasted on the wall captures his idea exactly: “Paint should not be applied thick. It should be like breath on the surface of a plane of glass.” It fittingly appears in the section on his 1870s series, Nocturnes, which is perhaps the pinnacle of atmospheric mood: Only the odd tiny red or white catchlight punctuates these saturated, minimalistic nighttime river scenes.

item.title: Keith Haring Mural May Decide the Fate of Public Art in Philly - Hyperallergic
item.description:
PHILADELPHIA — The fate of a Keith Haring mural in Philadelphia may be sealed this week in a decision that could also set a precedent for how to protect public art in the City of Brotherly Love.

At the height of his career in the 1980s, Keith Haring joined up with 14 high school students to paint a mural in a quiet pocket of South Philadelphia. The artist intentionally passed over better-trafficked areas of the city, instead selecting a wall on a residential building in the historically Black neighborhood of Point Breeze. A year after painting his legendary “Crack is Wack” mural in New York City, and three years before he died from AIDS-related complications, Haring drew bold, black outlines of his signature dancing figures that students filled in with bright colors and patterns. 

Today, after being restored twice over its 39-year lifespan, “We The Youth” (1987) is the only one of his collaborative murals that remains in its original location. 

At a public meeting scheduled for this Wednesday, September 16, the Philadelphia Historical Commission will entertain public comments as they discuss whether to recommend that “We The Youth” be added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places. The decision will be voted on by the entire commission on October 9. If approved, it would be the first time an outdoor mural in the “Mural Capital of the World” would receive the commission's protection. 

The wall the mural is painted on is co-owned by the Neighborhood Gardens Trust (NGT), an organization that preserves Philadelphia community gardens, and OCF Realty, a controversial real estate company often held responsible for the rapid gentrification of the Point Breeze neighborhood. Almost every key stakeholder has publicly supported the mural’s designation, including the Keith Haring Foundation, which told Hyperallergic in a statement that the move would be “preserving it as a unique cultural icon and providing the necessary legal protections against its loss.”

item.title: Lawsuit Alleges Warhol Forgery Scheme Spanning Florida, Peru, and Philadelphia - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Duped into buying more than $6.7 million worth of fake Andy Warhol paintings and prints, real estate investor Richard Perlman and his family have launched a multinational lawsuit against the players they say are complicit in the alleged scam.

Filed on September 9 in a Miami state court and first reported by the Wall Street Journal, the lawsuit accuses roughly half a dozen individuals and companies across Florida, Philadelphia, and Peru of acting as “suppliers, fake authenticators and distributors” within an elaborate forgery network. The lawsuit traces the alleged journey of the illicit works to Miami—from the painter employed in Peru, through their smuggling into the US, to the construction of a false provenance, including fabricated documents and a label for the canvas.

According to the lawsuit, the forgery was uncovered in 2023, when the Perlman family invited experts from Christie’s to assess a collection that included portraits they believed were by Warhol. The paintings depicted Liza Minnelli, Debbie Harry, and Queen Elizabeth II, among other famous faces. Christie’s instead raised suspicions about their authenticity, prompting Perlman to investigate.

The dealer at the center of Perlman’s earlier lawsuit, Leslie Roberts, sold the works from his Coconut Grove storefront. Perlman sued Roberts in 2024, a case that, according to the Journal, was resolved in January under undisclosed terms. Roberts has also admitted to wire fraud charges stemming from the alleged Warhol scheme. He pleaded guilty and is scheduled to be sentenced September 24. Roberts closed his gallery after the indictment and maintained that he believed the Warhols were authentic at the time. “I invested $3.3 million of my own money,” he said, explaining that he pleaded guilty because it was “the favorable way to get out of trouble.”

Perlman’s suit appears aimed at holding accountable every player who, as the complaint puts it, “created a pipeline of fraudulent works flowing across state and international lines.” The suit also names Philadelphia art dealer Nathan Isen. FBI agents raided his gallery, Dane Fine Art, in July.

Isen pleaded guilty in 2015 to money laundering as part of a scheme in which he used art to allegedly launder drug proceeds. That same year, Philadelphia magazine published a report on Isen that detailed allegations that he had sold counterfeit artworks.

Isen has denied any involvement in the alleged Warhol forgery.

The lawsuit also accuses two men in Peru of painting a series of works purportedly signed by Warhol and arranging for the canvases to be shipped to Roberts’s gallery. The forms listed values as low as $30, which the suit describes as “absurdly low values for purported original Warhol paintings.” Other collaborators named in the suit include a Florida dealer whom Roberts says he met at Art Basel Miami Beach and a retired dentist linked to an LLC called WarholandFriends.

“The Perlmans want to hold accountable every individual and every company that defrauded them and perpetrated this scheme to defraud other victims,” Luke Nikas, the Perlmans’ lawyer, told the Journal.

item.title: Madelon Vriesendorp’s Subconscious Cities - Hyperallergic
item.description:
LONDON — The British architect Sir John Soane and the Dutch artist Madelon Vriesendorp were born nearly two centuries apart, but despite differences in history, culture, technology, nationality, and gender, they share an undeniable kinship — a deep engagement with architecture, an affinity for collecting, and a penchant for mischief. The current exhibition at Sir John Soane’s Museum, Madelon Vriesendorp: Mind Games, brings together more than 50 works from across the artist’s career, celebrating shared connections while offering a quietly playful rebuke to its host’s neoclassical sensibility.

A significant portion of the exhibition centers around Vriesendorp’s best-known work, “Flagrant Délit” (1975), a delightfully surreal anthropomorphism of two iconic Manhattan skyscrapers caught in a post-coital moment by a spotlight atop the RCA Building. A few years later, Vriesendorp’s then-husband, architect Rem Koolhaas, chose the painting as the cover image for his Delirious New York (1978) — which he called, in the subtitle, a “retroactive manifesto” — helping secure its place in the iconography of the contemporary urban imagination. In fact, “Flagrant Délit” belongs to a larger series of paintings exploring the psychological and sexual aspects of contemporary architecture, several of which are on view, along with a 2026 cover commissioned by the New York Review of Architecture, testifying to the work’s ongoing influence. 

Drawings of Soane’s own projects, along with architectural drawings by his teacher George Dance, are on display in adjacent rooms. When Soane was awarded a travel stipend as an architectural student at the Royal Academy in 1778, it was still custom for upper-class British men to embark on a Grand Tour of Europe. Soane was no exception, and the many drawings, paintings, sculptures, and antiquities he brought back from two years of travel through Italy formed the beginnings of his house-and-office-turned-museum.

Vriesendorp and Koolhaas moved to New York in 1972, first to Ithaca and then to New York City, where the artist “discovered bad taste in a big way” and began to collect objects seriously. Compared with Soane’s collection, Vriesendorp's is decidedly more diverse and proletarian, shaped by the dizzying compilation of styles she encountered in the United States, encompassing small toys, figurines, models, postcards, and sundry quotidian objects. Mind Games includes a handful of postcards with an architectural focus; however, her full collection, which numbers in the thousands, includes such unexpected categories as Luna Parks, lighthouses, bus terminals, penitentiaries, airplanes, disasters, and babies — or, as she saw it, simply “Americana.” Soane’s neoclassical reverence is replaced with a postmodern embrace of the banal, the camp, and the kitsch; the Enlightenment regard for knowledge is traded for a critical examination of the dominant culture.

item.title: In ‘Ascent,’ Debra Baxter Explores the Power in Vulnerability, Mysticism, and Time - Colossal
item.description:
From elemental materials like alabaster, quartz, garnet, and bronze, Debra Baxter assembles jewel-like sculptures that explore consciousness, nature, anatomy, and spirituality. For her most recent body of work on view now in Ascent at Roq La Rue, the artist meanders into a more mystical side of history, infused with a tinge of punk and, somewhat paradoxically, a meditative calm.

Baxter contracted Covid in January 2022 that progressed into long Covid, during which she spent more time recuperating than being able to work with the heavy-duty equipment and materials characteristic of her practice. The sculptures on view in this show were initiated five years ago. However, her period of recovery, which she describes as a blessing, revealed an unexpected new direction. As she rested, she began to receive visions that confounded her sense of space, both physically and metaphysically.

Human hearts effervesce with crystals, such as in “The Day I Tried to Live” and “Fade Into You.” On one hand, these could be read as some kind of emotional or biological calcification. On another, these gleaming growths might represent a spilling forth of the spirit made tangible. “Fade Into You” consists of a hinge, allowing the work to become “open-hearted” but also to shut away its gleaming energy.

Baxter also uses materials derived from the earth that are explicitly solid, evoking an intimate tension between vulnerability and strength, the fleeting and the permanent. And in her smaller-than-life-size alabaster busts, she portrays women in an aesthetic representation historically granted to men. “The women depicted in these sculptures are trying to maintain higher consciousness, but keep fracturing and falling apart,” Baxter says. “They stem from my love of the history of sculptures from Greek busts to Bernini, and my interest in the innate truth of materials, and my ongoing belief in the power and intuition of woman.”

Pieces like “Veil” nod to the nature of seeing and awareness while also acknowledging the thinness of the boundary between our world and the next. “Life had a certain amount of permeability in a more spiritual and profound way than before, and she began to feel as if she started to embody the mystical concepts she had been researching,” the gallery says.

Ascent continues through October 3. See more on Baxter’s Instagram.

item.title: Activists Protest Bayeux Tapestry Sponsor’s Ties to Israeli Settlements - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Following reports that hedge-fund billionaire Igor Tulchinsky financed a community center in an illegal Israeli settlement in the Occupied West Bank, pro-Palestine activists took to the British Museum this Saturday, September 12, to protest Tulchinsky's financial backing of the new Bayeux Tapestry exhibit.

Activists from Energy Embargo for Palestine, who also denounced the British Museum's ongoing partnership with the oil giant BP, unfurled their own “People's Tapestry” in the museum's Great Court.

“We will continue to push for a Museum that is led by the interests of its workers and the general public,” the climate emergency group wrote in an Instagram post about the weekend action, specifying its call for an “end to collaboration and sponsorships by billionaires fueling climate breakdown and invested in 'Israel’s' settler-colonial occupation.”

The demonstration comes in light of last week's Middle East Eye report on Tulchinsky's “therapy yurt” for Israeli residents of Efrat — the de facto capital of a settlement bloc just south of Jerusalem within the Occupied West Bank called Gush Etzion. Tulchinsky's ties to the settlement may violate the United Kingdom's recently adopted sanctions and import ban on illegal Israeli settlements on Palestinian land.

The yurt, which hosts group therapy and movement programs for Israeli militants and civilians experiencing PTSD from “October 7, the ongoing war, and repeated reservist call-ups,” is part of a larger community center in Efrat that provides individual and family therapy for residents across Gush Etzion. As reported by the Jerusalem News Syndicate, Tulchinsky was present for the yurt's unveiling last November and dedicated it to “Israel's heroes,” referring to the new tent as “Israel's inner Iron Dome.”

Following the Middle East Eye's report, British politician and Green Party leader Zack Polanski has called on the UK government to investigate whether Tulchinsky's sponsorship with the British Museum violates the new sanctions. Earlier this month, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband outlined that the government will take action against “specific companies and individuals who provide services such as construction, infrastructure, financing, or real estate for settlement expansion.”

item.title: Europe’s Art Theft Problem Is Much Bigger Than the Louvre - Hyperallergic
item.description:
This week, two thieves broke into the Renoir Museum in southern France and seized two paintings in under five minutes. Earlier this year, three paintings by Renoir, Cézanne, and Matisse and four priceless Renaissance works were stolen from two museums in Italy. The thefts are only the most recent in a series of museum robberies across Europe over the past year, following the brazen daytime jewelry heist at the Louvre in Paris. 

In a new report last month, Europol warned that museum robberies were becoming “almost a weekly occurrence,” with offenders increasingly employing violent and forceful methods. But a succession of spectacular thefts can create the impression of an escalating trend without necessarily proving one, and Europol’s report does not provide the data needed to establish a long-term increase. According to Donna Yates, UNESCO Chair in Cultural Heritage and Emerging Crime at Maastricht University in the Netherlands, there has been little systematic research comparing the frequency, targets, methods, and perpetrators of these crimes.

There has also been speculation that the Louvre heist inspired a chain of copycat robberies, or that some of the thefts were commissioned or motivated by insurance payouts. There is little evidence yet to establish either explanation. 

But what the most recent thefts highlight is that extraordinary collections of cultural (and financial) value are not confined to Europe's largest institutions. Municipal and regional museums, like many of those targeted in the last year, hold objects of immense cultural and scientific significance while operating with far fewer resources than national institutions like the Louvre. 

“Most museums are increasingly underfunded and the fantasy security measures people propose to protect these objects in museums are laughable to anyone who knows museum budgets,” Yates told Hyperallergic.

These institutions could remove their most desirable objects from public display and lock them away permanently. But that would mean sacrificing the public purpose of museums to protect the collections entrusted to them. The recent thefts demonstrate the limits of security measures when confronted with fast, targeted, and sometimes violent attacks.

item.title: Art History and Pop Culture Converge in Friedrich Kunath’s ‘The Nearest Faraway Place’ - Colossal
item.description:
Friedrich Kunath describes that he aims to make his paintings “feel like songs.” The logo for the band Oasis turns up in a top corner of “Sometimes I’m Almost There,” and there is a kind of surreal, set-like quality to his vibrant, cinematic works. “Kunath explores themes of distance and (re)location, where a longing emerges between the place you’re in and the place you’re destined to be,” says a statement for his exhibition The Nearest Faraway Place, presented by Pace in Seoul.

The artist taps into art history with compositions redolent of the tradition of Weltlandschaft, or “the world landscape,” which can be traced to the Northern Renaissance. There’s also a strong nod to the Hudson River School, which drew on 19th-century European Romanticism. Kunath tips in references to pop culture, from the ubiquitous “The End” marking the finale of theatrical releases and phrases superimposed on uncanny situations, like the eponymous painting “The most beautiful world in the world” depicting an existential aerial advertisement.

Kunath is known for traversing realms of pop culture, irony, and fiction, often with a kind of nostalgic wistfulness and a tinge of the comedic. We’re initially drawn in to what appears like a traditional landscape, then quickly diverted by sticker-like additions of cartoonish, sometimes absurd characters.

As the basis of the artist’s works, romantic landscapes are already inherently invented; they may resemble real places, but the glistening light and idyllic absence of structures or people portray a kind of ideal. Kunath opens that door further. “By bringing together aesthetic contexts and familiar tropes, he materializes his subconscious,” the gallery says. “Feelings arise before we know where they come from.”

The Nearest Faraway Place continues through October 24. See more on Kunath’s Instagram.

item.title: Alice Diop to Take on Miu Miu’s 2026 Art Basel Paris Commission - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Miu Miu has announced that the recipient of its 2026 commission for the Art Basel Paris Public Program will be filmmaker Alice Diop.

Diop will stage Geste de Consolation (Gesture of Consolation) at both the Palais d’Iéna headquarters of France’s Economic, Social, and Environmental Council and the Miu Miu runway show. Diop’s takeover will mark the third commission by Miu Miu during Art Basel Paris, with Goshka Macuga’s Tales and Tellers (2024) and Helen Marten’s 30 Blizzards. (2025) preceding it.

Diop was invited by Miu Miu founder and ARTnews Top 200 Collector Miuccia Prada to make Geste de Consolation as a continuation of the artist’s 2025 short film Fragments for Venus (part of Miu Miu’s “Women’s Tales” series), which looks at the representation of Black women historically and today.  

Diop is best known for her documentaries looking at French society, including La Permanence (On Call, 2016), which looked at refugees being treated at a hospital in a banlieue northeast of Paris, and Nous (We, 2020), which focused on the mostly Black and immigrant communities living in the banlieues off the RER B line. (The latter film screened at the Museum of Modern Art in 2021.)

Her first feature film, Saint Omer, first screened at the 2022 Venice Film Festival, winning the Grand Jury Prize and the Luigi De Laurentiis Award for a debut film. The film is also Diop’s first narrative film, taking the court case of Fabienne Kabou, a Senegalese French woman who was ultimately convicted of murder for drowning her child, as inspiration. Diop attended Kabou’s trial as part of her research.

“I believe that by writing it I was creating a distance with the subject of this matter that was so corrosive, so difficult,” she told the New York Times in 2023. She “realized in the writing process that she needed another character whose reaction to Laurence could highlight the themes of maternal ambivalence she wanted to explore,” per the Times.

Geste de Consolation will mark Diop’s first foray into exhibition making, bringing together her work with that of others. Upon entering the space, visitors will first see a photograph by Zanele Muholi before coming across a two-channel film installation by Diop, which will collage together excerpts from her films and pieces of her archives, showing what has “shaped her gaze as a filmmaker through disturbing violent images and those that have consoled her,” according to a release.

The exhibition will also include a section called Chambre à soi (A room of one’s own), which will be decorated by textiles of Gee’s Bend quilter Mary Lee Bendolph and filled with books by the likes of Zora Neale Hurston, June Jordan, Audre Lorde, and Zadie Smith.

During the run of the show, October 21–25 (with a preview on October 20), a cast of performers will read from the text. The Chambre à soi will also serve as the setting for an adaption of choreographer Nadia Beugré’s Prophétique. Upon exiting, visitors will come across Simone Leigh’s 16-foot-tall bronze Sentinel (Mami Wata).

“Diop conceives of Geste de Consolation itself as a form of montage, with the guided path moving from one part of the exhibition to another functioning like a film edit moves from one shot to the next,” a release reads. “The visitor’s experience accumulates meaning through proximity and sequence rather than direct explanation, leading ultimately to cathartic release. Every placement—sound, word, voice, image—is composed for the body moving through it. Geste de Consolation offers a scenographic journey of remembrance and repair.”

item.title: Visual Glitches: Images from the Aesthetica Archives - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
The word “glitch” is thought to come from glitsh, Yiddish for “slippery place”, and from glitshn, meaning “to slide, or glide.” In the 1940s, radio broadcasters were using the term to refer to on-air blunders. Ten years later, it became part of the language of TV engineering. Today, in the digital age, it’s commonly employed in reference to computer faults and video game errors. Here, we explore five contemporary artists, previously featured in print editions of Aesthetica Magazine, who embrace and manipulate the beauty of digital and physical error. Their work explores the limitations of equipment used to create media and tests the boundaries of how software can edit and warp natural landscapes. 

Tommy Goguely

Interested in the cultural shift of how media becomes visible via malfunctions or disturbances, photographer Tommy Goguely (b. 1984) highlights the materiality of digital photography. The artist deliberately damages digital cameras by scratching, drilling and altering the photosensitive surface. The images taken with these cameras record their own degradation rather than the external world. Colours smear and glitch across the frame, or dissolve into speckles and “noise”.

tommygoguely.com | @tommygoguley

Naill Staines

Ireland-based Niall Staines (b. 1985) is an art director and digital creative turning serene coastlines into glitch-like scenes. Colours are smeared upwards; vertical stripes are dragged and pulled from natural panoramas. Crashing waves make way for bold lines of white and blue. Valleys transform into skies of kaleidoscopic green, pink and purple. Trees stretch infinitely skyward. The works make order out of chaos, gathering key information from organic landscapes and flattening them down to two dimensions. 

niallstaines.com |  @staines

Michel Lamoller

In Michel Lamoller’s (b. 1984) photographic reliefs, various prints are layered on top of one another in ways that mimic our increasingly stacked and urbanised behaviour – each composition representing a new, hyperreal existence in both form and structure. Through the acts of cutting and pasting – and further exaggerating the labyrinthine qualities of megacities – he explores what it means to exist in radically mechanised landscapes, whilst questioning the ultimate reality presented by images today. 

theravestijngallery.com | @michel.lamoller

Ellen Jantzen

The rise of digital cameras has meant that we no longer store photographs as pockets of light and darkness, but as strings of numbers, able to be edited instantly. Ellen Jantzen (b. 1946) draws attention to the editing processes that define much of today’s media – stretching, cutting and pasting samples from the organic world. Jantzen is interested in states of reality, attempting to make visual the ephemeral nature of sacred, spiritual realms by transplanting replica trees into the natural world.

ellenjantzen.com | @ellenjantzen

 

Andrea Alkalay

Andrea Alkalay’s Landscape on Landscape series (2020-2021) explores the “regimes of representation” – considering the visual information we are presented, and the manifold ways it is interpreted, as our relationship to the “real” world continues to become distorted. Beneath the folds of dramatic vistas, layers of digitised colour are stretched across the frame like barcodes. This intuitive process examines the poetic and political potential that arises from observation – as images become a complication of truth.

andrealkalay.com | @andrealkalay

item.title: Houston Center for Contemporary Craft Celebrates 25th Anniversary With Silver Exhibition - Colossal
item.description:
The most reflective element on Earth, silver has transformed the ways in which humans perceive, record, and understand the world. Presented on the occasion of the Houston Center for Contemporary Craft’s milestone 25th anniversary, A Material Inheritance employs silver as both subject and lens, inviting reflection on the institution’s past while considering the evolving future of contemporary craft.

Silver is the material through which cultures have learned to see and remember themselves. Its exceptional optical and metallurgical properties made possible advances in mirror-making, photography, and scientific instrumentation, while its weight, density, and malleability established it as a prime medium for currency, ceremonial objects, jewelry, and treasured heirlooms. Looking beyond the material’s status as a precious metal, the exhibition considers how silver has shaped systems of knowledge, value, and cultural exchange across centuries and continents. 

Featuring artists Shane R. Hendren, Edward Lane McCartney, Jaydan Moore, Leah Ying Lin, Anjali Srinivasan, and others, A Material Inheritance presents works spanning traditional metalsmithing and jewelry making as well as experimental glass, ceramic, and kinetic media practices that reveal silver’s remarkable conceptual and material range. 

McCartney and Moore, who are alumni of Houston Center for Contemporary Craft’s Artist Residency Program, are metalsmiths whose practices are deeply intertwined with the history of the organization, and each offers a compelling investigation into inherited silver heirlooms, particularly domestic serving ware. Working from antique platters, teapots, flatware, and gifted family objects, both artists transform inherited silver from repositories of memory into dynamic sculptural forms, asking how objects accumulate meaning as they pass through generations.

Across the works on view in A Material Inheritance, silver emerges as both substance and witness: a material shaped by histories of extraction, trade, migration, labor, and devotion, yet continually transformed through artistic experimentation. The exhibition positions silver as an active cultural agent that not only preserves histories but also continually refracts and reimagines them.

A Material Inheritance is on view through January 30, 2027, at the Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. Admission is free. 

Learn more at crafthouston.org. 

Installation view of “A Material Inheritance” at Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. Photo by Katy Anderson.

item.title: Good Muslim Artist, Bad Muslim Artist - Hyperallergic
item.description:
After Mahmood Mamdani published Good Muslim, Bad Muslim in 2004, artist Naeem Mohaiemen immediately recognized himself after 9/11 in its pages. “We naively thought if we were polite in the face of Islamophobia, it would wilt,” he recalls. Both a vital record and a call to action, his opinion today reflects on the haunting time period after the attacks, the South Asian community activism that rose up in response, and the 25 years since. Now a professor at Columbia University, Mohaiemen writes, “Thankfully, Mamdani’s son, Zohran, had other ideas.”

More to kick off your week in art below, from the end of the School of Visual Arts’s beloved Photography MFA program and our review of a Pope.L exhibition in Manhattan to our news team’s guides to the upcoming season of -ennials (tri- and bi- alike) and Brooklyn’s first craft supply library — as ever, librarians are holding it down.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor

Standing in the Shadow of No Towers

By August, the Tribeca nightclub Vinyl had gone into a Peter Gatien-era meltdown. Time magazine ran a dramatic cover story the year prior (“What Ecstasy Does to Your Brain”) and the dancefloor had posters warning about plainclothes sting ops. There was still talcum powder on the floor for dancing, but euphoric substances had vanished. In all my Sundays of dancing at Vinyl, I had never thought of how close it was to the Twin Towers — until that Tuesday in September when, by nightfall, the pavement outside was stacked with plastic bags of socks, t-shirts, and sweatpants we had collected for tower survivors who were expected to be pulled out “any moment now.” We waited until midnight, and by then it was clear — no one got out alive. | Naeem Mohaiemen

item.title: Tacita Dean Champions thePower of Analogue Filmmaking - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
Tacita Dean (b. 1965) is passionate about film. In a career that has spanned more than three decades and numerous awards, the Canterbury-born artist, now based between Berlin and Los Angeles, has created nearly 100 works on Super 8, 16mm and 35mm. But it is FILM, the monumental installation first produced for Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall in 2011, that stands as her defining tribute to the medium. Conceived at a time when analogue processes seemed in serious jeopardy of disappearing, Dean’s piece is a rallying cry for the world to take notice of photochemical motion pictures. In our current moment, where generative AI is threatening to reshape the future of cinema, this message takes on a renewed and urgent relevance.

For autumn 2026, Dean’s 11-minute-long, silent 35mm piece is on view at LA’s Marciano Art Foundation (MAF). It marks the first time the work has been exhibited in the USA, where it is once again projected onto a vertical screen reminiscent of the monolith in Stanley Kubrick’s 2001: A Space Odyssey. FILM appears to emerge from the gallery floor: a towering film strip onto which a variety of images are intercut, including a waterfall, a clock, a pine tree, a smokestack, a flickering bulb, a mountain, an eye and an enormous ostrich egg. Viewers will also see colour-filtered shots of Tate Modern’s former industrial architecture, painted in translucent hues of red, blue, orange, pink and green and often arranged in Mondrian-like grids. Each scene is framed by “sprocket holes” – a normally unseen technical detail that propels film through a projector – giving the piece a tactile quality. The effect makes one thing very clear: you are watching analogue.

To create this mesmerising work, Dean revived early 20th century techniques from the silent era, such as glass matte painting, gate masking and in-camera superimposition of multiple images. The colossal verticality was achieved by employing an anamorphic lens – used for wide landscape format, but here turned 90 degrees – which doubled the height of the frame. This combination of now largely abandoned processes speaks to Dean’s enthusiasm about the physical qualities of her medium, impossible to emulate digitally. She says: “My relationship to film begins at that moment of shooting and ends in the moment of projection. Along the way, there are several stages of magical transformation that imbue the work with varying layers of intensity. This is why the film image is different from the digital image: it is not only emulsion versus pixels, or light versus electronics, but something deeper – something to do with poetry.”

With this project, Dean joins a roster of contemporary artists in a quest to keep traditional printing and development processes alive. Recent examples include Japanese artist Hiroshi Sugimoto (b. 1948), whose Extinction exhibition in Tokyo was dedicated to the preservation of gelatin silver photography. Whilst Sugimoto’s show felt like an elegy, Dean’s piece unfolds as a celebration: a surreal collage that presents audiences with moments of absurdity, humour and surprise. As a variety of large-scale pictures flickers before their eyes, with no discernible narrative, FILM offers a welcome invitation for audiences to reconnect with the magic of cinema as it was when the medium was new, exciting and full of invention. As the gallery notes: “the end result has the effortlessness of an exhilarating magic trick.”

FILM by Tacita Dean is at Marciano Art Foundation, Los Angeles, from 18 September – 2 January.

marcianoartfoundation.org

Words: Eleanor Sutherland

Image Credits: Tacita Dean, FILM, (2011). (Still) 35mm colour and black and white portrait format anamorphic film with hand-tinted sequences, silent, 11 minutes, continuous loop. Large front projection; projection booth; free-standing screen; loop system. Commissioned as part of The Unilever Series for Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall, London, 2011- 2012. Courtesy of the artist, Marian Goodman Gallery, New York / Paris, and Frith Street Gallery, London.

The post Tacita Dean Champions the<br>Power of Analogue Filmmaking appeared first on Aesthetica Magazine.

item.title: Richard Avedon Honest Portraits of Getting Older - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
In a 2025 article, the BBC reported a 5% rise in cosmetic surgeries in the UK. There were a recorded 27,462 procedures, with more than nine in 10 of these being carried out on women. Reports also show that 65% of women feel pressured to look younger. Meanwhile, a recent study revealed that films are more likely to star an actor called Chris, or a talking animal, than a woman over 60. It’s clear that as a society, we prize youth in almost all facets of life. Yet, by 2030, 1 in 6 people in the world will be over 60. Many people are now resisting stereotypes and dated assumptions about what it means to get older. In 2023, UK company Ageism is Never in Style launched the “I look my age” campaign, pushing back against the assumption that people instinctively want to hide their age. It is in this climate that The Image Centre, Toronto presents an exhibition of Richard Avedon’s portraits that confront aging with honesty. 

Richard Avedon Immortal: Portraits of Aging, 1951-2004 asks viewers to confront the physical realities of getting older. The show features almost 100 images by the renowned photographer, featuring portraits of artists, writers, musicians and performers, all captured in a way that highlights their wrinkles, weary eyes and other signs of time’s inevitable passage. Paul Roth, Director of The Image Centre and exhibition curator, says: “The intensity and distinctive style of Avedon’s image continues to surprise people today, likely because they diverge so much from our expectations of portraiture. These photographs show that growing older is not something to hide. Instead, it is proof that a life has been fully lived. They can be honest and sometimes uncomfortable to look at, but they also show what it means to be human.” 

Born in New York in 1923, Avedon’s interest in photography began when he joined the armed forces in 1942 during WWII, serving as Photographer’s Mate Second Class in the US Merchant Marine. He described this experience: “my job was to do identity photographs. I must have taken pictures of one hundred thousand faces before it occurred to me I was becoming a photographer.” This experience became the bedrock of his creative career, working with Theatre Arls, Life, Look and Harper’s Bazaar, defining the USA’s tastes in fashion and contemporary art for decades. The artist was fascinated by the camera’s capacity for suggesting the personality and evoking the life of his subjects, famously saying: “my photographs don’t go below the surface. I have great faith in surfaces. A good one is full of clues.” 

This lifelong exploration of the human condition comes to the fore at The Image Centre. The collection includes portraits of Ronald Reagan, Toni Morrison, Gabriel García Marquez, Duke Ellington, Patti Smith, the Duke and Duchess of Windsor, Truman Capote and the Dalai Lama, among many other cultural icons. In each image, Avedon broke many conventions of portraiture. Instead of flattering angles and lighting, he controversially chose stark backgrounds and exacting details, often celebrating what he referred to as ‘the avalanche of age’ in his subjects’ features. Particular highlights include a shot of writer Toni Morrison, her stance is powerful as she gazes directly at the camera with her hands clenched in front of her chest. In a 1958 image of Ezra Pound, Avedon captures him with his eyes clenched shut and his shirt buttons undone, revealing a level of vulnerability rarely associated with the celebrated poet. 

Avedon made a name for himself as an artist who disrupted the status quo, reimagining the face of photography and fashion for new generations. Even now, 20 years after his death in 2004, the photographer continues to reveal new angles from which to view the world – and each other. 

Richard Avedon Immortal: Portraits of Aging, 1951–2004 is at The Image Centre, Toronto until 5 December: theimagecentre.ca

Words: Emma Jacob

Image Credits:

1. Richard Avedon, Louise Nevelson, sculptor, New York, May 13, 1975. gelatin silver print © The Richard Avedon Foundation. 
2. Richard Avedon, Toni Morrison, writer, New York, September 10, 2003, gelatin silver print © The Richard Avedon Foundation.
3. Richard Avedon, Samuel Beckett, writer, Paris, April 13, 1979, gelatin silver print © The Richard Avedon Foundation.
4. Richard Avedon, Ezra Pound, poet, at the home of William Carlos Williams, Rutherford, New Jersey, June 30, 1958, gelatin silver print © The Richard Avedon Foundation. Courtesy of Center for Creative Photography, Tucson, Arizona. Richard Avedon Archive, Gift of the Artist.

item.title: How Janine Antoni Simultaneously Disturbs and Delights - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Janine Antoni’s hands descend over the eyes of a creamy-colored bust to the sound of water pouring from a faucet. Bubbles froth at the sculpture’s chin and twinkle from grooves between sculpted strands of hair. She caresses the immobile features, then turns the statue to face her. In this 2003 video, little of the artist herself can be seen: A sliver of bare leg presses against the white enamel of a bathtub; her quick hands studiously encircle the simulated cartilage of the bust’s outer ear as she uses the tips of her thumbs to excavate soap from the concha. Then, it cuts to Antoni seated in her studio, her features the same as those of the bust. 

“For me, [this work is] about that conflict, that kind of love/hate relationship we have with our physical appearance,” she says. “And, really, the problem I have of looking in the mirror and thinking, ‘Is that who I am?’” Another cut reveals a chocolate version of the same statue. 

The footage, which originally appeared in an Art21 feature, captures Antoni remaking a bust from Lick and Lather (1993), an installation commissioned for that year’s Venice Biennale that encompasses 14 busts mimicking neoclassical marbles, seven made from chocolate and seven from soap. Cast from a mold of the artist’s head and chest, the sculptures’ features wear away as the artist gently washes and devours her own effigy, an erasure accomplished through apparent acts of tenderness. The piece—now her best known—has been remade on a few occasions due to the intense responses it invites; during the Biennale, a young woman licked and bit some works’ noses off in an inadvertent collaboration. While nonconsensual, the girl’s gesture was not far from Antoni’s own response to the art that then dominated museums. 

Antoni has chafed against the art historical canon since she first exploded onto New York’s art scene in the 1990s. Production, destruction, and gender are among her central themes—in her hands, they entangle and blur. Antoni is often misconstrued as a performance artist, perhaps because her objects bear palpable traces of the intimate and durational processes through which she molds and shapes them, operating as sensual surrogates for her body in space. 

Last spring, when I visited her home and studio in Brooklyn’s Park Slope neighborhood, I observed that many of her works take verbs as their titles: Lick and Lather, Gnaw (1992), Moor (2001), Tear (2008). In reply, she mused that museum wall labels list only materials, not how a work is created. “We have lost our connection to the way the objects we are in contact with every day are made,” she said. “This alienates us from our world.”

As an antidote to this material estrangement, Antoni uses her own body in the place of traditional tools. She has turned eyelashes and hair into paintbrushes, teeth and tongue into chisel and rasp, and bodies and bones into molds. While in her studio, Antoni and I sat surrounded by photographic works from her 2019 exhibition “I am fertile ground” at Brooklyn’s Green-Wood Cemetery. They show parts of the body—the sole of a foot, hands clasped in prayer, a hand resting against the lobe of an ear—and are housed in gilded frames, stamped by and molded from plastic casts of human bones of the kind found in anatomy classrooms and doctors’ offices. In our conversation, she described her fascination with the erotics of the traces a body leaves, comparing the forensic forms that her work takes to the warmth of a recently vacated seat. She framed her art as an interface between artist and audience, a mode of making space for another’s body to enter, adding, “The work is just an excuse to get close.”

BORN IN FREEPORT, Bahamas, in 1964 to Trinidadian parents, Antoni attributes her love of the body to her childhood in the Caribbean. While her mother kept house, her father worked as a physician at a clinic that he cofounded with his brothers. When, on occasion, neighbors would visit their home for emergency treatment, Antoni would play nurse, handing her father his tools while he attended to his patient. “He taught me the miraculousness of the body,” she reflected during our studio visit. 

That sense of wonder was complicated in 1977, when, at the age of 13, Antoni left to attend a Catholic girl’s high school in West Palm Beach, Florida. Keenly conscious of the different ways in which a gesture might be read in the US versus the Bahamas, she began to understand the body as socially conditioned, responsive not only to cultural context but to gender, race, and class. 

Thinking back to the concerns that motivated her as a young artist in the early 1990s, Antoni reflected, “In the early work, I was trying to understand how and why the world responds to me, given that I have this particular, gendered body.” Rooting works in persistent biological rhythms such as sleeping, eating, and bathing, she began to question differences in the body as it consumes and is consumed. Works like Loving Care (1993) and Butterfly Kisses (1996–99) saw the artist transform cosmetics and other beauty products into media for gestural mark-making, drawing attention to the commodified production of gender. 

Some of the same works also take on feminized gestures in the form of maintenance work and reproductive labor. In Loving Care, first staged live in 1993 at Anthony d’Offay Gallery in London, Antoni soaked her hair in a bucket of “natural black” hair dye from Clairol’s Loving Care trademark, the same brand used by her mother. On hands and knees, she “washed” the gallery floor with her dye-saturated hair, satirizing the gestural braggadocio of Abstract Expressionist action painting and the “human paintbrushes” of Yves Klein’s body prints. As black marks coated the gallery floor, onlookers were gradually expelled from the gallery. 

THESE WORKS GREW in part out of vital lessons Antoni took from feminist professors she encountered when she began her MFA at Rhode Island School of Design (RISD) in 1987. Teachers like Mira Schor and Roni Horn were then challenging the patriarchal bent of contemporary art. While Antoni was shaped by her contact with both artists, the lasting lesson was Schor’s, and it came from outside the classroom. After encouraging Antoni to familiarize herself with the work of other women, Schor sent her student to the library with a list of names. When the catalog failed to yield a scrap or mention of the women cited—as Schor knew it would—her point, about the art world’s marginalization and erasure of women, was made. Schor lent Antoni books from her own library, sparking an informal education in an alternative, feminist history of art. 

From that point on, Antoni began to figure herself in dialogue with earlier generations of women, particularly those active in the ’60s and ’70s, such as Mierle Laderman Ukeles, Carolee Schneemann, Hannah Wilke, and Ana Mendieta. In fact, when she was invited to show at the Wadsworth Atheneum in 1996—the same site where Ukeles had famously presented her Maintenance Art Performance Series in 1973—Antoni chose to repeat Loving Care, implicitly framing her version of floor-cleaning as a work of “maintenance art.”

Antoni’s first solo exhibition after graduating from RISD was a reckoning with a patriarchal art historical canon, with works undermining masculine-coded formalism through parody and play. Invited by New York gallerist Sandra Gering to produce an installation in her Broome Street space in February 1992, Antoni opted to appropriate Minimalist forms with a feminist twist. Gnaw began with a mold for a straight-edged cube, which she used to cast two blocks, each weighing 600 pounds: One was made from lard and the other from chocolate. The references she was dressing down were clear: The white of the lard suggests Sol LeWitt’s modular cubic frames, while the chocolate surface, mottled by blooms of sugar and fat, approximates the rusted gradations of Tony Smith’s steel Die (1962).

But Antoni didn’t stop there. With her teeth, she bit brittle mouthfuls from vertices and edges, the serrated enamel tracing grooves in the cubes’ malleable planes. In a 1994 Flash Art interview, she explained, “I was interested in the bite because it’s both intimate and destructive; it sort of sums up my relationship to art history.” She continued, “I feel attached to my artistic heritage and I want to destroy it: It defines me as an artist and it excludes me as a woman, all at the same time.” 

When it came to discussing Gnaw, Antoni stressed the physicality of her process—especially its stark contrast to the outsourced industrial-scale fabrication common among Minimalist sculptors. The act of biting challenged the cerebral distance of geometric form. Then the expelled chunks of material became the basis for additional objects exhibited in mirrored cases in the rear of the gallery: The lard was combined with beeswax and pigment to produce tubes of lipstick, while the excess chocolate was cast into heart-shaped bonbon boxes. Heightening the work’s oral drive, the Gering Gallery invitation card featured drawn cross-sections of infants suckling at both a woman’s breast and a baby bottle, underscoring Antoni’s embodied approach and emphasis on matrilineal legacies. The following year, the work took its place in the landmark 1993 Whitney Biennial, a show that marked a watershed turn toward social justice and identity politics. 

ANTONI’S EMPHATICALLY PHYSICAL practice soon led her to dance. In the summer of 1996, she was invited by curator France Morin to participate alongside nine other artists in The Quiet in the Land, a monthlong residency at the last active Shaker village, in Sabbathday Lake, Maine. Enmeshed in the community, the artists lived, worked, ate, slept, and attended services alongside their hosts. During the residency, Antoni shot the video Around the World, Around (1996) in the meeting house, inspired by the Shaker practice of ecstatic dance, an extension of their belief that physical labor is a form of prayer. The work opens on a shot of several rows of benches, spindled backrests visible one through the other. The camera shudders gently alongside Antoni’s footsteps, which echo through the space as it meanders over floorboards, a fireplace, and more worn seats. Gradually, she begins to turn, then spin. Windows flash into and out of sight. Her breath comes in fast, static bursts. The camera struggles to focus as her motion picks up speed, until all that we receive are streaks of color and light. Suddenly, we see stillness and a skew angle of woodgrain as she topples and lies straining for breath on the floor.

Antoni’s work grew even more corporeal following her diagnosis of breast cancer at age 33. By 1999, she had undergone surgery and completed several years of chemotherapy and radiation. Swapping observations on living through cancer with artist Guadalupe Maravilla in a 2021 interview for BOMB magazine, she recalled that ritual was vital to her battle with the disease, that it was “a process that provides the condition for transformation.” She incorporated somatic dance into her daily life; in 2005, she began to regularly attend 5Rhythms, a movement-based meditation practice rooted in gestalt therapy and developed by Gabrielle Roth in the 1970s. She also took classes with Emilie Conrad, who established Continuum Movement, a form of movement therapy that embraces a heightened attunement to the natural world.

“Dance was slowly taking over my entire life,” she told Abigail Levine in a 2016 interview for Movement Research. But, for Antoni, dance was merely another face of visual practice, and it didn’t take long for her to find a way back to sculpture again. In the summer of 2011, Antoni attended a workshop given by Anna Halprin, a pioneering choreographer of postmodern dance, at the Esalen Institute in Big Sur, and soon they were working together. Halprin invited Antoni to perform Paper Dance, Halprin’s improvisational choreography from 1965. The score is simple: Make sounds with paper, crumple and tear it, gather up as much as you can, and leave the stage. What originated as a movement-based and aurally oriented piece became, in Antoni’s hands, durationally drawn and sculptural. Halprin had instructed her, “Just do what you do in the studio with material, and the dance will make itself.” 

Antoni worked with Halprin over several years before Paper Dance was shown publicly. Over this time, Antoni thought about the intergenerational aspect of the work, noting that it was choreographed when she was an infant. “I was moved by… Anna’s gesture of giving her work away,” she reflected in her studio. “But something else also happened akin to transmission, which I am still trying to understand.” As they worked, Antoni installed a dance floor in her studio, eventually embarking on collaborations with other choreographers, including Stephen Petronio and Annie-B Parson. 

Antoni’s iteration of Paper Dance officially premiered in 2016 at the Fabric Workshop in Philadelphia and was shown again in 2019 at the Contemporary Austin. Attendees sat on and around crates containing Antoni’s past work, visible for some performances and sealed into their wooden armatures for others. In their midst, she moved, drawing with shadow and motion on the impressionable surface of a roll of brown paper, which blended into the nude planes of her skin. She talks of this work as an alternative to a mid-career survey, a history filtered through the lens of flesh. 

BY THE TURN OF THE century, Antoni was equally attuned to the lineage of feminist artists who had charted a path for her as she was to the generation that would follow. From 2000 until 2012, she taught a mentorship course at Columbia University, and spent one week each semester with a group of students in the MFA program. “The whole city was my classroom,” she recalls. “If I teach anything, I teach how to nurture the creative process.” 

Among her students number multimedia artist Chitra Ganesh, sculptor Aki Sasamoto, and performance and video artist Liz Magic Laser. Laser, who began her career at Columbia in the photography department, remembers an exercise in which members of her cohort each held a cube of ice in their hands until it melted. The activity directly inspired Laser’s first forays into performance, which has remained her primary medium since. 

Antoni’s role as mentor and peer continued with some students beyond their time together at Columbia. Laser attended 5Rhythms sessions with her former professor. Painter Allison Katz worked for several years in her studio, a period Antoni recalls with gratitude: “We wrote and thought together. That’s how I work: I think that my students and assistants have helped me make my work as much as I’ve had any influence on them.”

Now, Antoni is preparing for her first museum retrospective, opening at the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago (MCA) in December of next year. In a recent phone conversation, Joey Orr—MCA Deputy Director and Chief of Curatorial Affairs, co-organizer of the exhibition alongside independent curator Adrian Heathfield—said that while the show will primarily feature sculptures, drawings, photographs, and video, “there’s no way to walk out of the exhibition without having had an experience with the body.” 

Throughout her career, Antoni has considered how works are physically altered by time and how their resonance shifts in response to different cultural moments. In a 1999 interview with Stuart Horodner for BOMB magazine, she noted that she never saw live versions of some of the works that most influenced her practice: Carolee Schneemann staged Meat Joy (1964) the year Antoni was born, and Joseph Beuys’s I Like America and America Likes Me (1974) took place before she had immigrated to the US. For her, this fact was not entirely negative: She felt that her distance from the works permitted productive misinterpretation. “They become our works through projection,” she observed to Horodner. “I’m interested in how stories get passed down.” And her own works function in a way like performance documentation, objects bearing traces of a past action: For her iconic sculpture Saddle (2000), she cast cowhide over herself while planted on all fours, her body as much an absence as a presence.

The act of working on her own retrospective with the MCA’s curatorial team has pushed Antoni to reconsider her oeuvre. When I asked whether someone else might reperform Loving Care in her place—whether her works are open to the body more generally or are specific to her body in particular—she deliberated. “If you asked me 20 years ago, I would say no. Because all those works were about my relationship to myself.” But then, reflecting on the passage of time and its potential to transform her art, she mused, “I’m looking for new interpretations of the work that honor its past meanings and push them forward to meet our moment.”

item.title: “I Explore the Human Condition”: In Conversation with Atong Atem - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
Melbourne-based South Sudanese artist Atong Atem uses her body as a canvas, adorned with textiles, paint and symbolic objects. Her work explores inherited traditions and ancestral memories, societal norms around gender and race, and both emotional physical scars. Her images are richly layered and vibrant, connecting beauty and design with lineage of African studio photography, feminist aesthetics and diasporic narratives. National Gallery of Victoria presents Atem’s first major solo exhibition in Australia, presenting new and existing works that reveal her to be a leading f of her generation. The display tells a story of a culture that persists amid displacement, war and colonialism. We caught up with the artist ahead of the show’s opening to discuss what it means to look back at her impressive career. 

A: Take us back to the start. How did you begin working as an artist?

AA: I have always loved making art and responding to my world through creating artworks. As a kid I drew a lot and wrote tons of handwritten novels, all with illustrated covers and author photos. I initially wanted to be a writer like my father, but over time my interest in visual language took over. I went to art school after being an architecture school dropout and everything eventuated from there. 

A: How do you see photography as a tool for celebration and reclamation?

AA: Photography has one of the most fascinating histories of any of the mediums I use. It’s not ancient but it feels like it is and it’s so pervasive that it’s hard to imagine a time without it. I became interested in the camera as a weapon in writing histories and creating hierarchies. In the past, power structures were cultivated and weaponised and photography was very powerful in normalising these fictions. The moments when the subjugated take control of their own stories and yield the weapons used to oppress them are always the most powerful. That was what drew me to photography and its complex past; looking at studio photography in the African context as a significant moment of subversion. 

A: How has your own experience of migration shaped your practice?

AA: I’m still figuring it out. I think migration was an integral part of my early self identification and therefore my relationship to the world around me but I’m now sort of scattered in my identity. More than my experience as a displaced person who migrated, I’m now interested in what it means to make a home in a country like Australia, asking questions about whose permission granted me safety here and at whose expense. I’m also fascinated by what my identity means to my children, who have their own beautifully multi-faceted characters. I’m beginning to find a sense of truth in the fluidity of identities; I introduce myself in a different way depending on where I am and that’s something that I find really intriguing. 

A: You use your own body as a vessel to explore themes of race, gender and colonialism. What does being both subject and storyteller allow you to explore?

AA: At this point in my career, I don’t think about these ideas overtly. It’s kind of an instinctive thing, but it also feels somewhat natural. I enjoy it and that’s the best part of being the subject of my own work. 

A: Your work brings together personal memory, family history and cultural inheritance. How do you decide what to preserve and what to reimagine?

AA: I’m not sure if I do decide, or consciously at least. There’s so much intuitive thinking with the works. I give myself a lot of grace when it comes to the emotionality of my art making. It’s very personal sometimes, and I’m a very, very emotional person so art making can never really be routine for me. I think being a bit metaphysical about everything I do is a luxury and I find that it helps a lot.

A: Passage is the largest survey of your work to date. How do you feel ahead of its opening?

AA: I’m nervous but very excited. I’ve been able to engage with people from the South Sudanese community and I’m most excited for people to see and celebrate our community. 

A: What was it like to look back at the last decade of your career? Was there anything that stood out as a particular highlight or defining moment?

AA: It has to be deciding to have two young babies as my career started to stabilise. I must love drama. 

A: In Banksia, you prompt audiences to reconsider the foundations of Australian identity. What do you think Australian audiences still need to reckon with?

AA: There isn’t much that I can say that hasn’t been said before. At its core, I think this country I call home is still struggling to accept that it is presently colonised. Many places are not post-colonial but rather successful colonies – in that they were colonised so successfully that they cease to be broadly considered as such – or colonial apologists. I think Australia is one of those places. 

A: What can you tell us about As Above, the new installation created for the exhibition at NGV?

AA: It is is a large scale photographic work that was commissioned specifically for the survey exhibition. Its genesis was somewhere between thinking about astronomy/ology in my Tarot series, and mythology as a constant theme in my practice. It was also inspired by the idea of film; still frames in a sequence to make a moving image. I wanted to make a work that was about movement and stillness simultaneously. The endless starfield of the Southern Hemisphere as a backdrop for a body, obscured by beads, in the process of dance or death or fear. In making the work, I captured myself wearing an approximation of traditional Dinka beading and dancing our customary dance called Loor. This work synthesises so many elements of my practice and I think it’s a bit of a pivot into the interests I’m looking to explore into the future.

A: After 10 years of making, what about the themes of identity, belonging and home do you still feel like you want to explore?

AA: I still want to explore it all! I think my work heaves and breathes like an organism. There are minute and massive interests in flux. I can’t say exactly where I’m heading but as long as I am a person in a world with other people, I will always be interested in exploring the human condition through my own lens. 

Passage: The Art of Atong Atem is at NGV, Melbourne from 30 October: ngv.vic.gov.au

Words: Emma Jacob & Atong Atem

Image Credits:

2. Atong Atem, A yellow dress, a bouquet 32022, from the A Yellow Dress, A Bouquet series 2022. Art Gallery of New South Wales, La Prairie Art Award 2022 © Atong Atem.
3. Atong Atem, What we are given 2024. Commissioned by the National Maritime Museum, Amsterdam.

item.title: The Battle of New York - Hyperallergic
item.description:
September 7, noon: It’s Labor Day but some labor has to be done. I see a young man at a cafe wearing a hat embroidered with the words “Contemporary Art Market.” If only he knew, I mutter, and bury my head back into my laptop. 

September 8, morning: I meet Chilean artist Alfredo Jaar in Chelsea. We talk about the rise of authoritarianism, the decline of democracy, and other depressing things. In the evening, this gloominess turns cathartic as he delivers a moving lecture at the CUNY Graduate Center in Manhattan. They serve a buffet but I don’t touch any of it. On my way out, I stop in front of an exhibit in the hallway to educate myself about the Battle of New York in 1776. Outside, the Empire State Building is lit in red, blue, and gold. Turns out it’s to mark the 60th anniversary of Star Trek. Zohran T-shirts are still going strong in tourist souvenir shops. On Park Avenue, I pass by the ugliest public art I’ve ever seen. But I’ve never loved a city as much as I love New York.           

September 9, evening: We throw a pizza-and-wine party for Hyperallergic contributors at our Brooklyn office. I meet the loveliest people. Some days, everyone just seems beautiful to me. 

September 10, afternoon: We publish our first Pocket Review. These are fast, opinionated reviews of up to 300 words to read on the go. In the evening, I hop between several openings in Chelsea, including Johanna Unzueta’s sublime drawings at Casey Kaplan and a posthumous show of Yvonne Jacquette’s stunning aerial paintings at Karma. At the latter, I meet painter Katherine Bradford, who is looking for her lost purse. 

September 11, morning: A single-shot espresso at 7am. A double at 8:30am, and a large drip to sip on for the rest of the day. Kaveh Akbar’s Martyr plays in my headphones. Between two trees, One World Trade Center appears on the horizon.

—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

Artists Reflect on 9/11 and the Wounds of the “War on Terror”

Every year on September 11, New Yorkers pay tribute to the victims of the 2001 attacks on the World Trade Center — and to the wounds of the weeks and years after. That period was defined by grief, rebuilding efforts, and, almost immediately, a vicious campaign of Islamophobia and surveillance whose effects reshaped the world as they knew it. Iraqi-born artist Wafaa Bilal recalls, “I sensed at once that the comfort and security Americans had long taken for granted were gone.”

Bilal is one of several artists from Muslim, South Asian, and Southwest Asian and North African (SWANA) communities whose lives were indelibly altered by the United States’s weaponization of the 9/11 attacks to pass the PATRIOT Act and justify the invasions of Iraq and Afghanistan. Twenty-five years into “never forget,” Hyperallergic asked artists, curators, and culture workers to share personal and artistic reflections on how that day shaped their lives. These are their stories. | Lakshmi Rivera Amin
