item.title: What Does It Mean to Build a Museum for the Future? - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
Who gets to design the future and who is left to maintain it? Groninger Museum’s new programme begins with this tension, placing care, labour, imagination and collective life alongside questions of authorship, architecture and institutional power. Under artistic director Roos Gortzak, contemporary art is being used not as another area of programming but as a means of looking again at the museum itself, and its collection, building and histories. Four exhibitions opening this September bring domestic labour into conversation with childhood, speculative fiction, ceramics and the archive, asking who has the authority to shape shared worlds and who is expected to keep them functioning. What makes the programme interesting is that it does not present experimentation as a new institutional virtue, but attempts to recover an unruly proposition: that a museum might be most relevant when it refuses to behave like a single thing.

That proposition places the programme within a longer history of feminist art and institutional critique, where the supposedly ordinary has repeatedly been used to expose the structures behind cultural value. Feminist artists from the 1960s onwards challenged the division between productive and reproductive labour, asking why making a work could be recognised as creative while cleaning, caring, organising and maintaining remained largely invisible. Frances Stark’s The Architect & The Housewife, the 1999 publication from which the flagship exhibition takes its title, provides a pointed framework for this imbalance, contrasting the person permitted to imagine and construct with the person expected to live within and maintain what has been made. Gortzak and curator Clare Molloy extend that question beyond the domestic sphere, turning it towards the museum and the labour that makes its supposedly public spaces possible. Yet there is an unresolved contradiction here that makes the exhibition more compelling: can an institution critique hierarchy of labour without itself converting those inequalities into cultural material?

Maintenance art offers one answer, precisely because it refuses the distinction between what counts as an artwork and what merely keeps things going. Mierle Laderman Ukeles’ practice is central to this history, having insisted that cleaning, repair and institutional upkeep could themselves become subjects of artistic attention. Nicole Wermers’ Reclining Female #2 brings a related unease into the gallery, placing a reclining female form alongside the functional presence of a housekeeping trolley. Its ambiguity matters: the domestic object has not been transformed into something entirely separate from work, but remains stubbornly connected to the labour it evokes. Around it, practices by Margaret Raspé, Alison Knowles, Evelyn Taocheng Wang, Katie Schwab & Simon Worthington and Alida Pott widen the question of how making, repetition, use and care acquire value. Rather than resolving the politics of maintenance into a celebratory narrative, The Architect & The Housewifecan allow the discomfort to remain – particularly the possibility that once invisible labour becomes visible, it can also become aestheticised.

A different economy of value appears around the table, where usefulness and sociality complicate the status of the art object. Matthew Lutz-Kinoy and Natsuko Uchino’s Keramikos series treats ceramics not as isolated vessels but as carriers of relationships, rituals and histories, an approach embodied by Keramikos 2, a new acquisition comprising more than 300 pieces of dinnerware and accompanying tablecloths. Ursula K. Le Guin’s The Carrier Bag Theory of Fiction supplies the conceptual frame, replacing the heroic spear – traditionally associated with action, conquest and individual agency – with the carrier bag as an instrument of gathering and carrying. The metaphor shifts the emphasis from the exceptional act to the things that accumulate around it: food, objects, stories, encounters and the often unremarked structures of collective life. Curated by Gortzak with guest curator Nicolas Trembley, Keramikos Carrier Bag extends this logic into the museum collection, bringing the artists’ ceramic series into associative contact with historical objects. What is being carried, in other words, is a different idea of how cultural history might be assembled.

Archives are rarely neutral containers, however, and Nieuw Licht 1: Ani Schulze – The Convent of Pleasuremakes their instability particularly visible. Curated by Molloy, the exhibition invites Schulze to work with the museum’s De Ploeg collection as something that can be reactivated, disrupted and made strange rather than simply preserved. Her experimental soap opera draws together historical and literary references while addressing exile, gender-based violence, surveillance technologies and the political possibilities of entertainment. Its title comes from Margaret Cavendish’s 1668 comedy, in which women establish a community outside conventional social structures, giving Schulze a historical fiction through which to imagine another form of collective existence. The point is not to make the past behave as evidence for the present, but to allow incompatible times and ideas to collide. In that sense, the archive becomes less a storehouse of authorised memory than a contested material that contemporary practice can pry open.

Alida Pott’s position within this process is revealing because her relative historical invisibility becomes part of the exhibition’s argument. As the first female member of De Ploeg, Pott offers a particularly pertinent connection to Schulze’s interest in gender, constructed characters and alternative forms of community, while her watercolours and puppet-making acquire renewed significance through the contemporary encounter. Research undertaken for the exhibition has brought further attention to Pott, suggesting that collections do not simply contain histories – they also contain the conditions through which some histories become easier to see than others. Schulze’s newly commissioned Episode 4: Harlequin’s Arrival pushes this re-reading into the museum itself, transforming its architecture into convent, ship and spaceship. Groningen-based performers, choreographers and dancers populate the work, alongside a giant stuffed rabbit whose absurdity prevents the historical references from settling into solemnity. Fiction here is not an escape from institutional history; it is a way of making that history unstable enough to be questioned.

Childhood introduces another challenge to established hierarchies of knowledge. Playing House, curated by Judith Spijksma, asks which rules children inherit, which they accept and which they might disobey, treating imagination as a political capacity rather than a decorative quality associated with youth. Mercedes Azpilicueta, afra eisma, Petrit Halilaj, Eva Koťátková, Lina Lapelytė, sophie serber and Ola Vasiljeva bring together practices spanning installation, performance, sculpture and textiles, while the Biennial Kids have been involved in developing the exhibition. Participation is often presented by museums as an uncomplicated good, but handing audiences a role does not necessarily mean handing them power. Playing House becomes more interesting when understood through that distinction, since its real test is whether young participants can do more than supply an institutional appearance of openness. The question is uncomfortable but necessary: what happens when an institution genuinely allows its younger audiences to alter the terms on which knowledge is produced?

Eva Koťátková’s practice is especially suited to this problem because it repeatedly exposes the rules governing bodies, behaviour and social interaction. Her interest in situations where conventions become visible through disruption makes participation less about entertainment than about noticing the structures that ordinarily pass without comment. Petrit Halilaj approaches related questions through memory, belonging and the imaginative construction of environments, while the wider group in Playing House unsettles the assumption that artistic meaning must originate with a singular, authoritative maker. Spijksma describes the exhibition in terms of sensory connections between human and more-than-human life, alongside questions about how collections are formed and programmes constructed. Such an approach places the children’s biennial within a wider debate about museums attempting to move from speaking to audiences towards working with them. Its success will depend less on how participatory it looks than on whether that redistribution of attention changes anything beyond the exhibition itself.

Architecture gives these questions a physical history. Groninger Museum’s 1994 building was designed by Alessandro Mendini alongside Philippe Starck, Michele de Lucchi and Coop Himmelb(l)au, with different architects responsible for distinct pavilions corresponding to parts of the collection. The result rejected the smooth institutional whole, making difference and fragmentation part of the museum’s identity rather than problems to be concealed. Its postmodern language is inseparable from the 1990s, yet the underlying proposition remains strikingly pertinent – different disciplines and forms of knowledge can occupy the same institution without being forced into one vocabulary. Returning to that structure is therefore not simply an exercise in institutional nostalgia. It raises a harder question about whether contemporary museums, despite their increasingly sophisticated language around interdisciplinarity, are actually comfortable with the disorder that genuine interdisciplinarity produces.

Collections extend that disorder across time. Groninger Museum holds more than 60,000 objects spanning five millennia, bringing modern and contemporary art into contact with design, cultural history and East Asian ceramics. Its histories include Fluxus, De Ploeg, Studio Alchimia and Memphis, traditions in which distinctions between art and everyday life were already under pressure. New acquisitions by Lutz-Kinoy and Uchino, Eglė Budvytytė and sophie serber, alongside Schulze’s commissioned work entering the collection, make the relationship reciprocal: contemporary artists are changing what the collection will mean in future. That matters because collecting is never an innocent act of accumulation; every acquisition also participates in deciding what deserves durability, visibility and institutional memory. A contemporary programme that interrogates those decisions is therefore doing something more consequential than refreshing the walls – it is testing the museum’s authority to determine what survives.

Curation becomes the connective tissue between these otherwise divergent propositions. Gortzak, Molloy and Spijksma have structured the opening programme as a set of overlapping questions rather than four isolated exhibitions, while Trembley’s contribution to Keramikos Carrier Bag reinforces the emphasis on exchange and multiple perspectives. Gortzak describes the programme as a continuation rather than a restart, returning to the experimental impulse associated with the museum’s origins while addressing present conditions. Molloy’s emphasis on long-form programming similarly suggests a slower institutional rhythm, in which questions can develop across time rather than being exhausted within a single opening season. Yet continuity should not be mistaken for innocence: to revive an institution’s radical history is also to decide which parts of that history remain useful, which need scrutiny and which have become myths. The programme’s strongest gesture may be its willingness to make the museum part of the argument.

Museums are increasingly expected to account for the labour behind culture, revisit inherited collections and redistribute authority, yet these ambitions can easily become another institutional aesthetic. Groninger Museum’s new programme is most persuasive when it refuses that neat resolution – a housekeeping trolley remains both sculptural object and reminder of work; a collection becomes both archive and battleground; participation raises as many questions about authority as it appears to solve. The building offers an unusually apt setting because its original fragmentation already resists the fantasy of a single institutional voice. Rather than imagining the future as a finished model, the exhibitions place competing ways of living, making, remembering and gathering in productive tension. What remains unresolved is precisely what gives the programme its edge: who gets to maintain the institution, who gets to change it, and whether those roles can ever be cleanly separated. Perhaps a museum for the future begins there – not with a new identity, but with a willingness to examine the work of making one.

Find out more about Groninger Museum’s new programme: groningermuseum.nl

Words: Simon Cartwright

Image Credits:

All images courtesy Groninger Museum.

item.title: Standing in the Shadow of No Towers - Hyperallergic
item.description:
By August, the Tribeca nightclub Vinyl had gone into a Peter Gatien-era meltdown. Time magazine ran a dramatic cover story the year prior (“What Ecstasy Does to Your Brain”) and the dancefloor had posters warning about plainclothes sting ops. There was still talcum powder on the floor for dancing, but euphoric substances had vanished. In all my Sundays of dancing at Vinyl, I had never thought of how close it was to the Twin Towers — until that Tuesday in September when, by nightfall, the pavement outside was stacked with plastic bags of socks, t-shirts, and sweatpants we had collected for tower survivors who were expected to be pulled out “any moment now.” We waited until midnight, and by then it was clear — no one got out alive.

HBO Television, where I worked at the time, had a satellite office downtown. When I came out of the subway at Broadway-Lafayette, Amin Miah, the corner fruitseller who usually gave me the “best” banana, started saying in a frenzy, “Duita biman marse, ami dekhsi” (“two planes hit, I saw it” in Bangla). I spoke to him for a moment, looked down Broadway at the smoke plumes, and started walking to the office. It was 9:15am, I knew I was late for the staff meeting preparation, and most people on the street were also trying to get to work. I called Zahed Amanullah, co-editor of Altmuslim, because I figured that as a Berkeley resident, he may not know the news yet. His cellphone went to voicemail; later I learned he was in Cuba visiting José Marti’s grave when the tour guide said, “Something terrible — el cataclismo — has happened, we have to get back to the hotel.”

HBO’s Interactive Ventures head, Kevin Dowdell, did his best to pass on a semblance of “normal.” He insisted the staff meeting would start on time, at 10am. Then the South Tower collapsed. We watched it through the window, and then everything started happening in slow motion. Everyone was trying to call family, school, and of course all the phone lines were jammed shut (later we learned the shutdown was actually protocol to keep lines free for emergency communication). My girlfriend at the time, artist Reiko Yamamoto, had no cell phone — most people didn’t, it was still 2001 — and I had no way to reach her, so I biked down to Tribeca to find her. As crowds of businesspeople ran up the street, covered in a white powder, I wondered why nobody was stopping me. Nobody knows what to do anymore, I thought. I arrived at Chambers Street and of course the office had been evacuated already — Tribeca was in the blast radius of the towers, so residents had the sense to shut offices and leave. It was another four hours before Reiko made it home. The first thing I said to her was, “Please, you have to get a cell phone.” It’s likely a lot of people got over their aversion to the still-novel device that day.

The next week, I met comrades from South Asian activist organizations Youth Solidarity Summer (YSS) and Taxi Workers Alliance (TWA) outside a vigil. This was organized by Sreenath Sreenivasan of South Asian Journalists Association (SAJA) for a Sikh man who had been a victim of a hate-crime attack in the hours after 9/11. I had a tiny American flag attached to my bike handlebars. Filmmaker Dina Hossain had just finished work on a documentary about Leonard Bernstein for PBS and had started work on a new project on Islam in the world. The timing was absolutely eerie and she was hyper-aware of the loop of history.

“Where did you get that flag?” she asked.

“Somebody gave it to me, we are all mourning together,” I replied. 

Dina paused, looked at me, and said, “You will understand that you and I are not going to be allowed to be part of that ‘we,’ not anymore.”

Some had longer memories. My cousin Hassan remembered being attacked in 1979 in California as an “Eye-ranian” as the hostage crisis dragged out. Poet Saba Waheed, who had met us at the Vinyl club 9/11 relief point, went home and wrote “when they started bombing…” — memories of the first Gulf War. She ended with “oh no, not again.” I thought she was being extreme. People were in shock, but why would they “nuke Eye-raq”? 

It took a few days for us to learn that there had been several Bangladeshi waiters working at the Windows on the World restaurant in the first tower. In the citadel of capital, theirs were among the many working-class deaths. The media asked for names, biographies, photos. I understood, at that moment, that “Bangladeshi” had been interpellated as “Muslim.” Those stories of Muslim victims of 9/11 became suddenly essential as the beatings of taxi drivers and shop owners continued. In response, we built up the all-American narrative of model minorities. When scholar Mahmood Mamdani published Good Muslim, Bad Muslim: America, the Cold War, and the Roots of Terror three years later, I had the shock of recognition; I too had been one of those apologetic, get-along-go-along Muslims. We naively thought if we were polite in the face of Islamophobia, it would wilt. Our generation’s approach was to appeal to those in power — to ask, “allow us to go about life in peace.” Thankfully, Mamdani’s son, Zohran, had other ideas. Instead of appealing to the power structure, he worked his way up to being in a position to change the system itself.

I lived in Hell’s Kitchen and was sufficiently freaked out by the idea of “another attack” to want to move out of Manhattan. The landlord was thrilled at the chance to raise the rent. He returned my deposit with alacrity. The Russian bouncer at the strip club next door looked at my moving truck and waved at me. He had a scar down his right eye and had “seen it all.” I wondered if he was a veteran of the Chechen wars. On the drive to the Brooklyn storage space, I thought of the magazine profiles that talked about presidents finding God. Surely God was merciful; all the Abrahamic faiths made the same claim.

HBO had sponsored my green card application, and the card arrived in the mail in April 2001. It was an innocuous white envelope, and at first I thought it was a credit card offer from Burlington, Vermont. When I realized what it was, I called my immigration lawyer and asked if I could freely go to protests now (the Abner Louima and Amadou Diallo cases had thrown New York into a turmoil of protests against the police).

My Oberlin College roommate, Saif, was not so lucky. His green card due date was the end of the year. After September 2001, all such applications were ensnared in the dreaded loop of the security check. Saif had the bad luck of having an extremely common Muslim-Bangladeshi surname. You can imagine how that security check went. His H-1B visa timing ran out, and he returned to Bangladesh to work in the business sector. In a way, many countries benefited from this “reverse brain drain” as many immigrants got fed up with these visa mazes and returned home. Working-class migrants did not have those options, and large extended networks back home often depended on the money they sent back. So by and large they stayed, despite the mass arrests on Coney Island Avenue, or crossed into Canada.

item.title: School of Visual Arts Ends Photography MFA Program - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The School of Visual Arts (SVA) will be ending its graduate Photography, Video, and Related Media program in light of the institution's mounting deficit. SVA Provost and Vice President of Academic Affairs Jason Koth disclosed the program's termination in an email announcement shared with Hyperallergic.

In the announcement, Koth said the MFA Photo candidates will be able to complete their degree without interruption, and that the program would close out in its 40th year with the Class of 2028's graduation. The provost wrote that the “painful decision” to shutter the program was a direct result of “SVA's ongoing economic challenges, the nationwide decline in enrollment in graduate-level photography programs, and broader federal policy and financial headwinds that have made it untenable to sustain the program's current model.”

The termination of the MFA Photo program comes only months after SVA announced that it was ending its graduate degree track in curatorial practice next spring with the retirement of the founder and chair Steven Henry Madoff.

Founding Chair Charles Traub, who launched the Photography, Video, and Related Media program in 1988, lamented the MFA Photo program's closure during a call with Hyperallergic.

“I believe that the closure could have been avoided through better coordination and by rethinking how we were going to deal with the future of AI in a more aggressive way,” Traub said.

item.title: Joel-Peter Witkin’s God-Loving, Gender-Bending Art - Hyperallergic
item.description:
LOS ANGELES — Although octogenarian Joel-Peter Witkin’s photography has sparked controversy for its sometimes macabre subject matter, his five-decade retrospective at Fahey/Klein Gallery reveals the practicing Catholic’s ongoing dedication to the principle that “we are all God’s children.” From the 1970s through 2018, when Witkin was diagnosed with dementia, he created tableau vivant photographs, using live models, props, and elaborate sets to create morality tales that blend elements of mythology, the Bible, and art history to express compassion for the marginalized, including people with dwarfism, amputees, and members of the LGBTQ+ community, especially those who are intersex.  

Working exclusively with traditional cameras and black-and-white film, Witkin approaches each photo shoot like a director making a movie, building a set and developing his own prints. For expressive content, he often scratches a negative and treats an emerging print with bleach or encaustic, which can produce textural effects or color highlights. 

Witkin first explored gender bending in works such as “Ecce Homo, NYC” (1975), where a male hippie with sunglasses poses nude wearing high heels, his penis barely visible in dark shadows. The title equates him with art historical representations of Christ, while spotlighting his left foot on a draped table focuses on the female shoe and suggests that wearing it is a subversive act. A similar blend of dignity and edginess can be observed in multiple representations of intersex models, such as “The Three Graces, New Mexico” (1988), “Gods of Earth and Heaven, LA” (1988), which mimics Botticelli's “The Birth of Venus” (c. 1484–86), and “The Soul Has No Gender, Mexico” (2016), where a nude intersex person with long flowing hair is portrayed in radiant light holding a skull, in the tradition of memento mori portraiture. Three nails propped against the wall to the figure’s right suggest parallels between the persecution of Christ and the prejudicial abuses that people born with both male and female anatomy face today.

The controversial “The Kiss (Le Braiser)” (1982) is among Witkin’s most metaphorically potent works. The subject appears to be two men smooching, yet it was actually constructed from a corpse’s head split in half, with one side turned around and pressed against the other. While symbolically affirming the legitimacy of same sex lovemaking, the imagery also conjures associations with narcissism and Witkin’s status as an identical twin (to another artist, the painter Jerome Witkin).

item.title: French Artist Claude Lévêque Ordered to Stand Trial for Rape and Sexual Assault of Minors - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The famed French artist Claude Lévêque, who represented the nation at the 2009 Venice Biennale, has been ordered to stand trial in a French criminal court for rape and sexual assault of three minors, Libération has revealed.

His lawyers have filed an appeal, which is expected to further delay a trial in the northern Paris department of Seine-Saint-Denis; it has already taken years for the proceedings to reach this stage. According to court documents leaked to Libération, Lévêque is accused of using “his position and his aura as a renowned contemporary artist to create a context conducive to committing the sexual acts against the minors concerned and to establish, on a moral level, his influence over them.” The victims are listed as being between eight and 18 years old during the time of the alleged crimes, between 1989 and 2007.

More specifically, Lévêque is charged with sexual assault involving violence, coercion, threat, or surprise, as well as indecent assault on a minor under the age of 15 by a person in a position of authority.

Lévêque was once a prominent figure of the French and European art scene, known for his neon sculptures, which have been exhibited in major global institutions, including the Louvre and the Elysée Palace—the residence of French presidents. But following news of the investigation against him, his gallery, Mennour, dropped him, and venues began turning off the lights of his neon installations.

A judicial investigation of Lévêque began in 2019, after the artist Laurent Foulon claimed Lévêque had raped him in the 1980s, when he was between the ages of 10 and 17. Foulon also told investigators about several other boys who had similar experiences, most of which allegedly occurred while they worked as Lévêque’s assistants, joining him on lavish trips to international art events and exhibitions. During those trips, plaintiffs and witnesses said the artist would often have them stay in the same hotel room with him and sleep in the same bed, on the pretext that it wasn’t possible to book separate rooms. The parents were also given the same pretext.

Foulon is not counted among the victims in the current case because his allegations occurred outside the statute of limitations. Two other people claimed to have been abused by the artist during their childhood, according to Libération, but are also not included in the case headed to trial because the incidents took place too far in the past.  

Court documents outline how Lévêque allegedly manipulated underage boys over years, “gradually escalating the sexual acts imposed on them.”  Victims said they “felt compelled to conform to Claude Lévêque’s wishes so as not to disappoint him, given their emotional ties, but also in order to continue benefiting from access to the art world and these privileges.”

Lévêque has denied the accusations against him, but has also claimed that his relationships with these boys were consensual, despite urging them to remain silent about it. According to a later report by Le Monde published today, the new court order also spells out why that argument in itself is an inherent contradiction. “It is thus indisputable that a minor … is not capable of understanding the nature of sexual acts, of perceiving what is at stake in them, much less of asserting a desire of their own or of protecting themselves against an adult who would attempt to impose their own desire on them,” reads the legal document.

Lévêque’s lawyers, Patrick Klugman and Lucas Veil, told Libération that their client “actively cooperated with the investigation, during which, thanks to significant work on himself, he wished to offer his apologies to the civil parties and to help bring out the truth.” However, they explained they had appealed the court order because they disputed certain “legal classifications.” Once that is rectified, their client would be ready to face trial “within a reasonable timeframe and within a calmer context.”

Anastasia Pitchouguina, a lawyer representing two of the plaintiffs, said her clients “regret that Claude Lévêque, who talks about apologizing, chose to appeal, to contest the legal characterization of the facts. One cannot apologize while, at the same time, disputing the seriousness of what one has done.” Pitchouguina added that the appeal will delay the trial, and her clients “hope he will finally stop making excuses.”

item.title: Tschabalala Self’s Fourth Plinth Sculpture in London Receives Mixed Reviews - ARTnews.com
item.description:
London’s Fourth Plinth on Trafalgar Square has a new art star, and it’s New York–based artist Tschabalala Self, whose sculpture Lady in Blue is the 16th artwork to feature there since 1998.

The bronze sculpture shows a Black woman walking. Donning a baby blue dress with a slit and matching heels, she is “not a remote historic figurehead—but a tribute to everyday women. Monumental in scale—but at the same time relatable. London has already fallen in love with her,” said Justine Simons, London’s deputy mayor for culture and the creative industries, in an Instagram post.

Among the artworks to have previously appeared on the Fourth Plinth are Ecce Homo by Mark Wallinger in 1999, Alison Lapper Pregnant by Marc Quinn in 2005 and Nelson’s Ship in a Bottle by Yinka Shonibare in 2010. The plinth changes every two years and is funded by the Mayor of London with support from Arts Council England and Bloomberg Philanthropies.

Lady in Blue has mostly received glowing reviews so far. Laura Freeman, the chief art critic at the Times of London, gave the sculpture four stars out of five and wrote that “this Lady in Blue is a joyful sculpture with a sashay” and that she “walked away from Self’s Lady in Blue with a spring in my Birkenstocked step.” The Guardian’s Jonathan Jones gave the sculpture four stars, too, and said that “this striding sculpture fills the fourth plinth with humor and life.”

However, not everybody was a fan of the sculpture. The Daily Telegraph, a right-leaning newspaper, said that “Trafalgar Square’s Fourth Plinth welcomes yet another artistic dud” and awarded the sculpture two stars out of five. On X, Steven Barrett, the author of the Public Gallery Substack, wrote that “it must be deja vu, but I thought we did this years ago. And it was tacky then.”

It’s possible Barrett was referring to Self’s 2023 sculpture Seated, which appeared at the De La Warr Pavilion in Bexhill-on-Sea, a seaside town in East Sussex in England. When the sculpture appeared there, it was painted white by vandals.

In an interview with the Guardian on September 1, Self said she’s “ready for a whole gamut of reactions. I’m not nervous—I think everyone is entitled to their own opinion of the sculpture. Each will shed light on to some facet of the reality we’re all currently living.”

item.title: Tensions Ran High as Charlie Kirk Memorial Sculpture Was Unveiled in Times Square - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Shouting and a shoving match erupted as Italian-American artist Sergio Furnari unveiled his unpermitted life-size bronze memorial to slain right-wing activist Charlie Kirk in Times Square on Thursday, according to video footage posted by Al Jazeera and other media reports.

The sculpture was uncovered at 2:23 p.m., the same moment the Turning Point USA founder was assassinated one year ago at a speaking event at Utah Valley University in front of some 3,000 people. According to Getty, the sculpture was displayed on the back of a pickup truck that departed immediately after the unveiling.

The artist self-funded the sculpture, to the tune of $100,000, he said, telling the Guardian that he aimed to raise millions of dollars to take the statue on tour; what he found, instead, was that “People are cheap, man… it’s disgusting how cheap they are.”

Kirk’s alleged killer, 23-year-old Tyler Robinson, has been charged with aggravated murder. A Utah judge ruled on September 1 that there was enough evidence to proceed with the case. The next court date is set for October 23.

Prominent among the Kirk supporters on the scene on Thursday was right-wing activist Jake Lang, who served four years in prison for participating in the Janury 6, 2021 Capitol attack.

In a Fox News interview this week, the artist said that when people first suggested the monument, his response was, “No way. I cannot get involved with politics.” But the shoddy way he says Kirk’s widow and parents were treated, he said, catalyzed him to think again. No matter your politics, Furnari said, “you should have a little bit of empathy.” (Kirk famously said in 2022, “I can’t stand the word empathy, actually. I think empathy is a made-up, new-age term that… does a lot of damage.”)

Kirk was widely mocked online after his death, especially for dying by gunshot while having previously said, in the wake of a school shooting, “I think it’s worth to have a cost of, unfortunately, some gun deaths every single year so that we can have the Second Amendment to protect our other God-given rights.”

The artist told Fox, “It’s a monument to Charlie, but it’s a monument to freedom of speech.” Notably, right-wing activists hounded many people out of their jobs and harassed them, including with death threats, after they opined unsympathetically online about Kirk’s assassination, with vice president J.D. Vance urging his followers to report people to their employers. 

Speaking about Kirk, Furnari added, “He would have been a great president.”

item.title: Ancient Mausoleum Discovered Along Peruvian Coast - ARTnews.com
item.description:
An ancient mausoleum complex was found under a ruined citadel and uncovered by archaeologists in Peru’s northern coast, officials in the nation announced this week. This is the first time experts have found an untouched tomb in the city.

The Chan Chan site, once the capital of the Chimu kingdom, which ruled over much of Peru’s coast prior to the Inca, has been undergoing excavations for decades, with much of the area plundered due to centuries of conquest by the Inca, Spanish colonizers, and looters. Near present-day Trujillo, Chan Chan was the biggest city of the Americas in its prime, complete with gardens, plazas, pyramids, and mausoleums spread across nine square miles.

“It was a feeling of anxiety and urgency, to know if we were really in front of a chamber that had never been looted,” archaeologist Jorge Meneses, who is overseeing the excavations, told the New York Times. “In that moment we realized that the chamber had not been looted.” 

Inside the massive adobe brick ruins was a stairway descending eight feet into the middle of the mausoleum, with a chamber flanked on each side by a larger room. While one person was buried in the central chamber, the eastern room was almost empty and the western room contained a hoard of artifacts and the remains of some 20 people. Eighteen additional human remains were found in other parts of the complex.

A bright red pigment was identified on the skull and some additional bones on remains in the central chamber, along with two others on the funeral platform. Experts suspect the pigment may be cinnabar, a mercury sulfide mineral that held immense spiritual and ritualistic value for the Chimu, explicitly reserved for high-ranking members of society.

Ear ornaments, silver- or copper-plated necklaces, and jewelry made of quartz, shells, and semiprecious stones were also found among a number of the remains. A large amount of metal weapons and heavy beads were also uncovered, along with a wooden chest decorated with images of seabirds and monkeys that contained colorful textiles.

The design of the tombs, along with evidence from Chimu art, indicates that mausoleums of this kind were “designed to be open,” Gabriel Prieto, a professor of anthropology at the University of Florida, who was not involved in the research, also told the Times. Chimu people would leave bodies or offerings and take human remains “out of those burials to be placed on plazas and venerated as ancestors.”

Overall, the tomb contained a total of 38 bodies and countless artifacts intended as offerings for the dead, who are believed to be Chimu elite. The mausoleum, measuring 55 feet along each side and 16 feet high, is approximately 600 years old, dating to a period just before or possibly during the Inca conquest of the region in the mid-1400s.

Excavations at the site are still ongoing at this time, while the recovered remains are undergoing further analysis. This discovery stands to provide a wealth of information on Chimu burial practices and cultural elite, as well as a pivotal historical moment in the ancient Americas, as the established Chimu kingdom faced the rising Inca empire.

item.title: Pope.L Invites Us to Think Through the American Dream - Hyperallergic
item.description:
A headless man stares out with no eyes. An absurd study in portraiture both aesthetically and thematically coincident with Ralph Ellison’s 1952 novel Invisible Man and rendered here in acrylic, oil pastel, marker, pencil, and tape, interdisciplinary artist Pope.L’s painting, “Portrait a.k.a The American Dream Is to Be Able to Think,” (1989–90) beckons closer attention to the fraught materiality of race which inaugurated and continues to usher this nation along. 

Unadorned, bereft of a neck for fortitude, or a face one might identify, or eyes through which to see, existing as just one artwork in the Drawing Center’s sprawling posthumous Pope.L exhibition Certainly an Act: Works on Paper by Pope.L, the headless, and one might assume, brainless man appears to us here already excluded from the Dream. 

Through varying assemblages of black and white — white dress shirt, skinny black tie; white words set against a grainy black background, an undifferentiated Blackness set against and within an undifferentiated America — Pope.L’s probing of the founding racial contradictions which birthed the American Dream unspools here on this 250th year with even finer provocations: If the American Dream is the ability to think, then perhaps newer approaches to thought are needed.

Upon entering the space, thought in all forms abounds as one immediately encounters two walls organized with books. On one side is an archive of 161 previous exhibition catalogues from the Drawing Center; on the other is a celebration of the Center’s 162nd exhibition “Certainly an Act,” in partnership with the Detroit-based Black Art Library. If somehow, like me, you were unfamiliar with Pope.L before the show, which brought me to Soho on a breezy August afternoon, the selected texts which populate the Black Art Library might help to shape your expectations. Boasting names such as Zora Neale Hurston and Faith Ringgold alongside titles referencing Black art, African American mythology, and so on, the Black Art Library alerted me early on that, in this show, Blackness would sit at the very center of aesthetic consideration. Inching towards the glass doors which would deliver me into the exhibition, the exhibition wall text stated that for Pope.L, “drawing was never merely a medium but a mode of thinking about the world.”

item.title: George W. Bush Reveals New 9/11 Paintings: ‘When America Is in Trouble, Americans Respond’ - ARTnews.com
item.description:
To mark the 25th anniversary of 9/11, former US President George W. Bush has officially revealed a new series of paintings about that fateful day and the fallout from it. Titled “Remembering 9/11,” the series is making its debut at the George W. Bush Presidential Center in Dallas, Texas.

The paintings feature subjects such as American flags, grieving people, and images of Bush himself, addressing a reeling nation in 2001. The works “reflect on the courage, sacrifice, and resilience that emerged from one of the most defining moments in American history,” per a description on the website for the center, where the works will remain on view through September 30. (They do not address the criticism the Bush administration faced for its “Global War on Terrorism” in response to 9/11, which “set off a quarter-century of misgovernment in the United States,” as one adviser to Bill Clinton put it to the Guardian today.)

Notably not pictured are the attacks themselves, a topic that has been represented by artists less frequently than one might expect, as critic Jason Farago noted in a 2021 essay for the New York Times.

Bush himself appeared in Dallas this week to mark the anniversary. “When America is in trouble, Americans respond,” he said. “I got to see it firsthand…. It’s an amazing country.”

He also responded to a wave of Islamophobia that followed 9/11. Six days after the attacks, he visited the Islamic Center of Washington, where he denounced the harassment of women who wore hijabs on the basis of their religion.

“It became clear to me that if this was an ideological struggle – which is what I viewed it as – and we forgo one of the most important parts of our ideology, which is the freedom to worship the way you want to worship, all of a sudden, the enemy has won a victory,” Bush said in a statement this week.

Bush, who does not have a traditional art education, has previously painted an array of subjects, including himself for one series of self-portraits and a group of people that he deemed American heroes for another body of work. The self-portraits found an unexpected defender in the art critic Jerry Saltz back in 2013.

Below is a look inside Bush’s latest art exhibition.

item.title: UCR ARTS Presents Dispatches: The Photography of Douglas McCulloh, 1990–2025 - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Southern California photographer Douglas McCulloh spent nearly four decades developing conceptual photographic projects based on building systems to choose where he would point his camera. On view September 12 through December 20, 2026 in downtown Riverside, UCR ARTS: California Museum of Photography presents Dispatches: The Photography of Douglas McCulloh, 1990–2025, the first exhibition to survey the full breadth of his work. Two important tools — maps and chance operations — were central to his practice. He aimed to encounter the visual world as it actually exists, removing intention rather than following the edicts of conventional photography. 

The exhibition brings together McCulloh’s major series in extensive form, including Chance Encounters (1992–1999), in which McCulloh spoke with nearly everyone he met across 22,000 miles of chance-selected terrain; Lost Among the Stars (2003–2006), built around 90 fixed points in Hollywood history; Dream Street (1999–2009), a decade spent chronicling a Southern California subdivision from construction to the collapse of the housing bubble; and his final, most ambitious undertaking, American Cross (2013–2025) — a journey along locations defined by a giant X drawn across the country. He began the project in January 2013 and covered more than 5,352 miles of the route before passing away on January 5, 2025, following a short illness, just over 400 miles short of its completion.

The exhibition also includes The Great Picture: Revisiting The Legacy Project (2006), the Guinness World Record holder for the largest print photograph, which McCulloh made with five other artists inside a decommissioned Marine Corps hangar turned into a functioning pinhole camera. The final single gelatin silver print, which measures over 31 feet high and 111 feet wide, is not on display but this exhibition features behind-the-scenes documentation of the project and a new virtual re-staging developed using game engine technology, viewable in virtual reality or in a screen-based first-person mode.

For more information on the exhibition visit ucrarts.ucr.edu.

item.title: UK AIDS Memorial Quilt to Come Home to Scotland - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The UK AIDS Memorial Quilt is coming home to Scotland on Saturday, September 12, just two weeks after the quilt’s founder, Ally Van Tillo, died on August 30. Marking the first time that it will be exhibited in its entirety in its home country, the quilt will be on view at the Glasgow contemporary art venue Tramway through October 4.

Four years after American activist Cleve Jones began the US AIDS Quilt in San Francisco in 1985, the late Scottish activist Van Tillo started a separate edition to memorialize those who died from HIV and AIDS in the UK. After nearly two decades in storage and its exhibition at Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall last year, the quilt will be displayed alongside archival material detailing its Scottish origins.

First displayed at London's Hyde Park in 1994, the quilt has grown to 335 panels and now represents over 600 people lost to the deadly virus. The quilt is made primarily of three-by-six-foot panels, which correspond to the dimensions of a typical grave plot. Fashioned by loved ones, the panels depict hopeful messages, intimate embroideries, and patchwork mementos dedicated to the deceased. In one, rainbows spurt from a lighthouse toward intimate domestic vignettes on the perimeter. Freddie Mercury gestures out to the crowd mid-song in another panel, which is stitched into a patchwork tapestry populated with individual dedications. 

"At the time, it was a resource for loss, bereavement and education,” Van Tillo shared in a statement just before his death. “It helped people make sense of their loss, humanizing the death of individuals that our government and media were painting as perverts and social pariahs.”

item.title: Before Thieves Stole A Now-Missing Renoir Painting, Family Says Nazis Had Already Done So—And It Belongs to Them. - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The mystery has just deepened around who rightfully owns the two still-missing paintings by Pierre-Auguste Renoir, stolen on Tuesday from a museum in southern France, along with two other artworks by the Impressionist, which were ultimately abandoned in the museum garden.

According to Le Monde, the descendants of the Paris-based, Jewish dealer Jadwiga (also called Hedwig) Zak, who died in Auschwitz, had previously made a formal request for the restitution of one of the two missing Renoir paintings, Jeune femme au puits (1886).

The Canada-based Mondex Corporation, which advocates for people seeking to recover artworks that were often lost in the Holocaust, also confirmed to ARTnews that they have been working with Zak’s heirs to that end. Mondex founder James Palmer said over the phone that about a year ago, his team sent a petition to the French government arguing for the painting’s return to the Zak family, and were waiting to learn whether their request was approved when thieves got to the Renoir painting first.

“We are doing our best to cooperate with local authorities to expedite the recovery and ultimate restitution of this important painting,” said Palmer. Palmer explained Mondex had presented “a great deal of compelling evidence” to back their restitution request, and still felt confident French officials would recognize the family was the rightful owner of the artwork—even if the painting itself may never be recovered.

“At the time of the forced sale of that painting, the Aryanization of Jadwiga’s gallery had already commenced, and that was an important fact,” Palmer added.

Jadwiga Zak founded Galerie Zak in 1928 in Paris, where she showed modern European and South American art. She also married the Russian-Polish painter Eugeniusz (or Eugène) Zak. In 1941, her gallery and home were seized by French and Nazi officials, and in 1944, she and her son both perished in Auschwitz.

Zak’s heirs and the Mondex team hope the Renoir, a painted sketch depicting a woman drawing water from a well, will be recovered with minimal damage. If not, an alternative agreement involving payment from the artworks’ insurers could be one option, Palmer explained. “We have faith in the French authorities being able to resolve this matter,” he said, noting that the immediately recognizable Renoir work would be extremely hard for anyone to sell.

Paul Perrin, chief curator and director of conservation and collections at the Musée d’Orsay in Paris, corroborated some of the Zak family’s claim. He told Le Monde that during World War II, Jeune femme au puits was “seized by the German organization Otto: a black-market purchasing office, and then it ended up in Bavaria.” Perrin recently curated a traveling Renoir exhibition at the Musée d’Orsay, the institution that also lent on a long-term basis all four of the paintings that were stolen from the Renoir Museum in southern France.

“We share in [the Rodin Museum’s] grief and distress. We stand by their side,” Perrin said. He added that any restoration work would be “minimal” for the two recovered paintings that were left behind by the thieves, aside from their frames, one of which initially appeared to have sustained some damage. They are: Portrait of Madame Pichon (1895) and Coco Lisant (1905).

Additionally, ARTnews was able to confirm that both of the stolen and still-missing Renoirs were classified as Biens Musées Nationaux Récupération (MNR) [National Museums Recovery Property], or are informally known as “orphan” artworks, meaning their rightful owners are unknown. This can also support the Zak family’s claim and potentially speed up the restitution process. Lastly, the recovered painting Coco Lisant also has the MNR label.

Allied forces returned thousands of artworks to France from Germany after the war, based on records showing the objects had recently come from there. As a result, most, but not all, MNR-labeled objects were pillaged by Nazi’s during their occupation of France. Thus, the second stolen Renoir painting for which police are actively searching, titled Madame Colonna Romano (1913), has the MNR label, but it is not believed to have been Nazi loot. Records show it was sold without any apparent signs of duress by dealer Raphaël Gérard to the Abels gallery, which had been active in France during the war, and then it was acquired by an individual in Germany.

item.title: Bayeux Tapestry Sustained Minor Damage Discovered Following Trip to England, Artist Claude Lévêque Ordered to Stand Trial for Rape and Sexual Assault of Minors, and More: Morning Links for September 11, 2026 - ARTnews.com
item.description:
To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter.

Good Morning!

  • Conservators discovered two new “small breaks” in the Bayeux Tapestry, which appeared after its transfer to the British Museum from France.
  • Artist Claude Lévêque was ordered to stand trial in a French criminal court for rape and sexual assault of three minors. 
  • The Picasso Museum in Paris is making and selling eight exclusive bronze sculptures cast from Pablo Picasso’s original plaster molds to help pay for a planned renovation.

The Headlines

DAMAGE CONTROL. The Bayeux Tapestry sustained two new “small breaks,” discovered while checking its condition following its journey to London from France, said Thalia Bajon-Bouzid, one of the conservators responsible for the tapestry, via a written email sent to The New York Times. The news, which surprisingly contradicts widespread reports that the tapestry was not damaged at all during its controversial transfer to London, was buried near the end of a Times feature about the tapestry exhibit opening to the public yesterday at the British Museum. Most of the story addresses public reactions to viewing the 1,000-year-old relic, and what has been dubbed “Bayeux fever” in England. As for the damage, it is not considered major, with both breaks “a few millimeters long,” according to Bajon-Bouzid. Still, the news has worried some, like the founder of conservative French art publication La Tribune de l’Art, Didier Rykner. He reiterated what many experts feared: that moving the tapestry had been too great a risk. Plus, it still has a return trip to make.

FALLEN STAR. Claude Lévêque, 73, an international art star who represented France at the 2009 Venice Biennale, was ordered to stand trial in a French criminal court for rape and sexual assault of three minors, Libération revealed. His lawyers have filed an appeal, which could further delay a trial that has taken years to get to this stage. According to court documents leaked to Libération, Lévêque is accused of using “his position and aura as a renowned contemporary artist” to abuse three victims, aged between eight and 18 during the time of the alleged crimes, between 1989 and 2007.

The Digest

The Picasso Museum in Paris has secured the rights to make and sell eight exclusive bronze sculptures cast from Pablo Picasso’s original plaster molds, in order to help pay for a planned €50 million ($58 million) renovation of the museum. [Le Monde]

A recent renovation of the New York Studio School, a National Historic Landmark in Greenwich Village, revealed hidden murals by the artist and designer Robert E. Locher, as well as British artist Cecily Brown. [The New York Times]

Tschabalala Self’s bronze sculpture of a Black woman walking with confidence and flair was unveiled yesterday, becoming the 16th commission for the Fourth Plinth displayed in Trafalgar Square, London. [The Art Newspaper]

Today, a major Yayoi Kusama show opens in Amsterdam’s Stedelijk Museum, less than a month after the artist died at age 97. [France 24]

The Kicker

MEMORIAL BLUE. It’s been 25 years since the September 11 attacks, and many will remember, the sky was a strikingly clear blue that warm day, now known as “Memorial Blue.” For this anniversary commemoration, the 9/11 Memorial & Museum is inviting people around the world to participate in its annual campaign, “Remember the Sky,” by posting a photograph of the sky today (and tagging it), reports USA Today. The idea was inspired by artist Spencer Finch’s installation, “Trying to remember the Color of the Sky on That September Morning,” made of 2,983 watercolor squares painted shades of blue.

item.title: Say Hello to PÉPET, a Pear-Shaped, Palm-Size Paper Pal - Colossal
item.description:
Have you ever imagined a pear or an apple with a personality? If the fruit suddenly had two eyes and a stem-like nose, it might look a little like PÉPET, the palm-size “paper friend” produced by TAKEO Co., Ltd. Originally designed by Masae Nagao, the colorful characters come with names like “Dandel,” “Fuji,” and “Sky.” They’re each composed of more than 400 of layers of colorful paper, and they adorably wobble and ruffle when handled.

Inspired by the saturated red and green of apples and their leaves, TAKEO will release a new edition named “Pomme” on October 14. Follow updates on the company’s Instagram.

item.title: Artists Bear Witness to the Environmental Crisis - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
Worldwide, more than 47,000 species are threatened with extinction. Meanwhile, only 17.5% of land and 8.6% of oceans are protected. Explorers Against Extinction is a conservation charity, working across 30 countries to help protect endangered species from the forest to the ocean, as well as supporting reforestation and habitat protection. The organsation, as well as carrying out tangible, practical projects, believes in the art and photography to help raise public awareness of issues ranging from the illegal wildlife trade to climate change. This approach aligns them with major names like WWF who use imagery, exhibitions and photography books to help promote environmental activism.

 The visual arts exhibition brings together some of the world’s most celebrated artists, from Turner Prize winners to Indigenous voices across four continents, as an urgent reflection on humanity’s relationship with the natural world. The show features sculpture, photography, film and contemporary art, exploring humanity’s relationship with a changing planet. Works come from the studios of East London, the highlands of Scotland, the rainforests of Malaysia, the steppes of Mongolia and the atolls of the South Pacific, and each one has been donated by the artists themselves. This act of generosity is central to the spirit of Explorers Against Humanity, with creatives of international stature displayed alongside those whose communities are living on the frontlines of climate collapse, united in a common purpose: to bear witness to a planet under pressure and to imagine what renewal might look like.  

Visitors are welcomed by an audio introduction, narrated by Stephen Fry, before entering the first of four distinct sections. The opening zone, Extinction, is anchored in Happisburg Beach on the Norfolk coast, the oldest archaeological site in northern Europe at over 800,000 years old. Coastal erosion, accelerated by rising sea levels, has exposed fossils, bones and worked flints that have lain undisturbed for epochs. Highlights in this section include works by Turner Prize-winner Richard Deacon, who fashioned a piece from the fossilised teeth of three vanished species: the southern mammoth, steppe mammoth and straight-tusked elephant. All three were originally driven to extinction by historic climate shifts, whilst the teeth themselves washed from Happisburgh’s sediments. Meanwhile, Andy Goldsworthy, one of the pioneers of land art, contributes a video work in which ancient objects are reactivated and knowledge is honoured, and Emily Young contributes a sculpture of an ancient face, found within a fossil stone at the site. 

The second one turns to the present day, and the work of some of the most important documentary photographs of the past century: Sebastião Salgado, Daniel Beltrá, Richard Mosse, Cristina Mittermeier, Ami Vitale, Paul Nicklen, Michael Kenna, the Swedish duo Bigert & Bergström, and Beverly Joubert. Collectively, their work traverses the broad geography of the climate crisis: melting ice sheets, ravaged forests, drought-stricken landscapes and degraded habitats. Perhaps most powerful amongst the collection is an image from Sebastião Salgado, taken in the eastern Brooks Range in Alaska. It shows a stretch of rugged mountains, rising to over 9,800 feet, sliced by deep river valleys and numerous glaciers. The Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, spans ecozones and is the largest in the USA. It is warming and becoming wetter, with dire consequences for its ecosystem. 

In the latter half of the exhibition, audiences shift from establishing the extend of what is being lost to focus on what is losing it and the efforts to combat that loss. Here, stories of displacement, food insecurity, water shortage and the erosion of traditional ways of life come to the fore. Rashid Diab, exiled in Spain after war forced him to leave the Rashid Diab Art Centre he founded in Khartoum, paints in richly layered earth pigments that carry the weight of a landscape being lost to sand and silence. Jantsankhorol Erdenebayar, builds sculptures from animal horn and found materials, articulating a way of life now under acute pressure in Mongolia, a country that is warming at more than twice the global average rate. Iranian-American artist Nasim Hantehzadeh’s deeply personal work reflects a cultural duality, exploring personal and collective memory through Persian visual traditions, ancient textiles, and Islamic and pre-Islamic art, often looking to nature and Indigenous wisdom for insight.

Extinction: Renewal, Art of a Living Planet concludes on a note of hope. The final section spotlights people across the world who are restoring forests, recovering species, protecting ecosystems and finding new ways to live alongside nature. The curators describe this chapter as “deliberately optimistic,” focusing on creativity, collaboration and community-led responses to environmental change. It includes paintings and videos by Sophie Green, Gary Hodges, Emma Swift, Karen Laurence Rowe, Emily Lamb, and Anne London. The show concludes with Survivor’s Guilt, a powerful spoken-word film by conservation artist Luke Western, voiced by Sir Stephen Fry. It brings together the exhibition’s themes of extinction, climate change, community and hope, offering a moving reflection on humanity’s relationship with the natural world.

There is no shortage of exhibitions about the climate crisis, and in recent years, there has been much discourse about “climate fatigue.” Put simply: it’s getting harder to stop people looking away. In the face of such devastating activity, many struggle to look the situation in the eye. Extinction: Renewal, Art of a Living Planet walks a delicate line. It does not shy away from our situation or gloss over the unbelievable difficulties many communities currently face, but the show is not without hope. The exhibition leaves visitors with a powerful message: while much has been lost, the future of the living planet is ours to shape. 

Extinction: Renewal, Art of a Living Planet is at Eden Project, Cornwall from 18 September: edenproject.com

Words: Emma Jacob

Image Credits:

1. Daniel Beltra, Iceland #5 Hvita River.
2. Paul Goldstein, Big Blue.
3. Ami Vitale, Well.
4. Ashley Cooper, Russell Glacier.

The post Artists Bear Witness <br> to the Environmental Crisis appeared first on Aesthetica Magazine.

item.title: Artists Reflect on 25 Years Since 9/11 - Hyperallergic
item.description:
I was four years old when the Twin Towers fell, and my memory is a mishmash of confusion: my grandmother picking me up early from Pre-K, a pillar of smoke out the rearview window, asking my father why we suddenly had a sticker of the American flag on our car.

I was too young to understand then, but 25 years later, I’ve got a better view. In today’s featured piece, art world figures including artists Shahzia Sikander, Wafaa Bilal, Rina Banerjee, Michael Rakowitz, and our very own Editor-at-Large Hrag Vartanian recount their heartwrenching experiences of 9/11 and its fallout, from being surveilled by the NSEERS program to losing a family member to a forever war. But the future need not be as dark as our past — multiple contributors also mentioned the election of Zohran Mamdani, New York’s first Muslim mayor, as a milestone event that hopefully marks a better path.

Also today, the Rabkin Foundation named the winners of its 2026 prize, including our regular contributor Damien Davis, who has meditated on losing an archive, crushing debt traps, and more in our pages. Congratulations!

Plus, I’d also like to introduce you all to a new format we’re debuting: pocket reviews! At 250 words, they’re playful, pithy, and portable. Read yours truly on I Want Your Sex, in which Olivia Wilde plays a contemporary artist/ scammer/ dominatrix. Yes, it’s every bit as engrossing (and ridiculous) as it sounds.

—Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor

Artists Reflect on 9/11 and the Wounds of the “War on Terror”

Every year on September 11, New Yorkers pay tribute to the victims of the 2001 attacks on the World Trade Center — and to the wounds of the weeks and years after. That period was defined by grief, rebuilding efforts, and, almost immediately, a vicious campaign of Islamophobia and surveillance whose effects reshaped the world as they knew it. Iraqi-born artist Wafaa Bilal recalls, “I sensed at once that the comfort and security Americans had long taken for granted were gone.”

Bilal is one of several artists from Muslim, South Asian, and Southwest Asian and North African (SWANA) communities whose lives were indelibly altered by the United States’s weaponization of the 9/11 attacks to pass the PATRIOT Act and justify the invasions of Iraq and Afghanistan. Twenty-five years into “never forget,” Hyperallergic asked artists, curators, and culture workers to share personal and artistic reflections on how that day shaped their lives. These are their stories. | Lakshmi Rivera Amin

item.title: Family, Memory and Power:Carrie Mae Weems at C/O Berlin - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
Carrie Mae Weems’ (b. 1953) Kitchen Table Series (1990) is a landmark. It is one of the most iconic photography series of the 20th century, comprising twenty images which all play out at the kitchen table, under a bright overhead light. Weems plays the lead, sitting at the centre of the space, as children, friends and lovers move in and out of the frame. In one shot, a man reads a newspaper whilst she smokes a cigarette, lost in contemplation. In another, she applies lipstick alongside a young girl. Here, the domestic space becomes a stage to explore issues of love, partnership, motherhood, gender and self-determination.

The seminal body of work is now on display in The Heart of the Matter, an extensive retrospective taking place at C/O Berlin this autumn. Weems is a hugely influential contemporary artist, who, for more than four decades, has examined race, femininity, memory and power across a multidisciplinary practice. She is the recipient of a MacArthur Fellowship – one of the most prestigious awards in the world – and has work in the collections of New York’s MoMA and Metropolitan Museum of Art, as well as the Tate Modern, London. This Berlin show includes more than 100 installations, photographs and videos spanning 40 years.

Weems often uses her own biography as a starting point to investigate belonging, identity and representation. This is never clearer than in Family Pictures and Stories (1978–1984), also featured in The Heart of the Matter. Here, Weems combines images of loved ones with anecdotal texts. Likewise, the more recent video installation Leave Now! (2022) presents the story of her grandfather, Frank Weems, via a 19th century illusory stage technique known as Pepper’s ghost. Frank was a tenant farmer in Arkansas and member of the Southern Tenant Farmers’ Union. Through this piece, Weems exemplifies the realities of life for Black agricultural labourers in the American South. The Heart of the Matter also includes a new series about Black communities of faith, and their importance for solidarity and resistance. Preach (2024) combines early photographs with new images that trace religion and spirituality over generations.

The exhibition expands from the privacy of family life to public places and monuments around the world, giving special consideration to how these sites are seen and whose points of view they represent. Cultural institutions featured in Museums (2006-Ongoing) include The Louvre in Paris, London’s British Museum and the Guggenheim Bilbao. In each picture, Weems stands in front of a recognisable architectural façade, dressed in black and turned away from the camera. Here, Weems positions these spaces as places of memory and control, revealing how historical narratives are constructed. It’s a powerful assertion of presence in the face of buildings that often fail to equitably represent women and artists of colour.

The Heart of the Matter is an opportunity to come face-to-face with works by an artist for whom the personal is always political. Over many decades, Weems has created a genre-defying oeuvre that spans archival, documentary and staged approaches. Whatever the medium, her series share a common goal: to explore how images create history, form memory and determine who is seen and who remains invisible.

Carrie Mae Weems: The Heart of the Matter is at C/O Berlin from 12 September – 3 February.

co-berlin.org

Words: Eleanor Sutherland

item.title: Brooklyn Museum Displays Work of Artist Killed in 9/11 on 25th Anniversary - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Emerging Caribbean-American artist Michael Richards was in his studio on the 92nd floor of the World Trade Center's North Tower when the first plane crashed into the building 25 years ago, leaving no survivors above the 91st floor. The 38-year-old artist's remains were never recovered from Ground Zero, but his voice reverberates through time with the survival of his prescient, incisive sculptures that link aviation to Black freedom.

In acknowledgment of the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, the Brooklyn Museum has installed “Free F'All” (1997), the only work by Richards in its collection, in the lobby for public display.

“Richards's career was cut so short, so it's wonderful that the museum has this sculpture and that his legacy is really living on through his work,” Kimberli Gant, the museum's curator of modern and contemporary art, who organized the sculpture's reemergence, said in a phone call with Hyperallergic.

Made of fiberglass and resin and coated in rust oxide, “Free F'All” depicts a Black military pilot with closed eyes, arms pinned to his sides, and a slight bend in his right knee as he dons a parachute pack and an aviator's cap. Dozens of nails pierce his body from the collarbone to the mid-thigh, down the length of his arms, and through his hands and feet like that of a crucifixion.

Like much of Richards's practice, the sculpture directly references the Tuskegee Airmen — the first African American aviators to serve in the United States armed forces. The nails embody the racial discrimination and violence that these Black pilots endured while putting their lives on the line as segregation was still enforced in the US military during World War II.

item.title: Tschabalala Self’s Splendid “Lady in Blue” Graces London’s Fourth Plinth - Hyperallergic
item.description:
LONDON — Tschabalala Self’s “Lady in Blue” was unveiled today as the latest sculpture for the Fourth Plinth on Trafalgar Square in London, perhaps the most famous public art commission in the United Kingdom. At nearly 17 feet tall, donning a glamorous turquoise dress and statement jewelry as she takes a purposeful step forward, the towering figure is Self’s largest sculpture to date.

Born and based in New York, Self is best known for her joyful depictions of Black women rendered in paint, fabric, and collage elements. Fabricated from bronze, her Fourth Plinth sculpture is patinated with Lapis Lazuli, a vibrant blue pigment made by grinding the semi-precious stone. Prized since antiquity, the color also appears in many historical paintings, including some at the nearby National Gallery. 

Despite this reference to art history, Self’s sculpture is resolutely a woman of today. In a speech at the unveiling Thursday, September 10, the artist emphasized that “Lady in Blue” is “not an idol to venerate or a historical figure to commemorate.” 

“She’s an everyday woman like the many who occupy the square daily,” Self said.

item.title: Qatar Is Building a Permanent Pavilion for Gerhard Richter to Open in November - ARTnews.com
item.description:
A new permanent pavilion devoted to the artist Gerhard Richter will open later this fall in Qatar, in MIA Park outside Doha’s Museum of Islamic Art. The building was designed by Richter himself and is being constructed in collaboration with Selldorf Architects, the firm led by art-world design favorite Annabelle Selldorf (whose credits include the Frick Collection, the Art Gallery of Ontario, galleries David Zwirner and Hauser & Wirth, and many more).

“Doha Pavilion has been designed by Gerhard Richter as a free-standing work of art and architecture housing a distinct body of his paintings and sculpture,” according to a press release issued by the Qatar Museums group behind the project, which will open on November 20 as part of Rubaiya Qatar, a new quadrennial for contemporary art from around the world.

About his vision for the building, Richter said, “My trip to Doha in 2013 came two years into developing my Strip paintings, and the city’s architecture and history sparked an idea for a pavilion that could unite the thematic threads of that body of work. The Pavilion’s exterior features decorative tiles based on the Patterns that first led me to the Strips. Inside, Strip paintings hang alongside Mirrors and the Strip Tower.”

He added: “Doha is the right place and the only place for my Pavilion.”

Patterns on the outside walls, created by way of mathematically inclined digital processes, “recall the carefully constructed geometries of Islamic art, where interlaced arabesques and endlessly repeating tiles dazzle the eye and act as windows into the spiritual world,” according to the release. Inside, two large Mirrors works positioned between Strip paintings will offer “a literal reflection, or meditation, on painting and image-making.”

Selldorf, the architect, said, “It is an uncommon honor to assist Gerhard Richter in realizing his vision for this project—a major addition to his endlessly probing and fascinating body of work—as well as a privilege to contribute to Doha’s extraordinary ensemble of contemporary architecture.”

Rubaiya Qatar opens on November 21 and runs through April 2027, featuring 25 new commissions and six public art installations among other offerings with “particular attention to artists from outside the Western Hemisphere.”

item.title: Anna Ortiz Traverses the Multiple Realities of the Borderlands - Colossal
item.description:
In Mesoamerican folklore, the jaguar is a prominent nagual, a being with the power to morph into an animal. Moving from one realm into another allows this hybrid creature to act as a spiritual guide through unknown territories. For Anna Ortiz, the jaguar is also a fitting metaphor for entering into a mythic borderland.

Drawing on her Mexican-American heritage, the artist renders remote landscapes through limited, yet vibrant palettes. Ortiz favors subtle shifts in tone and saturation, painting jungle terrain in shades of blues, greens, and pinks. The focused palette emphasizes the fantastic world we’ve entered into, one that appears variable and as a manifestation of myth.

In her new body of work, Shapeshifter, Ortiz expands upon her interest in the borderlands and what happens when time and space collapse. Recurring motifs of an explosive volcano, double moon, and reflective pools of water position this uncanny realm as one in which multiple realities coexist and change is inevitable.

Ortiz’s pieces feel like visual pairings to the work of feminist writer Gloria Anzaldúa, whose conceptions of mixed heritage, the borderland, and the nagual the artist echoes in paint. Anzaldúa’s 1992 essay “The New Mestiza Nation” is a fitting companion to Ortiz’s practice, particularly the following passage:

Certain aspects of identity don’t disappear, aren’t assimilated or repressed when they are not in the foreground. Identity is a changing cluster of components and a shape-shifting activity. To refer to a person who is changing identity I use the Náhuatl term nagual… We shift around to do the work we have to do, to creative the identities we need to live up to our potential.

Ortiz’s Shapeshifter is on view through October 31 at Chart Gallery in Tribeca. Explore more of the artist’s work on her website and Instagram.
