item.title: UAE Minister Says Guggenheim Abu Dhabi Will Tell a New Story About the Middle East, Despite the Ongoing War - ARTnews.com
item.description:
All eyes are on the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi as it prepares for opening on December 11 after two decades of delays.

The cost of the project has neared $1 billion and the country is getting excited for what’s to come. Just last month, the museum named Valerie Hillings as the institution’s inaugural director, where she will oversee the largest branch in the Guggenheim’s four-country museum network.

In a short interview with the German culture magazine Monopol, Noura bint Mohammed Al Kaabi, minister of state at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the United Arab Emirates, said that she’s proud that artists from the region and the Emirates are not “merely featured as supporting actors, but are at the heart of the exhibition.”

The Guggenheim Abu Dhabi is opening on Saadiyat Island, which is an hour’s drive away from Dubai and home to the arts with such institutions as the Zayed National Museum, Louvre Abu Dhabi, Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi, and Frieze Abu Dhabi.

Al Kaabi said that her vision for the island is to attract tourism as it’s “important for our economy. But for our cultural institutions, tourism isn’t the primary goal. It has to go beyond that. The primary goal is an audience that wants to return. How can we create an intensity that engages people?”

In the last year, the Middle East has been caught in the middle of the Iran war and its aftermath has affected many countries including the UAE, which is one of the region’s most affluent destinations. Al Kaab said that the shock of the Iran war “certainly wasn’t easy. There were support programs for tourists who couldn’t continue their travels, but also for the tourism industry — a model we already know from the pandemic. But museums have a different priority, and that hasn’t changed. We continue to build these institutions. The community pulled together, which was very inspiring.”

Despite the conflict in the region, the opening of the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi is confirmed without further delay. Al Kaab said that with this new museum “we want to further stimulate the debate and continue the conversation with our partners. We’re telling a new story.”

item.title: See Inside Maurizio Cattelan’s Highly Anticipated Berlin Show, Featuring a Sculpture Made with Human Remains - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Maurizio Cattelan, the provocateur sculptor famed for duct-taping a banana to a wall and calling it art, has returned with his latest exhibition, a much-hyped show at Berlin’s Neue Nationgalerie. It’s billed as a survey, but in typical form for Cattelan, who once did a Guggenheim Museum retrospective in which many of his sculptures were strung together and hung in the center of the rotunda, the exhibition is something funkier than that.

The genesis of the show is equally funky. Cattelan, who was born in Padua, Italy, and is now based between New York and Milan, is this year’s winner of the Preis der Nationalgalerie, an award that has historically gone to artists with some connection to Berlin. That makes Cattelan a befuddling choice, the Neue Nationalgalerie has sought to position him as an artist with ties to the German capital. He co-curated the 2006 Berlin Biennale, the museum points out.

No, the banana is not in the Neue Nationalgalerie show, which is titled “NIGHT” and which was curated by Lisa Botti, working in collaboration with Klaus Biesenbach, the museum’s director, and Cattelan himself. But there are a few other famous works, including Him (2001), a sculpture of a kneeling Hitler that has previously proven controversial. There are also new works such as a sized-down version of Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate and Dust (2026), a fire extinguisher that Cattelan filled with human ashes.

The exhibition appears to be an unusually sedate affair, and that may be because Cattelan conceived it as something akin to a space for worship. “The Neue Nationalgalerie already has something ritualistic: its scale, symmetry, silence and distance from everyday life,” he said in a statement. “I imagined the space almost like a contemporary church: a central nave, side aisles and a sequence of presences.”

Below, a look inside the show, accompanied by descriptions of some of the works that Cattelan wrote for the exhibition.

item.title: Billionaire Igor Tulchinsky, Who Sponsored the Bayeux Tapestry’s UK Sojourn, Also Funded a Mental Health Facility in an Illegal West Bank Settlement - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The historic voyage of the Bayeux Tapestry to London’s British Museum has been a popular sensation, with VIPs like the UK’s King Charles and French president Emmanuel Macron attending a reception to welcome the famed 11th-century embroidery. Tens of thousands of people vied for tickets. The fragile artwork was allowed to travel only after the French supreme court tore up a lawsuit aiming to stop the loan and a painstaking French study said it would be safe to undertake the trip.

It has now emerged that Belarus-born billionaire Igor Tulchinsky, who supported the history-making voyage, to the tune of £5 million ($6.8 million), according to Middle East Eye, also supported a yurt in a community center in Efrat, an illegal Israeli settlement in the occupied West Bank. The British Museum did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As reported in the Jerusalem News Syndicate (JNS), Tulchinsky is the primary sponsor of the structure, which opened November 13, 2025, as part of the Mondlak Center, meant to serve mental health needs of those living in the area. “This warm and inviting wood-lined space is designed for group therapy activities, yoga and martial arts sessions for individuals coping with mental health challenges,” per JNS. 

The UK announced sanctions on illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, as the BBC reported this week, “accusing Israel’s government of turning a blind eye to the ‘ethnic cleansing’ of Palestinians by settlers.”

At the inauguration of the yurt, Tulchinsky dedicated the center to “Israel’s heroes,” JNS reported, calling the yurt “Israel’s inner Iron Dome,” referring to the country’s high-tech defensive system. “Just as we train our soldiers to run toward fire, we must train our citizens to run toward healing with the same courage,” he said. “Every survivor who stands back up again declares to the world: ‘You can wound us, but you will never break us!’”

Born in Belarus and now living in New York, Tulchinsky is a venture capitalist and founder of World Quant, an investment firm with $17 billion in assets under management; Forbes estimates his net worth at $1.7 billion.

item.title: The Largest Ancient Roman Wall Mosaic Ever Found Goes on Public View - ARTnews.com
item.description:
What may be the largest ancient Roman wall mosaic ever found has been open to the public for limited viewing. Roberto Gualtieri, the mayor of Rome, unveiled the 1st-century CE mosaic, along with a fresco discovered at the same time, in the city this week.

The artworks were first identified during excavations in the 1990s at the Baths of Trajan, located on Oppio Hill near the Colosseum, but never fully uncovered until now. Dedicated by Roman emperor Trajan in 109 CE, the baths were an enormous leisure complex that extended over 15 acres and featured areas for cultural activities and sports as well as bathing pools.

Occupying an underground gallery beneath the baths, the mosaic measures 33 feet high and over 50 feet across. In its original state it may have been even bigger; its uppermost section was cut off when the Baths of Trajan were built, while its base has yet to be fully excavated.

The work’s top levels depict human and mythological figures arranged between rows of columns; below them is a detailed rendering of a port city. Researchers are not sure whether it is a city that existed at the time or an idealized town.

“Either way,” Francesco Pacetti, an archaeologist involved in the excavation, said in a statement, “it has been painted in great detail. You see the stone walls and a main gate with two towers and a glimpse of a temple.”

Elsewhere in the chamber archaeologists found a fresco showing a bird’s-eye view of another Roman town with a theater, a temple, and residences. It is believed that the artworks adorned either a domus—a private home belonging to a wealthy Roman family—or the Domus Aurea, a palace built by the Roman emperor Nero and covered over after his death.

Beginning this month, the mosaic and the fresco will be available for public viewing, initially to small groups of 15 people. The fragile artworks will be monitored during this trial period to see if they can withstand greater crowds.

item.title: Hannah Buechler Loops Thousands of Colorful Loom Bands like Brushstrokes - Colossal
item.description:
A decade ago or so, parents were finding loom bands in the couch cushions and underfoot during a craze for the analog toys. Kids made bracelets and other items, and in the vein of LEGO and other build-your-own entertainment, YouTube creators provided tutorials for elaborate projects. The toy fad may have waned, but for artist Hannah Buechler, the small, colorful rubber bands proved an accessible material for an inventive application.

At a glance, Buechler’s works appear like expressionist paintings, with gestural brushstrokes and carefully chosen colors. But our senses are piqued by the unusual texture, and upon closer inspection, we observe thousands of loom bands in vibrant relief.

Buechler draws upon her interest in fabrics and mark-making techniques of the Impressionists. She’s interested in pushing the boundaries of textiles by using found and recycled materials, and her works often plumb the relationship between natural and synthetic media.

Utilizing a felt template, which also serves as the substrate, Buechler loops the bands onto small tufts of colorful wool roving. Soft and malleable, these segments can be curved and nestled in among one another to create any shape, assembled almost like a puzzle. The finished work retains its textile-like pliability, but when framed and installed on the wall, it assumes the character of a painting.

See more on Buechler’s work on Instagram.

item.title: Princess Diana’s Revenge Dress Returns to Sotheby’s With $300,000 Price Tag - ARTnews.com
item.description:
It’s been 32 years since Princess Diana stepped out at the Serpentine Gallery’s summer party wearing a black Christina Stambolian dress, otherwise dubbed “the revenge dress.” The dress has served as a reference point for fashion designers on the international runways and for costume designers on shows such as Netflix’s “The Crown.” Now, the dress is coming to auction at Sotheby’s London on December 9 for an estimate of $150,000 to $300,000.

The famous black dress was last offered for sale when the late princess gave 79 of her dresses to a charity auction for cancer and AIDS research. At Sotheby’s London, the dress will be sold with the original catalog from 1997 that was numbered and signed by Princess Diana and crediting Prince William with the idea of the sale. This time around, part of the proceeds from the dress sale will be donated to NHS Lothian Charity on behalf of the Royal Edinburgh Hospital.

The identity of the consignor has not been revealed, but it’s understood to be a Scottish businessman. “My late husband and I knew that this dress was something special. Princess Diana was walking into the worst night of her life and you would never know it to look at her. It went from a cocktail dress to a statement in the time it took to photograph her,” said the wife of the consignor in a statement. “Thirty years on, you can say the words anywhere in the world and everyone knows exactly which dress you mean. Bidding at auction and winning it was one of the great days of our life together. With him gone, that chapter has closed, and so should this one. I hope it goes to someone who will enjoy owning it as much as we did.”

Princess Diana wore the dress in 1994 on the night that her ex-husband, then Prince Charles was giving a televised interview with Jonathan Dimbleby confessing to his affair with Camilla Parker-Bowles. The day after, the dress was on the front page of every newspaper. “Fashion can be a language when words fail or are simply not enough. Princess Diana understood that instinctively. What makes this dress extraordinary is not merely that it was worn by the princess, nor that its appearance at the Serpentine event made headlines around the world. It is what it communicated,” said Morgane Halimi, Sotheby’s global head of handbags and fashion in a statement. “On her own terms, Princess Diana turned the dress into one of the most powerful messages she ever made, during one of the most scrutinized and emotionally charged episodes of her life.”

The revenge dress will be on display at Sotheby’s London from September 18 to 24, coinciding with London Fashion Week, before traveling to Hong Kong, Geneva, and New York, where it will be on show at Sotheby’s Breuer Building from December 2. The dress has drawn many comparisons, from Odile the black swan in Tchaikovsky’s “Swan Lake” to John Singer Sargent’s Portrait of Madame X (1884). In 2022, Taylor Swift referenced Diana’s revenge dress in her record “Vigilante Shit,” singing, “I don’t dress for women/ I don’t dress for men/ Lately I’ve been dressing for revenge.”

item.title: Sandra Vásquez De La Horra’s Dreamlike Drawings Unite Nature and Humanity - ARTnews.com
item.description:
As a young child visiting her grandparents in the Chilean countryside, Sandra Vásquez de la Horra went missing. “Nobody could find me. They searched for hours and hours, until finally they found me with a pig who had just given birth. I was sleeping with the piglets,” the artist recently recalled, beginning to laugh. “My relationship with nature is that I’m part of it. I don’t feel separation.”

For more than four decades, Vásquez de la Horra has made work that speaks to the profound connection between humanity and Mother Earth. Meditating on migration, sexuality, and gender, she creates drawings in graphite, gouache, and watercolor on handmade paper, which she then dips in beeswax or folds into delicate three-dimensional houses or accordion-like leporellos. Riddled with symbolism and inspired by religious and spiritual practices from around the world, her works feature figures who exist between dreams and reality: hips rendered as mountains, limbs as branches, eyes as leaves, veins as rivers, breasts as volcanoes.

Measuring 84 by 61 inches, Saludos a Olorum (2021), for instance, shows the body of a naked female figure in a field of saturated cobalt blue, her arms lifted as head and torso dissolve into a milky sun ringed with concentric rainbow bands. Yemanyá (2024–25), a three-part leporello, depicts a woman’s body emerging from cresting waves, rendered in full color on one side and sepia tones on the other. Both titles allude to deities of the African diasporic religion Santería: Olorúm, the supreme ruler of the heavens, and Yemanyá, the orixá of the ocean and motherhood.

Born in 1967 and raised in a Catholic family, Vásquez de la Horra came of age during Pinochet’s military regime, which lasted from 1973 to 1990. She grew up in the coastal town of Viña del Mar and made her first foray into the arts at 12, when her parents, hoping to channel her hyperactive energy, enrolled her in the Escuela Municipal de Bellas Artes de Valparaíso. “Art was the only thing I could do for hours and hours without any trouble,” she said.

In 1995, she moved to Germany to study at Kunstakademie Düsseldorf. She then went on to attend the Kunsthochschule für Medien in Cologne during the early aughts, and later moved to Berlin, where she has been based ever since.

It was during the ’90s that Vásquez de la Horra adopted many of the stylistic choices she still favors today. She started working with handmade paper, inspired in part by fellow Chilean artist and poet Cecilia Vicuña, whose practice prioritizes precarious materials. Around this time, Vásquez de la Horra first started finishing her drawings by dipping them in beeswax, beginning with the series “Botánica de la Evolución” (1999). “I argued that we come from plants, not animals,” she said of that body of work. “I collected old plant illustrations and drew heads on them to explain how a seed is an embryo—a potential plant, a potential soul. I started dipping them into wax as an alchemical process. It felt like giving the works some kind of protection, an aura.”

Although Vásquez de la Horra has been making art for more than four decades, her practice reached a turning point when Cecilia Alemani included her in the 2022 Venice Biennale. For that exhibition, titled “The Milk of Dreams,” she installed her works within a wooden house structure: two-dimensional drawings lined the exterior walls, three-dimensional pieces filled shelves inside, and at the center stood one of her signature houses, assembled from handmade paper. The installation drew considerable attention, including from Raphael Fonseca, a curator at the Denver Art Museum, and from gallerist Tanya Bonakdar, who began representing her earlier this year.

“Before then, I didn’t know her work, and I was struck by her use of paper, her unique approach to the human body, and how she connects it to landscapes,” Fonseca recently told ARTnews. “Even though the work is very spiritual and mysterious, as an artist she is a deep researcher who always seems to be challenging herself.” That encounter led Fonseca to curate Vásquez de la Horra’s first museum show in the United States, “The Awake Volcanoes,” a sprawling retrospective at the Denver Art Museum in 2024; the exhibition then traveled to Santiago de Chile, Buenos Aires, and Los Angeles.

This week, Vásquez de la Horra will open her first New York solo show, “Reading the Waves,” at Tanya Bonakdar Gallery in Chelsea. Featuring a series of historical works and new pieces created by the artist on-site during the past month, the exhibition focuses on water and transmutation as its central motifs.

“For her first show with the gallery, Sandra is transforming the way that artworks inhabit the space,” Bonakdar said. “Her magical way of thinking is part of a larger gesture toward nature, an invitation to transcend our own limits. I feel that the work is very healing and rejuvenating, especially as we all look for ways to find solace and peace in a turbulent moment.”

Indeed, Vásquez de la Horra sees herself as a healer. To this end, she’s sought to personally discover and research a range of mystical practices that in turn inform her practice. “For me, relating to a religion or spiritual practice is about falling in love with a worldview,” she explained. “When I first turned to Buddhism, for example, I was meditating to build concentration skills, but then I discovered the idea of ‘karma,’ and it just fascinated me. Then I fell in love with Santería, and seeing the world through those beliefs changed everything. Now I look at a river and think, Oh wow, this is a divinity. There are so many layers—everything becomes magical.”

Speaking of the ways this relationship to the sacred has informed her process, Vásquez de la Horra described herself as a channel. “My work is not intellectual, it’s something that wants to speak through me, so it’s a surprise, even to me. Whatever wants to come comes, and I’m in the middle, like a medium, taking it all down,” she said.

Among the works on show in her New York debut will be Cósmicos (2023), a large-scale drawing of a palm rendered in soft graphite gray, its fingertips glowing with white orbs and a center resembling a face contoured by rainbow lines; Volcánica (2023), which featured in the DAM show and depicts two female figures within a landscape teeming with volcanoes beneath a smoky violet-and-crimson sky; and Sanando el Árbol (2026), a leporello of a woman’s body, this time featuring a tree emerging from the figure’s womb. 

During her time in New York prepping for the show, Vásquez de la Horra said she felt greatly influenced by the energy of the Hudson River: “I’ve been thinking a lot about the water crisis, we’re not gentle with what we have around us. We are these ecosystems. It’s a kind of collective suicide, what we’re doing to this planet. We’re destroying ourselves.”

item.title: Announcing the 2026 Rabkin Prize Winners - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Marking a decade of support for arts writers, the Rabkin Foundation has named its 2026 recipients of the Rabkin Prize, awarding eight visual arts journalists $50,000 each in recognition of their creative and intellectual contributions to the field.

The 2026 Rabkin Prize winners are: 

  • Damien Davis – an artist, educator, and writer whose work explores how power, race, and cultural narratives are constructed and circulated.
  • Melaine Ferdinand-King – a cultural strategist, poet, and writer focused on historical and community narratives, and the inaugural curator of the African American Museum of Rhode Island.
  • Tyler Green – a critic, author, and longtime host of The Modern Art Notes Podcast.
  • Alicia Inez Guzmán – a critic and award-winning investigative journalist focused on culture and land use.
  • Julia Halperin – a critic, editor, investigative data journalist, and co-founder of the Burns Halperin Report, which tracks equity and representation in the art world.
  • Sarah Lewis – an award-winning author, associate professor of African and African American Studies at Harvard University, and founder of Vision & Justice, an initiative that reveals the role of culture in representational democracy. 
  • Jan Tumlir – an author, editor, educator, and founding editor of the Los Angeles-based contemporary art journal X-TRA.
  • Kaelen Wilson-Goldie – a journalist and critic with decades of international reporting experience who writes often about the relationship between art and politics.

The Rabkin Foundation has distributed $4.1 million in Rabkin Prizes since 2017. An independent jury — comprised of Irene Borger, a writer, teacher, and founding director of the Herb Alpert Award in the Arts; Jaime DeSimone, chief curator at the Farnsworth Art Museum in Rockland, Maine; and Legacy Russell, a curator, writer, and executive director and chief curator of The Kitchen, an artist-driven collective in New York City — selected the winners from a pool of nominees. 

The Rabkin Prize is the central initiative of the Dorothea and Leo Rabkin Foundation, an artist-endowed foundation based in Portland, Maine. Leo Rabkin was an artist who worked and exhibited in New York. He and his wife, Dorothea, valued art discussion and created a landmark collection of what historically has been termed folk and outsider art. The foundation’s headquarters is home to a destination gallery, where all are welcome to explore Leo Rabkin’s work.

Writers are eligible until they win a Rabkin Prize.

Learn more about the foundation and prize at rabkinfoundation.org.

item.title: After a Turbulent Decade and Multiple Delays, Brussels’s Kanal-Centre Pompidou Will Open in November. Not Everyone Is Happy About It. - ARTnews.com
item.description:
This past spring, an eclectic mix of journalists donned hard hats and dusty boots to join Kasia Redzisz, the artistic director of the Kanal-Centre Pompidou in Brussels, on a tour through the institution’s colossal former Citroën garage from the 1930s ahead of its long-awaited reopening. After a crisis-ridden decade of planning and renovations and more than €250 million ($290 million), the 430,000-square-foot complex is set to open on November 28, when it will become the Belgian capital city’s only major modern and contemporary art museum.

Bordering the low-income neighborhood of Molenbeek, the Art Deco structure is known for its 90-foot-high glass façade. Looking down from inside the cavernous glass showroom, with its four floors removed, the space recalls the nave-like Turbine Hall at Tate Modern in London. But Redzisz, who previously worked as a curator at Tate Modern, matter-of-factly pointed out why that comparison is inaccurate. “Turbine Hall is a destination, with an entrance; here everything is a passage, so it’s very different,” she said during the tour.

The layout of Kanal is also quite different: two streets intersect its campus, and over 215,000 square feet of it—including workshops, libraries, an auditorium, a cinema, a café and restaurant, a rooftop bar, a bakery, and a playground designed by the Turner Prize–winning collective Assemble—are all ticket-free, forming what the museum calls a “city within a city.” Another 85,000 square feet are for offices, tech facilities and storage, while 130,000 square feet are dedicated to exhibition spaces. A portion of the latter is curated with the Centre Pompidou in Paris, as part of a renewable partnership that expires in 2031. All told, Brussels’s new Kanal is in fact much larger than the original Tate Modern.

Per their agreement, the Pompidou has about 21,500 square feet in which to collaborate on semi-permanent displays every 18 months, mainly drawn from its collection. Plus, it will contribute works to additional temporary shows. Meanwhile, Kanal is slowly building its own, budding collection with an annual budget of €250,000 ($290,350); it currently numbers about 100 objects.

But not everyone has been thrilled about such an ambitious art museum coming to the European capital city.

To balance this year’s €957 million ($1.1 billion) projected deficit for the Brussels-Capital Region government, lawmakers announced plans earlier this year to slash its funding of Kanal to €10 million ($11.5 million) annually starting in 2029, down from the original €35 million ($40 million). The cuts have already progressively begun, with the current budget of €28 million dropping to €24 million in 2027, and €22 million in 2028. They also echo broader austerity measures across Brussels’ municipal, regional, and federal governing systems, which have impacted everything from drug-prevention services to art institutions and now-shuttered tourist offices. In Kanal’s case, they threaten the future of the museum as it was initially conceived.

This looming financial blow to the museum is bolstered by long-standing accusations that Kanal was a poorly planned vanity project initiated in 2013 by Socialist Party leaders, who lost dominance of the city’s regional coalition government in June 2024, though they have managed to hold onto a close second place as a coalition governing partner. The center-right, francophone Mouvement Réformateur (MR) party now leads the seven-party coalition government, after over 600 days spent in deadlock without a government.

“There is a political will to see this project through—whatever it costs,” Gaëtan Van Goidsenhoven, a center-right MR member of the Belgian parliament, told ARTnews. If Kanal doesn’t manage to find an alternative to “hyper-dependence” on public subsidies, however, “the risk is that this immense ship accumulates disappointments, empty spaces, periods of closure, all of which will obviously have very major repercussions on a project that, to guarantee its ambition, must have very high attendance and needs to be open permanently.”

Van Goidsenhoven added, “We set the bar very high.”
 

How Much Could a Museum Cost?

Some critics of the budget cuts argue that the bar may be high but merited, given what the museum has to offer Brussels in terms of art, direct and indirect employment, and revitalizing the surrounding, low-income neighborhood. Yves Goldstein, Kanal’s founding general director, believes the proposed funding drop presents an existential threat to the museum, and hopes lawmakers will reconsider their current budget. “The reality is that [for] the museum that we built, of course it’s not possible to do it with €10 million,” he said, noting that the building alone costs about €10 million a year to maintain and secure.
Kanal recently won a €60 million government loan to finalize construction, and it has one year to pay it back. A portion of that money will be used to repair damage to the roof of one of its buildings from a fire that broke out in early July in the air conditioning system. (The cause of the fire in the new building dedicated to Kanal Architecture, formerly called the International Centre for the City, Architecture and Landscape (CIVA), is still undetermined.) Goldstein said it was the “cherry on top of the complexities and difficulties that we’ve met over these last 10 years.” Or to use a French expression, the protracted job was not unlike a chemin de croix (“cross to bear”), he said, half-joking.

The delays are indeed numerous. Beyond the current budget crisis and government-less period, the pandemic and the war in Ukraine added €40 million ($46 million) to the initial projected cost of €150 million ($173 million) to renovate the Citroën campus. An early setback began when, rather than renovate, Atelier Kanal designers—a team consisting of the architectural offices EM2N, noAarchitecten, and Sergison Bates—had to erect three new, temperature-controlled buildings, or “boxes within boxes,” to house exhibitions on art and architecture, as well as offices and an auditorium, when the existing structure, with its vast, open spaces, proved unsuitable to actually display most artworks. Some of Kanal’s underground galleries also kept filling with water that had to be pumped back into the nearby canal. And much of the metal foundation supporting the building’s central glass showroom had deteriorated to the point of becoming unstable.

Another significant, though supporters say fair, expense is the museum’s partnership with the Pompidou, which costs a total of €12 million or €2 million annually for five years until 2031, plus nearly €2 million for an early preparatory and consulting phase, including the “Kanal Brut” pre-opening exhibition from May 2018 to June 2019.

Local detractors of the partnership include leaders of other Belgian cultural institutions, like Dirk Snauwaert, director of the Wiels contemporary art center in Brussels. He sees it as a French-first initiative that is closely tied to government cultural policies, which risk overshadowing Belgium’s art scene, despite efforts to include Belgian artists in Kanal’s programming. He added that the Pompidou is “extracting financial means from regions like Brussels, which is virtually broke.”

Pompidou director Julie Narbey refuted those accusations, saying that the Pompidou has “curatorial and artistic independence” from the French government and that her institution’s involvement comes down to “partnerships with a friend.” She insisted the Pompidou is “not taking root” and “establishing itself in Brussels.” Narbey also characterized the €12 million licensing fee as “not very expensive,” though she noted that it is helping to finance the Pompidou’s major renovation, which has closed the museum for five years. Redzisz, Kanal’s artistic director, similarly defended the partnership, saying “we run an autonomous program of temporary shows, curated mostly in-house or by guest curators.”

Claire Leblanc, director of the Ixelles Museum in Brussels, said Kanal’s troubles reflect a lack of coordination and common vision with the local art scene. She, too, is at work on reopening a small modern and contemporary art museum: the 135-year-old Ixelles has been closed for renovations for the past nine years and will reopen in March. But she hopes for a positive outcome for Kanal. “They’ve gone so far that I really wish them success,” said Leblanc. “We can’t imagine that the region could have given so much money for something that doesn’t work out in the end. That’s just not possible.”

Shifting Priorities

Jan Wostyn, an economist who has written about Brussels politics and finances, believes the Kanal project was too grandiose to begin with. “Some in the political class felt this absolute urge to put Brussels on the map in a big way, and that’s a thing that you often have with Brussels politicians: They always look at Paris … but they forget that Brussels does not have the means and size of Paris.”
Snauwaert agreed, characterizing Kanal as the product of a “megalomaniacal” political initiative by francophone authorities. (Brussels has separate Dutch- and French-speaking political parties). He worries the cumbersome “mega-structure” will “drain so much money into infrastructural means” that instead of actually funding the arts ecosystem in Brussels, the money will “go into keeping that machine going [so as] to not lose face.”

Kanal is the only cultural institution currently receiving significant subsidies from the Brussels-Capital Region, which typically does not fund the arts. (This does not count a now abandoned museum project dedicated to illustrator Philippe Geluck’s cat cartoons, itself plagued by skyrocketing construction costs, nor Kanal Architecture, formerly CIVA.) Private funding, along with projections for ticket sales and other revenue generated onsite, will round out Kanal’s budget. Other cultural institutions often receive a mix of public funding from the federal to the local commission levels. The BCR’s exception made for Kanal, with financial backing that dwarfs the operating costs of other institutions—Wiels runs on €2.5 million to €2.6 million annually—has added tensions within the local art community, according to multiple sources interviewed for this article.

The Brussels governing system is notoriously splintered along linguistic communities, which is one reason the Brussels-Capital Region failed to form a new government between June 2024 and February 2026. Kanal has borne the brunt of these rifts and was kept in financial limbo during those nearly two lame-duck years.

Even still, Goldstein, Kanal’s general director, argued that “Brussels needs to have this kind of institution.” Without a major modern and contemporary art museum, he said there is “a real lack in the ecosystem,” which is otherwise vibrant. Prior to his role at Kanal, Goldstein served as chief of staff to former Minister-President of the Brussels-Capital Region, Rudi Vervoort, a francophone member of the Socialist Party. Goldstein plans to step down from Kanal after it opens, having accomplished his mission.

“We did our best to build a museum that is different, not only in Brussels, but even in Europe, and maybe the world,” he said, pointing to Kanal’s goal “to attract people who think that museums are not for them, which is the large majority of our population, and to lead them toward a kind of ownership of a museum, which is the biggest challenge that we have.”

Nevertheless, given the museum’s precarious finances, the move has raised some questions. If the budget hadn’t been slashed, “I’d say he’d have been keener to stay on,” said Wostyn. But with the current outlook, Goldstein knows the next manager will “have to optimize every possible income and cost and find private sector partners— that was not his vision for this project.”

Finding the Money

The Kanal team is currently searching for alternative investment and looking into event-space rental opportunities as a way to stymie the expected loss of €25 million ($29 million) in funding. So far, they have secured some commercial privatization and sponsorships, including hiring out event space for founding sponsor ING Belgium. The museum anticipates 100 to 200 private hire events per year; added to other resources such as ticket sales, food and beverages, they are targeting at least €15 million ($17.3 million) in revenue. Tickets cost €24 for adults who want access to all art shows, including the temporary exhibition. It expects to welcome between 400,000 and 500,000 visitors per year.

In late August, Kanal’s team also met with officials from Kazakhstan and agreed to begin collaborating with the Museum of Contemporary Art in Almaty by October, “with a view to Kanal receiving payment for its services,” such as curatorial exchanges and joint exhibitions, according to a representative from the Brussels museum. It is still unclear how much they would receive from the private museum or the Kazakh government.

Goldstein thinks even Kanal’s staunchest critics will change their tune come November. “The first step—after so many years of criticism, of problems—is to open,” he said, arguing that the financial future of the museum, including its real expenses and revenue, can’t be accurately determined until the institution is open.

Kanal’s inaugural 10 exhibitions showcasing over 250 artists remain “rooted in a local context,” according to Redzisz. They include several shows that will highlight Belgium-based artists, such as “NO SHOW,” curated by artist duo Deborah Bowmann (Amaury Daurel and Victor Delestre), and Maoupa Mazzocchetti; “La première fois” (The first time), featuring a light and sound installation by Joëlle Tuerlinckx and Christoph Fink; “Blindsight,” a sound work by Manon de Boer; Joshua Serafin’s new film installation, Whispering pleas of the eternal echoes; and “Département des Pièges: Metabolic Museum-University,” which includes loans from Brussels museums combining historical artifacts and contemporary works, as well as paintings by Belgian and international artists from the 17th to the 21st centuries, such as  Kasper Bosmans and Guillaume Bijl. Additionally, Antwerp-based Otobong Nkanga was commissioned to make a site-specific, large-scale installation.

Another highlight is the show “An infinite woman: Black archives in two acts,” which excavates the Citroën company’s historic financing of colonial propaganda, notably through depictions of African Mangbetu women. That imagery is then subverted by contemporary artists of African descent, including the Belgian-based Agneskena and Agnes Lalau, paired with international artists such as Simone Leigh, Carrie Mae Weems, Faith Ringgold, and Barbara Walker.

The largest exhibition, titled “A truly immense journey,” however, features 350 works from the 1900s to the present, largely from the Pompidou and complemented by contributions from Kanal’s collection, plus private and public Belgian collections. Artists include Henri Matisse, Alberto Giacometti, Lygia Clark, Sonia Delaunay, and Wilfredo Lam, with works gathered around the theme of movement and migration, whether it be people or ideas.

All things considered, Goldstein is still optimistic about Kanal, seeing the project as “a breakthrough for Brussels” that will bridge two different parts of the city, which he said is “necessary in this time of more [political] radicalization.” By the end of 2027, he said, “let’s see if there’s a kind of Guggenheim effect.”

item.title: Getty Center Closes After Fire Breaks Out Along Los Angeles’s 405 Freeway - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Los Angeles’s Getty Center closed early on Wednesday after a fire broke out along the 405 Freeway.

Per the Los Angeles Times, the fire was reported to the city’s Fire Department at 4:30 p.m.; it has already burned five acres. The Fire Department has issued an evacuation warning for an area that includes the Getty Center, a complex that includes museum buildings host to Renaissance and Old Master paintings, the Getty Research Institute, and a Robert Irwin–designed garden.

According to CBS News, the Getty Center asked visitors to exit through the parking garage and closed the museum at 4:45 p.m. “The Getty Center is closed due to a nearby fire,” reads a notice on the museum’s website.

On Wednesday night, the Getty said in a statement that the fire had been contained and that the museum complex would remain closed on Thursday.

It was not immediately clear whether there was any damage to the Getty Center. ARTnews has reached out to the Getty for comment.

Of the zone impacted by the blaze, which is already being called the Getty Fire, Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said, “Anyone in the area should prepare to evacuate should conditions worsen. Please stay vigilant and follow all instructions from first responders.”

This is not the first time in recent history that a fire has broken out near the Getty Center. In 2019, a wildfire near the 405 consumed 745 acres.

The Getty Center was designed by Richard Meier with fires in mind. Features such as crushed rocks on the roof, a travertine skin, and plants on the campus have helped spare the museum complex from significant damage in the past. “The safest place for the artwork to be is right here in the Getty Center,” he told the New York Times in 2017, the year another fire came near the complex.

item.title: Lonnie Bunch’s Resignation Is a Wake-Up Call - Hyperallergic
item.description:
In 2003, a PhD candidate at the University of Texas at Austin successfully defended a dissertation based on meticulous research across French, Spanish, and English. Kevin D. Roberts’s Slaves and slavery in Louisiana: the evolution of Atlantic world identities, 1791-1831 articulated an argument about how enslaved people resisted bondage by forming alternative social and cultural structures, contending that Black Americans “employed a variety of tools — cultural traditions, secret and overt resistance, and a distinctive ideology of politics ‘from the ground up’ — to tweak, alter, and challenge” white supremacy.

Like most dissertations, it wasn’t necessarily groundbreaking but rather an example of the methodical expansion of knowledge that is the purpose of academic research. Ultimately, Roberts landed a tenure-track job at New Mexico State University, where he taught for two years and was remembered fondly after he left. That was precisely what surprised the faculty in 2021, when Roberts was named the director of the Heritage Foundation, the ultra-conservative think tank responsible for the bulk of the dystopian Project 2025 that is currently enacting a veritable Kulturkampf across American society. Perhaps the most cynical conclusion is that Roberts, a White researcher, studied Black history as a means to better understand and continue the oppression of Black Americans and others deemed unworthy in the eyes of the regime.

I thought about Roberts when reading the disturbing news that Dr. Lonnie G. Bunch III is planning to retire as secretary of the Smithsonian Institution by end of the year, following relentless harassment from the Trump administration. Prior to his appointment to the position in 2019, Bunch had served in several different roles throughout the Smithsonian museums, including as founding director of the acclaimed National Museum of African American History and Culture. As Hyperallergic Senior Editor Valentina Di Liscia and Staff Writer Anna Lee reported yesterday, “Bunch has repeatedly clashed with and stood up against the Trump administration” in its dogged pursuit of historical revisionism as a means of not just White-washing American history, but indeed in facilitating a radical cultural takeover. (They also reported that, “in an interview with the Washington Post, Bunch said Trump’s pressure did not play a role in his decision to step down.”)

Like Roberts, Bunch is a specialist in African-American history. Unlike Roberts, Bunch has used his expertise as a means of presenting to the public the most up-to-date, critically informed, and scholarly rigorous information. That Bunch resigned does nothing to diminish his admirable — even heroic — work but underscores the tremendous pressures that might have led him to this decision.

item.title: The Counterpublic Triennial’s New Kind of Public Space - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The third edition of the Counterpublic Triennial, Coyote Time, has expanded significantly across five main sites and opens tomorrow, Thursday, September 10, in St. Louis. But as artistic director and co-founder James McAnally explains, this expansion moves beyond mere scale, aiming to support artistic practices rooted in real change. The triennial frames itself as an invitation to experience public space differently, guided by core concepts such as accountability, access, climate, infrastructure, agency, and Native sovereignty.

Unlike traditional biennials, Counterpublic relies on a curatorial "ensemble" rather than a team, balancing individual authorship with a collective voice to present multiple perspectives. Selected from 80 peer-recommended candidates, the ensemble members curated sections organized around specific themes across St. Louis. Stefanie Hessler and Wanda Nanibush focus on the ecology of the Mississippi River and the city's disconnect from its three major North American watersheds. Jordan Carter examines scores, staging, and rehearsals of the future in The Ville, a neighborhood in St. Louis, including an operational high school, and other institutional spaces; Raphael Fonseca leverages his teaching background to design collaborative projects with students and work at a refugee resettlement center; and Nora N. Khan explores speculative infrastructures and technology at Sauget, the former Monsanto town, and elsewhere throughout the city.

Presented on a three-year cycle and on view for three months, Counterpublic echoes the late artist Vito Acconci’s idea that in order for something to be "public," it must connect at least three people. When I asked artistic director James McAnally which artists’ practices have influenced his approach, he cited Richard Serra, whose first permanent public work, “Twain,” (1982), is installed in downtown St. Louis, adding that he also takes inspiration from the intimacy engendered by artists like Chloe Bass, whom he is married to, and Felix Gonzalez-Torres. 

Sara Reisman: I’d like to start with The Luminary, which you founded in 2007, and how Counterpublic grew out of it, first as an exhibition in 2015 and later as a triennial launched in 2019. Both platforms connect art, thought, and action to drive social change. What was your motivation for founding The Luminary, and how did you approach establishing it as a space for these ideas?

James McAnally: Both The Luminary and Counterpublic are rooted in linking art with social change. Inspired by the alternative space movement, The Luminary created a context for artists beyond mainstream institutional viewpoints. When we founded the organization, I was a musician, and co-founder Brea Youngblood was an artist and photographer, and others brought varied perspectives. The common thread was the understanding that there was a lack of space for artists to gather, think, and build together. Over time, that commitment sparked projects like Contemporary Art Review and March.

Our core ambition was to move beyond institutional critique. Critique alone isn't enough; if we can’t imagine and build the institutions we want, critique becomes another instance of speaking to power without changing it. Writing as a critic for outlets like Hyperallergic, I reflected on how biennials and triennials repeatedly draw the same criticisms regarding their processes, audience, and resource distribution. Counterpublic grew out of asking whether we could build the alternatives we imagined.

item.title: Remembering Jean-François Leroy, Lucien Smith, and Jibby Beane - Hyperallergic
item.description:
In Memoriam is published every Wednesday afternoon and honors those we recently lost in the art world.

Jean-François Leroy (1956–2026)
French photographer who founded an influential photojournalism festival

He co-founded and directed the leading photojournalism festival Visa Pour l’Image, bringing attention to world conflicts and environmental disasters and bolstering the careers of photographers. He was also a photographer in his own right, and edited Photo Magazine during the late 1980s.

Lucien Smith (1989–2026)
Fixture of NYC's downtown art scene

The abstract painter and nonprofit founder channeled the community ethos of New York in the 1970s. Best known as an artist for his Rain Paintings series (2011–12), he also founded the organization Serving the People in 2017, which hosted weekly discussions and meetings around artists’ ideas, processes, and work in major cities across the world.

Read the obituary

Jibby Beane (d. 2026)
British gallerist and fashion icon

She bridged the fashion and art worlds, modeling for designers like Vivienne Westwood and opening a home gallery in 1994 that supported emerging talent, including British artist and composer Martin Creed.

item.title: Striking Workers Shutter Three V&A London Locations - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The Victoria and Albert Museum (V&A) preemptively closed three of its London locations last Friday, September 4, as its unionized staff went on a planned, two-day strike that weekend. Making up over half of the organization's workforce, some 700 workers organized under the Prospect Union's heritage division and the Public and Commercial Services Union (PCS) took part in the strike.

The strike led the V&A to close the East Museum, the East Storehouse, and the Young V&A (its children's museum in Bethnal Green) through Saturday, September 5.

Many staff members rallied outside the three locations throughout the action, equipped with punny and confrontational signs calling for fair pay and access to water.

“The decision to close three V&A sites underlines the point we have been making; our members are critical to the operation of the museum,” said Prospect's National Secretary for heritage, Paula Lamont, in a statement shared with Hyperallergic.

She also said that Prospect won't hesitate to execute further strikes, including one at the V&A flagship in South Kensington, if necessary.

item.title: Lucas Museum of Narrative Art Faces Lawsuit over Whether It Truly Is a Private Museum at All - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, the newly inaugurated institution spearheaded by collectors George Lucas and Mellody Hobson, may finally have opened to the press and founding members after $1 billion in costs and more than a decade of bureaucratic wrangling, but a new lawsuit alleges that the museum should’ve faced yet more hurdles during its construction.

The Los Angeles Times reported on Wednesday that the museum is currently the subject of four lawsuits by contractors, one of whom is J.E. Snyder Electric, which worked on the museum as a subcontractor for Siemens Industry, Inc. and not directly for the Lucas Museum. Per the LA Times report, J.E. Snyder Electric’s lawsuit centers on whether the Lucas Museum really is a private museum at all. (ARTnews was not able to independently locate the documents for the lawsuit.)

The institution “actively promoted, contracted, and labeled the construction as a ‘private, non-profit development’ to bypass the rigorous administrative, registration, and bonding mandates of the California Public Contract Code, Civil Code, and Labor Code,” the lawsuit alleges.

It would be more appropriate to call the Lucas Museum a “public work,” the lawsuit goes on to claim: “In truth and in law, the Project is, and at all times was, a ‘public work,’ because it is a work of construction paid for in part out of public funds, which explicitly includes the transfer of public assets for less than fair market value and the lease of public land for nominal or below-market rent.”

By way of example, the lawsuit scrutinizes California’s land lease agreement with the museum. In 2017, after failed attempts by Lucas to realize his museum in Chicago and San Francisco, the Lucas Museum struck a deal with the state-run California Science Center, which is also located in Exposition Park, that would see the Lucas pay $30 a year for land usage for the next 99 years. This kind of agreement usually indicates that such an institution is a public one in California, the suit alleges. “We contend this rent concession makes the project a public work,” a lawyer for J.E. Snyder Electric told the Los Angeles Times.

The Lucas Museum rebutted the lawsuit to the Times, with an attorney stating: “The Lucas Museum is one of the largest private cultural gifts in American history: more than $1 billion, every penny of it private. No public funds. No public financing. No public debt. The claim that this is a ‘public work’ is a fiction, manufactured for leverage in a routine payment dispute by a subcontractor who has no direct contract with the Museum.”

According to the Lucas Museum’s lawyer, the institution was clear with the state of California that it was a private museum and agreed to provide public benefits during its construction. Those included the payment of $2.1 million to cover a lack of surface parking during construction, the upgrading of a nearby soccer park, and the maintenance of park space.

The lawsuit also contends that J.E. Snyder Electric has not received payment from Siemens for work done on the Lucas Museum. A Siemens spokesperson did not immediately respond to ARTnews’s request for comment.

The Lucas Museum focuses broadly on “narrative art,” which its founders define as any kind of art that tells a story. The offerings there include a self-portrait by Frida Kahlo, an illustration of Pokémon, recreations of cave paintings in Lascaux, and sculptures of characters from Star Wars, the film franchise created by Lucas himself.

Critics have been polarized by the museum, with many in the film trade singing its praises while others in the art world have panned it. “In hindsight, the $1 billion price tag was perhaps the best indication that the Lucas is, ultimately, a vanity project,” wrote ARTnews Senior Editor Maximilíano Durón in his review of the museum.

item.title: Dimitris Daskalopoulos Collection Donates 51 Artworks to Four Museums in Greece and Scotland - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The D. Daskalopoulos Collection announced a donation of 51 artworks to four museums across Greece and Scotland.

The majority of the works will be spread across the Museum of Contemporary Art of Crete, the Museum of Contemporary Art (MOMUS), and the National Gallery of Greece, all in Greece, with three pieces heading to the National Galleries of Scotland.

The donation continues the collection’s “commitment to making contemporary art accessible to wider audiences,” the announcement stated. It added, “This initiative seeks to ensure the long-term preservation of the works while sustaining an ongoing dialogue with the art of the future.”

The National Gallery of Greece will receive 29 modern artworks by leading Greek artists, including Io Angeli, Konstantinos Andreou, Spyros Vikatos, George Vorres, Kostis Georgiou, Apostolos Yayannos, Giorgos Golfinos, Christos Karas, Costa Coulentianos, Yiannis Maltezos, Christos Sarakatsianos, Aristotelis Solounias, Yiannis Spyropoulos, Thanos Tsingos, Alekos Fassianos, and Yiannis Psychopedis. This donation will bolster the museum’s collection by adding works created during three highly productive decades that span the 1960s through to the 1990s. These artists, in particular, connected Greek artistic production with international postwar avant-garde movements.

Three works by the artists Nobuko Tsuchiya, Ioanna Pantazopoulou, and Nana Sachini are slated to head to the Museum of Contemporary Art of Crete.

MOMUS will receive 16 works by artists Jay Heikes, Subodh Gupta, Seth Price, Josh Tonsfeldt, Kelley Walker, Elias Kafouros, Haluk Akakҫe, Catharina Van Eetvelde, Stefanos Tsivopoulos, and Alex Hubbard that form a larger dialogue with existing pieces already held in the museum’s collection.

The National Galleries of Scotland will receive three works in total. Two, by Mike Kelley and Bruce Nauman, were featured in the 2013 exhibition “From Death to Death and Other Small Tales.” The third is a work by Greek artist Margarita Myrogianni.

Many of these pieces were acquired early in Dimitris Daskalopoulos’s collecting career and were part of the formation of one of the foremost international private collections of contemporary art. Daskalopoulos is an ARTnews Top 200 collector.

In 2022, more than 350 works and the majority of the collection were donated to four major museums: EMST, Tate, the Guggenheim Museum, and the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago. Subsequently, in 2025, six more works were donated to the Guggenheim Bilbao.

Below is a look at some of the most significant works donated in this cycle.

item.title: Trust in US Museums Grows Across Party Lines, Survey Finds - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Trust in museums is rising across partisan lines, according to newly published data from a survey conducted by the American Alliance of Museums (AAM) and Wilkening Consulting, an audience research firm specializing in the culture sector.

In an August 17 visual infographic story, AAM compiled new polling data from January with past annual surveys of American museum-goers conducted from 2021 to 2025. Each year, researchers partner with museums to determine the public's most trusted sources of information across 10 categories. With friends and public libraries tying for first, museums trailed just behind, surpassing the public’s level of trust in researchers and scientists, local and national news agencies, and the United States government.

On a scale of 1 (least trustworthy) to 10 (most trustworthy), conservative respondents gave museums an average score of 7.3, exceeding their 2021 and 2025 ratings. Moderates followed a similar upward trend with an assigned score of 7.2, a 0.6 jump from the 2021 number. Liberal participants scored museums at 7.8, matching last year's average and moving slightly above their 2021 rating.

"People generally do not want political interference in museum content," Susie Wilkening, principal of Wilkening Consulting and the survey’s lead author, told Hyperallergic. "It can be perceived from all parts of the political spectrum, particularly with what's happening with the Smithsonian."

President Donald Trump's escalating attacks on the Smithsonian have included attempts to whitewash its presentations of US history and accusations that its museums promote "extreme political activism." After threatening to strip federal funding from the Smithsonian network, Trump proposed one of the lowest budgets for the institution in a decade. Amid the chaos, Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch announced his year-end resignation this week.

item.title: Diminutive Seahorses Top the 2026 Ocean Photographer of the Year Contest - Colossal
item.description:
As deep swells from an offshore hurricane were further empowered by king tides in Southern California over the past several days, residents experienced firsthand the impacts of human-generated climate change. Erosion is an innate process along coastlines, where waves and wind constantly shift the sand and gnaw away at bluffs. Infrastructure projects and residential development over the last several decades have also meant changes to the natural coastline, and beaches are regularly refilled with tons upon tons of sand. Even so, in just a couple of days, some of the region’s beaches virtually disappeared.

This example is just one in an increasing array of low-lying places where our oceans, which continue to warm and rise, demonstrate their impressive authority. That’s where Oceanographic magazine and Blancpain’s annual Ocean Photographer of the Year competition aims to highlight some of the most beloved, impressive, and little-seen aspects of our planet’s most expansive waters.

The annual contest announced its winners of 2026 this week, awarding top honors to Julien Anton for his black-and-white portrait of a seahorse accompanied by two very tiny juveniles. British photographer Jenny Stock received the Female Fifty Fathoms Award, which recognizes an overall practice that pushes the boundaries of women in ocean photography.

Peruse more images below, plus others from this year’s contest, and see all the winners in the online gallery.

item.title: Women Painters Lead Brazil’s New Wave of Figuration - Hyperallergic
item.description:
After years of institutional exhibitions of Brazilian painting often limited to early-modernist figuration and mid-century abstraction — and the work of Tarsila do Amaral, Anita Malfatti, Lygia Clark, Lygia Pape, and Mira Schendel being feted internationally — a new wave of Brazilian artists is injecting the medium with a sense of urgency and vigor. 

Brazil previously saw a “return to painting” with the Geração 80 (‘80s Generation) and abandonment of strict geometric abstraction; though, as evidenced by some of that era’s artists, including Luiz Zerbini, Beatriz Milhazes, Leda Catunda, and José Leonilson, abstraction never fully went away. Instead, it fused with the materiality of the medium, resulting in a hybrid approach still present in contemporary painting.

While Brazilian women artists have certainly challenged stereotypes of beauty and womanhood before — Anna Bella Geiger and Lenora de Barros immediately come to mind — the frankness with which Brazilian women painters depict eroticism today, be it through their dogged, unvarnished portrayals of the female body and desire, or their bracing examinations of violence against women, seems uniquely of the moment.

Here are five artists to know.

Panmela Castro

Upon seeing Castro’s somber yet invigorating 2021–22 solo show at Galeria Luisa Strina in São Paulo, curated by Daniela Labra, I was immediately struck by its title: To Flaunt is to be alive. Here, flaunting didn’t mean flagging one’s status or possessions, but rather presenting one’s body candidly and intimately to affirm its resilience. In a series of nudes, Castro sometimes depicts a sitter twice, as if imagining her own painting already hanging on the sitter’s wall. Such doubling brought to mind the paucity of institutional archive imagery that preserves the memories of Black-Brazilian communities — the fact that representation, or lack of it, is always a political act.

Castro conveys grit in works including a neon sign that reads “Cada Día Peor” (Worse Every Day) (“Vulcanica Pokaropa,” from the Vigil series, 2021) and a three-dimensional text-based sculpture that reads “Eu Sobrevivi” (I survived),  from the Residency series (2021). Psychological and physical pain recur in Castro’s works, where the act of commemoration through portraiture or a self-reflexive testimonial gesture toward symbolic recovery.

item.title: Amateur Metal Detectorist Finds Finland’s Largest Viking-Age Silver Hoard - ARTnews.com
item.description:
A hoard of thousands of silver coins was unearthed by an amateur metal detectorist in southern Finland. Experts at Lahti Museums believe it’s the largest Viking-era coin hoard found in the country, Heritage Daily reported.

Kalle Lappinen made the find with a metal detector near Sysmä church village on September 3. Archaeologists have since inspected the site and recovered a trove of almost 10 pounds of silver coins, with individual pieces still to be cleaned, separated, and counted.

The silver hoard was discovered inside two straw containers nearly 18 inches below the ground and about 40 feet apart. It includes coins, a fragment of silver, a bracelet, a clasp, and a bead. Each object will undergo conservation and analysis to determine the exact age and material composition. It is roughly from Finland’s Late Iron Age, which includes the Viking Age.

It is unclear who owned it, why the treasure was buried, and if the two vessels were simultaneously or separately buried.

Researchers expect to learn more about how valuables were concealed due to the survival of the straw containers. The coins and remnants could also reveal trade connections and wealth patterns from the period.

The last time a hoard of this size was discovered was in Nousiainen in 1895. Just shy of five pounds, it contained some 1,700 coins and other objects.

item.title: Karla Wong’s Folkloric Portraits Conjure Mysterious Portals to Another World - Colossal
item.description:
Although Karla Wong has always been passionate about drawing, it was her degree in law that ultimately spurred her current practice. The Mexican artist spent her adolescent and early adult years in Oaxaca, where she attended university and eventually became a forensic and witness sketch artist for the local justice department. Rendering a figure’s likeness based solely on a description is a deeply imaginative process and one that continues to inform the artist’s practice today.

In Journeys of Being on view now at Chicago’s Intuit Art Museum, Wong presents a vibrant body of work that entwines her Oaxacan roots with her Chinese heritage and experiences as a trans woman living between the U.S. and Mexico. Included are vibrant portraits with skeletal figures evocative of Day of the Dead, the folk art sculptures known as alebrijes, and a desert landscape pocked with agave. Victorian garb and faces adorned with makeup gesture toward the performance of gender, too, and the ways we signify beauty and self-expression.

Surrealism and the uncanny inspire much of Wong’s work, and mysterious pockets of clouds and small openings also appear like portals to another world. Paintings like “Our Brief Passage Through Life (Nuestro breve paso por la vida)” share an affinity with the alchemical works of Spanish artist Remedios Varo, who portrayed more-than-human figures with odd proportions.

Playing with scale and atypical pairings of objects and motifs is characteristic of Wong. Unlike the lifelike renditions she created as a sketch artist, these vivid paintings stray from any predetermined script and instead envision a world entirely her own.

If you’re in Chicago, see Journeys of Being through January 10. Keep up with Wong’s work on Instagram.

item.title: Could a Kid Do It? The Wa Transforms Buildings into Childlike Drawings - Colossal
item.description:
Although there’s no official count, the amount of World War II bunkers, battery platforms, defensive bollards, and other structures found along European coastlines probably number in the tens of thousands. Bunkers were typically made of concrete, and several thousand are located along what’s known as the Atlantic Wall, an extensive coastal network of defenses built by the Nazis between 1942 and 1944 in anticipation of attacks by Allied forces. Disused now for decades, they’re a blight on the landscape, but one that The Wa sees as a blank canvas for something much more playful and bright.

In his series A Kid Could Do It, The Wa transforms otherwise nondescript structures into jubilantly youthful drawings, literally scribbling in saturated colors and adding blocky windows, doors, and flowers. The title of the project, of course, will sound familiar to any artist working in abstraction or museum-goer who has stood looking at a Jackson Pollock or Franz Kline painting and heard someone nearby murmur derisively, “My kid could do that.”

The Wa turns the table on this sentiment, including in a large-scale rendition on an empty house in Stuttgart as part of this year’s PFFFestival. We encounter windows with purple curtains in seemingly random places, a door that’s narrower on the bottom than the top, a roof with scalloped shapes that could be shingles or clouds, and of course, huge scrawls of bright blue and red.

For PFFFestival, as with his earlier bunker paintings, the artist follows what he describes as “one simple rule: the unfiltered creative logic of a child.” A Kid Could Do It also nods to the collaborative nature of how the project began, as The Wa started the series by working alongside his mother. In a manner of speaking, a kid really did do it.

See more on The Wa’s Instagram.

item.title: Valie Export Was Ahead of Her Time and as Subtle as She Was Provocative - ARTnews.com
item.description:
One chilly but sparkling afternoon this past January, I made a pilgrimage. The destination was a somewhat unlikely site for work by one of the most iconoclastic (in every sense of that term) feminist artists of the last century: a Roman Catholic church. The Pöstlingberg basilica gleams atop the steep hill of the same name, looking out upon a wide vista of the Danube flowing through Linz—where VALIE EXPORT, born Waltraud Lehner in Nazi-era Austria, spent her formative years. 

I was led to the summit, admittedly not on foot, by Dagmar Schink, managing director of the VALIE EXPORT Center, established in the artist’s hometown in 2017, five decades after EXPORT changed her name in an acute rejection of patronymics and all they represented in her postwar milieu. After we reached the late-Baroque structure, brimming inside with billowing gilt ornament and trompe-l’oeil frescoes, my intrepid guide convinced a parish employee to lend us a key that unlocked a stairwell. We were greeted at the top by a shock of silver and the crisp, sweeping curves of a pipe organ designed by EXPORT and installed there in 2022. Across the instrument’s undulating facade, in cut-out letters backlit by colored lights, are words that began to appear in her work in the 1970s. Whoever understands has wings, the organ proclaims, projecting this sentence, like a piercing chord, toward the altar at the opposite end of the church.

A few months after this sojourn, the world lost EXPORT. Her death came during a time defined by compounding grief, especially for those invested in the feminist project out of which the artist’s work emerged. By comparison, the period of second-wave feminism can seem like—or, more accurately, can be idealized as—a moment of both endless possibility and political cohesion. 

In the wake of her passing, at least one prominent online obituary included a video of TAP and TOUCH CINEMA, first performed in 1968 and later becoming something of a synecdoche both for EXPORT’s work and feminist performance art writ large. The video shows passersby on the street reaching inside a box, figured as a miniature movie theater and worn around the artist’s torso, in order to feel her breasts. The surviving footage was originally aired by the ORF, Austria’s national public broadcaster. Just before a man reaches into the “theater” surrounding EXPORT’s upper body, there’s a quick cut to a shot from another part of the program (blink and you’ll miss it). In this other segment, EXPORT runs toward the camera while it tracks backward. Barreling forward, she chants a dizzying list: “…expanded movies… film objects… communication actions… multimedia programs…” 

Hiding in plain sight, in the midst of arguably her best-known work, EXPORT’s sprinting incantation speaks to the urgent yet playful experimentation that drove her practice, spanning performance, conceptual photography, televised video, publications, curatorial ventures, three feature films… you can lose your breath trying to keep up.

But what did participants (who were not only men, it should be noted) encounter in their confrontation with EXPORT’s body in this performance? The answers—a critique of male cinematic voyeurism, an assertion of female bodily autonomy—are important, but often come too quickly. Blunted certainty about the stakes of 1960s and ’70s feminism runs the risk of not only mummifying the period’s radically open-ended modes of questioning, but also fueling, in the process, our current fascist turn. For all its insistence on the gendered body, EXPORT’s work refuses too-easy answers to that insidiously transphobic question: “What is a woman?” 

In the prominent phrase on the organ she designed for Linz, the German verb for “understand,” begreifen, has the sense, resonating with English, of “grasping” something with the mind, acting like the hand. Understanding is here, if anything, a deeply physical, embodied act. But in EXPORT’s phrasing, primate fingers and opposable thumbs loosen, transforming into feathered wings. Her legacy, that most petrified of terms, resides precisely in the ways her art unsettles what we think we understand about the overlapping historical, political, and mediatic landscapes in which it intervened. Through some uncharted territory, I imagine her running breathlessly on, even to the point, eventually, of taking flight.

item.title: Christie’s to Auction Peter Simon’s $172 M. Art Collection, Led by Bacon, Mondrian, Warhol Works - ARTnews.com
item.description:
An art collection, estimated to be worth £87 million to £127 million ($118 million to $172 million), featuring works by Francis Bacon, Ben Nicholson, Barbara Hepworth, Piet Mondrian, Pablo Picasso, Jeff Koons, and more, is coming to Christie’s on October 14 and 15 during Frieze Week. The collection belongs to British businessman and art collector Peter Simon, who has appeared on each edition of ARTnews’ Top 200 Collectors list since 2005.

The sale of “Monsoon: The Peter Simon Collection” is the highest-value single-owner collection offered to date at Christie’s London. Comprising nearly 200 works, the sale will be spread across three auctions: an evening sale, a day sale, and an online auction.

Simon is the founder of fashion retailer Monsoon and Accessorize. In a statement, he explained that in the early days of Monsoon, he would sit with “fashion and textile designers sifting portfolio after portfolio” selecting work that could be converted onto fabric. Handpicking colors and prints, he added, informed his taste and ability to “zero in on the best combination of color and composition in a picture.”

When he was building his art collection, he first started with British artists, notably Bacon, Nicholson, and Hepworth. Simon’s aim was to always “build links and foster dialogue across different worlds” and now he wants to start collecting in “a new direction.”

The highlight lot includes two Bacon’s works: Figure in Movement (1978) estimated for £14 million to £18 million ($19 million to $24.4 million) and Study for a Figure (ca. 1945) estimated for £4 million to £6 million ($5.4 million to $8 million). The Mondrian Composition A, with Double Line and Yellow (1935) is estimated to go under the gavel for £8 million to £12 million ($11 million to $16 million), while Joan Miró’s Peinture (Les amants – Adam et Eve), 1925, is estimated for £7 million to £10 million ($9.5 million to $14 million).

The collection also includes works from Frank Auerbach, Leon Kossoff, Fernand Léger, Willem de Kooning, and Andy Warhol’s Diamond Dust Shoe (1980) estimated for £1.8 million to £2.5 million ($2.4 million to $3.4 million), which spans more than two meters in height and is a nod to the artist’s career as a commercial illustrator in the 1950s, where he had earned the moniker “Leonardo da Vinci of the shoe trade” by Women’s Wear Daily.

Katharine Arnold, Christie’s vice chairman of 20th and 21st century art in Europe, described Simon’s collection as “dynamic” and “unbridled by geography and time.”

item.title: Lonnie G. Bunch Has Had Enough - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Lonnie G. Bunch III has had it. After months of incessant harassment and political prodding from the Trump White House, the Smithsonian Secretary announced that he's quitting his job with “very mixed emotions." What a sad way to kick off the fall season. 

It's also sad to see New York artist Lucien Smith die at the very young age of 37. Once a market darling, he had abandoned the commercial art world for more community-focused work. Associate Editor Phillip Pyle looks back at his life and career.    

Also in the news: Another week, another museum heist in Europe. This time, two paintings disappear from the Renoir Museum in southern France. According to police, the thieves dropped two other paintings in the museum’s garden while officers chased them. 

Much more to read below, including John Yau on Law & Order writer and producer René Balcer, who also happens to be a photographer. Maybe Balcer can help Europe with its museum heist problem ... DUN DUN.  

—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

The Law & Order Writer Who Moonlights as an Artist

Is René Balcer a street photographer, a documentary photographer, or a landscape photographer? All the above and more.

Despite his achievements as a producer and writer for Law & Order — including a Primetime Emmy Award and multiple Edgar Awards — the throughline of Balcer’s life was direct photography.

After studying poetry and photography at Concordia University in Montreal and taking a six-month seminar taught by the French New Wave filmmaker Jean-Luc Godard, Balcer worked as a cameraman, war reporter, editor, scriptwriter, documentary filmmaker, and film critic. Like Godard and other New Wave filmmakers, Balcer wrote reviews and made films, merging commentary and creativity. | John Yau
