item.title: Jenny Holzer and Andy Goldsworthy Win $95,000 Praemium Imperiale Award - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Artists Jenny Holzer and Andy Goldsworthy are among the five recipients of Japan’s 37th Praemium Imperiale award—one of the world’s largest art prizes, dubbed by some the “Nobel Prize of the Arts.” They will each win 15 million yen (about $95,000).

The award celebrates lifetime contributions to painting, sculpture, architecture, music, and theater/film on a global scale. Fellow laureates this year include actor Cate Blanchett, who has won Academy Awards for performances in Blue Jasmine (2013) and Elizabeth (1998); Polish American architect Daniel Libeskind, known for his Jewish Museum design in Berlin; and the 99-year-old Swedish American symphony conductor Herbert Blomstedt, who is often considered one of the world’s greatest.

Holzer, chosen for the award’s painter category, has been using language and text as a conduit for shifting the ways we address questions of power, memory, and justice. Often with clear-eyed wit, the New York–based artist has her way with words that can appear on posters, electronic signs, stone carvings, light projections, large installations, and—yes!—on paintings, as the award category suggests.

“Her practice explores the political and social implications of public speech and the relationship between language and space,” states a press release. Holzer’s text-based works have been exhibited at the Venice Biennale, where she won the Golden Lion in 1990; the Guggenheim Museums; the Louvre Abu Dhabi; and the Museum of Modern Art in New York, to name a few. She also has a major solo exhibition coming up at the Musée d’Orsay in Paris this fall, and a current exhibit at the Fundação de Serralves in Porto on view until November 1.

Goldsworthy, selected in the sculpture category, is world-renowned for his large-scale installations and sculptures made in and with un-manipulated natural materials found in the environment. They are often ephemeral, made from things like snow, twigs, and leaves, arranged in poetic displays that speak to the passage of time. The British artist’s works can be found in the National Gallery of Art, Washington, D.C.; Storm King Art Center, New York; Yorkshire Sculpture Park, West Bretton, UK, and he recently had a major retrospective at the Royal Scottish Academy. A solo exhibition at the Parrish Art Museum in Water Mill, New York, runs until November 8.

In addition, the Japan Art Association has awarded a grant of 5 million yen (about $32,000) to France’s La Source Garouste association for its work supporting young artists.

Past winners have included Anish Kapoor, William Kentridge, James Turrell, the late Yayoi Kusama, Sophie Calle, Peter Doig, Olafur Eliasson, Doris Salcedo, and Marina Abramović.

item.title: How Jutta Koether Made A Color Her Signature Style - ARTnews.com
item.description:
When you walk through a show,” Martin Kippenberger observed to Jutta Koether when she interviewed him in 1991, “some of the pictures are good and some of them are bad. Then there’s possible controversy.” It may seem like a simple observation—until he explains that that’s what he was for. “And not, please, where everything is equally good…. When everything is good, none of it counts. God, in the beginning, wanted that a bit differently. Both good and bad were supposed to exist. But contrasts and dialectic,” Kippenberger lamented, “have disappeared in art.”

Had oppositional energy and the willingness to test the good against the bad really walked off the field of art? If only Kippenberger had looked more deeply into the art of his interlocutor, he would not have been so sure. Just five years younger than Kippenberger, Koether was part of a new cohort on the Cologne art scene—which in the ’80s and early ’90s was certainly the most dynamic and socially ebullient in Europe, populated by the most audacious artists—and she was already painting her way toward what she’d later call “the limit where knowledge offers itself as a resource for acting, no longer for the peace of the understanding but at the mercy of the alluring forces of chaos.”

Yet the fact that Koether felt it necessary to distance herself from the context that gave her the problems that became the material of her work seems characteristic. German painting circa 1980—what was that? It was, for instance, the pure chill of Gerhard Richter’s “capitalist realism,” seemingly an armor with no chinks in it; this did not have much to offer an artist like Koether. Or it was the raucous hullabaloo of Jörg Immendorff’s “Café Deutschland” series, with its colorfully convivial disorder. Perhaps most sympathetically, though Koether has said she was slow to appreciate him, it was the mercurial presence of Sigmar Polke, who always seemed to play hide-and-seek with his identity as a painter and to contradict himself at every turn.  

KOETHER WAS BORN in Cologne in 1958 and studied not at the renowned nearby art academy of Düsseldorf, where professors such as Bernd Becher, Joseph Beuys, Nam June Paik, and Richter had held forth—the age of famous and charismatic women professors was still in the future there—but rather at Cologne’s university, where she studied philosophy as well as art. Or rather, as she explained to Benjamin Buchloh in a long 2016 interview that remains the best account of her work’s history, she was “part of a philosophically oriented seminar with a pedagogue…who had studied with Joseph Beuys and then gone to Paris and studied with Jacques Lacan.” 

She considered doing a PhD on writer-director Antonin Artaud, of Theatre of Cruelty fame. There must have been a lot to sort out at that time of strong ideological conflicts: Philosophy versus art (or, let’s say, writing versus making) would have been only the beginning. If art, then the question would be, in what form? Painting itself was contested—for or against? (And those against would have been happy to declare: No contest.) And then of course, since as it turned out Koether did opt to make painting central to her art (without making it her exclusive focus), there was the problem of how to pursue the claims of feminism in the face of an art scene in which painting was marked by a notoriously macho ethos. 

Right from the beginning of her practice, Koether already knew that problems are just the material you have to work with. As she told Kim Gordon in a 2011 interview, “I also like to incorporate living social facts from a point of view that is shaped by the female experience. I like to do things with painting that men cannot do. And yet finding the knowledge of the other doesn’t mean to limit yourself, or self-marginalization…. Not to stabilize expectations but to confound them. Even those of your friends. Even your own.”

Even after Koether started exhibiting as an artist in 1985, she kept one foot outside the art world. “My home base,” she told Gordon, “was not a gallery or the bar but Spex magazine,” to which she’d begun contributing in 1981. Spex was a legendary music magazine—“legendary” meaning that even those of us who could not read German were aware of it as a cultural force, and “music magazine” meaning, as I understand it, not the specialist self-containment of a fan magazine or trade journal but a publication that uses music as the lens through which to take a wide-ranging critical view on culture and politics. As with so many of us, Koether had grown up with music. As she told me, her childhood included “classical piano lessons, school choir, church singing, and the limited but eclectic record collection of my father—Maria Callas, military trumpet music, Ray Charles—and all kinds of music on the radio,” all of which led to her “early interest in rock/pop music culture as a nonhierarchical way of cultural learning, gaining access, participation, into a public realm.” 

Koether’s been making her own music ever since, often in collaboration with fellow artists: Her 2010 LP XXX Macarena was a collaboration with Tony Conrad and John Miller, while her untitled cassette with Steven Parrino was released in 2005, the year Parrino died in a motorcycle accident. She’s also made music with fellow painter Rita Ackermann, as well as Koether’s late husband, the musician Tom Verlaine, whose pioneering band Television had been a mainstay of the CBGB scene in the 1970s.

In the ’80s, Koether also began writing sharp, opinionated criticism for Flash Art, which is how I first came into contact with her during my brief tenure as an editor there. If the likes of Richter, Immendorff, and Polke were established totems of German art when Koether was starting out, there were also younger figures in the limelight. Just slightly older than Koether were the so-called Neue Wilde of Neo-Expressionism, mostly forgotten now (whether rightly or wrongly), who seemed to emerge with great energy but not a lot of critical thinking—whereas Koether set out to marry the two—or their sharper, more disillusioned, more derisive contemporaries: Kippenberger and his pals Werner Büttner, Georg Herold, and the Oehlen brothers. Their work has a staying power that is certainly rooted in its oppositional stance, and they must have made an impression, but there was no way Koether was going to try to become one of the “bad boys.”

That’s not just a matter of gender. It also has to do with her way of inhabiting the role of thinker-writer alongside that of intuitive artist. This combination is something that also struck her fellow painter Cecily Brown, who had long been acquainted with Koether and her work but grew closer to her when they made a two-person show together at Bortolami gallery in New York in 2023. As Brown put it, Koether “is the opposite of the ‘dumb painter.’ She straddles ‘painter’ and ‘intellectual’ while making very painterly things. She puts the absurdity of being a painter into a very visual form.” 

Koether’s paintings have been mostly figurative, and have not taken photography or abstraction as a paradigm: This is what she has in common with most of the boomer-generation German artists who came on the scene just before she did (excepting Albert Oehlen). Painterly gesture is the basis of both her pictorial vocabulary and theirs. But the nature of those gestures is very different. The facture of a painting by Kippenberger or, say, Büttner is typically heavy, punchy, almost coarse, with a blunt energy that does not promise freedom as the Abstract Expressionist gesture might be thought to do. Instead, that generation’s gesture seems to be stymied or to miss its target and end in bitterness—which is precisely what gives these artists’ work at its best a poignancy on the other side of its aggression and humor. Koether’s gesture, by contrast, is typically light, almost nerveless—intentionally weak-looking, it seems, somehow only approximating the forms it sketches out. Her drawing may, like theirs, court a deliberate awkwardness, but the effect is usually less mordant, even affectionate.

WHILE THE TENUOUS yet quietly insistent way of handling paint at which Koether eventually arrived stands as an implicit dissent from the macho—one might even say emo—approach of the male painters who dominated the German scene in her early days as an artist, she did not find it all at once. Take the 1983 painting Edie, for instance. (It was shown in 2020 in a show at Lévy Gorvy Dayan, New York, comprising both then-new paintings and ones from the 1980s; interrupted by the Covid lockdown, this has been, as far as I know, the largest Koether show in a city that by now should have been the setting for a proper retrospective. But to start, this fall, fans can look forward to a show at Buchholz Galerie’s new New York location.) This thickly painted little canvas depicts a naked, wide-hipped woman, her head cropped off by the top of the canvas, with handless arms folded just above her vulva; against the blank background, red on one side, black on the other, float a couple of egglike forms. It’s as if she wanted to prove that she could pursue the themes of feminist art (from Louise Bourgeois onward) in a painterly idiom that, burdened with the weight of tradition and complicit with what theorist Laura Mulvey had dubbed the “male gaze,” might have been thought inimical to feminism.

Or, on the contrary, might it have been imagery of body-oriented feminist art that was the target of Koether’s gimlet eye? The critic Jan Avgikos deemed one untitled 1983 painting in the Lévy Gorvy show “so hideous it’s funny,” adding that in making such a work, Koether had outdone her colleagues: “Many of the infamous male artists in Cologne embraced ugliness with a vengeance, which was adumbrated by a knowingly stupid breed of rotgut humor. Koether also made sport of sacred cows, but with the super-small scale of her work and its amateurish style, she also conveyed vulnerability—something the guys never could have pulled off.” 

Another of the show’s early paintings, Some Esoteric Sipping (1986)—a title Koether used for more than one painting around this time—is less heavily painted than Edie, and plays with the imagery of organic abstraction, with a vaguely flowerlike form at the top and three tentacular lines springing down from it. This organic metaphor, like the more direct invocation of the female body as an icon, seems to represent another aspect of ostensible artistic sincerity that Koether shows herself inclined to distrust. Her path would not be that easy.

The one thing about Some Esoteric Sipping that does predict Koether’s future course is its color palette: mainly a range of reds. On the face of it, there’s something strange about a painter choosing a certain color as a stylistic signature, but—although she has also made black paintings, for instance—Koether has, especially in the last couple of decades, made the low-frequency end of the visible light spectrum her painting’s home territory. 

I DIDN’T MEET Koether in person until she moved to New York in 1991. I remember being vaguely surprised that she’d done so. I think we suspected Cologne was hipper than New York, and it looked like a very self-referential club that would be difficult to join—so why resign from it? “I had to leave all that behind,” she later explained to Buchloh, “to find my coordinates as an artist on my own. I totally ‘abandoned’ the German cultural sphere and developed a kind of structural sense of disobedience for avoiding the ruts of the patriarchal models still dominant in schools, in the art world, even in activism.” Maybe Koether felt misunderstood in her home country. The critic Isabelle Graw recalled in Artforum in 2006 that “few people in Cologne in the ’80s and early ’90s knew quite what to make of Jutta Koether’s paintings,” while her “writings seemed nearly irreconcilable with her deliberately clumsy, apparently crude pictures.” Her canvases seemed to flirt with a Neo-Expressionism that their milieu—and her own thinking—had decisively rejected. 

Of course, it’s an exaggeration to say that Koether abandoned the German cultural sphere entirely; she has continued to exhibit her work regularly in her home country, her works are in the collections of many German museums, and for 14 years (beginning in 2010) she was a professor at the Hochschule für bildende Künste Hamburg. Today, she maintains a studio in Berlin as well as in New York.

I first went to see her in her studio when she had just arrived, and remembered only recently that this studio visit was part of a kind of group show, organized by artist Eric Oppenheim. The show took place not in a gallery but in a dispersed way across the artists’ studios. “Oppenheim was supposed to bring people by,” Koether told Buchloh, “which he never did. But I used it as a frame for experimenting with my own thing and inviting guests/visitors myself…. I asked people one-on-one to come and look at the painting in progress, and then sit with me and speak about the experience of seeing the painting.” With the painting came a book—she called it a “manual”—containing “all the drawings and visual trajectories of what I was involved in. It was also an emerging social sketchbook, which meant I made reports of each session every night.” 

The studio had been converted into a kind of theater in which both Koether and I were improvising performers, and the point of the performance was to generate self-consciousness about everything that goes into the ongoing process of art: its making and its reception, its solitary aspects and its social aspects.

KOETHER’S LAST NEW York presentation of recent work, “eVEryTHinG WilL ChaNGe” at Reena Spaulings in 2022, persists in my memory as swirls of light, open, translucent touches of red, orange, yellow, green, and blue—but mostly red—that somehow seemed to float just in front of the white ground of the canvas rather than to be truly fixed upon it. 

The imagery? It seemed to come and go in the air like clouds forming, dissipating, re-forming. The most prominent bit of imagery in Fly Now (2022) is the front of an airplane with its door open and boarding stairs at the ready; the name koether is inscribed on the fuselage next to the door. Beyond that, the canvas mainly features lots of little red circles—bubbles, I’d call them—and a few stray strokes of light green, vaguely reminiscent of foliage; at the top, a Valentine’s heart contains the unintelligible inscription ollodnxx and a couple of neutral-faced (straight-mouthed) emojis. At the bottom, the painting’s title is inscribed, and the words seem to emerge from and lead into a series of letterlike marks that don’t quite add up to any sort of writing. 

Fly Now might be the poster for an artform conceived of as a vehicle for transport in and out of the realm of determinate meaning. If so, another of the paintings in the show would appear to advise the traveler as to how to identify one’s home in this transient existence. The World (2022) depicts a standing figure in a striped dress, seen from behind, with bare arms outstretched; next to it is the name apollo, lettered once vertically, once horizontally. Whether this is meant to evoke the Greek god of poetry and prophecy or the American space program of the 1960s and ’70s may be a moot question; more important, perhaps, is the inscription in smaller letters at the foot of the painting, which expands on its title: when they ask you where you’re from. the world. It’s a recommendation of cosmopolitanism from an artist who has spoken of herself as “interested in space and time travel,” whose work “comes from a kind of mental traveling, an ongoing search, because you don’t have a fixed historical vision.”

Paintings like these seem to celebrate a kind of active uncertainty. Koether’s mark in them is very hard to correctly articulate. I am tempted to call it hesitant, tentative, or approximate, and yet that’s not really right at all. That is, the mark may be approximate or tentative in adumbrating a form—the form may seem to come and go—but in itself, as a presence, the painterly mark asserts itself in a very definite manner, even if that definiteness embodies translucency, sparingness, indirection. They are what Koether has called “plays of lines and colors suggesting the motions of the mind celebrating with garlands…” (excuse me, but I have to interrupt the artist and repeat with an exclamation point that phrase “with garlands”: with garlands!—the phrase suggests an arcadian or pastoral mode, which is perhaps not surprising in an artist who has made paintings inspired by those of the Baroque artist Nicolas Poussin) “…the fact that we still do not know where Bewusstsein, or consciousness, occurs in the human mind.”

This garlanded play of mind, as it is communicated through Koether’s art, has nothing heavy or brooding about it. This has something to do with her idea that painting is intertwined with performance, which contributes a peculiar energy to her work. Still, it’s easy to think of her as simply a painter: In fact, when I started writing this, I had the impression that I’d never seen one of Koether’s performances, but then I remembered that that’s not quite the case—there was that studio-visit-as-performance I’d played a small part in. 

This bears out something that Koether’s former student Ei Arakawa-Nash, the performance artist who is representing Japan at this year’s Venice Biennale, told me: “What I learned from Jutta is a certain form of appropriation in which the artist’s persona is not something to hide behind, nor something to present as authentic. Instead, it can be treated as material.” He added, “Jutta’s work has been very influential for me, especially in thinking about performance not only as an event but also as a way of making visible the conditions surrounding art, authorship, and public appearance—even as it risks collapsing into itself.” The fact that I hadn’t remembered our first studio visit as a performative event may even mean that it was quite successful: I incorporated this self-consciousness into my thoughts about painting without leaving a remainder to be set apart as “performance.” And yet it fed into my awareness that painting is always performed, and so is the appreciation of painting. In Koether’s case, I see that the process can go on indefinitely.

item.title: Geles Cabrera, Trailblazing Mexican Sculptor, Dies at 100 - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Mexican artist Geles Cabrera, who was celebrated as her country’s first professional female sculptor and associated with the Generación de la Ruptura (Breakaway Generation), died on September 1 at age 100, as first reported by the Spanish magazine Bonart.

Over seven decades, she built a sculptural practice that explored the human figure through abstracted, voluptuous forms, often ones made of rough volcanic stone. Over the years, she effectively led the way for younger generations of modern and contemporary Mexican artists, for whom she was a “tireless promoter,” as the National Institute of Fine Arts and Literature (INBAL), Mexico City, put it in a past tribute. The institution also announced her death earlier this month.

“It is with deep sadness that we pay tribute to Geles Cabrera… a pioneer of modern sculpture in Mexico and an artist whose work transformed the way we think about the body, movement, and space,” stated OMR gallery in Mexico City, which has worked with the artist. “She was both an artist and her own muse. She didn’t wait for the world to make a place for her — she shaped it with her own hands.”

When Cabrera began her long career, few other women in Mexico were taken seriously as artists, and sculpture was something that only men were expected to do. While she enjoyed some early recognition, famously becoming the first Mexican sculptor to have a solo show at the Mont-Orendáin Gallery at age 22 in 1949, major institutions only started noticing her pioneering work much later in her life.

“They wouldn’t let women in. It was so hard to achieve anything,” she told artist Pedro Reyes in a 2018 filmed interview in time for a major solo exhibition at Mexico City’s Museo Experimental El Eco, titled “Geles Cabrera: Mexico’s First Female Sculptor.” That 2018 show marked a turning point in the recognition of Cabrera’s decades of contributing to local art history. “They built museums for all the [male] artists, but they never supported me,” she said. “Tell me the Mexican art system isn’t sexist; of course it is.”

But Cabrera, a mother of five, managed not only to push through many of those sexist barriers, but to carry others along with her. With 52 other artists, she founded the Salón de la Plástica Mexicana in 1949 to promote modern Mexican art. In 1966, she opened the Museo Escultórico in Coyoacán, the country’s first independent artist-run museum by a living artist; it operated until 2006. The museum did not charge admission, and Cabrera personally helped support it with her salary as an art teacher. It showed fellow contemporary sculptors and permanently exhibited over 50 of her own pieces.

She was born under the name Ángeles María Cabrera Alvarado in 1926. Her father, a civil engineer, was involved in archaeological excavations of pre-Hispanic artifacts from Mexico City, while overseeing new building projects there. Seeing those ancient sculptures would have a lasting impact on Cabrera, whose work contained forms that recall pagan ritual and prehistoric objects. One of her aunts, Rosario Cabrera, was also an artist who led Open-Air Painting Schools.

In the 1940s, Cabrera enrolled in Mexico’s San Carlos Academy, plus dance school, joining Alfonso Pallares’s experimental troupe. Her time spent dancing quickly spun itself into Cabrera’s dancer-like, strong figurative sculptures that could as easily evoke fertility or appear as merged couples. She got an early break when her family moved to Cuba when she was in her 20s. There, she enrolled in the San Alejandro Academy and started exhibiting, even winning two awards. After returning to Mexico City in 1949, Cabrera continued studying at La Esmeralda School of Painting, Sculpture, and Engraving.

Around the same time, she expanded beyond the medium of terracotta and experimented with a variety of other materials that invite touch. They range from wood to plant fibers, bronze, and, particularly, her signature black or gray, porous volcanic stone, recinto, which was also used in Indigenous buildings. The latter material adds a raw dimension that says as much about the sensual curves of her figures as their unvarnished material. “I left them like that on purpose. I don’t like to polish them. That is why I barely ever worked with marble,” she told Reyes.

Cabrera’s abstract leanings, which differed from nationalist motifs then popular with Mexican muralists, drew her closer to the Generación de la Ruptura movement of artists, beginning in the 1950s. According to the Art Newspaper, she also joined the GUCADIGOSE avant-garde collective with Angela Gurría and Mathias Goeritz, among others.

In her final years, belated museum exhibits started rolling in. In 2022, she had her first solo in the US at the Americas Society in New York; in 2025, Mexico City’s Museo del Palacio de Bellas Artes mounted a retrospective. In 2023, she went on to win Mexico’s highest honor for lifetime achievements in the arts, the Medal for Fine Arts. For many, her win suggested that if female artists can just manage to live long enough, they may very well see the fruits of their labors given their fair due.

item.title: The Artist Residency That Never Was - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Like hundreds of other visual artists around the world, 25-year-old airbrush painter Syd Sauer Wilson opened their email inbox on Friday, June 5, to what appeared to be the opportunity of a lifetime: an invitation to participate in an artist residency program hosted by Abstract Mag — a popular art-focused social media platform that had over 1 million followers — taking place overseas this summer.

The residency promised an all-expenses-paid retreat in the mountainous regions of southern Georgia, where for two weeks in August, 40 visual artists would live in a “historic chateau” and pursue their practices while also exploring the country’s culture and traditions through a series of expeditions and activities. For the emerging artist hungry for any opportunity to create works in a historic environment without having to pay for travel, materials, or accommodations, a residency like this would be a dream come true.

This was the case for Wilson, an early-career artist in Los Angeles. They had applied to last year’s residency, hosted in the 18th-century Château De Forbin in Marseille, for a $40 fee after seeing the open call for artists on Abstract Mag’s social media pages. Though Wilson didn’t apply to this year’s residency in Georgia, they received an email in June from a member of the program’s artist selection committee informing them that, after being shortlisted last year, they were personally invited to participate this August.

“We look forward to welcoming you to Georgia this summer,” the end of the email obtained by Hyperallergic reads, with a link that directs the artist to submit more information about their availability, travel information, and any materials they will require during the residency.

“ I was super, super excited,” Wilson told Hyperallergic. “I dropped down to the ground on my knees, and I was just like, ‘Oh my God.’ Throughout the day, I just kept looking up at the sky and saying, ‘Thank you, thank you, thank you.’ I called my parents, I shared the news with them, I shared the news with my friends.”

But the dream began to crumble after Wilson opened social media to find hundreds of artists coming forward online with reports that they had received similar emails also inviting them to Abstract Mag’s Georgia summer residency this year, raising speculation within the art community about the program’s legitimacy.

In July, Abstract Mag announced in since-deleted Instagram posts that 40 artists had been accepted. But artists say they were ghosted after the summer residency’s social media pages all went dark.

item.title: The Pine Trees That Would Not Leave Me - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Six years ago, on August 4, 2020, a massive explosion at the Port of Beirut killed more than two hundred people, wounded thousands, and devastated large parts of the capital. 

This August, sitting with a friend at a family-run restaurant amid the pine trees of Dhour El Choueir, a mountain town overlooking Beirut, I found myself unable to shake off a painting and a poem I had translated two decades earlier. 

Lebanese painter Moustafa Farroukh’s watercolor “A Group of Pines in Bekfaya” was painted just a few miles from here in 1936. Born and first trained in Beirut under the painter Habib Serour, Farroukh later studied in Rome and Paris before returning to establish his practice in his native city. Through portraits and idealized landscapes, he offered a vivid vision of Lebanon’s people and terrain. Farroukh became a foundational figure in modern Lebanese painting, his art helping shape a visual language for the country while its political and cultural identity was still taking form under the French Mandate. 

The painting of the pine grove was seared into my memory when I first saw it in 2003 in a catalog accompanying a Sursock Museum exhibition of Farroukh’s works. (The watercolor was on loan from the private collection of Emile Nasrallah.) Sursock itself later became a victim of the Beirut Port explosion. The blast shattered its stained-glass windows and damaged the historic building as well as dozens of artworks. The museum reopened on May 26, 2023, with five exhibitions, one of them titled Beyond Ruptures. 

In August 1937, the Armenian poet Vahan Tekeyan was also here in Dhour El Choueir when he wrote the sonnet “To a Lebanese Pine Tree.” 

I reconnected with the sonnet after returning home. I corrected a few errors in my translation, adjusted the wording and rhythms, and tried to bring the English closer to the movement of Tekeyan’s Armenian. 

Here is the translation as I read it now, at twice the age I was when I first attempted it, with many more years of witnessing Lebanon from near and far.

To a Lebanese Pine Tree

By Vahan Tekeyan
Dhour El Choueir, Lebanon, August 1937

Your pain unfolds from the past, O soft-shadowed
pine tree… Barely risen from the ground
you have lost your maiden branch, the trace of which
appears on you, dried and jutting, like a severed arm.

Then countless others followed it, one after another…
Until, once they thought your trunk had grown large enough,
they let your upper branches sprout and thicken,
and slowly adorn themselves with translucent tresses.

And upon them too, how many fresh traces of the saw —
all your grandchildren and great-grandchildren, dead too soon,
whose open grave you have become beneath the skies…

But you do not at all inspire, O green tree of the mountains,
with memories of so many victims, any thought of mourning;
you ever bring forth new life and sway in joyous mood…

Born in Constantinople in 1878, Tekeyan came of age in an Armenian literary world that would be shattered during his lifetime. Poet, editor, teacher, and public figure, he belonged to a generation whose intellectual and literary lives cannot be separated from the violence that dispersed Ottoman Armenians across new geographies.

By 1937, Lebanon had become one of the epicenters of Armenian revival in the Middle East. Survivors of the Armenian Genocide had reconstituted community life away from their ancestral towns, rebuilding around churches and secular institutions.

Tekeyan participated directly in this process of revival. In September 1937, he became the first editor of a new Armenian newspaper in Beirut, Zartonk (“Awakening,” still published today). Tekeyan included “To a Lebanese Pine Tree,” written the previous month in Dhour El Choueir, in the paper’s inaugural issue, nestled among news items ranging from the upcoming parliamentary elections in French Mandate Lebanon and domestic politics in Palestine to the Spanish Civil War and Mussolini’s visit to Germany. 

For all the Armenian resonances of Tekeyan’s wounded tree, the poem is emphatically Lebanese. Reading it in Lebanon in August 2026, I was struck less by what the pine might stand for than by how closely its contradictions seemed to belong to the country around me. 

The poem begins with history lodged in the body. “Your pain unfolds from the past,” Tekeyan tells the tree.

The first wound appears low on the trunk. The lost branch resembles a human limb, its trace “dried and jutting, like a severed arm.” Before long, the instrument of amputation appears explicitly: the saw.

The mutilations accumulate. “Then countless others followed it, one after another.” Yet the tree continues upward. Its higher branches are eventually allowed to sprout and thicken, adorning themselves with “translucent tresses.” Tekeyan lets us glimpse flourishing before making us look again: those branches, too, bear “fresh traces of the saw.”

And then Tekeyan shifts the metaphor. The injured body becomes a genealogy. Its branches are its “grandchildren and great-grandchildren, dead too soon.” The ancestor remains standing as its descendants disappear around it.

Tekeyan then reverses the natural order of generations: The ancestor becomes the grave of its descendants, “whose open grave you have become beneath the skies.”

Everything in the sonnet seems to carry us toward grief.

Until it doesn’t.

“But you do not at all inspire,” Tekeyan writes, “any thought of mourning.”

And he tells us why: “You ever bring forth new life.”

In writing and conversation about Lebanon, the word “resilience” is tossed around liberally. But endlessly celebrating people’s resilience can normalize what they are repeatedly forced to endure.

No less common in Western media is the portrayal of Lebanon as hedonistic: its nightlife and crowded beach clubs, where the party continues amid economic collapse and political crisis. For decades, such coverage has treated the revival of Beirut’s bars and clubs as evidence that the country is “back.”

It is a seductive shorthand. But like the celebration of resilience, this framing romanticizes precarity and escapism while obscuring the scars of war and the uneven costs of crisis. 

Tekeyan’s pine offers us something more compelling. Farroukh’s pines, in turn, offer a key to reading the poem. 

Farroukh’s trees stand together. 

Seen in this light, what is often flattened into hedonism may instead be understood as one manifestation of solidarity: an insistence on gathering with friends and family against the odds, even while bearing the traces of violence.

My grandparents were child survivors of the Armenian Genocide who found refuge in Lebanon, where my parents and I were born. I grew up during the Lebanese Civil War and came of age in its aftermath. When I first translated Tekeyan’s poem in 2003 and encountered Farroukh’s painting in the exhibition catalog that same year, I was still living there. Three years later came another war. Soon thereafter, I moved to the United States.

But it was only in Dhour El Choueir, in August 2026, that the poem and the painting came together for me, revealing something about Lebanon beyond the familiar scripts.

The wounds remain. The tree sways.

Acknowledgment: The author would like to thank Rowina Bou Harb, Head of Archives at the Sursock Museum, for her assistance.

item.title: In Queens, Immigrant Women Sew a Truer Atlas - Hyperallergic
item.description:
This article is part of a series focusing on underrepresented craft histories, researched and written by the 2025 Craft Archive Fellows, and organized in collaboration with the Center for Craft.

How can we delve into the archives of the present? Is it possible to unveil and touch the documents that communities are creating today to record and remember their history, or does understanding only arise with the passage of time? When does an object become an archive?

For the past two years, I have been working with two immigrant-led costureros: circles of women from all over Latin America that gather to create textiles together. Located in different community centers in Northwestern Queens in New York City, these spaces have become a safe haven for many undocumented, working-class immigrants who are enduring racial profiling and persecution under the current immigration crackdown. Amid this terror, the intimacy and secrecy of the costurero set a table where gossip and generosity sit side by side with threads and needles.

The first group, BordeAndo, was founded in 2018 as a community engagement initiative of the Queens Museum, though it soon grew beyond the institution to become an independent collective. Its name plays with multiple meanings in Spanish: bordar (to embroider), borde (border or frontier), and the suffix -ando, which evokes movement or walking. Most of its members come from the Ecuadorian highlands (la Sierra), though others are from the Dominican Republic, El Salvador, and Mexico. They range in age from 30 to 83 and have lived in the United States for between 10 and 50 years.

Las Comadres Bordadoras was founded in 2021 in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic by two Mexican immigrants, who sought to bring women out of isolation and foster a mutual support network. Their name, also difficult to translate, gestures toward camaraderie and kinship. The comadre refers specifically to women who are, in their words, “a midpoint between friend and family.” The comadres come from Mexico, Cuba, El Salvador, Uruguay, Colombia, Ecuador, and Argentina; range in age from 35 to 75; and have lived in the United States for between two and 30 years. They mostly embroider Mexican cloth napkins, but all forms of needlework are welcome. This costurero calls itself “nomadic” because it has moved around community gardens, public libraries, and schools in the area since its conception. Both circles are intergenerational, international spaces of confluence for transnational, working-class, largely undocumented immigrant women.

Last year, BordeAndo and Las Comadres Bordadoras were the protagonists of Thread of Voice / Un hilo de voz at the Queens Museum. The exhibition, which I curated, featured Andrés Altamirano’s photographs of the costurero members along with film by documentarian Eleonora Privitera. The visual narrative and documentation of this project was also done in collaboration with Altamirano.

I see these costureros as living archives — as sites where craft traditions converge, and concrete embodied and material practices connect geographies of affect and displacement, like a woman knitting a stitch learned by her grandmother back home or another embroidering a napkin for the altar of a dead loved one whose grave she cannot visit because of her migratory status. “Text” and “textile” share an etymological root — the Latin verb texere — that reveals both that texts are woven and textiles written. In this sense, textiles are texts that we have forgotten how to read, encoded with bodily gestures, storytelling practices, and materialities that could, if safeguarded, be called archives.

item.title: José Antonio Rosas Discusses Photographing Collective Euphoria - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
Over 10 years, José Antonio Rosas has photographed some of the world’s greatest celebrations – from Glastonbury and Holi to Kumbh Mela, Carnaval, the pilgrimages of Lalibela and Qoyllur Rit’I, and the dances of Candelaria. The artist works from within these vast gatherings, capturing the charged moments when cultural and social boundaries dissolve and collective euphoria takes hold. Yet, even within these immense crowds, individuality persists. In each expression of ecstasy, devotion or abandon, something irreducibly personal breaks through. What emerges is a portrait of a universal human yearning – to surrender to something larger than oneself in search of release, connection and transcendence. This decade-long project is now the subject of a book from Kehrer Verlag, spotlighting what it means to come together in deeply human moments of celebration, worship and collective release. 

A: Take us back to the start. Where did you get your first camera? 

JAR: I bought a compact film point-and-shoot just before my honeymoon in 2000. But I really started to get serious about photography a few years later, when digital came along. In 2004, my wife got pregnant with our first child, and I bought the Canon Digital Rebel to record my family life. I started immersing myself in the world of photography, getting more and more interested in the craft. What started as a hobby gradually evolved into a dedication, first in the natural world, and then into other people and cultures. 

A: You first experienced this feeling of collective euphoria at Glastonbury in 2015. What exactly happened to you in that crowd that made you want to spend the next ten years pursuing that feeling?

JAR: As a lifelong fan of rock music, I had already experienced a sense of connection with crowds at concerts and festivals. I went to Glastonbury expecting a grander experience, in terms of scale and musical offerings. But what struck me most wasn’t any of that. It was a deep sense of community, a shared euphoria among total strangers. For a few days, everyday life ceased to exist. People who had never met before connected over a collective state of release and elation. At the time, I was contemplating leaving my business career, so that feeling of release felt especially poignant. 

A: What were you searching for when you began following this feeling across different cultures, continents and gatherings? 

JAR: At first, I wasn’t consciously looking for anything in particular. It took me a couple of years after Glastonbury to start photographing celebrations in Peru. In those, I took a documentary approach, not yet fully aware of the similarities between those festivals and Glastonbury. That realisation started to manifest itself during the COVID-19 lockdown. I had just come back from Holi in India, and began to reflect on what we lose when unable to get together: a collective joy that we can only experience when gathered in crowds. After the pandemic, I became conscious of trying to capture that feeling across different traditions. 

A: Why do you choose to document from within the crowd rather than from a distance? 

JAR: From a distance, these massive gatherings might seem like a sea of indistinct bodies. It is easy to imagine that in the middle of the crowd, individuality dissolves completely. However, when examining each gesture from deep within the group, I have found something else happening. In each pair of closed eyes, each open mouth, each expression of ecstasy, there is an individual striving for something personal, perhaps a release from the pressures of everyday life, a deep connection not found in the normal world or a search for transcendence. Whatever the reasons, by letting themselves go during the communal frenzy, people end up setting themselves apart from the crowd and releasing a deep expression of their being. 

A: When you’re part of a crowd where so many things are happening at once, what is it that makes you pick up the camera and capture an image? 

JAR: At these gatherings, I always have my camera in hand, ready to go. There are a few moments during which I get so lost in the crowd that I forget about taking pictures, but most of the time I will be watchful of everything going on around me, looking for those special moments gestures and expressions of emotion from individuals that show them as connected to the crowd, while setting themselves free. 

A: Many of the images you capture are of moments of intense worship or cultural celebration. How do you approach photographing people in vulnerable or private moments? 

JAR: That is one of the most challenging parts of this project: how to capture a special moment of deep worship, contemplation or revelry without disrupting or interfering with the experience. For me, the answer lies in always showing respect and care for the people and their traditions. Establish eye contact, show that I am present in the moment as an observer, be mindful of not standing in the way of a ritual or celebration and be ready to step away if I sense that I am causing discomfort.  

A: Do you have a particular experience that has stuck with you from your 10 years on this project? 

JAR: During my first time at Holi in India, I went with a group of photographers to a remote temple for a celebration called Huranga. We stepped into the courtyard, which was filled with men dancing, then the women appeared, all dressed in colourful saris. Each of them roped a man with her silk shawl, stripped him of his shirt and started flogging him with it, while water rained from pipes above. I later learned that it was a playful enacting of revenge. At the moment, I was so absorbed that I didn’t realise that my group had left and I was the only foreigner in the courtyard. Suddenly, I felt a pull at the back of my t-shirt. It was a young woman, trying to rip my shirt apart. Even though her elders disapproved, she tore my shirt from me and started flogging me hard with it, while her friends laughed. I emerged from the temple shirtless, soaked and filled with powder up to my nostrils, to general laughter from young locals. It remains a special moment, because I started the day as an observer of a foreign ritual and ended it as a full participant.

A: You’ve been across the world, from India’s Holi to the candlelit devotion of Christmas in Lalibela. What have you found unites these disparate events

JAR: These festivals originate from different traditions and are driven by various motives, but they share common characteristics: multi-day gatherings that suspend societal norms, halt regular life, dissolve social categories and encourage people to give in to uninhibited joy. These factors lead to the emergence of a phenomenon called “collective effervescence,” first described by the sociologist Émile Durkheim at the beginning of the 20th century. The act of gathering generates an electricity that runs through everyone in the crowd, driving people to shed their regular identities and allowing for a freer version of themselves. 

A: Tell us about the title – Somewhere We Feel Free. What does this mean? 

JAR: When thinking about a title for the book, I listened carefully to the lyrics of my favorite songs. A line in “Wildflowers” by Tom Petty struck a chord: “You belong somewhere you feel free.” That “somewhere” implies a place different from where you are now, away from troubles and worry, as the song later says. Then there’s the “feel free,” the sense of release and liberation one experiences. I changed the “you” for “we”, in order to give it the meaning of community and connection. And so, the title became Somewhere We Feel Free, a special place where we gather to find connection and release. 

A: Are there any events or celebrations that you want to photograph, but haven’t had the chance? 

JAR: After 10 years, I’m taking a break from big gatherings. I arrived at each of the seven celebrations featured in the book under different circumstances and driven by various motives. I didn’t reach any of them with a prior intention of incorporating them into this book. There was chance involved in how I arrived at them, and how I found the similarities that ended up making them part of the same project. So, I would rather let chance continue to take me to the next event. 

José Antonio Rosas: Somewhere We Feel Free is published by Kehrer Verlag: kehrerverlag.com

Words: Emma Jacob & José Antonio Rosas

Image Credits:

item.title: Taryn Simon’s LandmarkNew Project at The Guggenheim - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
American artist Taryn Simon (b. 1975) has a particular talent for revealing the hidden systems of power that shape the world we inhabit. She is perhaps best known for The Innocents (2000), which traces the stories of individuals imprisoned for crimes they did not commit. Her approach, which often examines the politics of images, has led to widespread acclaim; Simon is a Guggenheim Fellow who has exhibited everywhere from the Tate Modern and MoMA to the United Nations. This September, she unveils Father Country I Do Love You, a body of work ten years in the making. The show, taking place at Guggenheim, New York, is significant for several reasons, not least because it marks the first time the institution has dedicated its entire Frank Lloyd Wright-designed rotunda to a photography-based practitioner.

The presentation also coincides with the 250th anniversary of the United States, and is the first time Simon has integrated personal stories into her practice. Father Country I Do Love You is dedicated to the artist’s father, who worked for the US government and, during that time, lived in Thailand and travelled to Russia, Afghanistan, China, Iran, Israel, Korea and elsewhere. He later changed career, pivoting to manufacture and sell arcade games. Simon never got his full story, and, upon his diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease, she realised she never would. “’But America,’ he always said, ‘was the best story on earth, if you could ﬁnd someone to tell it,’” she recalls. Father Country I Do Love You feels like an attempt to recount that tale.

The project draws on the real life of Simon’s father to trace one unnamed federal agent through 42 individual artworks, including photographs, text, videos and sculptures. It is the largest presentation of new work the Guggenheim has ever staged – an immense undertaking that unfolds as a “labyrinth of sagas” in which Simon uncovers the ripple effects of her protagonist’s actions and inactions. “The federal agent acted as a middleman, witnessing events great and small and collecting evidence for someone else to slot into the bigger picture. Everything he touched ricocheted to the outer boundaries of nations and lives he’d never know.” The narration recounts victims, predators, survivors and the mechanics of justice. As the exhibition winds up the building’s iconic ramps, visitors step into a narrative Simon has assembled.

In Father Country I Do Love You, Simon tells stories through objects and symbols – a technique she has employed with great success in celebrated series such as Paperwork and the Will of Capital (2015), which recreated flower arrangements present at the signing of international treaties, and An American Index of the Hidden and Unfamiliar (2007), which examined objects and sites in the US that are off-limits to the public. At the Guggenheim, audiences will see a box of Quaker Life Multigrain Cereal go up in flames in One little room on fire. You have to backfill it shows a high-heeled shoe crawling with insects. There’s no start or finish features an American flag dangling over a cascading waterfall. Here, mundane items are transformed into evidence.

With this exhibition, Simon harnesses personal family history as a route into examining American mythology, government, national identity and power. In so doing, she joins a list of contemporary names whose recent projects have traced paternal histories to similar ends. Magnum photographer Diana Markosian’s Father (2014-2024), for example, recounts her own experience of being separated from her father after moving from Russia to California with her brother and mother, without a chance to say goodbye. Fifteen years later, Markosian travelled in search of him. Then there’s the powerful Las flores mueren dos veces by Foam Talent nominee Cristóbal Ascencio, in which the Mexican creative attempts to make sense of his father’s suicide through photogrammetry and glitched family snapshots. Together, these bodies of work show how paternal relationships can become a means not only of personal healing, but of tackling wider questions, too. Father Country I Do Love You does just that. It is an ambitious, sprawling achievement that makes the tension between the intimate and the political impossible to ignore.

Taryn Simon | Father Country I Do Love You is at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York.

18 September – 14 March.

guggenheim.org

Words: Eleanor Sutherland

item.title: Vietnam Veterans File Restraining Order to Block Progress on Trump’s 250-Foot Triumphal Arch - ARTnews.com
item.description:
A group of Vietnam veterans filed for a temporary restraining order on Friday to stop progress on one of Trump’s projects to alter the landscape of the nation’s capital, a 250-foot triumphal arch. 

The plaintiffs are veterans Michael Lemmon, Shaun Byrnes, and Jon Gundersen, along with architectural historian Calder Loth, who are represented by the Public Citizen Litigation Group, of Washington, D.C. They filed their motion for a 14-day restraining order on Friday, after Interior Secretary Doug Burgum wrote on X on Thursday that “excavation work” for the arch would come within two weeks, promising that the arch would be “one of the Great Pieces of American Architecture, honoring the history and significance of Arlington Cemetery and befitting the most powerful Capital in the World.”

The arch, however, has not received congressional approval. It is slated to go up at Memorial Circle, across the Potomac River, in Arlington, Virginia, from the Lincoln Memorial. The president debuted a model of the monument in October 2025, telling CBS News that the arch is dedicated to himself. Trump wants his arch, at 250 feet, to be taller than the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, which rises to 162.5 feet. The plaintiffs argue that the arch would disrupt sightlines between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

The veterans first filed suit in February against Trump; Vince Haley, of the president’s office; and the National Park Service (NPS), aiming to stop progress on the project, absent authorization from Congress. In April, they agreed to dismiss their motion in exchange for assurances that NPS would not authorize construction without posting a notice of its authorization online and that NPS would provide at least 14 days’ notice prior to beginning construction or demolition ahead of construction. 

“The imminent course of action that Secretary Burgum has announced to the American people is unlawful many times over,” the Friday filing reads, further alleging that it violates the court’s April order. It adds that “once a building project has begun, a later order to reverse course raises ‘significant’ practical problems,” and that the defendants “have offered no evidence that beginning construction of a commemorative arch is a matter of such exigency that blocking construction until this Court has had the opportunity to rule on the project’s legality will irreparably harm Defendants or the public interest.”

“This court,” conclude the plaintiffs, “should enter a temporary restraining order blocking Defendants’ efforts to blaze ahead with an unlawful course of conduct in the hope that they can render the arch a fait accompli before this Court has had the chance to reach a final determination as to whether Defendants’ project is authorized by law.”

In a responding filing entered “to clarify Plaintiffs’ misunderstanding and avoid any potential for further confusion,” the Trump administration argues that the new activity will be “long-disclosed Phase 1B archaeological survey work,” conducted to ensure compliance with statutes such as the National Historic Preservation Act. “This activity is not construction, or demolition in preparation for construction, of an arch,” it says, noting that the work will consist of digging four test pits. 

The planning of the District of Columbia has been subject to great deliberation ever since it was founded in the late 18th century, notes the plaintiffs’ filing, with Congress responsible, since 1912, for authorizing any additional monuments and structures. 

The Trump administration has shown no regard for Congressional or any other authority in his campaign to remodel the White House and Washington overall to suit his taste. This has included gilding large monuments near the Lincoln Memorial, adding Trump’s name to the Kennedy Center in violation of its founding documents, and abruptly removing a major Joel Shapiro work from the center’s grounds.

Most dramatically, he razed the East Wing of the White House without warning last October to make way for one of his favored projects, a massive ballroom-cum-military bunker that preservationists say would be out of proportion with the rest of the White House. Nonetheless, the Supreme Court ruled this week, 5–4, that construction could go ahead absent approval from Congress, saying that the National Trust for Historic Preservation, a nonprofit chartered by Congress to guard public buildings, which brought suit against the administration, did not have standing.

item.title: Beyoncé Gives the Studio Museum in Harlem a $2 M. Gift on Her Birthday - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Beyoncé Knowles turned 45 on September 4, and to mark the occasion, the global superstar entertainer made an unusual birthday gift, of $2 million, not to herself but to the Studio Museum in Harlem. 

“Art tells all our stories; the past and the present, but is not always accessible to everyone,” said Beyoncé in a press release. “I have always been impressed with the Studio Museum in Harlem because of its intention to make the museum an integral part of the community. I have been introduced to several of my favorite young and upcoming Black artists through exhibits at the Museum. It is a place of inspiration where all audiences can discover new stories through the canvases of diverse storytellers that reflect our humanity.”

The museum did not immediately respond to an email asking how the funds will be used; this story will be updated with any new information from the institution.

Beyoncé is married to rapper, music mogul, and ARTnews Top 200 collector Jay-Z (born Shawn Carter). The couple famously shot large parts of the video for their 2018 single “Apeshit” at the Louvre Museum in Paris.

“Each time Beyoncé releases new music, it might as well be considered an art-world event too,” wrote Alex Greenberger for ARTnews in 2020. “She’s been known to include works by vaunted artists in her videos, and with her husband Jay-Z, she’s built up an important collection of Black art.” He was writing on the occasion of the release of an 85-minute visual album titled Black Is King, which is “filled with artworks of note, and includes contributions from art-world figures behind the scenes.”

One of the most-awarded performers of all time, Beyoncé has won 35 Grammy Awards, more than any other artist. As a solo musician, she has sold over 200 million records worldwide, and she is one of the highest-grossing live acts in history. Her net worth is estimated by Forbes to be $1 billion. 

Founded in 1968 in a temporary space on the second floor of a Fifth Avenue loft building, the Studio Museum opened its new $160 million David Adjaye–designed home on 125th Street in November after a seven-year closure. Writing for ARTnews, Maximilíano Durón called it “stunning.” In 2023, the financier Joseph Perella and his wife Amy gave the museum a Jean-Michel Basquiat painting, making it one of the few US museums to own one. Also among the masterpieces on view at the reopening were works by Barkley K. Hendricks, Kerry James Marshall, Howardena Pindell, Faith Ringgold, and Carrie Mae Weems.

“I am deeply grateful to Beyoncé, both for the generosity of this gift, especially on her birthday, and for recognizing the vital role that the Studio Museum plays in people’s lives,” said museum director and chief curator Thelma Golden. “Our institution was founded to shift the arts landscape and reimagine who that landscape serves. This gift will allow us to continue strengthening our work for Harlemites, New Yorkers, and audiences across the globe.”

item.title: Huiling Chen Documents Life in China’s Rural Communities - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
In China’s Hengnan County, Hunan Province, long-term migration to cities is reshaping family structures and village life. As younger generations leave for education and employment, many older residents continue to care for homes, cultivate land and maintain everyday routines. Those Who Remain, a photo series by London-based Chinese visual artist Huiling Chen, focuses on older people living in agricultural communities like Hengnan. Through portraits taken in domestic spaces as well as scenes of daily labour, the body of work observes how rural existence is being reshaped by an ageing population.

“Rather than portraying these communities through nostalgia or decline, the project considers how everyday life continues and adapts amid social change,” the artist explains. “Those photographed are not simply presented as people “left behind,” but as active participants sustaining families, relationships and a continuing connection to place.” This is indicative of Chen’s wider fine art practice, which incorporates documentary observation of individuals to make broader cultural and socio-political shifts visible. Her previous projects include A House in Three Tenses, following three generations of women sharing one home, and The Lane Becomes a Table, in which a private birthday celebration expands into village streets. Chen’s subjects include rural societies and families in China, as well as migrants living and working in the UK.

The documentary genre brings with it a particular set of responsibilities: How do you tell someone else’s story? Who owns the photograph? How much are the pictures influenced by the person behind the camera? Chen explicitly aims to “avoid sentimental or victimising representations,” collaborating with participants to construct their own image – “rather than treating them as symbols of rural ageing.” The result is that the camaraderie between subject and photographer is often palpable. In one shot, a woman looks up from her phone, meeting Chen’s gaze with familiarity. Elsewhere, a man grins, walking by holding a bamboo cane. Other compositions take a wider view: depicting figures in the fields, a shock of yellow flowers behind them, or tilling the soil, deep in concentration. These are people with agency. Chen’s perspective moves between intimate portraits like these – taken in the home, or whilst individuals are at work – and empty interior spaces devoid of human presence. The latter shots are occupied solely by tools of their owner’s trade – buckets, stools and nets – and are reminiscent of still life paintings. Each featured object, perhaps passed down through generations, resonates with silent histories of family and labour.

In Those Who Remain, Chen places herself within a longer tradition of portrait photography concerned with ageing. Examples include Imogen Cunningham’s posthumous After Ninety (1977), Richard Avedon’s Portraits of Aging (1951–2004) and Martine Franck’s Le Temps de Vieillir (A Time to Grow Old) (1980). Today, a closer contemporary parallel can be found in the work of Joanne Coates (b. 1990). Whilst Coates does not explicitly focus on what it means to be “getting old”, her explorations of rural life and class in North East England – including The Lie of the Land and Daughters of the Soil – centre on portraying and telling the stories of farmworkers. Like Chen, she uses photography to give visibility to lives and experiences that are often overlooked, narrating “a story of gender and class that has long been forgotten, or never told.”

This collection of pictures is shaped by the absence of those who have left. Younger family members who have migrated are rarely physically present in the photographs, yet their distance influences the homes, relationships and routines Chen records. However, Those Who Remain makes it clear that these villages are not static, untouched remnants of the past. They are ever-changing environments in which older generations continue to adapt, work and sustain everyday life. That is where the series holds its power. And it has not gone unnoticed: Those Who Remain was recently named an Official Selection in the 2026 International Photography Awards (IPA), a major international competition which champions “the world’s finest photographers.” It’s a selection that establishes Chen as one to watch, positioning her alongside other acclaimed contemporary image-makers working in the space between fine art and documentary.

huilingchen.art

Words: Eleanor Sutherland

Image Credits:
All images courtesy of Huiling Chen, from the series Those Who Remain.
