item.title: Kehinde Wiley Responds to the Trump Administration’s Removal of His Painting With an ‘Aesthetically Terrifying’ T-shirt - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Kehinde Wiley’s artwork at the US Embassy in the Dominican Republic continues to cause a stir. Erin Scavino, director of Art in Embassies in a podcast interview with Sean Spicer, called the painting Young Artists After Siamesas 1960 (2013) “aesthetically terrifying” last week, but now in an unearthed radio interview from April, US ambassador Leah Campos described the painting as a lesbian picnic, according to the New York Times.

In the interview conducted in Spanish, Campos said that she saw a “huge painting of a picnic in a park with flowers and some lesbians.” She wrongfully contends in the interview that the Biden administration wanted being “that ideology here to the Dominican people.” The painting was commissioned during the Obama administration by the State Department in 2013.

Wiley hasn’t come out publicly to address the controversy around his painting, but on his official e-commerce Instagram, he posted a black T-shirt retailing for $120 with the words “aesthetically terrifying,” which he borrowed from Scavino, who describes his work as such. “A response. A reclamation. A reminder that art has never needed permission to be beautiful, provocative, or powerful,” Wiley’s post reads.

The Trump administration has been slowly changing artwork in its embassies to reflect “American patriotism and the beauty of our great country” as Campos put it in an Instagram post in August when describing the swap of Wiley’s painting for an image of the American flag accompanied by the Twisted Sister’s song We’re Not Gonna Take It.”

At the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C., the same act is taking place as workers began to disassemble Joel Shapiro’s monumental 24-foot-tall sculpture Blue. The American sculptor gave the center the work as a gift in 2019. The New York Times reported that Shapiro’s work was “targeted for elimination after President Trump’s takeover of the center.”

In December, the center’s board, led by Trump and filled with his allies, voted to inscribe his name on the building’s facade, triggering an ongoing legal struggle with the federal court system.

item.title: Adam Lindemann Sued by Nature Conservancy for Allegedly Installing Julian Schnabel Sculpture Without Permission - ARTnews.com
item.description:
In a lawsuit filed earlier this month, dealer Adam Lindemann is facing allegations that he installed a 25-foot-tall Julian Schnabel sculpture on a Long Island estate without permission.

Filed on August 20 in New York’s Eastern District, the lawsuit was brought by the Nature Conservancy, a preserve in Montauk. Lindemann, the founder of New York’s now-defunct Venus Over Manhattan gallery, has a property next to the vast preserve.

Newsday, a publication focused on Long Island’s Nassau and Suffolk Counties, first broke news of the lawsuit on Thursday.

Lindemann is accused of trespassing on the Andy Warhol Visual Arts Preserve, which the conservancy currently owns and which was once the property of Pop artist Andy Warhol. Lindemann is accused of installing Schnabel’s Ahab without the Nature Conservancy’s permission.

Known as Eothen (“from the East” in Greek), Lindemann’s adjacent estate is a six-acre property with a house and six cottages that Lindemann purchased from J.Crew CEO Millard Drexler for $50 million in 2015, according to the Real Deal. There was an additional 24-acre horse farm that Lindemann did not purchase.

The conservancy is an Arlington, Virginia–based nonprofit dedicated to environmental preservation. In 1992, the New York property was donated by the Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts. As part of the donation at that time, the conservancy agreed to “preserve a section of the ecologically significant Montauk Moorlands and to promote the visual arts,” per the lawsuit.

After it discovered Lindemann had installed a sculpture on the preserve, the conservancy allegedly asked Lindemann to remove the sculpture in question within 90 days in an initial December 2024 letter, with additional correspondence about the sculpture’s removal. The nonprofit also found Lindemann parking personal vehicles in its lot, mowing its lawn, and planting shrubs, according to the suit.

“Despite TNC’s repeated demands and efforts towards amicable resolution, Defendant has refused to remove the Sculpture and continues to enter the property without permission,” William H. Taft V, the conservancy’s attorney, wrote in the suit.

According to the lawsuit, Lindemann agreed to remove the sculpture by August 31, 2025, after a meeting with conservancy officials in May.

On September 7, 2025, however, Lindemann sent the nonprofit an email, saying, “as promised I’m moving the sculpture!” He added, “Sure hope that makes you happy as it’s expensive and disruptive but it’s happening as you wished and I agreed. All the best to you and I’ll send pics as soon as the move is completed, we are currently organizing this with the local artist, the famous local artist Julian Schnabel’s team.”

Taft explained, “In a show of good faith — and with the intent to resolve these issues amicably — TNC noted that Defendant may not have been aware of the exact boundary lines between the Preserve and Defendant’s property and offered to meet with Defendant on site to walk their shared boundary.”

On February 6, 2026, conservancy officials allegedly sent Lindemann a cease-and-desist demanding he stop entering and parking on the property, as well as maintaining “any part of the preserve.” It also demanded the artwork’s removal within within 30 days.

The sculpture has allegedly still not been removed.

“To date, Defendant continues to park personal vehicles in the Preserve’s parking area, mow the Preserve adjacent to his property, and refuses to remove the Sculpture from the Preserve,” Taft said.

The conservancy has requested a jury trial and is seeking an injunction that would stop Lindemann from entering the property, a declaration that the conservancy has exclusive control of the preserve, a declaration that Lindemann does not own the sculpture, a declaration the conservancy can remove the sculpture, and attorneys’ fees.

The protection of the preserve is “important for migratory birds, rare species, and other wildlife,” the lawsuit claims. “The Preserve’s location along the Atlantic Flyway — a major north-south migration route used by birds in North America — makes it an important feeding ground and stop-over site for Neotropical migratory birds.”

Lindemann did not respond to ARTnews’s request for comment by the time of publication.

item.title: An Incisive Exhibition in Buffalo Defies Expectations of What Latinx Painting Should Look Like - ARTnews.com
item.description:
There is a painting at the Buffalo AKG Art Museum that I still can’t get out of my head, six months after I saw it. It only measures 40 by 30 inches, and I missed it on my first walk through the gallery. Made by Los Angeles–based artist Karla Diaz in thinned-out acrylic paint, it shows two Latino men, both with mustaches, one carrying the other on his shoulders. The painting’s joyful casualness belies its subject matter, clues to which can be found in the coyote on one of the men’s shirts and in the work’s title, Uncle’s Crossing (2022).

Diaz depicted her late uncle, who was a coyote, or someone who helps undocumented people cross into the United States. The role of the coyote is controversial in Latinx communities, often regarded as a necessary evil: someone who may help you get into the US but exploit you along the way. Growing up, Diaz recalled, talking about her uncle’s job was taboo at home. “He would whisper, ‘Okay, I’m leaving for work,’ and I was like, ‘Okay, why are you whispering? You’re just going to work.’” At the time, she didn’t know exactly what job her uncle was leaving for; it was only later that she learned the truth.

Four years ago, shortly after her uncle passed away, Diaz was recovering from a stroke and had to relearn how to talk, walk, and paint. Throughout this rehabilitation, memories of her uncle returned to her. “It was a vulnerable time,” she said. “I’m the type of person, when something is very vulnerable and scary, instead of running away from it, I confront it. Even if that means putting myself in a space that is scary emotionally, I feel I can grow and learn a lot from it.”

She felt compelled to make this tender work because it was an image she had never seen before in art history: a portrait of a coyote. “In a way, it’s something that has been erased. It’s a controversial story to tell. I hope that people come with questions more than anything. I know that my uncle, in the most humane way of being able to do that, was trying to help people.”

The work, she added, asks “What does it mean to make taboo stories visible and tell others about them?”

Uncle’s Crossing features in “Let Us Gather in a Flourishing Way,” which closes this weekend in Western New York. Painting surveys like “Let Us Gather,” which will soon depart on a national tour to Iowa, Phoenix, and Seattle, were once a standard feature of contemporary art museums, though they have recently fallen out of favor. The exhibition is an exciting intervention into the history of painting surveys, ambitious in scope yet thoughtfully executed in both its installation and its creation of new scholarship.

In focusing on one medium, Andrea Alvarez, the exhibition’s curator, wanted to explore “the breadth and the richness of that discipline—to reveal the richness of the Latinx population.”

Alvarez said she included works that most might not consider traditional paintings—oil or acrylic on canvas or linen—to “push the boundaries of what is painting and what that means today.” These range from Moises Salazar Tlatenchi’s Cruising Queens (2024), which imagines a queer version of Washington crossing the Delaware and features a crocheted frame; Manuela Gonzalez’s Inanna (2024), made of painted textiles sewn together into a diamond shape that reference the history of hard-edge abstraction and painters like Frank Stella and Mary Heilmann; and Nery Gabriel Lemus’s Querida Niña Migrante and This Is the Air We Breathe (both 2020), each consisting of 15 painted floor mats installed on the floor.

Works like these, Alvarez said, “resist the materiality of painting itself—what should and shouldn’t fine art be made out of. … Every single material choice is intentional and deliberate.” Speaking on an artist panel, Sarah Zapata, who contributed another textile-based work, said she welcomed her inclusion in the exhibition because “an important part of the lineage [of painting] is thinking about how textiles largely are the reason that painting exists.”

 “My hope is that what visitors take away is an experience of the richness, the diversity, and the complexity of what these artists are doing,” Alvarez said, and in doing so “they can also expand that in their mind to the population more broadly to understand that this population of the diaspora of Latinx people in the United States are similarly rich, culturally productive and diverse, and meritorious of all of this sort of celebration.”

Another legacy that Alvarez had to contend with is the perception of Latinx painting, more specifically the stereotypes that have historically been attached to it by outsiders: colorful, figurative, folkloric. “There are going to be people who walk through the exhibition with certain expectations that they will be surprised to see the breadth of work that they encounter,” she said. “But I didn’t see a lot of the artists still wrestling with that. It feels to me like a lot of the artists have liberated themselves from those historical obligations. The exhibition does do the work of undoing some of those stereotypes.”

Now curator at the Buffalo AKG, Alvarez joined the museum as a curatorial fellow in 2018 and shortly afterward began thinking about how she might introduce contemporary Latinx art to the people of Buffalo. After her promotion to assistant curator in 2021, she began planning the exhibition in earnest, conducting her initial studio visits across the country, from Los Angeles to Miami, Chicago to Phoenix, and Texas to Puerto Rico. “That’s when I started homing in on the discipline of painting,” she said. The museum’s deep holdings in 20th-century painting were also a plus, as frequent visitors might more easily begin to connect with the works on view.

“Let Us Gather” features 58 artists, though Alvarez could have included dozens more. “The question I asked myself over and over again is: Is this artist actively contributing to the discourse of what is contemporary Latinx painting?” As she continued her research, “I did start to observe shared concerns or interests among these different artists. In some cases, these artists weren’t in dialogue with one another—they might not even know each other’s work until this exhibition.”

These observations led Alvarez to organize the exhibition into seven themes, including “Identity/Place,” which looks at how the people who live in a place shape it and how, in turn, its topography shapes them, and “Pinturx,” a gender-neutral version of the Spanish word for “painter” that encompasses various genres of painting.

Each theme acts as its own microcosm of the overall exhibition’s approach, showcasing varied perspectives on a single topic. In the “Community” section, for example, artists including Aliza Nisenbaum, David Antonio Cruz, and Shizu Saldamando consider “community as a verb, community as a noun—different kinds of communities, whether those are blood relations or chosen family” and explore “the importance of community, in many cases, to marginalized groups for survival and thriving.”

Other artists subvert expectations of the themes, as illustrated by an abstraction by Eamon Ore-Giron featured in “(New) Histories,” which tackles the legacy of history painting; Kristopher Raos’s painted close-up of the Cheer laundry detergent logo in “Abstractions”; and still lifes by Salomón Huerta, featuring a gun paired with a glass of milk or a pink pan dulce, in “Bodies & Figures.” The latter works are actually portraits of the artist and his father, who each night would “take his revolver out of the holster, set it down on the table, and ask someone to bring him a snack,” according to Alvarez. “It’s a tender image actually that represents his father and the care that they had for one another.”

After settling on a final list in summer 2024, Alvarez felt it was important to involve the artists in selecting which of their works would be featured in the exhibition. Often, she explained, L.A.-based artists or artists from the Caribbean have shown together, but because artists from different places were going to be presented in the same galleries, “I wanted everyone to have a little bit more agency,” she said, noting that ultimately, as the curator, she did have the final say. “I wanted to hear what they had to say—I have my preferences; I have the works that have stuck out to me for whatever reason—but I wanted to know what’s more resonant for them.”

An example of this is also one of the largest works on view, Man on Trampoline (2023), by Larry Madrigal. Initially, artist and curator considered showing a selection of four or so smaller paintings before settling on this monumental canvas. Measuring 7.5 feet by 6.3 feet, it depicts a jumble of figures suspended in midair above the titular bouncing device, with the composition referencing El Greco’s The Resurrection (1597–1600) and the subject resembling something you’d see on America’s Funniest Home Videos. In blending these two sources, Madrigal said he aims to bring “humor, earnestness, and humanity—all in the painting.”

“His work is one that celebrates the improvised moments of family life—of a big family, a chaotic family—and what it feels like to be the father of a growing family,” Alvarez said. “It encapsulates all those elements [of community], while also still addressing the studied way the artist thinks about art history.”

Art history, meanwhile, factors broadly into the exhibition, too. “Painting has such a potent and undeniable history,” Alvarez said, connecting it not just to its primacy within the discipline but also how it was a tool of imperialist power in spreading aesthetic conventions to various colonies, like the Americas. “These artists are using painting, engaging with its traditions—and subverting its legacies—because of that history. Painting felt like a particularly loaded medium to unpack.”

Guadalupe Maravilla’s personal story of migration, from El Salvador to the U.S. during the 1980s, acts as a call to think about the ongoing mass deportations being conducted by ICE. In Pupusa Retablo (2023), the artist shows three women grilling masa for the titular dish and, in a painted caption, recalls how, while in Honduras on this sojourn, he ate pupusas: “A woman on the neighboring table told her friends that I was a Salvadoran refugee child because she noticed that I ate my pupusas with my hands. I remember feeling terrified of being sent back to El Salvador.” That experience, likely shared by countless others, was “an early lesson in assimilation,” Alvarez said.

While the works on view may all seem disparate, Alvarez said what connects the art and the artists together is “a deep sense of care for community, for heritage, for one another, lifting one another up.”

That sense of community informs the exhibition title, which borrows its name from Juan Felipe Herrera’s 2008 poem “Let Us Gather in a Flourishing Way.” Alvarez came across it early in her research for the show and felt a strong connection to it because of its fluid use of Spanglish. “I’ve always read poetry because I don’t understand it. I’m the kind of person who’s like, I’m going to bang my head against the wall because I want to understand why I don’t understand it. But for the first time, reading a poem in Spanglish, it felt like, oh, somehow, I understand this.”

In the poem, Herrera describes people coming together with “pearls / of corn flowing árboles de vida en las cuatro esquinas” where we are “contentos llenos de fuerza to vida / giving nacimientos to fragrant ríos / dulces frescos verdes turquoise…” Alvarez printed out his words and hung them up, contemplating them for months. “I started to understand the poem as a celebration of abundance, as this invitation to gather together,” she said. “As I was trying to figure out the title of the exhibition, I realized that was exactly what I was doing: inviting these artists to be present in their fullest expression in the galleries.”

To mark the exhibition’s realization, the Buffalo AKG commissioned Herrera to write a poem, “So Many Years We Dreamed the Colors / Tantos años soñamos los colores” (2024), that directly responded to the checklist. Printed on the walls of the exhibition and reproduced in the accompanying catalog, it reads, in part, “so many years we dreamt / the colors the shapes the gathering / … / so we stand on this wall you can see us / you can study our language & thought / never studied you can taste our colors / never loved…”

The exhibition also features three commissioned artworks by Zapata, rafa esparza, and Justin Favela. Zapata has made three textile-covered columns, two of which hang from the ceiling, while the third leans against a wall. esparza contributed Tratos: Después de Pedro Valtierra Entre Redadas (2025–26), an adobe painting inspired by Valtierra’s 1998 photograph taken after the Acteal Massacre of the Indigenous group “Las Abejas” (The Bees), in Chiapas, Mexico. Supported by a steel armature, the work encourages visitors to walk on the adobe path behind it, where a coiled US flag is embedded. Into the work, esparza’s has also added a scene from the Florentine Codex showing a Spaniard whipping an Indigenous person and images of ICE raids in LA and Chicago, connecting centuries of oppression together.

Favela’s contribution is St. Maarten (1972), After Marisol, installed on a large wall that faces a window overlooking the museum’s front lawn. The piece’s subject is difficult to see from the gallery, but when viewed from outside, its reference to a watercolor by Marisol in Buffalo AKG’s collection becomes clear.

St. Maarten is part of Favela’s “piñata murals” series, which he began in protest after being asked by an art school professor to “make something about being Mexican.” His fellow white classmates hadn’t been asked about that, but he took it as a challenge. He responded by making a piñata, “a symbol that represented Latinidad that I thought would be so corny, so cheesy, that they’d say, ‘Oh, he’s making fun of our request,’” as he recalled. His teachers loved it, though he suspects his critique went over their heads—and so did he, finding it a fertile artmaking mode for the past 20 years. When the exhibition travels to the Des Moines Art Center next month, Favela will make a new piñata mural based on a work in that institution’s collection.

I imagine “Let Us Gather in a Flourishing Way” will linger long after it comes down in Buffalo. Since 2022, the museum has been acquiring works for its permanent collection in anticipation of the show, beginning with Patrick Martinez’s Promised Land (2022), followed soon after by works by Guadalupe Maravilla, Ilana Savdie, and Eamon Ore-Giron. Since the exhibition opened in March, the museum has also added pieces by Felipe Baeza, Yvette Mayorga, and Salomón Huerta, as well as Alfonso Gonzalez Jr.’s towering Abogados Tierra Caliente (Billboard)—and it hopes to acquire even more in the coming months.

An exhibition like “Let Us Gather in a Flourishing Way,” with its layered and nuanced approach to discussing both painting and Latinx identity, was urgently needed even at the time of its conception five years ago. Given today’s political climate, one that’s only grows more fraught, its message will likely be just as necessary five years from now.

To that end, Alvarez hopes that “Let Us Gather in a Flourishing Way” is just the beginning for exhibitions of this kind. “This is just the tip of the iceberg,” she said. “By design, the project gives people a peek into the discipline, and it’s an invitation to want to learn more. This exhibition is not a comprehensive survey—I am resisting the word ‘survey’ because that comes with the connotation that it’s a complete story.”

item.title: Trump to Break Ground on “Triumphal Arch” Before Federal Approval - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Excavation efforts are set to begin within the next two weeks for President Donald Trump’s controversial “Great Triumphal Arch,” according to a statement Interior Secretary Doug Burgum posted on X on Thursday, September 3. The announcement was made before the project has even received the green light from a federal review panel.

The National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC), which evaluates design proposals throughout Washington, DC, preliminarily approved Trump's project on July 9, but issued several comments the president must address before earning the committee's final approval. The NCPC's primary concern is the height of the 250-foot-tall structure, which could violate the 130-foot cap imposed by the 1910 Height of Buildings Act and obstruct the sightlines of dozens of historical landmarks.

"This will be one of the Great Pieces of American Architecture, honoring the history and significance of Arlington Cemetery and befitting the most powerful Capital in the World," Burgum added in his post on Thursday, a month before the NCPC's next scheduled review on October 1.

Sitting on the highly trafficked Memorial Circle near Arlington National Cemetery, the white granite-clad arch will include a “Military Observation Deck” and be topped by two statues of gold eagles and one of a golden winged figure. While the project has been presented as a celebratory marker of the country's 250th anniversary, Trump has also dedicated the monument, which many have deemed the “Arc de Trump,” to himself.

item.title: LA’s Lucas Museum Displays “Narrative Art” for the Few, Not the People - Hyperallergic
item.description:
LOS ANGELES — After nearly two decades of planning and construction, a spate of layoffs, and staffing controversies, the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art will open its doors to the public later this month in South Los Angeles’s Exposition Park. This week, members of the press were invited to tour the new institution and get a taste of the random and facile smorgasbord of art that awaits visitors. 

Founded by filmmaker George Lucas and his wife Mellody Hobson, co-CEO of Ariel Investments, the reportedly $1 billion building designed by Ma Yansong/MAD Architects houses their collection of 40,000 works representing what they call “visual storytelling.” These include illustrations, history paintings, comic art, films, murals, and other genres that “have not always received the respect they deserve,” as press materials explain. The five-story, undulating, spaceship-like structure sits on an 11-acre campus of rolling green hills designed by Mia Lehrer of Los Angeles’s Studio-MLA, who also designed the building’s green roof.

“For thousands of years, that was the only way you could tell a story, with pictures,” Lucas said during a press preview on Wednesday, September 2 (seemingly disregarding traditions of oral histories or song). “Pictures and stories are very powerful. Put them together, and those two elements make a society.” 

“Narrative Art creates groups of people with common belief systems, which allows them to work together and not kill each other,” he continued, as if to finally resolve the question of what Narrative Art is, exactly, a query that has surrounded the museum for years.

Ironically, there is very little narrative at all in the Museum of Narrative Art, at least curatorially. The collection is spread throughout 100,000 square feet of gallery space, divided into 30 or so thematic galleries — Adventure, Romance, Motherhood, Civic Life, Science Fiction, Comics, Sports, and others — with a few dedicated to individuals such as famed fantasy artist Frank Frazetta, American regionalist Thomas Hart Benton, and Norman Rockwell, whose specific brand of folksy Americana can be felt throughout. Artworks are displayed free of context or even any wall text aside from shiny, metal letters announcing each section. The thematic arrangement mashes together artworks of different styles and eras, linked by the flimsiest of threads, as if to say “Look, we’re all the same: we play sports, we work, we raise children!”, with little interest in exploring the specific cultural or social conditions from which they emerged.

item.title: Ann Patchett and Crying at The Met - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Ever shed a tear in a museum? You’re not alone, my friend. There’s something cathartic about that rare moment, when you find yourself in front of a work of art that seems tailor-made for the very grief or joy or uncertainty you’re experiencing. Critic Lavinia Liang tries to locate this emotional connection with art — or a lack thereof — in Ann Patchett’s new novel, Whistler, which follows a single family’s unraveling and reunion bookended by the halls of the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

Our reports on ICE’s seizure of 22,000 smuggled artifacts in Florida, coverage of the Chinese Pavilion’s withdrawal from the Gwangju Biennale in South Korea in protest of the Taiwan Pavilion, guide to Upstate New York art shows this month, and more in this edition.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor
